clozeText: Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci are arranged in chains.
extraNote: This microscopic arrangement is a primary morphological distinction between the two genera.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This test differentiates Staphylococci (positive) from Streptococci (negative).

clozeText: Catalase is a virulence factor that allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of {{c1::H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide)}} within neutrophils.
extraNote: Chronic Granulomatous Disease patients are susceptible to catalase-positive organisms because they cannot supplement the missing oxidative burst.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: In the laboratory, {{c1::S. aureus}} usually ferments mannitol and hemolyzes red blood cells, whereas coagulase-negative species do not.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to destroy red blood cells and recover {{c2::iron}} for use in cytochrome enzyme synthesis.
extraNote: This process results in the characteristic beta-hemolysis seen on blood agar.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::β-lactamase}}, which is often encoded on plasmids.
extraNote: This enzyme renders standard penicillin G ineffective against most staphylococcal infections.

clozeText: MRSA is resistant to nafcillin and methicillin due to altered {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}} in the cell membrane.
extraNote: These altered PBPs are encoded by the mecA gene.

clozeText: The altered protein {{c1::PBP2a}} in MRSA can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This is the structural basis for methicillin resistance.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) almost always produces {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin relatively rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is associated with necrotizing skin lesions and severe pneumonia.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursor.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} is a major virulence factor that binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on phagocytes from binding the antibody, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus is induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} and peptidoglycan, which trigger macrophages to release {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: This mechanism allows S. aureus to cause shock despite lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is poorly immunogenic, with serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} causing the majority of human infections.
extraNote: The microcapsule helps the organism resist phagocytosis.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, with approximately 30% colonization rate.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of ~5% of women, predisposing them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: The most important mode of S. aureus transmission in clinical settings is {{c1::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Handwashing is the most effective way to decrease transmission.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to S. aureus infections, along with IV drug use and CGD.
extraNote: Compromised immunity or high glucose levels facilitate staphylococcal growth and invasion.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Abscesses are characterized by central necrosis and pus formation.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::epidermidis}} is a common cause of infections on prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and forms biofilms on plastic/metal surfaces.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::saprophyticus}} is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections in young women.
extraNote: It is second only to E. coli in this demographic.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This 'NO Staph' mnemonic (NOvobiocin) helps differentiate coagulase-negative staph.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles.
extraNote: Presents as multiple small pustules, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: {{c1::Impetigo}} presents as honey-colored crusts and can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is characterized by desquamated skin in infants, caused by an S. aureus exotoxin.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of hospital-acquired {{c1::pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of septicemia and endocarditis.

clozeText: The most common MRSA strain in the United States is the {{c1::USA300::strain name}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired outbreaks.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which differentiates them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, protecting the bacteria from oxidative killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike coagulase-negative species, Staphylococcus aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta-hemolysis::type of hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron from hemoglobin, which is used for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: The major protein in the S. aureus cell wall is {{c1::Protein A}}, which inhibits phagocytosis by binding to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on macrophages and neutrophils from binding the antibody.

clozeText: In the cell wall of staphylococci, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the bacteriophage surface receptors.

clozeText: S. aureus can induce septic shock without endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} and {{c2::lipoteichoic acid}} stimulate macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: These components activate the complement and coagulation cascades, mimicking Gram-negative sepsis.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are chronic carriers, which increases their risk for skin infections.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a has low affinity for beta-lactams but can still perform its transpeptidase function for cell wall synthesis.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, whereas relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains do.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a toxin that can lead to necrotizing infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot produce H2O2 to kill catalase-positive organisms.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in these patients.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of skin {{c1::abscesses}}, which are characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Abscesses are the classic pyogenic lesion associated with S. aureus infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common cause of infections involving prosthetic heart valves, prosthetic joints, and intravenous catheters.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and is coagulase-negative.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin, whereas Staphylococcus saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This sensitivity is a key laboratory test to differentiate the two common coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is naturally resistant to novobiocin.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This frequently manifests as right-sided endocarditis or skin abscesses.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus and presents with widespread desquamation.
extraNote: It typically affects infants and young children.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts::physical finding}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a common superficial skin infection in children.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains produce {{c2::beta-lactamase}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: These strains are usually treated with beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin or oxacillin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis::joint infection}}.
extraNote: Hematogenous spread of the bacteria often leads to these deep tissue infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::disease name}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is a systemic vasculitis that primarily affects young children.

clozeText: S. aureus is one of the most common causes of {{c1::hospital-acquired pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is frequently associated with infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: For staphylococci, {{c1::handwashing}} is a critical intervention to decrease transmission, as hand contact is a primary mode of spread.
extraNote: Skin colonization among hospital personnel is a major reservoir for healthcare-associated infections.

clozeText: The antibiotic of choice for treating non-MRSA (MSSA) staphylococcal infections is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: Nafcillin is a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin.

clozeText: Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by the ingestion of a preformed {{c1::enterotoxin}}.
extraNote: S. aureus is a common cause of rapid-onset vomiting and diarrhea.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is associated with S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}} in approximately 5% of women.
extraNote: It is mediated by the TSS toxin-1 (TSST-1), which acts as a superantigen.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as {{c1::gram-positive cocci}} arranged in {{c2::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: This morphology differentiates them from streptococci, which appear in chains.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule consists of {{c1::polysaccharide}}, and serotypes {{c2::5 and 8}} cause the majority of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: There are two medically important genera of gram-positive cocci: Staphylococcus and {{c1::Streptococcus}}.
extraNote: These two genera are the primary cause of many pyogenic infections in humans.

clozeText: Microscopically, {{c1::streptococci}} appear in chains, whereas staphylococci appear in grapelike clusters.
extraNote: Chain formation is a hallmark of the genus Streptococcus and helps distinguish it from the clusters of Staphylococcus.

clozeText: Biochemically, staphylococci produce catalase, whereas {{c1::streptococci}} do not.
extraNote: Streptococci are catalase-negative, a critical diagnostic point for distinguishing them from Staphylococci.

clozeText: Streptococci are {{c1::nonmotile}} and do not form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: This differentiates them from other gram-positive organisms like Bacillus or Clostridium which are spore-formers.

clozeText: Catalase is an enzyme that degrades {{c1::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}} into {{c2::oxygen (O2) and water (H2O)}}.
extraNote: Because Streptococci lack this enzyme, they are generally more susceptible to the oxidative burst of neutrophils.

clozeText: Bacteria that lack {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, such as streptococci, are more vulnerable to the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.
extraNote: Catalase-positive organisms like S. aureus use the enzyme as a virulence factor to survive phagocytic killing.

clozeText: Impetigo is a skin infection that can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: Both organisms are primary causes of this common childhood skin infection.

clozeText: The classic lesion of {{c1::impetigo}} is a crop of vesicles with a {{c2::"honey-colored"}} crust.
extraNote: This appearance is characteristic regardless of whether S. pyogenes or S. aureus is the causal agent.

clozeText: Streptococci are {{c1::spherical}} gram-positive cocci.
extraNote: The term 'coccus' refers to their round or spherical morphology.

clozeText: One of the two main criteria to differentiate gram-positive cocci is the microscopic arrangement: staphylococci in clusters vs. streptococci in {{c1::chains}}.
extraNote: Linear chain formation is due to cell division in a single plane.

clozeText: One of the two main criteria to differentiate gram-positive cocci is the biochemical {{c1::catalase}} test.
extraNote: Catalase-negative = Streptococcus; Catalase-positive = Staphylococcus.

clozeText: {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}} is one of the two most important human pathogens described in the gram-positive cocci chapter.
extraNote: S. pyogenes is often referred to as Group A Streptococcus (GAS).

clozeText: Streptococci stain {{c1::positive (purple)}} on Gram stain.
extraNote: Their thick peptidoglycan layer retains the crystal violet-iodine complex.

clozeText: Impetigo lesions typically begin as crops of {{c1::vesicles}} before progressing to crusting.
extraNote: These small fluid-filled sacs are a standard clinical finding in early impetigo.

clozeText: Unlike Staphylococci, {{c1::Streptococci}} do not possess the catalase virulence factor that survives the killing effect of H2O2 in neutrophils.
extraNote: This metabolic difference is fundamental to their interaction with the host immune system.

clozeText: The two medically important genera of gram-positive cocci are distinguished by their arrangement: {{c1::clusters}} (Staphylococcus) and {{c2::chains}} (Streptococcus).
extraNote: Microscopic morphology is the first step in identification from a specimen.

clozeText: Streptococci and staphylococci are both classified as {{c1::non-spore forming}} bacteria.
extraNote: This is a key contrast to gram-positive rods like Bacillus and Clostridium.

clozeText: In the differentiation of gram-positive cocci, {{c1::Streptococcus}} is always catalase-negative.
extraNote: A simple bubble test with H2O2 confirms the absence of catalase.

clozeText: Both staphylococci and streptococci are characterized as {{c1::nonmotile}} cocci.
extraNote: They lack flagella and do not move independently in clinical samples.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is a common cause of {{c1::skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs)}}, including impetigo.
extraNote: S. pyogenes is a major contributor to superficial and deep skin infections.

clozeText: The specific species of Streptococcus noted for causing honey-colored crusts in impetigo is {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: While S. aureus is also common, S. pyogenes is the classic organism associated with this presentation in pediatric populations.

clozeText: Catalase degradative activity involves the reaction: 2 H2O2 → {{c1::2 H2O + O2}}.
extraNote: This oxygen production creates the visible bubbles in a positive catalase test.

clozeText: Streptococci are differentiated microscopically from staphylococci because they do not form {{c1::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: Instead, their division occurs along a single axis, resulting in chains.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the nose, but {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}} is also a major pathogen sharing similar skin infection niches.
extraNote: Both can cause impetigo and other pyogenic skin conditions.

clozeText: While staphylococci produce catalase to survive within {{c1::neutrophils}}, streptococci must rely on other mechanisms because they lack this enzyme.
extraNote: Catalase protects bacteria from the reactive oxygen species produced during the oxidative burst.

clozeText: Cocci arranged in {{c1::chains::microscopic pattern}} that test catalase-negative are identified as {{c2::Streptococcus}}.
extraNote: This dual finding is definitive for the genus in a clinical lab setting.

clozeText: Streptococci are spherical organisms, a morphology they share with the genus {{c1::Staphylococcus}}.
extraNote: Both are Gram-positive cocci, distinguishing them from Gram-positive rods.

clozeText: A gram-positive coccus that does NOT degrade hydrogen peroxide belongs to the genus {{c1::Streptococcus}}.
extraNote: The absence of H2O2 degradation (catalase activity) is the hallmark of Streptococci.

clozeText: Microscopically, Streptococci are distinguished from Staphylococci because they appear in {{c1::chains::arrangement}} rather than clusters.
extraNote: Streptococci divide in a single plane, resulting in the characteristic chain-like formation seen on Gram stain.

clozeText: All Streptococci are characterized biochemically as being {{c1::catalase}}-negative.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from Staphylococci, which produce catalase to degrade hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is a common cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a honey-colored crust.
extraNote: Both Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes can cause this skin infection.

clozeText: The major virulence factor of S. pyogenes that inhibits phagocytosis by interfering with complement (C3b) is the {{c1::M protein}}.
extraNote: M protein is highly antigenic; however, molecular mimicry with cardiac myosin leads to Rheumatic Fever.

clozeText: Streptococcus pyogenes is also known as {{c1::Group A}} Streptococcus based on its Lancefield carbohydrate antigen.
extraNote: Lancefield classification is based on the C-carbohydrate found in the cell wall.

clozeText: Unlike S. aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes possesses a capsule made of {{c1::hyaluronic acid}}, which is non-immunogenic.
extraNote: Because it mimics human ground substance, the capsule helps the bacteria evade the immune system.

clozeText: In the laboratory, S. pyogenes is identified by its sensitivity to {{c1::bacitracin}}.
extraNote: This is a key test to differentiate GAS from other beta-hemolytic streptococci like S. agalactiae.

clozeText: Scarlet fever is caused by {{c1::erythrogenic::toxin name}} toxin produced by S. pyogenes.
extraNote: The clinical triad includes fever, 'strawberry tongue,' and a sandpaper-like rash.

clozeText: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) can occur after both pharyngitis and {{c1::skin infections::site}}.
extraNote: Rheumatic fever, by contrast, occurs only after pharyngitis, not skin infections.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae is the most common cause of {{c1::neonatal sepsis::condition}} and meningitis.
extraNote: Pregnant women are screened at 35–37 weeks gestation for vaginal/anal colonization.

clozeText: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Strep) is identified by a positive {{c1::CAMP}} test.
extraNote: The CAMP factor enlarges the area of hemolysis produced by S. aureus.

clozeText: The {{c1::Hippurate::test name}} hydrolysis test is used to identify S. agalactiae.
extraNote: S. agalactiae can hydrolyze sodium hippurate to benzoate and glycine.

clozeText: Streptococcus pneumoniae appears on Gram stain as {{c1::lancet-shaped::shape}} diplococci.
extraNote: They are often seen in pairs and are exquisitely sensitive to optochin.

clozeText: S. pneumoniae is characterized by {{c1::alpha::hemolysis type}}-hemolysis and optochin sensitivity.
extraNote: Alpha-hemolysis results in a greenish tint on blood agar due to partial hemoglobin breakdown.

clozeText: The virulence of S. pneumoniae is primarily due to its {{c1::polysaccharide capsule}}.
extraNote: The capsule is the target of the PPSV23 and PCV13 vaccines.

clozeText: The {{c1::Quellung::reaction name}} reaction causes the S. pneumoniae capsule to swell when exposed to specific antibodies.
extraNote: This is a classic diagnostic laboratory technique for encapsulated organisms.

clozeText: S. pneumoniae is the #1 cause of the 'MOPS' infections: Meningitis, Otitis media, Pneumonia, and {{c1::Sinusitis}}.
extraNote: It is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP).

clozeText: The Viridans group streptococci are {{c1::optochin::drug}}-resistant alpha-hemolytic organisms.
extraNote: This resistance differentiates them from S. pneumoniae.

clozeText: Streptococcus mutans causes dental caries by synthesizing {{c1::dextrans}} from sucrose.
extraNote: Dextrans allow the bacteria to adhere to tooth enamel and form biofilm (plaque).

clozeText: Viridans streptococci (e.g., S. sanguinis) are a leading cause of {{c1::subacute}} bacterial endocarditis.
extraNote: They typically infect previously damaged heart valves (e.g., following dental work).

clozeText: Streptococcus bovis (S. gallolyticus) bacteremia is strongly associated with underlying {{c1::colon cancer}}.
extraNote: Identification of S. bovis in the blood mandates a colonoscopy.

clozeText: Rheumatic fever is diagnosed using the {{c1::JONES}} criteria.
extraNote: Joints (Polyarthritis), Carditis, Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis is {{c1::Penicillin G::drug}}.
extraNote: Resistance to penicillin has not yet been documented in S. pyogenes.

clozeText: S. pneumoniae develops resistance to penicillin via alterations in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}.
extraNote: Unlike Staph, this resistance is not typically due to beta-lactamase production.

clozeText: Necrotizing fasciitis caused by S. pyogenes is often associated with the production of {{c1::Exotoxin B::toxin}}.
extraNote: Exotoxin B is a protease that rapidly destroys tissue (flesh-eating bacteria).

clozeText: To diagnose a previous S. pyogenes skin infection, the {{c1::Anti-DNase B}} titer is more sensitive than the ASO titer.
extraNote: ASO titers may not rise significantly following pyoderma/impetigo.

clozeText: Streptococcus pneumoniae is {{c1::bile-soluble::biochemical property}}, which distinguishes it from Viridans strep.
extraNote: Bile salts activate autolysins that dissolve the S. pneumoniae cell wall.

clozeText: Toxic Shock-Like Syndrome (TSLS) from S. pyogenes is mediated by {{c1::SpeA::toxin}}.
extraNote: SpeA (Pyogenic Exotoxin A) acts as a superantigen, cross-linking MHC II and T-cell receptors.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase-positive bacteria can survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci typically form chains.
extraNote: This arrangement is due to division in multiple planes versus a single plane.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and causes hemolysis of red blood cells.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth in the human host.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids}} that encode β-lactamase, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: This necessitated the development of β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: MRSA strains are resistant to nafcillin due to alterations in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}} encoded by the mecA gene.
extraNote: The altered protein, PBP2a, performs transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is distinguished from healthcare-acquired MRSA by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common strain of CA-MRSA in the United States.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) occurs when {{c1::d-lactate}} is substituted for d-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: These resistance genes are typically acquired from enterococci via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.
extraNote: The Fc receptor on the phagocyte cannot bind the antibody if the Fc portion is already occupied.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} in the cell wall of S. aureus mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the bacteriophage receptors.

clozeText: Septic shock in S. aureus infections can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} through the induction of IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids act similarly to the endotoxin (LPS) of gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is poorly immunogenic, and serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the majority (85%) of human infections.
extraNote: This poor immunogenicity has hindered the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus possesses endotoxin-like properties, allowing it to stimulate cytokine production and the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite being gram-positive.

clozeText: The main reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose}}, with approximately 30% of the population colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose are at an increased risk for recurrent skin infections.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is often associated with high-absorbency tampon use or colonized surgical wounds.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are particularly prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive and neutralizes the limited H2O2 these patients' neutrophils can produce.

clozeText: The characteristic lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which features central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Examples include furuncles and boils; they often require drainage.

clozeText: {{c1::Foreign bodies}} such as sutures and intravenous catheters are major predisposing factors for S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Bacteria often form biofilms on these surfaces, protecting them from antibiotics and the immune system.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and is typically coagulase-negative.

clozeText: To differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It results in widespread desquamation and is most common in infants.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: Infection can progress to deeper forms like furuncles or carbuncles.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing metabolic factor to infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia and impaired neutrophil function contribute to this increased risk.

clozeText: S. aureus, particularly MRSA, is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: Common presentations include endocarditis (often right-sided) and skin abscesses.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for S. aureus in hospital settings is via {{c1::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Rigorous handwashing is the most effective way to decrease hospital-acquired transmission.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may potentially be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is a vasculitis that primarily affects medium-sized arteries in children.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase is an important virulence factor that allows bacteria to survive the oxidative killing burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive cocci, but their arrangement on microscopy is a primary morphological distinction.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: S. aureus is unique among medical staphylococci for its ability to {{c1::ferment mannitol}} and hemolyze red blood cells.
extraNote: Coagulase-negative species like S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus typically do not ferment mannitol.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin for the synthesis of energy-producing {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth during infection.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain {{c1::plasmids}} that encode β-lactamase, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin are required for these strains.

clozeText: MRSA strains are resistant to nafcillin because of the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but does not bind β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is distinguished from healthcare-acquired strains by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves a gene cassette that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This cassette is the same one found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE).

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major S. aureus virulence factor that binds the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG, preventing phagocytosis.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, the bacteria prevent the neutrophil's Fc receptors from recognizing the antibody.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids::Polymer}} are ribitol phosphate polymers in the staphylococcal cell wall that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: Septic shock in S. aureus infections can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which trigger the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This occurs despite S. aureus lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is an important virulence factor, with serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} causing 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is often referred to as a microcapsule and is poorly immunogenic.

clozeText: S. aureus peptidoglycan possesses {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, allowing it to activate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains clinical findings of septic shock in the absence of Gram-negative LPS.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, which is colonized in approximately 30% of the population.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a deficiency in the NADPH oxidase system, making it difficult to clear catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Abscesses include clinical presentations like furuncles and boils.

clozeText: In women, S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}} (found in ~5% of women) predisposes to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is toxin-mediated and often associated with tampon use or focal infections.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is resistant to novobiocin and is a common cause of UTIs in young women.

clozeText: Impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust and can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin and soft tissue infections like folliculitis and cellulitis.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a desquamating skin disease in infants caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus.
extraNote: The skin appears "rolled up" and desquamated due to the toxin's action.

clozeText: S. aureus, particularly MRSA, is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users}}.
extraNote: Common infections include endocarditis and skin abscesses.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia, septicemia, and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: The presence of foreign bodies like sutures or catheters significantly increases the risk of infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::Disease}}, a pediatric vasculitis of unknown etiology, may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: This syndrome is characterized by high fever, conjunctivitis, and strawberry tongue.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora but is a major cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and joints.
extraNote: Its ability to form biofilms on plastic/metal surfaces is a key virulence factor.

clozeText: The primary mode of S. aureus transmission in healthcare settings is via {{c1::hand contact}}, making handwashing the most effective prevention.
extraNote: Colonized hospital personnel serve as common vectors for transmission to patients.

clozeText: S. aureus causes food poisoning through the ingestion of a preformed {{c1::enterotoxin}}.
extraNote: Symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea typically occur rapidly after ingestion (2–6 hours).

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major systemic predisposing factor to recurrent S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Compromised immunity, including low neutrophil levels, also increases susceptibility.

clozeText: Staphylococci are distinguished from Streptococci biochemically by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide.
extraNote: Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, {{c1::Staphylococci}} appear in grapelike clusters, whereas {{c2::Streptococci}} appear in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive cocci; morphology is a key preliminary diagnostic feature.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}, which activates prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: Thrombin then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and displays {{c2::β-hemolysis::type of hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for energy production (cytochrome enzymes).

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain {{c1::plasmids}} that encode {{c2::β-lactamase}}, an enzyme that degrades many penicillins.
extraNote: Nafcillin is often used for non-MRSA strains that produce this enzyme.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves enzymes that substitute {{c1::d-lactate}} for {{c2::d-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This substitution prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: The major cell wall protein of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which acts by binding to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages as the Fc receptor cannot be engaged.

clozeText: In the S. aureus cell wall, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells and serve as part of the {{c2::bacteriophage}} receptors.
extraNote: These are polymers of ribitol phosphate.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in S. aureus play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mechanism mimics the action of gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: Most S. aureus infections (85%) are caused by capsule serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}}.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause the clinical findings of septic shock despite lacking endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} can stimulate macrophages and the complement cascade.
extraNote: The peptidoglycan possesses endotoxin-like properties.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, with approximately {{c2::30}}% of the population being chronic carriers.
extraNote: Hand contact is a major mode of transmission; handwashing is critical for prevention.

clozeText: Vaginal colonization by S. aureus in approximately 5% of women predisposes them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen exotoxin.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, allowing it to neutralize the small amount of H2O2 produced by CGD neutrophils.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Pyogenic means pus-producing; S. aureus causes disease by inducing inflammation and producing toxins.

clozeText: {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora that frequently causes infections of {{c2::prosthetic heart valves}} and orthopedic implants.
extraNote: It is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in the lab.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a significant cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young women.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It results in widespread areas of desquamated skin, particularly in infants.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust, can be caused by either {{c2::S. aureus}} or {{c3::S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a common superficial skin infection in children.

clozeText: Almost all strains of Community-Acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a factor less commonly found in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that destroys leukocytes.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections.

clozeText: Diabetes is a major predisposing factor for infections by {{c1::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: Other risks include intravenous drug use and the presence of foreign bodies like sutures.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is at high risk for MRSA endocarditis and skin infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is characterized by systemic vasculitis in children.

clozeText: The diagnostic feature of an S. aureus gram stain is gram-positive cocci in {{c1::irregular clusters}}.
extraNote: Microscopy is often the first step in identifying the causative agent of an abscess.

clozeText: S. aureus recovers iron for growth from {{c1::hemoglobin}} via the action of hemolysins.
extraNote: The iron is then used for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes for energy production.

clozeText: Staphylococci are {{c1::catalase}}-positive, which distinguishes them from Streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, allowing bacteria to survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus that binds the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase is an enzyme that causes plasma to clot by activating prothrombin to form thrombin.

clozeText: Coagulase catalyzes the conversion of {{c1::fibrinogen}} into {{c2::fibrin}} clots.
extraNote: This mechanism is thought to wall off the infection, contributing to abscess formation.

clozeText: S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and shows {{c2::beta}}-hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: In contrast, S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus do not ferment mannitol and are non-hemolytic.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall subunits.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of healthy individuals are colonized at any given time.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in the S. aureus cell wall can induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF, leading to {{c2::septic shock}}.
extraNote: These components act similarly to the endotoxin (LPS) found in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, while S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This biochemical test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in urine cultures.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are highly susceptible to S. aureus because the organism is {{c2::catalase}}-positive.
extraNote: CGD patients lack NADPH oxidase and cannot produce H2O2; catalase-positive organisms further deplete available peroxide.

clozeText: On Gram stain, staphylococci appear as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: This morphology is due to cell division occurring in multiple planes.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::beta-lactamase}}, which is typically encoded on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins like penicillin G; beta-lactamase-resistant drugs like nafcillin are required.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are cell wall polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin that results in widespread desquamation of the skin in infants.
extraNote: The condition involves the exfoliatin toxin, which targets the epidermis.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Abscesses are characterized by central necrosis and the accumulation of pus (neutrophils and dead tissue).

clozeText: Almost all strains of {{c1::community-acquired (CA-MRSA)}} produce P-V leukocidin.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a toxin that kills white blood cells and is associated with severe skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: It shares this clinical presentation with Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: The drug of choice for methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA) infections is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: These are beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins.

clozeText: S. aureus produces hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin for use in {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Acquisition of iron is essential for bacterial energy production and growth.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: It is the most frequent pathogen isolated from bone and joint infections across most age groups.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a pediatric vasculitis that may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: The etiology is unknown, but a superantigen-mediated mechanism is suspected.

clozeText: The {{c1::capsule}} of S. aureus is an important virulence factor, with types {{c2::5 and 8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a frequent cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its resistance to novobiocin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a major cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: Contaminated hands of hospital personnel are a common mode of transmission.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus possesses {{c1::endotoxin}}-like properties.
extraNote: It can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines and activate the complement cascade, potentially causing septic shock.

clozeText: Presence of S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}} of approximately 5% of women predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is often associated with the use of highly absorbent tampons which promote toxin production.

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae are gram-positive, {{c1::club-shaped}} rods often arranged in V or L shapes (Chinese letters).
extraNote: This characteristic morphology is also referred to as being 'coryneform' or pleomorphic.

clozeText: The metachromatic granules seen in Corynebacterium diphtheriae are also known as {{c1::Babes-Ernst}} granules.
extraNote: These granules represent stored inorganic polyphosphates and appear red/purple when stained with methylene blue.

clozeText: To enhance the production of metachromatic granules, Corynebacterium diphtheriae is typically grown on {{c1::Loeffler}} coagulated serum medium.
extraNote: Loeffler medium is a classic enrichment medium that favors the development of characteristic granules over other bacteria.

clozeText: On cystine-tellurite blood agar, Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces {{c1::black}} colonies.
extraNote: The organism reduces tellurite to tellurium, which precipitates and colors the colonies black or gray.

clozeText: The tox gene that encodes the diphtheria toxin is introduced into C. diphtheriae via a {{c1::lysogenic bacteriophage}}.
extraNote: This process is called lysogenic conversion; only strains infected by the beta-prophage are toxigenic.

clozeText: The mechanism of Diphtheria toxin involves the {{c1::ADP-ribosylation}} of a specific host cell protein.
extraNote: It is an A-B exotoxin where the A subunit provides the enzymatic activity.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin inhibits host cell protein synthesis by inactivating {{c1::Elongation Factor-2 (EF-2)}}.
extraNote: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Exotoxin A) uses the exact same mechanism of action as Diphtheria toxin.

clozeText: The respiratory form of diphtheria is characterized by a thick, gray-white {{c1::pseudomembrane}} in the pharynx.
extraNote: The membrane consists of fibrin, leukocytes, necrotic epithelial cells, and bacteria; it is firmly adherent and bleeds if scraped.

clozeText: A classic clinical sign of severe pharyngeal diphtheria is massive swelling of the neck, known as {{c1::bull neck}}.
extraNote: This is caused by extensive cervical lymphadenopathy and edema.

clozeText: Systemic absorption of diphtheria toxin can lead to {{c1::myocarditis}}, which is a major cause of death.
extraNote: Patients may develop arrhythmias, heart block, or congestive heart failure several weeks after the initial infection.

clozeText: Neurotoxicity from diphtheria toxin often manifests as {{c1::cranial nerve palsies}} (e.g., soft palate paralysis) or peripheral neuropathy.
extraNote: The toxin causes demyelination, which can also lead to ocular motor nerve dysfunction and difficulty swallowing.

clozeText: The {{c1::Elek}} test is an in vitro immunodiffusion assay used to detect the production of diphtheria toxin.
extraNote: It uses filter paper impregnated with antitoxin placed on agar; precipitation lines form where toxin and antitoxin meet.

clozeText: The diphtheria vaccine is a {{c1::toxoid}} vaccine, typically administered as part of the DTaP series.
extraNote: The toxoid is a formal-inactivated toxin that induces protective IgG antibodies.

clozeText: In the acute treatment of suspected diphtheria, the most critical step is the administration of {{c1::diphtheria antitoxin}}.
extraNote: Antitoxin provides passive immunity by neutralizing circulating toxin before it enters host cells.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin production is regulated by the concentration of {{c1::iron}} in the environment.
extraNote: High iron levels activate the DtxR repressor, which shuts down toxin production; low iron levels trigger toxin release.

clozeText: The preferred antibiotics for eliminating the carrier state or treating active Corynebacterium diphtheriae infections are {{c1::erythromycin}} or penicillin G.
extraNote: Antibiotics stop further toxin production by killing the bacteria but do not neutralize already circulating toxin.

clozeText: Unlike many other pathogens, Corynebacterium diphtheriae is non-invasive; it stays in the {{c1::pharynx}} while its toxin disseminates.
extraNote: The bacteria themselves do not enter the bloodstream (no bacteremia).

clozeText: Metachromatic (polyphosphate) granules in C. diphtheriae stain {{c1::red}} with Albert's stain or methylene blue.
extraNote: This contrast with the blue color of the rest of the bacillus helps in rapid identification.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for Corynebacterium diphtheriae is {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: The organism is maintained in the population by asymptomatic carriers who harbor it in their oropharynx or skin.

clozeText: The pseudomembrane in diphtheria can lead to death by {{c1::airway obstruction}} (asphyxiation).
extraNote: The membrane can extend into the larynx or trachea, blocking the flow of air.

clozeText: Corynebacterium species that are non-pathogenic skin flora are collectively referred to as {{c1::diphtheroids}}.
extraNote: Examples include C. xerosis and C. hoffmannii; they are often contaminants in blood cultures.

clozeText: The B subunit of the diphtheria toxin binds to the {{c1::heparin-binding epidermal growth factor}} (HB-EGF) receptor.
extraNote: The high density of these receptors on heart and nerve cells explains the toxin's specific organ damage.

clozeText: Cutaneous diphtheria typically presents as a chronic, non-healing {{c1::ulcer}} covered by a gray membrane.
extraNote: It is more common in tropical climates and among indigent populations.

clozeText: The {{c1::Schick}} test was historically used to determine if a person was immune to diphtheria.
extraNote: A positive test (skin redness/swelling) indicated a lack of neutralizing antibodies (susceptibility).

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a {{c1::catalase}}-positive, non-motile organism.
extraNote: These biochemical features help differentiate it from other gram-positive rods like Listeria (which is motile).

clozeText: The A subunit of the diphtheria toxin contains the enzyme {{c1::ADP-ribosyltransferase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme transfers the ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ to EF-2.

clozeText: Transmission of Corynebacterium diphtheriae occurs primarily via {{c1::respiratory droplets}}.
extraNote: It can also be spread by direct contact with skin lesions in cutaneous cases.

clozeText: One reason for the re-emergence of diphtheria in certain populations is a decrease in {{c1::herd immunity}} due to low vaccination rates.
extraNote: Booster doses (Td or Tdap) are required every 10 years to maintain protective antibody levels.

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a gram-{{c1::positive}} rod that is often described as appearing in {{c1::V or L shapes::arrangement}} resembling Chinese characters.
extraNote: This arrangement is due to snapping division after binary fission.

clozeText: The characteristic shape of Corynebacterium diphtheriae is described as {{c1::club-shaped}} (coryneform).
extraNote: The word 'koryne' is Greek for club.

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae contains {{c1::metachromatic (Babes-Ernst) granules}}, which are storage polymers of inorganic phosphates.
extraNote: These granules appear red when stained with methylene blue.

clozeText: To visualize metachromatic granules in Corynebacterium diphtheriae, {{c1::methylene blue}} stain is typically used.
extraNote: The granules stain a different color (red/purple) than the rest of the blue-stained cell.

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces black colonies when grown on {{c1::cystine-tellurite agar}}.
extraNote: Tellurite is reduced by the bacteria to produce the black metallic color.

clozeText: The specialized medium used to promote the development of metachromatic granules in Corynebacterium is {{c1::Loeffler medium}}.
extraNote: It is a protein-rich medium that supports rapid growth of C. diphtheriae.

clozeText: The diphtheria toxin gene is introduced into C. diphtheriae via a {{c1::lysogenic bacteriophage::vector}} (beta-prophage).
extraNote: This process is known as lysogenic conversion; only strains carrying the phage are toxigenic.

clozeText: The mechanism of Diphtheria toxin involves the {{c1::ADP-ribosylation::biochemical reaction}} of elongation factor-2 (EF-2).
extraNote: The toxin targets a specific modified amino acid on EF-2 called diphthamide.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin inhibits host cell {{c1::protein synthesis}} by inactivating EF-2.
extraNote: This mechanism is identical to the Exotoxin A produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin is classified as an {{c1::A-B}} toxin, where the B subunit binds to cell receptors and the A subunit provides the active enzymatic function.
extraNote: The B subunit specifically binds to heparin-binding epidermal growth factor receptor.

clozeText: The hallmark clinical finding of respiratory diphtheria is a thick, gray {{c1::pseudomembrane::lesion}} in the oropharynx.
extraNote: The membrane consists of fibrin, leukocytes, and dead respiratory epithelial cells.

clozeText: Severe cervical lymphadenopathy in diphtheria results in a characteristic {{c1::bull neck}} appearance.
extraNote: This is a sign of severe, potentially fatal respiratory disease.

clozeText: A dangerous systemic complication of Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection is {{c1::myocarditis}}, which can lead to heart failure or arrhythmias.
extraNote: The toxin has a high affinity for cardiac and neural tissue.

clozeText: Diphtheria toxin can cause neurologic damage, most commonly manifesting as {{c1::cranial nerve palsies}} or paralysis of the soft palate.
extraNote: Regurgitation of fluids through the nose while swallowing is a classic symptom of palatal paralysis.

clozeText: The {{c1::Elek test::laboratory test}} is an in vitro precipitation test used to determine if a strain of C. diphtheriae is toxigenic.
extraNote: It involves an antitoxin-soaked paper strip placed on an agar plate.

clozeText: The most important immediate treatment for a patient suspected of having diphtheria is the administration of {{c1::diphtheria antitoxin}}.
extraNote: Passive immunization with antitoxin must be given immediately to neutralize circulating toxin before it binds to tissues.

clozeText: The DTaP vaccine contains diphtheria {{c1::toxoid}}, which induces protective antibodies against the toxin.
extraNote: A toxoid is a toxin that has been treated (usually with formaldehyde) to destroy toxicity but retain immunogenicity.

clozeText: The preferred antibiotics for treating Corynebacterium diphtheriae are {{c1::erythromycin}} or penicillin.
extraNote: Antibiotics stop the production of further toxin but do not treat the toxin already present in the body.

clozeText: Attempting to scrape the pseudomembrane of diphtheria usually results in {{c1::bleeding}} of the underlying mucosa.
extraNote: This is a key clinical differentiator from other forms of exudative pharyngitis.

clozeText: In the ADP-ribosylation of EF-2, the ADP-ribose moiety is derived from {{c1::NAD+::molecule}}.
extraNote: This is a common motif among many bacterial A-B toxins.

clozeText: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a non-{{c1::motile}} and non-{{c1::spore}}-forming organism.
extraNote: Unlike Bacillus and Clostridium, it does not form spores.

clozeText: Cutaneous diphtheria typically presents as a {{c1::non-healing ulcer}} covered by a gray membrane.
extraNote: This form is more common in tropical climates or among the homeless population.

clozeText: C. diphtheriae is aerobic or {{c1::facultatively anaerobic}}.
extraNote: It can grow in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor environments.

clozeText: The Diphtheria toxin is regulated by {{c1::iron}} levels; toxin production is maximal when iron is {{c2::low::high/low}}.
extraNote: The DtxR repressor binds to the tox gene operator only in the presence of iron.

clozeText: The {{c1::Schick test}} (historically used) determines if a person has protective immunity against diphtheria toxin by injecting a small amount of toxin intradermally.
extraNote: A positive skin reaction indicates a lack of immunity (no antibodies).

clozeText: Diphtheroids are {{c1::non-pathogenic}} Corynebacterium species that are part of the normal human flora.
extraNote: They must be distinguished from C. diphtheriae in clinical cultures.

clozeText: Diphtheria can cause airway obstruction if the pseudomembrane dislodges and is {{c1::aspirated}}.
extraNote: This represents a surgical emergency requiring tracheostomy.

clozeText: {{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}} is a Gram-{{c2::positive}} rod that is a frequent cause of meningitis in neonates and the elderly.
extraNote: It is one of the few Gram-positive organisms that produces endotoxin-like effects despite being a non-spore-forming rod.

clozeText: Listeria exhibits {{c1::tumbling}} motility in broth at room temperature (25°C).
extraNote: This motility is due to peritrichous flagella, which are not produced at 37°C.

clozeText: Listeria is a {{c1::facultative intracellular}} pathogen, allowing it to avoid host antibodies.
extraNote: Clearance of Listeria requires cell-mediated immunity (Th1 response), which is why the immunocompromised are at high risk.

clozeText: Listeria uses the protein {{c1::ActA}} to induce {{c2::actin polymerization::process}}, creating 'actin rockets' to spread between cells.
extraNote: This mechanism allows the bacteria to move directly from the cytoplasm of one cell into an adjacent cell, avoiding the extracellular environment.

clozeText: The pore-forming toxin {{c1::Listeriolysin O}} allows Listeria to escape from the {{c2::phagosome}} into the host cell cytoplasm.
extraNote: It is activated by the acidic pH of the phagolysosome.

clozeText: Listeria can be distinguished from Group B Streptococcus (GBS) because Listeria is {{c1::catalase}}-positive.
extraNote: Both organisms are beta-hemolytic and cause neonatal meningitis, making the catalase test a key differentiator.

clozeText: Listeria can grow at temperatures as low as {{c1::4::number}}°C, a characteristic used in the lab technique called {{c2::cold enrichment}}.
extraNote: This property allows it to contaminate and multiply in refrigerated foods.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Listeria is the consumption of contaminated {{c1::unpasteurized dairy}} or {{c2::deli meats::food type}}.
extraNote: Outbreaks are often linked to soft cheeses (like queso fresco) and cold cuts.

clozeText: In pregnant women, Listeria infection can cause {{c1::amnionitis}} and lead to spontaneous abortion or stillbirth.
extraNote: Pregnant women are often advised to avoid deli meats and soft cheeses to prevent this.

clozeText: {{c1::Granulomatosis infantiseptica}} is a severe neonatal infection caused by Listeria, characterized by disseminated granulomas and abscesses.
extraNote: This occurs via transplacental (in utero) transmission.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating *Listeria monocytogenes* is {{c1::Ampicillin}}.
extraNote: Listeria is naturally resistant to all cephalosporins, which is a common 'pimp' question on rounds.

clozeText: For empiric treatment of meningitis in patients over age {{c1::65::age}}, Ampicillin must be added to cover Listeria.
extraNote: The standard regimen of Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone does not cover Listeria.

clozeText: Listeria is {{c1::positive::positive or negative}} for the CAMP test, which enhances the zone of hemolysis produced by *S. aureus*.
extraNote: While GBS is the classic CAMP-positive organism, Listeria also produces a positive result.

clozeText: Listeria uses {{c1::Internalins}} to facilitate adherence and entry into host cells, such as {{c2::enterocytes}}.
extraNote: Internalin A binds to E-cadherin on epithelial cells.

clozeText: Listeria is typically {{c1::beta}}-hemolytic on blood agar, though the zone of hemolysis is often very {{c2::narrow::wide or narrow}}.
extraNote: The narrow zone of hemolysis can sometimes be obscured by the colony itself.

clozeText: Healthy adults infected with Listeria most commonly develop {{c1::febrile gastroenteritis}}.
extraNote: Symptoms include watery diarrhea, fever, and nausea, usually occurring after a large inoculum.

clozeText: In patients with a penicillin allergy, {{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)}} is the preferred alternative for Listeria.
extraNote: It provides excellent CNS penetration for meningitis cases.

clozeText: The CSF in Listeria meningitis may show a predominance of {{c1::monocytes}} or {{c2::neutrophils::alternative cell}}.
extraNote: Despite being a bacterial infection, the 'monocytogenes' name reflects the monocytosis observed in infected rabbits.

clozeText: Listeria is a non-{{c1::spore}}-forming, Gram-positive rod.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Bacillus and Clostridium species, which are spore-formers.

clozeText: Listeria is particularly dangerous for {{c1::renal transplant}} patients and others with impaired T-cell immunity.
extraNote: Cell-mediated immunity is the primary defense against intracellular pathogens.

clozeText: Listeria produces {{c1::Phospholipase C}} to help break down the double-membrane vacuoles formed during cell-to-cell spread.
extraNote: This enzyme works in conjunction with Listeriolysin O.

clozeText: Listeria is a {{c1::siderophilic}} organism, meaning it requires iron for growth and can be more virulent in iron-overload states.
extraNote: Patients with hemochromatosis may be at increased risk of severe infection.

clozeText: The characteristic motility of Listeria seen on a wet mount is called {{c1::tumbling}} motility.
extraNote: On semi-solid media, it may produce an 'inverted umbrella' pattern of growth.

clozeText: Transplacental transmission of Listeria typically leads to {{c1::early}}-onset neonatal disease.
extraNote: Early-onset disease is characterized by granulomatosis infantiseptica; late-onset is usually meningitis acquired during birth.

clozeText: Listeria is resistant to cephalosporins due to altered {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}.
extraNote: Even 3rd generation cephalosporins like Ceftriaxone fail to bind effectively to Listeria's PBPs.

clozeText: Listeria's ability to cross the {{c1::blood-brain barrier}} and the {{c2::placenta}} is a hallmark of its tissue tropism.
extraNote: It also crosses the intestinal barrier to enter the bloodstream.

clozeText: Listeria is the only Gram-positive rod that is a {{c1::common}} cause of meningitis.
extraNote: While other GP rods like Corynebacterium exist, they rarely cause meningitis in the general population.

clozeText: The reservoir for *Listeria monocytogenes* includes {{c1::soil}}, water, and the GI tracts of animals.
extraNote: It is a ubiquitous organism in the environment.

clozeText: {{c1::Listeria monocytogenes}} is a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming bacillus often transmitted via unpasteurized dairy or {{c1::deli meats}}.
extraNote: Listeria is one of the few bacteria that can cross the placental, intestinal, and blood-brain barriers.

clozeText: Listeria exhibits a characteristic {{c1::tumbling}} motility when observed in broth at 22–25°C.
extraNote: This motility is due to flagella, which are not produced at 37°C.

clozeText: The virulence factor {{c1::Listeriolysin O::toxin}} allows Listeria to escape the phagosome into the host cell cytoplasm.
extraNote: It is a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin that is activated by the acidic pH of the phagolysosome.

clozeText: Listeria uses the {{c1::ActA::protein}} to induce host cell actin polymerization, forming "actin rockets."
extraNote: This mechanism allows the organism to propel itself into adjacent cells, avoiding the extracellular immune response.

clozeText: Listeria is classified as a {{c1::facultative intracellular}} pathogen, which explains why cell-mediated immunity is required for clearance.
extraNote: Patients with impaired T-cell immunity (e.g., transplant recipients, HIV) are at significantly higher risk.

clozeText: Listeria can be isolated using {{c1::cold enrichment::technique}} because it is capable of growing at temperatures as low as 0–4°C.
extraNote: This unique property allows it to contaminate and multiply in refrigerated foods.

clozeText: {{c1::Granulomatosis infantiseptica}} is a severe, early-onset neonatal infection caused by Listeria acquired in utero.
extraNote: It is characterized by disseminated abscesses and granulomas in multiple organs.

clozeText: Listeria is a top-three cause of neonatal meningitis, alongside {{c1::Group B Streptococcus}} and {{c1::Escherichia coli}}.
extraNote: Late-onset neonatal listeriosis (acquired during or after birth) typically presents as meningitis 2–3 weeks after birth.

clozeText: The empiric treatment for suspected meningitis in patients >65 years old must include {{c1::Ampicillin}} to cover Listeria.
extraNote: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins.

clozeText: Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, a fact often remembered by the mnemonic {{c1::LAME::mnemonic}}.
extraNote: LAME: Listeria, Atypicals (Mycoplasma/Chlamydia), MRSA, Enterococci.

clozeText: On blood agar, Listeria monocytogenes produces a {{c1::narrow::size}} zone of β-hemolysis.
extraNote: The hemolysis is often so subtle it can be mistaken for α-hemolysis or confused with Group B Strep.

clozeText: Unlike Group B Streptococcus, Listeria is {{c1::catalase}}-positive.
extraNote: This is a key biochemical test used to differentiate these two common causes of neonatal meningitis.

clozeText: Listeria shows a positive {{c1::CAMP}} test, demonstrating enhanced hemolysis when streaked near Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: The effect appears as a rectangular/blunt zone rather than the sharp "arrowhead" seen with S. agalactiae.

clozeText: The primary immune response against Listeria involves {{c1::cell-mediated::type}} immunity (specifically CD8+ T cells and activated macrophages).
extraNote: Humoral (antibody) immunity is largely ineffective because the bacteria remain intracellular.

clozeText: Listeria entry into intestinal epithelial cells is mediated by the interaction between {{c1::Internalin}} and host E-cadherin.
extraNote: This interaction triggers receptor-mediated endocytosis of the bacterium.

clozeText: In healthy adults, Listeria infection typically manifests as a self-limited {{c1::febrile gastroenteritis}}.
extraNote: Symptoms usually occur within 24 hours of ingesting a large inoculum via contaminated food.

clozeText: Pregnant women are at 10x higher risk of Listeria infection, particularly in the {{c1::third}} trimester due to physiological T-cell suppression.
extraNote: Maternal listeriosis can be asymptomatic or cause a mild flu-like illness but results in fetal risk.

clozeText: For a patient with a severe penicillin allergy, the alternative treatment for Listeria is {{c1::Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)}}.
extraNote: Listeria is naturally resistant to vancomycin-intermediate levels in some cases, but TMP-SMX remains effective.

clozeText: In semi-solid motility agar, Listeria produces an {{c1::umbrella-shaped}} growth pattern.
extraNote: This pattern forms because motility is more active at room temperature than at body temperature.

clozeText: Listeria is a Gram-positive {{c1::rod (bacillus)}} that can sometimes appear in V-shaped or L-shaped pairs.
extraNote: This morphology can lead to misidentification as Corynebacterium (diphtheroids).

clozeText: Listeria utilizes {{c1::Phospholipase C}} enzymes to help degrade the two-layered membrane of the primary and secondary vacuoles.
extraNote: This acts synergistically with Listeriolysin O to allow cytoplasmic escape and cell-to-cell spread.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Gentamicin}} is often added to Ampicillin for synergistic effect when treating Listeria endocarditis or meningitis.
extraNote: Aminoglycosides help increase the bactericidal activity against the organism.

clozeText: Unlike Bacillus anthracis, Listeria monocytogenes is {{c1::non-spore-forming}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from other medically important Gram-positive rods.

clozeText: CSF analysis in Listeria meningitis may uniquely show a predominance of {{c1::monocytes}} rather than neutrophils.
extraNote: This is reflecting the organism's name (monocytogenes) and its intracellular nature.

clozeText: Neonatal listeriosis acquired during delivery (late-onset) usually results in {{c1::meningitis}} or sepsis.
extraNote: This occurs via exposure to Listeria in the vaginal tract or fecal contamination during birth.

clozeText: Listeria is a common cause of meningitis in patients with {{c1::iron overload::condition}} (e.g., hemochromatosis).
extraNote: Listeriolysin O is an iron-dependent toxin, and the organism thrives in high-iron environments.

clozeText: Avoidance of {{c1::soft cheeses}} (e.g., Brie, Camembert) is a standard recommendation for pregnant women to prevent Listeriosis.
extraNote: These cheeses provide an ideal environment for Listeria growth during storage.

clozeText: The ActA protein of Listeria is located on the {{c1::surface}} of the bacterial cell.
extraNote: ActA mediates the recruitment of host Arp2/3 complexes to initiate actin filament assembly.

clozeText: Gardnerella vaginalis is a {{c1::gram-variable}} pleomorphic rod associated with bacterial vaginosis (BV).
extraNote: While it has a gram-positive cell wall structure, the peptidoglycan layer is thin, often causing it to stain gram-negative or variable.

clozeText: Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) is characterized by a decrease in the normal flora, specifically {{c1::Lactobacillus::genus}}, and an overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes.
extraNote: Lactobacilli normally maintain an acidic pH by producing lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide.

clozeText: The characteristic vaginal discharge in Gardnerella-associated BV is described as {{c1::thin, gray-white}} with a fishy odor.
extraNote: This is distinct from the cottage-cheese discharge of Candida or the yellow-green frothy discharge of Trichomonas.

clozeText: The pathognomonic finding on a saline wet mount of vaginal secretions in BV is the presence of {{c1::clue cells}}.
extraNote: Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells covered with Gardnerella bacteria, giving them a 'stippled' or 'shaggy' appearance.

clozeText: In the diagnosis of BV, the addition of 10% KOH to vaginal secretions produces a fishy odor, known as a positive {{c1::Whiff test}}.
extraNote: The odor results from the volatilization of amines (like cadaverine and putrescine) produced by anaerobic bacteria.

clozeText: The vaginal pH in a patient with Gardnerella vaginalis infection is typically {{c1::> 4.5::greater than or less than 4.5?}}.
extraNote: A pH > 4.5 is one of the four Amsel criteria for diagnosing BV.

clozeText: The first-line antibiotic treatment for Gardnerella vaginalis (BV) is {{c1::metronidazole}}.
extraNote: Clindamycin is an alternative treatment option.

clozeText: Unlike Trichomoniasis or Candidiasis, Gardnerella vaginalis infection (BV) typically lacks {{c1::vaginal inflammation}} (redness/pain).
extraNote: This is why the condition is termed 'vaginosis' rather than 'vaginitis'.

clozeText: Gardnerella vaginalis works synergistically with anaerobes such as {{c1::Mobiluncus::genus}} to cause BV.
extraNote: Mobiluncus is a curved, gram-variable anaerobic rod often seen on gram stains of BV samples.

clozeText: Bacterial Vaginosis is not traditionally classified as a {{c1::sexually transmitted infection (STI)}}, although it is associated with sexual activity.
extraNote: Treatment of male partners is generally not recommended as it does not prevent recurrence.

clozeText: The Amsel criteria for BV diagnosis require 3 of 4: thin discharge, pH > 4.5, positive whiff test, and {{c1::clue cells}}.
extraNote: Clue cells are the most specific of the Amsel criteria.

clozeText: Gardnerella vaginalis produces {{c1::vaginolysin}}, a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin that targets human cells.
extraNote: Vaginolysin is a pore-forming toxin specific to human vaginal epithelial cells.

clozeText: Pregnancy complications associated with Gardnerella vaginalis infection include an increased risk of {{c1::preterm labor}}.
extraNote: BV is also associated with premature rupture of membranes and chorioamnionitis.

clozeText: Gardnerella vaginalis can form a {{c1::biofilm}} on the vaginal epithelium, which protects the bacteria and anaerobes from the host immune system.
extraNote: The biofilm contributes to the high recurrence rates of BV after antibiotic treatment.

clozeText: Normal vaginal flora is dominated by Lactobacillus, which produces {{c1::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}} to inhibit the overgrowth of Gardnerella.
extraNote: Loss of H2O2-producing Lactobacilli is a key step in the development of BV.

clozeText: On Gram stain, Gardnerella vaginalis appears as small {{c1::coccobacilli}}.
extraNote: They are typically described as gram-variable or gram-negative due to their thin cell walls.

clozeText: The amine odor in the Whiff test is caused by the breakdown of proteins into {{c1::amines}} (e.g., putrescine, cadaverine) by anaerobes.
extraNote: These amines become volatile and smell 'fishy' when the pH is raised by KOH.

clozeText: The {{c1::Nugent score}} is a gram-stain-based scoring system used in research settings to diagnose BV.
extraNote: It quantifies the number of large Gram-positive rods (Lactobacillus), small Gram-variable rods (Gardnerella), and curved Gram-variable rods (Mobiluncus).

clozeText: Metronidazole treats BV by targeting the {{c1::anaerobic}} bacteria that proliferate alongside Gardnerella.
extraNote: Metronidazole is activated in anaerobic cells to form free radicals that damage DNA.

clozeText: Gardnerella vaginalis is a {{c1::facultative anaerobe}}.
extraNote: While it can grow in both environments, it thrives in the anaerobic conditions of a dysbiotic vagina.

clozeText: A saline wet mount shows epithelial cells with {{c1::obscured borders}} due to the high density of Gardnerella organisms.
extraNote: This 'obscuring' of the cell margin is what defines a clue cell.

clozeText: The discharge of Gardnerella-associated BV is typically {{c1::non-viscous}} and coats the vaginal walls evenly.
extraNote: Unlike the clumped discharge of yeast infections.

clozeText: The most specific diagnostic finding for Gardnerella vaginalis on a vaginal smear is the {{c1::clue cell}}.
extraNote: Presence of clue cells on >20% of epithelial cells is highly diagnostic of BV.
