clozeText: Vibrio vulnificus can cause rapidly progressive {{c1::cellulitis or necrotizing fasciitis}} following exposure to seawater.
extraNote: Wound infections occur when open cuts are exposed to contaminated water or shellfish.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::liver disease (cirrhosis)}} or {{c2::hemochromatosis::iron disorder}} are at high risk for V. vulnificus septicemia.
extraNote: The organism's growth is enhanced by high serum iron levels.

clozeText: The most important intervention in the treatment of cholera is {{c1::Fluid and electrolyte replacement::Management}}.
extraNote: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) containing glucose and salts is highly effective.

clozeText: While rehydration is primary, the antibiotic of choice to shorten the duration of cholera is {{c1::Doxycycline::Drug}}.
extraNote: Azithromycin is an alternative, especially in children or pregnant women.

clozeText: V. cholerae serogroups {{c1::O1}} and {{c2::O139}} are the only ones associated with epidemic and pandemic cholera.
extraNote: Non-O1/non-O139 strains generally cause milder, sporadic diarrheal illness.

clozeText: Vibrio vulnificus septicemia carries a high mortality rate and often presents with {{c1::hemorrhagic bullae::skin finding}}.
extraNote: These lesions are a hallmark of systemic V. vulnificus infection in immunocompromised hosts.

clozeText: The {{c1::String test}} is used in labs to differentiate Vibrio from Aeromonas; Vibrio colonies lyse in sodium deoxycholate and release DNA that can be pulled into a string.
extraNote: Aeromonas is string test negative.

clozeText: Vibrio cholerae is described as having {{c1::shooting star::description}} motility on dark-field microscopy.
extraNote: This motility is attributed to its single polar flagellum.

clozeText: In the laboratory, Vibrio species grow well in alkaline media, such as {{c1::alkaline peptone water::medium}} (pH 8.5–9.5).
extraNote: This alkaline pH inhibits most other intestinal flora.

clozeText: Vibrio parahaemolyticus and V. vulnificus are distinguished from V. cholerae by their inability to grow in {{c1::0% NaCl (distilled water)}}.
extraNote: V. cholerae can grow without added salt, whereas the others are obligate halophiles.

clozeText: The most common biotypes of V. cholerae O1 are {{c1::Classic}} and {{c2::El Tor}}.
extraNote: El Tor is currently the dominant biotype in the ongoing seventh pandemic.

clozeText: Vibrio cholerae infection results in {{c1::metabolic acidosis::acid-base status}} due to the loss of bicarbonate in the stool.
extraNote: Stool bicarbonate concentrations in cholera are very high.

clozeText: V. parahaemolyticus produces the {{c1::Kanagawa hemolysin::toxin}}, which is detected by β-hemolysis on high-salt blood agar.
extraNote: Strains that are 'Kanagawa positive' are more likely to be pathogenic.

clozeText: The treatment for V. vulnificus wound infections or sepsis involves a combination of {{c1::Ceftriaxone}} and {{c2::Doxycycline}}.
extraNote: Rapid antibiotic administration and surgical debridement are critical.

clozeText: Proteus species are {{c1::Gram-negative::Gram stain}} rods that do not ferment {{c2::lactose::sugar}}, placing them in the same category as Salmonella and Shigella on MacConkey agar.
extraNote: They appear as clear/colorless colonies on MacConkey agar because they cannot ferment lactose.

clozeText: A defining cultural characteristic of Proteus is {{c1::swarming motility::movement pattern}}, which results in concentric rings of growth on blood agar.
extraNote: This is due to the differentiation of vegetative cells into hyper-flagellated 'swarmer' cells.

clozeText: Proteus species produce the enzyme {{c1::urease::enzyme}}, which hydrolyzes urea into {{c2::ammonia::product}} and CO2.
extraNote: The production of ammonia raises the pH of the urine, making it alkaline.

clozeText: The increase in urinary pH caused by Proteus leads to the precipitation of {{c1::struvite::composition}} stones, also known as magnesium ammonium phosphate stones.
extraNote: These stones are often called 'staghorn calculi' because they take the shape of the renal pelvis.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is distinguished from Proteus vulgaris by the {{c1::indole::biochemical}} test; P. mirabilis is {{c2::negative::positive/negative}}.
extraNote: P. mirabilis is indole-negative, whereas P. vulgaris is indole-positive.

clozeText: On Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) agar, Proteus produces {{c1::H2S (Hydrogen Sulfide)::gas}}, which results in a {{c2::black::color}} precipitate.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from other urease-positive organisms like Klebsiella.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)::infection type}}, particularly in patients with {{c2::long-term catheters::risk factor}}.
extraNote: Alkaline urine and biofilm formation contribute to its persistence in the urinary tract.

clozeText: The characteristic smell of Proteus cultures is often described as {{c1::burnt chocolate::odor}} or fishy.
extraNote: This distinct odor can help identify the organism in the laboratory setting.

clozeText: Staghorn calculi associated with Proteus can act as a {{c1::nidus::site}} for recurrent infection by sequestering bacteria within the stone.
extraNote: Complete surgical removal of the stone is often necessary to eradicate the infection.

clozeText: Proteus species use {{c1::peritrichous flagella::structure}} to facilitate their rapid movement and swarming behavior.
extraNote: The switch from swimmer to swarmer cells involve a massive increase in flagella density.

clozeText: In the laboratory, Proteus is {{c1::oxidase-negative::biochemical test}}, which helps differentiate it from Pseudomonas species.
extraNote: Pseudomonas is oxidase-positive, while Proteus (like all Enterobacteriaceae) is oxidase-negative.

clozeText: The alkaline environment (pH > {{c1::7::number}}) created by Proteus promotes the formation of {{c2::magnesium ammonium phosphate::chemical name}} crystals.
extraNote: This environment also damages the urothelium and inhibits local immune function.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is generally {{c1::sensitive::sensitive/resistant}} to penicillins like ampicillin, unlike many other Gram-negative enteric rods.
extraNote: However, P. vulgaris is typically more resistant and often requires broader-spectrum antibiotics.

clozeText: The {{c1::Weil-Felix::diagnostic}} reaction uses Proteus antigens to cross-react with antibodies against {{c2::Rickettsia::organism}}.
extraNote: This is an older diagnostic test for Rickettsial diseases, based on shared O-antigens.

clozeText: Proteus possesses {{c1::endotoxin::toxin type}} in its cell wall, which can trigger systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) if it enters the bloodstream.
extraNote: Like all Gram-negative bacteria, the Lipid A component of LPS is the toxic moiety.

clozeText: A significant complication of Proteus-induced staghorn calculi is {{c1::hydronephrosis::condition}}, caused by the obstruction of the renal pelvis.
extraNote: Chronic obstruction can lead to renal atrophy and failure.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis uses {{c1::MR/P fimbriae::structure}} (mannose-resistant Proteus-like) to adhere to the epithelial cells of the urinary tract.
extraNote: Adherence is the crucial first step in the colonization of the bladder and kidneys.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::ammonium::ion}} in the urine, produced by Proteus, is directly toxic to the {{c2::renal tubular::cell type}} cells.
extraNote: This local toxicity contributes to the pathogenesis of pyelonephritis.

clozeText: On Hektoen Enteric (HE) agar, Proteus colonies appear green with a {{c1::black center::appearance}}.
extraNote: The black center indicates H2S production, similar to Salmonella.

clozeText: Proteus species can be differentiated from Salmonella by the {{c1::urease::test}} test, as Proteus is {{c2::positive::positive/negative}}.
extraNote: Salmonella is urease-negative and H2S-positive; Proteus is both urease-positive and H2S-positive.

clozeText: Proteus is a common cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired::setting}} infections, particularly pneumonia and wound infections in surgical patients.
extraNote: It is considered an opportunistic pathogen in the clinical environment.

clozeText: The swarming motility of Proteus is inhibited on certain media by adding {{c1::bile salts::additive}} or increasing the concentration of agar.
extraNote: MacConkey agar inhibits swarming due to the presence of bile salts.

clozeText: Proteus vulgaris is often treated with {{c1::Cefotaxime::antibiotic}} or Fluoroquinolones due to its innate resistance to many beta-lactams.
extraNote: Indole-positive Proteus (P. vulgaris) is generally more antibiotic-resistant than P. mirabilis.

clozeText: The {{c1::IgA protease::virulence factor}} produced by some Proteus strains helps the bacteria degrade host antibodies on mucosal surfaces.
extraNote: This aids in the colonization of the urinary mucosa.

clozeText: Struvite stones caused by Proteus are {{c1::radiopaque::radiographic property}} on X-ray.
extraNote: They are easily visible on plain abdominal films due to their mineral content.

clozeText: The pore-forming toxin {{c1::HpmA hemolysin::toxin}} is a virulence factor of Proteus that contributes to tissue damage in the kidneys.
extraNote: HpmA facilitates the escape of the bacteria from phagosomes.

clozeText: In patients with Proteus UTIs, urinalysis will typically show {{c1::alkaline::pH}} pH and the presence of {{c2::triple phosphate::crystal type}} crystals.
extraNote: Triple phosphate crystals have a classic 'coffin-lid' appearance under the microscope.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is a member of the {{c1::Enterobacteriaceae::family}} family.
extraNote: As a member of this family, it is a fermentative, Gram-negative, oxidase-negative rod.

clozeText: Proteus species are characterized by {{c1::swarming}} motility on blood agar, often described as concentric circles or a "bull's eye" pattern.
extraNote: This motility is due to peritrichous flagella that allow the bacteria to move rapidly across the surface of the medium.

clozeText: Proteus is a {{c1::urease}}-positive organism, which splits urea into ammonia and CO2.
extraNote: Urease production is a critical virulence factor that leads to the alkalinization of urine.

clozeText: The alkalinization of urine by Proteus (pH > {{c1::7}}) leads to the precipitation of magnesium ammonium phosphate.
extraNote: The resulting stones are known as struvite stones.

clozeText: Struvite stones associated with Proteus infections often take the shape of the renal pelvis, forming {{c1::staghorn}} calculi.
extraNote: These large stones can cause renal obstruction and serve as a reservoir for recurrent infection.

clozeText: Proteus-induced stones are composed of {{c1::magnesium ammonium phosphate::mineral name}}, also known as triple phosphate.
extraNote: These stones are radiopaque on X-ray.

clozeText: Proteus {{c1::mirabilis}} is the most common species isolated from clinical infections, particularly urinary tract infections.
extraNote: It is generally more sensitive to antibiotics than P. vulgaris.

clozeText: Proteus {{c1::vulgaris}} can be distinguished from P. mirabilis by being {{c2::indole::biochemical test}}-positive.
extraNote: P. mirabilis is indole-negative. This is a common board-distinguishing feature.

clozeText: The {{c1::Weil-Felix}} reaction uses Proteus antigens to detect anti-Rickettsial antibodies in patient serum.
extraNote: This cross-reactivity occurs because certain Proteus strains (OX19, OX2, OXK) share O-antigens with Rickettsia.

clozeText: Proteus is a Gram-{{c1::negative}} rod that is part of the {{c2::Enterobacteriaceae}} family.
extraNote: Like other members of this family, it is a facultative anaerobe.

clozeText: On MacConkey agar, Proteus species appear as {{c1::non-lactose fermenters::metabolic property}}.
extraNote: They produce colorless/pale colonies because they do not ferment lactose.

clozeText: Proteus produces {{c1::hydrogen sulfide (H2S)}} on Triple Sugar Iron (TSI) agar, resulting in a black precipitate.
extraNote: This helps differentiate it from other non-lactose fermenters like Shigella.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is typically sensitive to {{c1::ampicillin::drug class}}, unlike many other Gram-negative enteric rods.
extraNote: However, resistance is increasing, and treatment should be guided by sensitivity testing.

clozeText: Proteus-associated urinary tract infections often produce a distinct {{c1::fishy}} odor.
extraNote: The smell is attributed to the production of volatile amines and ammonia.

clozeText: Urease-mediated ammonia production by Proteus is toxic to the {{c1::uroepithelium::tissue type}}.
extraNote: The resulting tissue damage facilitates bacterial invasion and persistence.

clozeText: Proteus is often associated with UTIs in patients with {{c1::long-term urinary catheters}}.
extraNote: The bacteria can form biofilms on the surface of the catheter.

clozeText: In the Weil-Felix test, the strain {{c1::OX-19}} reacts strongly with antibodies against Rickettsia prowazekii (Epidemic typhus).
extraNote: This is a classical, though now rarely used, diagnostic method.

clozeText: Proteus species possess {{c1::peritrichous}} flagella, which are essential for their characteristic swarming behavior.
extraNote: During swarming, the bacteria differentiate into elongated, hyper-flagellated "swarmer" cells.

clozeText: Urinalysis of a patient with Proteus UTI will typically show {{c1::alkaline}} pH and {{c2::triple phosphate}} crystals.
extraNote: The crystals have a characteristic "coffin-lid" appearance under microscopy.

clozeText: For multi-drug resistant Proteus infections, {{c1::fluoroquinolones}} or {{c2::third-generation cephalosporins}} are often used.
extraNote: Examples include ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.

clozeText: Proteus can be differentiated from Salmonella on TSI agar because Proteus is {{c1::urease-positive}} while Salmonella is urease-negative.
extraNote: Both produce H2S (black precipitate), making the urease test vital for differentiation.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for Proteus is the {{c1::human intestinal tract}}.
extraNote: It is considered part of the normal colonic flora in many individuals.

clozeText: Proteus species are {{c1::oxidase-negative}}, which distinguishes them from Pseudomonas.
extraNote: All Enterobacteriaceae are oxidase-negative.

clozeText: In the context of the Weil-Felix test, the {{c1::OX-K}} strain is used to diagnose Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi).
extraNote: OX-19 and OX-2 are usually negative in Scrub typhus.

clozeText: Proteus mirabilis is {{c1::ornithine decarboxylase}}-positive, helping to distinguish it from Proteus vulgaris.
extraNote: Metabolic profile differences are key for species-level identification.

clozeText: Proteus species can cause {{c1::bacteremia::condition}}, particularly in elderly patients with urinary tract obstructions or catheters.
extraNote: Urosepsis is a significant complication of untreated Proteus UTIs.

clozeText: Unlike E. coli, Proteus is unable to ferment {{c1::lactose}}.
extraNote: E. coli is a strong lactose fermenter (pink on MacConkey).

clozeText: Staghorn calculi formed by Proteus can lead to chronic {{c1::pyelonephritis}} and eventual renal failure if not treated surgically.
extraNote: The stone itself must be removed to completely eradicate the infection.

clozeText: Proteus species are characterized by the production of {{c1::phenylalanine deaminase}}.
extraNote: This test involves the conversion of phenylalanine to phenylpyruvic acid, which turns green with ferric chloride.

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-{{c1::negative::stain}} rod that is an {{c1::obligate aerobe::respiration}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Enterobacteriaceae, which are facultative anaerobes.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is characteristically {{c1::oxidase::enzyme}}-positive and {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}-positive.
extraNote: The oxidase test helps differentiate it from members of the Enterobacteriaceae family.

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces a blue-green pigment called {{c1::pyocyanin::pigment}} and a yellow-green fluorescent pigment called {{c1::pyoverdin::pigment}}.
extraNote: Pyocyanin generates reactive oxygen species to kill competing microbes and damage host tissues.

clozeText: On MacConkey agar, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a {{c1::non-lactose fermenter::metabolism}}.
extraNote: It appears as colorless or pale colonies because it cannot ferment lactose.

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is known for producing a distinct {{c1::grape-like::description}} or fruity odor in culture.
extraNote: This odor is often helpful for early identification in the clinical lab.

clozeText: The primary virulence factor of Pseudomonas, Exotoxin A, acts by {{c1::inactivating elongation factor-2 (EF-2)::mechanism}} via ADP-ribosylation.
extraNote: This is the same mechanism of action as the Diphtheria toxin produced by C. diphtheriae.

clozeText: In patients with {{c1::Cystic Fibrosis::condition}}, Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces an {{c1::alginate::substance}} capsule that facilitates biofilm formation.
extraNote: This mucoid phenotype is highly resistant to phagocytosis and antibiotics.

clozeText: {{c1::Ecthyma gangrenosum::Clinical sign}} is a necrotic skin lesion caused by Pseudomonas bacteremia, characterized by a black eschar.
extraNote: It typically occurs in immunocompromised or neutropenic patients due to perivascular bacterial invasion.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is a frequent cause of {{c1::otitis externa::condition}}, also known as 'swimmer's ear'.
extraNote: Chronic infection can progress to malignant otitis externa in elderly diabetic patients.

clozeText: Malignant otitis externa caused by Pseudomonas typically affects {{c1::diabetic::patient population}} patients and can invade the temporal bone.
extraNote: It may lead to cranial nerve palsies, particularly of the facial nerve (CN VII).

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis::condition}} in intravenous drug users and following {{c1::puncture wounds to the foot::trauma}}.
extraNote: Puncture wounds through rubber-soled sneakers are a classic USMLE presentation.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is a common cause of {{c1::hot tub folliculitis::condition}}, which presents as a pruritic papulopustular rash.
extraNote: This occurs due to inadequate chlorination of heated water sources.

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major cause of {{c1::corneal ulcers::condition}} in individuals who wear {{c1::contact lenses::risk factor}}.
extraNote: The bacteria can contaminate lens cleaning solutions or the lenses themselves.

clozeText: Pseudomonas uses {{c1::Phospholipase C::virulence factor}} to degrade cell membranes and {{c1::Elastase::virulence factor}} to destroy connective tissue.
extraNote: Elastase is particularly important for damaging blood vessels, leading to hemorrhage and necrosis.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is a common cause of {{c1::nosocomial::setting}} infections, particularly Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP) and UTIs from catheters.
extraNote: It thrives in moist environments like sinks, respirators, and humidifiers.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Pseudomonas often includes {{c1::Piperacillin-Tazobactam::antibiotic}} or {{c1::Ceftazidime/Cefepime::antibiotic}}.
extraNote: Antipseudomonal penicillins and 3rd/4th generation cephalosporins are essential first-line agents.

clozeText: The monobactam antibiotic {{c1::Aztreonam::drug}} is used to treat Pseudomonas in patients with a severe {{c1::penicillin::allergy}} allergy.
extraNote: Aztreonam binds to PBP3 and is effective only against Gram-negative aerobes.

clozeText: The fluoroquinolone {{c1::Ciprofloxacin::antibiotic}} is an effective oral treatment for Pseudomonas infections.
extraNote: Levofloxacin is also used, but Ciprofloxacin typically has better antipseudomonal activity.

clozeText: In patients with Cystic Fibrosis, inhaled {{c1::Tobramycin::antibiotic}} is frequently used to manage Pseudomonas colonization.
extraNote: Aminoglycosides are often combined with beta-lactams for synergistic effects against Pseudomonas.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is naturally resistant to many antibiotics due to the presence of {{c1::efflux pumps::mechanism}} and low porin permeability.
extraNote: Multi-drug resistance is common, requiring susceptibility testing for clinical isolates.

clozeText: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a significant pathogen in {{c1::burn::injury type}} victims, often leading to sepsis.
extraNote: The loss of the skin barrier and the moist environment of the wound favor Pseudomonas growth.

clozeText: Pseudomonas belongs to the group of {{c1::Gram-negative non-fermenters::classification}}, which do not utilize glucose fermentatively.
extraNote: This differentiates them from the Enterobacteriaceae in TSI (Triple Sugar Iron) agar tests.

clozeText: Pseudomonas can produce {{c1::endotoxin (LPS)::toxin}}, which can trigger {{c1::septic shock::condition}} in systemic infections.
extraNote: The lipid A component of LPS induces cytokine release (TNF-alpha, IL-1).

clozeText: Pseudomonas infections are particularly dangerous in patients with {{c1::neutropenia::blood count abnormality}}, such as those undergoing chemotherapy.
extraNote: Severe neutropenia is a major risk factor for Pseudomonas bacteremia and ecthyma gangrenosum.

clozeText: {{c1::Ceftazidime::antibiotic}} and {{c1::Cefepime::antibiotic}} are the only two cephalosporins commonly used for Pseudomonas.
extraNote: Most other cephalosporins (like Ceftriaxone) lack sufficient activity against Pseudomonas.

clozeText: Pseudomonas is a common cause of UTI in patients with {{c1::indwelling catheters::medical device}}.
extraNote: It is often associated with recurrent infections and multi-drug resistance in hospital settings.

clozeText: Pseudomonas uses a {{c1::Type III secretion system::virulence mechanism}} to inject toxins directly into host cells.
extraNote: ExoS and ExoT are examples of effector proteins injected via this needle-like apparatus.

clozeText: Pseudomonas can be differentiated from other non-fermenters by its ability to grow at {{c1::42::temperature}}°C.
extraNote: This thermal tolerance is a classic laboratory identification feature for P. aeruginosa.

clozeText: Biochemically, staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O; it is a virulence factor allowing bacteria to survive within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: In the coagulase reaction, thrombin catalyzes the activation of {{c1::fibrinogen}} to form the {{c2::fibrin}} clot.
extraNote: This process provides a physical barrier (the clot) that can protect the bacteria from phagocytosis.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, Staphylococcus aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol::biochemical test}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain plasmids encoding {{c1::β-lactamase}}, an enzyme that degrades many penicillins.
extraNote: Nafcillin and other β-lactamase-resistant penicillins were developed specifically to treat these strains.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin/methicillin (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins, rendering the drug ineffective.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin relatively rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States is USA300.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This is the same mechanism found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), often carried on a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and acts as a virulence factor by binding the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By occupying the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils, inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce cytokines leading to septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids induce IL-1 and TNF from macrophages, similar to the action of endotoxin.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for Staphylococcus aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized at any one time; chronic carriers have increased risk of skin infections.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: Common manifestations in this population include endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the respiratory burst to produce H2O2; since S. aureus is catalase+, it destroys the small amount of H2O2 produced.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a condition in infants caused by an {{c2::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus.
extraNote: The condition presents with widespread areas of desquamated, 'rolled up' skin.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, is caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a superficial skin infection highly contagious among children.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, whereas Staphylococcus saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in clinical samples.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::saprophyticus}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::epidermidis}} is a common cause of infections on prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and is known for producing biofilms on medical devices.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause clinical findings of septic shock without possessing {{c1::endotoxin}} because its peptidoglycan has endotoxin-like properties.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines and activate the complement cascade.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSST-1 acts as a superantigen, causing massive cytokine release.

clozeText: S. aureus microcapsules are poorly {{c1::immunogenic}}, which has complicated the development of an effective vaccine.
extraNote: Types 5 and 8 capsular polysaccharides cause 85% of human infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is an acute febrile vasculitis primarily affecting children.

clozeText: For epidemiologic purposes, S. aureus strains can be differentiated by {{c1::phage typing}}, which utilizes surface receptors including teichoic acids.
extraNote: Specific staphylococcal bacteriophages bind to these surface receptors.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, characterized by small pustules on the chin and neck.
extraNote: It is an infection of the hair follicles that can progress to furuncles or carbuncles.

clozeText: MRSA accounts for more than {{c1::50%}} of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients in the United States.
extraNote: This highlight's the importance of empiric vancomycin for suspected S. aureus infections in healthcare settings.

clozeText: Infections related to {{c1::foreign bodies}} (e.g., sutures and intravenous catheters) are significantly predisposed by S. aureus.
extraNote: Foreign material provides a surface for bacterial colonization and protects organisms from the immune response.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of bacterial {{c1::conjunctivitis}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a frequent cause of healthcare-acquired pneumonia and septicemia.

clozeText: Helicobacter pylori is a {{c1::Gram-negative}} curved (spiral) rod.
extraNote: Its morphology is often described as 'seagull-shaped' or spiral.

clozeText: H. pylori is {{c1::urease}} positive, which allows it to survive in the acidic stomach by creating an alkaline microenvironment.
extraNote: Urease converts urea into ammonia and CO2.

clozeText: H. pylori is motile via multiple {{c1::polar flagella}}, which allow it to penetrate the gastric mucus layer.
extraNote: Motility is essential for the bacteria to reach the neutral-pH environment of the gastric epithelium.

clozeText: H. pylori is {{c1::microaerophilic}}, meaning it requires low levels of oxygen for growth.
extraNote: This is a characteristic shared with Campylobacter jejuni.

clozeText: Biochemically, H. pylori is {{c1::oxidase}} positive and catalase positive.
extraNote: These biochemical markers help distinguish it from other Gram-negative rods.

clozeText: The {{c1::CagA}} protein is a high-yield virulence factor injected into host cells via a Type IV secretion system.
extraNote: CagA is associated with an increased risk of gastric adenocarcinoma.

clozeText: The {{c1::VacA}} toxin induces large vacuoles in gastric epithelial cells and promotes apoptosis.
extraNote: VacA stands for Vacuolating cytotoxin A.

clozeText: H. pylori primarily colonizes the {{c1::antrum}} of the stomach.
extraNote: Colonization here often leads to chronic antral gastritis.

clozeText: H. pylori infection leads to decreased {{c1::somatostatin}} production by D-cells in the gastric antrum.
extraNote: Loss of somatostatin (an inhibitor) leads to hypergastrinemia and increased acid production.

clozeText: Chronic infection with H. pylori is the leading cause of {{c1::duodenal}} ulcers (approximately 90%).
extraNote: It is also associated with 70% of gastric ulcers.

clozeText: H. pylori is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen because it causes {{c1::gastric adenocarcinoma}}.
extraNote: The chronic inflammation leads to intestinal metaplasia and eventually cancer.

clozeText: H. pylori is strongly associated with {{c1::MALT lymphoma}} (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue lymphoma).
extraNote: MALT lymphoma is a type of B-cell marginal zone lymphoma.

clozeText: Treatment of H. pylori can result in the complete regression of {{c1::MALT lymphoma}}.
extraNote: This is a unique example of a malignancy curable with antibiotics.

clozeText: The {{c1::urea breath test}} involves swallowing radiolabeled urea to detect isotope-labeled CO2 in the exhaled breath.
extraNote: Used for both initial diagnosis and confirming eradication.

clozeText: The {{c1::stool antigen}} test is a highly specific non-invasive test used to confirm eradication of H. pylori.
extraNote: Standard practice is to test 4+ weeks after completing therapy.

clozeText: On histology, H. pylori can be visualized using the {{c1::Warthin-Starry}} silver stain.
extraNote: Giemsa and silver stains are superior to standard H&E for visualizing the bacteria.

clozeText: The first-line 'Triple Therapy' for H. pylori includes a PPI, {{c1::Clarithromycin}}, and Amoxicillin.
extraNote: Metronidazole can be used in patients with a penicillin allergy.

clozeText: In areas of high macrolide resistance, {{c1::Bismuth}}-based quadruple therapy is the preferred treatment.
extraNote: Components: PPI, Bismuth, Metronidazole, and Tetracycline.

clozeText: H. pylori produces {{c1::ammonia}} from urea, which directly damages gastric mucosal cells.
extraNote: This creates the 'protective cloud' against stomach acid.

clozeText: H. pylori utilizes the {{c1::BabA}} adhesin to bind to Lewis b blood group antigens on the gastric epithelium.
extraNote: BabA stands for Blood group antigen-binding adhesin.

clozeText: The rapid {{c1::urease test}} (CLO test) involves placing a gastric biopsy into a medium containing urea and a pH indicator.
extraNote: A color change from yellow to pink indicates a positive result.

clozeText: Unlike S. aureus, H. pylori transmission is primarily via the {{c1::fecal-oral}} or oral-oral route.
extraNote: Intrafamilial clustering is common.

clozeText: H. pylori causes {{c1::Type B}} gastritis, which is the most common form of chronic gastritis.
extraNote: Type A gastritis is autoimmune and affects the fundus/body.

clozeText: H. pylori produces {{c1::proteases}} and mucinases that degrade the protective gastric mucus layer.
extraNote: This exposes the underlying epithelium to gastric acid.

clozeText: Increased levels of {{c1::Gastrin}} are seen in H. pylori antral-predominant gastritis due to D-cell inhibition.
extraNote: This differentiates H. pylori gastritis from other forms where gastrin might be normal.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Blood group O}} are at a statistically higher risk for developing duodenal ulcers from H. pylori.
extraNote: This is due to increased binding affinity of the bacteria to certain surface antigens.

clozeText: H. pylori is a common cause of iron deficiency {{c1::anemia}} even in the absence of visible GI bleeding.
extraNote: Mechanisms include sequestration of iron by the bacteria and decreased absorption.

clozeText: PPIs must be discontinued at least {{c1::2 weeks}} prior to urea breath or stool antigen testing to avoid false negatives.
extraNote: PPIs inhibit the growth and urease activity of H. pylori.

clozeText: Helicobacter pylori is a {{c1::Gram-negative::Gram stain}} curved rod that is {{c2::catalase::enzyme}}, oxidase, and urease positive.
extraNote: Its curved/spiral shape and flagella help it penetrate the thick mucus layer of the stomach.

clozeText: The primary virulence factor of H. pylori is {{c1::urease::enzyme}}, which produces ammonia to {{c2::neutralize::effect}} stomach acid.
extraNote: Urea + H2O → Ammonia + CO2; this creates a local alkaline environment (protective cloud) for the bacteria.

clozeText: H. pylori most commonly colonizes the {{c1::antrum::anatomical region}} of the stomach, leading to Type B gastritis.
extraNote: Chronic infection here causes decreased somatostatin and increased gastrin, predisposing to duodenal ulcers.

clozeText: H. pylori is associated with approximately {{c1::90%::percentage}} of duodenal ulcers and 70% of gastric ulcers.
extraNote: It is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) worldwide.

clozeText: The {{c1::Urea Breath Test::Diagnostic test}} requires patients to swallow radiolabeled urea; detection of labeled {{c2::CO2::molecule}} in the breath indicates active infection.
extraNote: This test is highly sensitive and specific for active infection and for confirming eradication after treatment.

clozeText: H. pylori is a major risk factor for {{c1::MALT lymphoma::Cancer type}} and gastric adenocarcinoma.
extraNote: MALToma (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue) is a B-cell lymphoma that often regresses after antibiotic treatment.

clozeText: Standard 'Triple Therapy' for H. pylori includes a PPI, {{c1::Clarithromycin::Macrolide}}, and {{c2::Amoxicillin::Beta-lactam}}.
extraNote: Metronidazole is substituted for Amoxicillin in patients with penicillin allergies.

clozeText: Bismuth quadruple therapy consists of a PPI, Bismuth, {{c1::Tetracycline::Antibiotic}}, and {{c2::Metronidazole::Antibiotic}}.
extraNote: This is often used in areas with high clarithromycin resistance or after failure of triple therapy.

clozeText: The {{c1::CagA::Virulence factor}} protein is an oncoprotein injected into host cells that remodels the actin cytoskeleton and promotes inflammation.
extraNote: Strains carrying the cag pathogenicity island are more likely to cause ulcers and cancer.

clozeText: H. pylori can be visualized on gastric biopsy using {{c1::Silver (Warthin-Starry)::Stain name}} or Giemsa stains.
extraNote: Histology is the gold standard for diagnosis but is invasive.

clozeText: {{c1::VacA::Virulence factor}} is a pore-forming toxin produced by H. pylori that induces massive vacuolation in epithelial cells.
extraNote: It leads to host cell apoptosis and facilitates the leakage of nutrients into the extracellular space.

clozeText: Chronic H. pylori infection in the stomach body (corpus) can lead to {{c1::atrophic::type}} gastritis and intestinal metaplasia.
extraNote: Metaplasia is characterized by the presence of goblet cells in the gastric mucosa, increasing adenocarcinoma risk.

clozeText: H. pylori is considered {{c1::microaerophilic::oxygen requirement}}, meaning it requires low levels of oxygen to grow.
extraNote: This is consistent with the environment found beneath the gastric mucus layer.

clozeText: The {{c1::Stool Antigen Test::Non-invasive test}} is used to diagnose active infection and monitor the success of eradication therapy.
extraNote: Unlike serology, stool antigen only remains positive during active infection.

clozeText: Patients with H. pylori-related duodenal ulcers typically experience pain that {{c1::improves::effect}} with food intake.
extraNote: In contrast, gastric ulcer pain often worsens with food, leading to weight loss.

clozeText: H. pylori uses {{c1::Lophotrichous::Flagella arrangement}} flagella for motility through the gastric mucus.
extraNote: Mutants lacking flagella are unable to colonize the gastric mucosa.

clozeText: The {{c1::Rapid Urease Test (CLO test)::Diagnostic test}} involves placing a biopsy specimen in a medium containing urea and a pH indicator.
extraNote: A color change from yellow to pink/red (alkaline pH) indicates the presence of urease.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::oxidase::enzyme}} helps H. pylori transfer electrons to oxygen during aerobic respiration.
extraNote: H. pylori is oxidase-positive, distinguishing it from many other enteric rods.

clozeText: In the antrum, H. pylori-induced inflammation inhibits {{c1::D cells::Cell type}}, leading to reduced somatostatin production.
extraNote: Low somatostatin removes the 'brake' on G cells, resulting in hypergastrinemia.

clozeText: H. pylori does not invade the gastric epithelium; it remains in the {{c1::mucus layer::location}} overlying the cells.
extraNote: Despite being non-invasive, it causes significant damage via secreted toxins and the host immune response.

clozeText: Eradication of H. pylori is the primary treatment for {{c1::low-grade::grade}} MALToma.
extraNote: Antibiotics alone can lead to complete remission in many localized cases.

clozeText: PPIs in H. pylori therapy increase the {{c1::pH::parameter}}, which enhances the stability and activity of antibiotics like Amoxicillin.
extraNote: Higher pH also encourages H. pylori to enter a replicative state, making them more susceptible to antibiotics.

clozeText: {{c1::Serology::Diagnostic method}} for H. pylori cannot distinguish between a current active infection and a past treated infection.
extraNote: IgG antibodies persist for months to years after the bacteria are cleared.

clozeText: H. pylori is the most common cause of {{c1::Type B::classification}} chronic gastritis.
extraNote: Type A gastritis is autoimmune and involves the fundus/body.

clozeText: H. pylori infection is associated with an increased risk of {{c1::Iron deficiency::deficiency}} anemia.
extraNote: This is due to occult GI bleeding from ulcers and impaired iron absorption from the stomach.

clozeText: The {{c1::BabA::Virulence factor}} adhesin helps H. pylori bind to Lewis b blood group antigens on gastric epithelial cells.
extraNote: Adherence is crucial for the delivery of toxins like CagA into host cells.

clozeText: The combination of {{c1::Metronidazole::Antibiotic}} and alcohol can cause a disulfiram-like reaction in patients treated for H. pylori.
extraNote: This presents as flushing, nausea, and tachycardia due to acetaldehyde accumulation.

clozeText: H. pylori infection is typically acquired during {{c1::childhood::life stage}} via the fecal-oral or oral-oral route.
extraNote: Prevalence is higher in developing countries and low-socioeconomic status households.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is classically described as having a {{c1::comma or S-shape::shape}} that resembles "seagull wings."
extraNote: This characteristic morphology is seen on Gram stain as Gram-negative curved rods.

clozeText: Campylobacter is a {{c1::Gram-negative::Gram stain}} rod that is {{c2::oxidase::biochemical test}}-positive.
extraNote: The oxidase-positive status helps distinguish it from other Enterobacteriaceae.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni grows best at a temperature of {{c1::42°C::temperature}}.
extraNote: The mnemonic 'Campy likes the hot campfire' helps remember this thermophilic property.

clozeText: Campylobacter species are {{c1::microaerophilic::oxygen requirement}}, meaning they require low levels of oxygen for growth.
extraNote: They typically require approximately 5% oxygen and 10% carbon dioxide.

clozeText: The most common source of Campylobacter jejuni infection is the consumption of {{c1::undercooked poultry::food source}}.
extraNote: Contaminated water and unpasteurized milk are other significant sources of transmission.

clozeText: Exposure to {{c1::infected puppies::animal reservoir}} is a high-yield zoonotic source of Campylobacter transmission in children.
extraNote: Petting zoos or new household pets can be culprits for fecal-oral transmission.

clozeText: The primary clinical presentation of Campylobacter enteritis is {{c1::bloody::type}} diarrhea.
extraNote: It causes inflammatory diarrhea with fecal leukocytes and blood, often preceded by a prodrome of fever and headache.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is the most common antecedent infection for {{c1::Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)::neurological complication}}.
extraNote: GBS is an ascending paralysis caused by molecular mimicry between the bacterial LPS and peripheral nerve gangliosides.

clozeText: Guillain-Barré syndrome occurs after Campylobacter infection due to {{c1::molecular mimicry::mechanism}}.
extraNote: Antibodies against the Campylobacter lipooligosaccharide (LOS) cross-react with gangliosides like GM1 in the myelin.

clozeText: A post-infectious complication of Campylobacter associated with the HLA-B27 marker is {{c1::reactive arthritis::condition}}.
extraNote: This was formerly known as Reiter's syndrome and presents with the 'can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree' triad.

clozeText: Campylobacter motility is described as {{c1::darting::description}} motility.
extraNote: This is facilitated by a single polar flagellum at one or both ends.

clozeText: To isolate Campylobacter from stool, selective media such as {{c1::Skirrow's agar::medium}} or Campy-BAP is used.
extraNote: These media contain antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin, polymyxin, trimethoprim) to inhibit the growth of normal colonic flora.

clozeText: The drug of choice for severe or persistent Campylobacter jejuni infection is {{c1::azithromycin::drug (macrolide)}}.
extraNote: Fluoroquinolones were once the standard but resistance is now widespread.

clozeText: Campylobacter species are {{c1::catalase::biochemical test}}-positive.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from some other anaerobic or microaerophilic species.

clozeText: Campylobacter infection can cause severe abdominal pain that mimics {{c1::appendicitis::surgical condition}}.
extraNote: This is due to mesenteric adenitis or pseudoappendicitis similar to Yersinia enterocolitica.

clozeText: Unlike C. jejuni, {{c1::Campylobacter fetus::species}} is a common cause of systemic bacteremia in immunocompromised patients.
extraNote: C. fetus has a surface S-protein that prevents C3b binding, making it resistant to serum killing.

clozeText: The {{c1::S-protein::virulence factor}} of C. fetus allows it to inhibit opsonization and resist complement-mediated killing.
extraNote: This factor acts as a capsule-like structure for systemic survival.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a major cause of {{c1::inflammatory::classification}} diarrhea.
extraNote: It invades the lining of the small and large intestines, leading to the presence of PMNs in the stool.

clozeText: A high {{c1::infectious dose::threshold}} is generally required for Campylobacter infection because the organism is sensitive to {{c2::gastric acid::defense mechanism}}.
extraNote: Patients on PPIs are at higher risk due to reduced gastric acidity.

clozeText: The incubation period for Campylobacter gastroenteritis is typically {{c1::2 to 5 days::timeframe}}.
extraNote: This is longer than the incubation period for preformed toxins like S. aureus.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni contains {{c1::lipooligosaccharide (LOS)::toxin component}} in its outer membrane, which lacks the long O-antigen chains of LPS.
extraNote: LOS is the critical component involved in the molecular mimicry leading to GBS.

clozeText: The {{c1::O:19::serotype}} serotype of Campylobacter jejuni is most frequently associated with the development of Guillain-Barré Syndrome.
extraNote: Specific serotypes carry LOS structures that closely resemble human nerve gangliosides.

clozeText: In stool samples, Campylobacter can be visualized using {{c1::dark-field microscopy::technique}} to see its characteristic motility.
extraNote: The 'darting' motion is a classic board-exam descriptor.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is the leading cause of {{c1::bacterial::type}} gastroenteritis worldwide.
extraNote: It often surpasses Salmonella and Shigella in incidence in developed countries.

clozeText: Chronic infection with Campylobacter is rare, but carriage can occur in {{c1::biliary tract::anatomic site}} in rare cases.
extraNote: This is much less common than the biliary carriage seen with Salmonella Typhi.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is {{c1::urease-negative::test}}, which helps distinguish it from Helicobacter pylori.
extraNote: H. pylori is urease-positive to survive the acidic stomach environment.

clozeText: Most cases of Campylobacter enteritis are {{c1::self-limiting::prognosis}} and do not require antibiotics.
extraNote: Supportive care with fluid and electrolyte replacement is the mainstay of therapy.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni produces {{c1::cytolethal distending toxin (CDT)::toxin}}, which causes cell cycle arrest in host cells.
extraNote: This toxin contributes to the localized tissue damage and inflammation in the gut.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a {{c1::Gram-negative}} rod that is characteristically {{c2::comma- or S-shaped::shape}}.
extraNote: They are often described as having a "seagull wing" appearance on microscopy.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is {{c1::thermophilic::temperature preference}}, growing optimally at {{c2::42::degrees}}°C.
extraNote: This temperature preference helps in isolating it from other enteric pathogens that grow at 37°C. "Campy is hot."

clozeText: The preferred atmosphere for Campylobacter growth is {{c1::microaerophilic::oxygen requirement}}, requiring low levels of oxygen.
extraNote: Typically requires 5% O2 and 10% CO2 for optimal recovery in culture.

clozeText: On microscopy, Campylobacter exhibits a characteristic {{c1::"darting"::motility type}} motility.
extraNote: This motility is provided by a single polar flagellum, creating a corkscrew-like movement.

clozeText: Campylobacter is {{c1::oxidase::enzyme}} positive, which helps distinguish it from the Enterobacteriaceae family.
extraNote: Most enteric Gram-negative rods (like Salmonella/Shigella) are oxidase negative.

clozeText: The most common source of Campylobacter jejuni infection in humans is {{c1::poultry::animal reservoir}}.
extraNote: Contaminated, undercooked chicken is the leading vector for human transmission.

clozeText: Campylobacter can be transmitted through the consumption of {{c1::unpasteurized milk::food source}} or contact with {{c2::infected puppies::animal source}}.
extraNote: Fecal-oral transmission is the primary route, often involving pets or contaminated farm products.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a major cause of {{c1::bloody/inflammatory::diarrhea type}} diarrhea, especially in children and young adults.
extraNote: It is one of the "Big 3" bacterial causes of bloody stools alongside Salmonella and Shigella.

clozeText: Campylobacter infection may present with severe abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis, a condition known as {{c1::pseudoappendicitis::clinical syndrome}}.
extraNote: This is caused by mesenteric adenitis (inflammation of the lymph nodes in the mesentery).

clozeText: A high-yield neurologic complication of Campylobacter infection is {{c1::Guillain-Barré syndrome::syndrome}}.
extraNote: This is an ascending paralysis caused by molecular mimicry between the bacteria and human nerves.

clozeText: Guillain-Barré syndrome follows Campylobacter infection due to {{c1::molecular mimicry::mechanism}} between bacterial LPS and host {{c2::gangliosides::target}}.
extraNote: Cross-reacting antibodies attack the myelin of peripheral nerves.

clozeText: Following a Campylobacter infection, patients with the {{c1::HLA-B27::genetic marker}} serotype are at risk for developing {{c2::reactive arthritis::condition}}.
extraNote: This is part of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

clozeText: The antibiotic of choice for severe or persistent Campylobacter jejuni infections is {{c1::Azithromycin::drug name}}.
extraNote: Macrolides are the first-line treatment if antibiotics are indicated; otherwise, treatment is supportive.

clozeText: Resistance to {{c1::Fluoroquinolones::antibiotic class}} is increasing in Campylobacter due to their use in agricultural poultry.
extraNote: Ciprofloxacin was formerly used, but high resistance rates have shifted preference to Macrolides.

clozeText: In contrast to C. jejuni, {{c1::Campylobacter fetus::species}} is known for causing systemic infections and bacteremia.
extraNote: C. fetus is often resistant to the bactericidal activity of serum due to its S-protein capsule.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is {{c1::urease::enzyme}} negative, which helps differentiate it from Helicobacter pylori.
extraNote: Both are curved, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rods, but only H. pylori produces urease to survive gastric acid.

clozeText: The incubation period for Campylobacter enteritis is typically {{c1::2 to 5::days}} days.
extraNote: The onset is usually characterized by prodromal fever, headache, and myalgia followed by abdominal cramping.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni produces {{c1::cytolethal distending toxin (CDT)::toxin}}, which leads to host cell cycle arrest.
extraNote: CDT has DNase activity that causes double-strand breaks in host DNA.

clozeText: Stool examination in Campylobacter infection often shows the presence of {{c1::fecal leukocytes::finding}}.
extraNote: This indicates an invasive/inflammatory process rather than a purely toxigenic one.

clozeText: Campylobacter is one of the most common precursors to {{c1::Miller Fisher::variant}} syndrome, a variant of GBS.
extraNote: Characterized by the triad of ataxia, areflexia, and ophthalmoplegia.

clozeText: For patients with {{c1::hypogammaglobulinemia::immune defect}}, Campylobacter infections can be severe, recurrent, or lead to bacteremia.
extraNote: Humoral immunity is critical for clearing the organism from the GI tract.

clozeText: The Gram stain of Campylobacter may require longer exposure to the counterstain or the use of {{c1::carbol fuchsin}} to be visualized clearly.
extraNote: They stain weakly with standard safranin counterstain.

clozeText: Campylobacter {{c1::jejuni}} accounts for approximately 90% of human Campylobacter infections, while C. {{c2::coli}} accounts for most of the remainder.
extraNote: Both cause nearly identical clinical gastroenteritis.

clozeText: The infectious dose of Campylobacter is relatively {{c1::low::dose level}}, often requiring fewer than 1,000 organisms to cause disease.
extraNote: This is similar to Shigella and much lower than the dose required for Vibrio cholerae.

clozeText: Campylobacter-related diarrhea is often described as {{c1::steatorrhea-like::negative finding}}? No, it is usually watery followed by {{c2::bloody}} stools.
extraNote: It is an invasive infection of the intestinal mucosa of the colon and ileum.

clozeText: In the United States, the incidence of Campylobacter infection peaks during the {{c1::summer::season}} months.
extraNote: This seasonality is likely linked to increased poultry consumption and outdoor activities.

clozeText: Most Campylobacter infections are {{c1::self-limiting::prognosis}} and do not require antimicrobial therapy.
extraNote: Hydration and electrolyte replacement are the mainstays of treatment for simple enteritis.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci by degrading hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β-hemolysis}} on blood agar, unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron from hemoglobin, which is utilized for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: The major virulence factor in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc portion from binding to receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In the cell wall of staphylococci, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in S. aureus is encoded by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which produces an altered {{c2::PBP2a}}.
extraNote: PBP2a is a transpeptidase that retains its function but does not bind β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: The most common strain of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}, and it typically produces {{c2::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few strains of healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA) produce P-V leukocidin.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This resistance is often carried on a transposon found on a plasmid, similar to resistance in enterococci.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose::anatomical location}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized in the nose at any one time; chronic carriers have an increased risk of skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the NADPH oxidase system, making patients susceptible to catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which characterized by central necrosis and pus drainage.
extraNote: S. aureus causes disease both through toxin production and inducing pyogenic inflammation.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is distinguished from S. saprophyticus by being {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is resistant to novobiocin and is a common cause of UTIs.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This includes serious conditions like endocarditis and sepsis.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus, leading to desquamated skin.
extraNote: This is especially common in infants and neonates.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored}} crusts, can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a common superficial skin infection in children.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines, showing {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite being Gram-positive and lacking LPS.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90%}} of S. aureus strains contain plasmids that encode {{c2::β-lactamase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins, necessitating the use of β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is poorly immunogenic, and types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the majority (85%) of infections.
extraNote: The capsule's poor immunogenicity has historically hindered effective vaccine development.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and is frequently associated with {{c1::surgical-wound}} infections.
extraNote: It also commonly infects sites of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora and is a leading cause of infections on prosthetic heart valves and hips.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and does not produce Protein A.

clozeText: A predisposing factor for toxic shock syndrome is S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}}, which occurs in about 5% of women.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: Staphylococci typically appear as Gram-positive cocci in {{c1::grapelike clusters}} under the microscope.
extraNote: In contrast, streptococci typically form chains.

clozeText: Hand contact is a major mode of transmission for S. aureus, and {{c1::handwashing}} is the primary method to decrease transmission in hospitals.
extraNote: Colonization on the skin of hospital personnel is a major reservoir for HCA-MRSA.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections by Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia and impaired neutrophil function contribute to this susceptibility.

clozeText: {{c1::Phage typing}} of S. aureus strains for epidemiologic purposes is possible because of surface receptors, including teichoic acids.
extraNote: Specific staphylococcal bacteriophages bind to these receptors.

clozeText: Strains of S. aureus with {{c1::intermediate}} resistance to vancomycin are known as {{c2::VISA}}.
extraNote: Full resistance is categorized as VRSA.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicle for which S. aureus is the most common cause.
extraNote: It presents as multiple small pustules, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of bacterial {{c1::conjunctivitis}} in addition to its role in skin and soft tissue infections.
extraNote: It can also cause deep-seated infections like osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.

clozeText: Staphylococci are {{c1::catalase}}-positive, whereas streptococci are {{c1::catalase}}-negative.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into oxygen and water, helping bacteria survive oxidative killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in {{c1::chains}}.
extraNote: This morphological distinction is the first step in differentiating Gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: {{c1::S. aureus}} is distinguished from other staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c2::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: {{c1::MRSA (Methicillin-resistant S. aureus)}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of necrotizing fasciitis, pneumonia, and sepsis in immunocompetent patients.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is a(n) {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the leading cause of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs).

clozeText: Unlike coagulase-negative species, S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β (beta)}} hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain plasmids encoding {{c1::β-lactamase}}, which degrades many penicillins.
extraNote: Nafcillin or oxacillin are used to treat β-lactamase-producing (MSSA) strains.

clozeText: MRSA resistance is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a maintains transpeptidase function but does not bind β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Almost all strains of {{c1::CA-MRSA (Community-Acquired)}} produce {{c2::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin relatively rare in HCA-MRSA.
extraNote: The most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States is USA300.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance (VRSA) occurs when the bacteria substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} is a virulence factor that prevents phagocytosis by binding the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on neutrophils from binding the antibody.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate the {{c2::adherence}} of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by triggering the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mechanism is analogous to the action of Gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}, with a colonization rate of ~{{c2::30}}%.
extraNote: Chronic carriers are at increased risk for developing skin infections.

clozeText: Vaginal colonization with S. aureus in 5% of women predisposes them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are highly susceptible to S. aureus because the organism is {{c2::catalase}}-positive.
extraNote: CGD neutrophils lack the oxidative burst to kill catalase-producing organisms.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common member of skin flora and a frequent cause of {{c2::prosthetic valve/hip}} infections.
extraNote: It is notably novobiocin-sensitive and coagulase-negative.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a common cause of UTIs and is distinguished by being {{c2::novobiocin}}-resistant.
extraNote: It is the second most common cause of community-acquired UTIs in young women.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, which presents as small pustules on the chin and neck.
extraNote: It can also lead to more severe lesions like furuncles and carbuncles.

clozeText: Impetigo presents as vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust and is caused by S. aureus or {{c2::S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a desquamating disease of infants caused by an S. aureus {{c2::exotoxin}}.
extraNote: The toxin causes cleavage of the epidermis.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause clinical findings of {{c1::septic shock}} despite lacking endotoxin because its {{c2::peptidoglycan}} stimulates cytokine production.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan can also activate the complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: The capsule of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic, but types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the majority of human infections.
extraNote: There are 11 known serotypes of the polysaccharide capsule.

clozeText: In intravenous drug users, S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::endocarditis}}.
extraNote: It often involves the right-sided valves (tricuspid).

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may potentially be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It primarily affects children and involves medium-vessel vasculitis.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: These are pyogenic infections often requiring long-term antibiotics and drainage.

clozeText: The most common MRSA strain currently circulating in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: It is frequently associated with skin and soft tissue infections in the community.

clozeText: Bacteria that produce {{c1::catalase}} can survive within neutrophils by neutralizing {{c2::hydrogen peroxide}}.
extraNote: This is a key differentiator between staphylococci and streptococci.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by their ability to produce {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This test is the primary biochemical marker used to distinguish the two medically important genera of gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: The classic lesion of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} pyogenic infection is an abscess, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}, an enzyme that activates prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: Coagulase causes plasma to clot by converting fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: S. aureus cell walls contain {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils.
extraNote: By occupying the Fc portion, the antibody cannot bind to Fc receptors on macrophages or neutrophils.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin/methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: The primary site of S. aureus colonization in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, with approximately 30% of the population being chronic carriers.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock via IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids act similarly to endotoxin by stimulating cytokine release from macrophages.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves a transposon that encodes enzymes substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This same resistance cassette is found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and produces {{c2::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis allows the bacteria to recover iron from hemoglobin for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust, can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: S. aureus is also the most common cause of folliculitis, a localized infection of the hair follicles.

clozeText: Most community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, whereas relatively few hospital-acquired strains do.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: S. aureus causes Scalded Skin Syndrome via the production of an {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} that leads to desquamation.
extraNote: This typically presents as widespread areas of rolled-up skin in infants.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common member of skin flora that typically infects prosthetic heart valves and artificial joints.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. saprophyticus by its sensitivity to Novobiocin.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections and is resistant to {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: A quick mnemonic is 'Saprophyticus is Second' (cause of UTIs in young women) and 'Resistant' to Novobiocin.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill catalase-positive bacteria.
extraNote: Catalase degrades the small amount of hydrogen peroxide produced by the host cells, neutralizing the oxidative burst.

clozeText: S. aureus peptidoglycan has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, meaning it can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines even though the bacteria lack true endotoxin.
extraNote: This explains the induction of septic shock and the complement/coagulation cascades.

clozeText: Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) is associated with S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}}, which occurs in approximately 5% of women.
extraNote: This syndrome is mediated by TSS toxin-1 (TSST-1), a superantigen.

clozeText: The capsule of S. aureus is composed of {{c1::polysaccharide}} and is poorly immunogenic, with serotypes {{c2::5 and 8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The poor immunogenicity of the capsule has hindered vaccine development.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users::patient group}}.
extraNote: Common infections include endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Epidemiologic typing of S. aureus strains can be performed using {{c1::phage typing}}, which utilizes receptors made of teichoic acids.
extraNote: Surface receptors for specific bacteriophages allow for tracking of infection outbreaks.

clozeText: Approximately 90% of S. aureus strains are resistant to penicillin G because they possess {{c1::plasmids}} encoding {{c2::beta-lactamase}}.
extraNote: Nafcillin is a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin used to treat these strains.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: It is a vasculitis that primarily affects young children.

clozeText: Predisposing factors for S. aureus infection include diabetes and the presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}} such as sutures or catheters.
extraNote: Foreign bodies provide a surface for biofilm formation and protective niches for the bacteria.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: Both are nonmotile, non-spore-forming, gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus, making {{c1::handwashing}} the most effective prevention measure.
extraNote: Transmission is especially common between hospital personnel and patients.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired}} pneumonia and septicemia, as well as surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a significant cause of infections at cardiac pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: The enzyme coagulase catalyzes the activation of {{c1::fibrinogen}} to form {{c2::fibrin}}.
extraNote: This occurs after coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin.

clozeText: Staphylococci are {{c1::gram-positive}} cocci that are both nonmotile and do not form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: Their cell wall is thick and holds the crystal violet stain.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses, pneumonia, and sepsis in intravenous drug users.
extraNote: MRSA is also an important cause of necrotizing fasciitis in immunocompetent patients.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive cocci and are nonmotile and non-spore-forming.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}, which activates prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: Thrombin then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: In contrast to coagulase-negative species, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol::metabolic process}} and causes hemolysis of red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: The virulence factor {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.
extraNote: This is the major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus but is absent in coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids::cell wall component}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while lipoteichoic acids can induce septic shock.
extraNote: Septic shock is induced via the release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: Full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan structure.
extraNote: This resistance cassette is often carried on a transposon on a plasmid, similar to vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a factor rarely found in healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA).
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of developing S. aureus skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the ability to produce reactive oxygen species to kill catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause septic shock despite lacking endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} has endotoxin-like properties that stimulate cytokine production.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan can activate both the complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which characterized by central necrosis and pus drainage.
extraNote: Organisms may also disseminate from these local sites via the bloodstream.

clozeText: Impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust and can be caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a common skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI) in children.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is uniquely {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin, whereas Staphylococcus saprophyticus is resistant.
extraNote: This lab test is crucial for differentiating coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::saprophyticus}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus, leading to widespread desquamation.
extraNote: This is typically seen in infants and young children.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, predisposing them to Toxic Shock Syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is associated with superantigen-mediated cytokine release.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: Folliculitis can progress to furuncles or boils if not managed.

clozeText: The major predisposing metabolic factor for S. aureus infections is {{c1::diabetes}}.
extraNote: Other factors include reduced humoral immunity or foreign bodies like catheters.

clozeText: S. aureus capsule serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} are responsible for approximately 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The microcapsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: The {{c1::USA300}} strain is currently the most common strain of MRSA identified in the United States.
extraNote: It is associated with aggressive community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Epidemiologic "phage typing" of S. aureus is possible because specific {{c1::teichoic acids}} serve as receptors for bacteriophages.
extraNote: This method is used to track outbreaks by identifying specific staphylococcal strains.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids}} that encode beta-lactamase, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: These strains remain sensitive to beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin unless they are MRSA.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora but can cause infections of {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and hips.
extraNote: Its ability to form biofilms on foreign bodies is a key pathogenic mechanism.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: It is a pediatric vasculitis often presenting with fever and systemic inflammation.

clozeText: Iron required for S. aureus growth is obtained by recovering iron from {{c1::hemoglobin}} after red blood cell lysis.
extraNote: This iron is essential for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes used in energy production.

clozeText: Chlamydia is a(n) {{c1::obligate intracellular}} organism because it cannot synthesize its own ATP.
extraNote: This is why Chlamydia cannot be grown on standard agar and requires cell cultures (e.g., McCoy cells).

clozeText: The {{c1::Elementary body::Form?}} is the small, dense, infectious form of Chlamydia that enters the cell via endocytosis.
extraNote: EB = Enters / Extracellular / Infectious.

clozeText: The {{c1::Reticulate body::Form?}} is the metabolically active, replicating form of Chlamydia that divides by binary fission.
extraNote: RB = Replicates / Reproduction.
