extraNote: Relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains produce this specific toxin.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan layer.
extraNote: The cassette of genes for this resistance is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and works by binding to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis because the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages cannot bind the occupied antibody.

clozeText: In the cell wall, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} induce septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids trigger the release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages and activate complement, possessing {{c2::endotoxin-like}} properties.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The {{c1::nose (nares)}} is the primary reservoir for S. aureus, with approximately {{c2::30::%}} of humans colonized at any time.
extraNote: Chronic nasal carriers have an increased risk of developing skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, allowing it to neutralize the minimal H2O2 produced by CGD neutrophils.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and septic arthritis.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5::%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is often associated with the use of highly absorbent tampons.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common cause of infections involving prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora and is coagulase-negative.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, while S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This biochemical test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections, especially in young women.
extraNote: Unlike S. aureus, it does not produce coagulase and does not ferment mannitol.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a condition in infants caused by an exotoxin that results in widespread {{c2::desquamation}}.
extraNote: The toxin causes the top layers of the skin to roll up and peel off.

clozeText: Impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a superficial skin infection most common in children.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicles, most commonly caused by {{c2::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: It presents as multiple small pustules, often on the chin, neck, or areas with frequent friction.

clozeText: In the laboratory, {{c1::S. aureus}} usually ferments {{c2::mannitol}}, whereas coagulase-negative species do not.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used for S. aureus.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is frequently involved in infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: The capsule of S. aureus is poorly {{c1::immunogenic}}, making the development of an effective vaccine difficult.
extraNote: Types 5 and 8 are responsible for 85% of clinical infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is found in S. aureus, but is {{c2::absent}} in coagulase-negative staphylococci.
extraNote: This protein is a key diagnostic and virulence marker for S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::disease}}, which is a pediatric systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology.
extraNote: Specific strains of S. aureus may play a role in its development.

clozeText: Effective treatment for non-MRSA S. aureus infections usually involves {{c1::beta-lactamase-resistant}} penicillins such as {{c2::nafcillin}}.
extraNote: Over 90% of S. aureus strains produce beta-lactamase encoded on plasmids.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus is a gram-{{c1::positive}} rod that is known for its ability to form {{c2::spores}}.
extraNote: Unlike B. anthracis, B. cereus is motile and lacks a capsule.

clozeText: The emetic type of Bacillus cereus food poisoning is classically associated with the consumption of {{c1::reheated rice}}.
extraNote: Commonly known as 'fried rice syndrome'; spores survive initial boiling and germinate when rice is left at room temperature.

clozeText: The emetic toxin produced by B. cereus is called {{c1::cereulide}}, which is {{c2::heat-stable}}.
extraNote: Because the toxin is preformed and heat-stable, reheating the food does not prevent the illness.

clozeText: The emetic form of B. cereus infection has a short incubation period of {{c1::1 to 5}} hours.
extraNote: This rapid onset resembles food poisoning caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

clozeText: The diarrheal form of B. cereus is caused by a {{c1::heat-labile}} enterotoxin.
extraNote: The enterotoxin is produced in vivo after the ingestion of contaminated meat, vegetables, or sauces.

clozeText: The incubation period for the diarrheal form of B. cereus is {{c1::8 to 16::range}} hours.
extraNote: The longer incubation is required for the bacteria to germinate and produce toxin within the gut.

clozeText: The mechanism of the B. cereus diarrheal enterotoxin involves increasing {{c1::cAMP}} levels.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the heat-labile toxin of ETEC and Cholera toxin, leading to watery diarrhea.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus is a leading cause of severe {{c1::endophthalmitis}} following penetrating eye trauma with soil-contaminated objects.
extraNote: This is a surgical emergency and can lead to rapid loss of vision within 24 hours.

clozeText: On blood agar, Bacillus cereus typically demonstrates {{c1::beta}}-hemolysis.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Bacillus anthracis, which is non-hemolytic (gamma-hemolysis).

clozeText: Unlike Bacillus anthracis, Bacillus cereus is {{c1::motile::motility status}}.
extraNote: Motility is a key diagnostic feature used to differentiate B. cereus from the non-motile B. anthracis.

clozeText: The diarrheal form of B. cereus poisoning is most commonly associated with {{c1::meats or vegetables}}.
extraNote: Unlike the emetic form which is associated with starch/rice.

clozeText: B. cereus produces the enzyme {{c1::lecithinase}}, which can be detected on egg yolk agar.
extraNote: The production of lecithinase results in an opaque zone around the colonies.

clozeText: Most strains of B. cereus are resistant to {{c1::penicillins}} because they produce {{c2::beta-lactamase}}.
extraNote: Vancomycin or clindamycin are typically used for systemic or ocular infections.

clozeText: The primary clinical symptom of the emetic form of B. cereus is {{c1::vomiting}}, whereas the diarrheal form presents with watery diarrhea and {{c2::cramps}}.
extraNote: The emetic form is mediated by a preformed toxin; the diarrheal form is mediated by toxin produced in the gut.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus is a {{c1::facultative anaerobe}}.
extraNote: It can grow in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, though it prefers aerobic environments.

clozeText: The emetic toxin (cereulide) is a {{c1::ionophore::biochemical class}} that is resistant to proteolysis and low pH.
extraNote: Its stability allows it to pass through the stomach acid without being degraded.

clozeText: B. cereus spores are highly resistant to {{c1::desiccation}} and heat.
extraNote: They are ubiquitous in the soil and frequently contaminate raw agricultural products.

clozeText: Diagnosis of B. cereus food poisoning is usually {{c1::clinical}}.
extraNote: While the organism can be cultured from food, it is rarely cultured from patient stool due to the transient nature of the illness.

clozeText: In intravenous drug users, B. cereus can rarely cause {{c1::endocarditis}} or sepsis.
extraNote: The spores can contaminate drug paraphernalia or the drugs themselves.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating B. cereus endophthalmitis is often {{c1::vancomycin}} combined with an aminoglycoside.
extraNote: Aggressive treatment is required due to the rapid progression of the infection.

clozeText: The diarrheal toxin of B. cereus is similar in action to the toxin produced by {{c1::Clostridium perfringens}}.
extraNote: Both cause watery diarrhea with a similar incubation period (8-16 hours).

clozeText: B. cereus colonies on agar are often described as having a {{c1::frosted glass}} appearance.
extraNote: They are large, grayish-white, and granular.

clozeText: The emetic toxin of B. cereus acts by stimulating the {{c1::vagus}} nerve.
extraNote: This triggers the vomiting center in the brain, leading to rapid emesis.

clozeText: Bacillus cereus does not possess a {{c1::capsule}}, which is a major virulence factor for B. anthracis.
extraNote: B. anthracis has a unique polypeptide capsule (D-glutamate).

clozeText: Treatment for B. cereus food poisoning is primarily {{c1::supportive}}.
extraNote: Antibiotics are not indicated for food poisoning as the symptoms are toxin-mediated and self-limiting.

clozeText: One of the reasons B. cereus can cause serious wound infections is the production of {{c1::collagenases}} and proteases.
extraNote: These enzymes contribute to tissue destruction and spread of the organism.

clozeText: B. cereus is widely distributed in the {{c1::soil}}, which serves as its primary reservoir.
extraNote: This allows for easy contamination of various food products and traumatic wounds.

clozeText: In the laboratory, B. cereus can be differentiated from other Bacillus species by its sensitivity to {{c1::bacteriophages}} and biochemical profiles.
extraNote: However, beta-hemolysis and motility are the most common rapid identifiers in clinical labs.

clozeText: Staphylococci are gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci are arranged in chains.
extraNote: This microscopic arrangement is a key morphological differentiator in the Gram stain of pus or culture.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into oxygen and water.
extraNote: Catalase-positive organisms can survive the oxidative burst (H2O2) within neutrophils.

clozeText: The primary biochemical test used to distinguish S. aureus from other staphylococci is the {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}} test.
extraNote: S. aureus is coagulase-positive, while S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS).

clozeText: Coagulase activates {{c1::prothrombin}} to form {{c2::thrombin}}, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.
extraNote: The fibrin clot may protect the bacteria from phagocytosis and isolate the infection site (abscess).

clozeText: S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar, distinguishing it from CoNS.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar (MSA) is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to recover {{c2::iron}} from hemoglobin for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth during human infection.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids}} that encode {{c2::β-lactamase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins like penicillin G, necessitating the use of beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins (e.g., nafcillin).

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a functions as a transpeptidase but has low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) typically produces {{c1::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}, a toxin less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursors.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a cell wall component that binds the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, it prevents the antibody from properly orienting to bind to Fc receptors on macrophages/neutrophils.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the {{c2::adherence}} of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Adherence is the crucial first step in colonization and infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}}.
extraNote: This triggers a systemic inflammatory response similar to the endotoxin (LPS) of gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The S. aureus polysaccharide capsule is categorized into 11 serotypes, with types {{c1::5 and 8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: S. aureus peptidoglycan possesses {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, including the ability to activate the {{c2::complement and coagulation}} cascades.
extraNote: This allows S. aureus to cause septic shock even though it lacks true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately {{c2::30::%}} of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: In women, S. aureus colonization in the {{c1::vagina}} (found in 5% of women) predisposes to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: Vaginal colonization is the source of the TSST-1 toxin-producing strains during menses.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections due to a defect in {{c2::neutrophil killing::mechanism}}.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the NADPH oxidase required to generate reactive oxygen species.

clozeText: The hallmark lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which features central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Abscesses must often be drained (I&D) in addition to antibiotic treatment.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} and is characterized by large areas of {{c2::desquamated::peeling}} skin.
extraNote: This condition typically affects infants and young children.

clozeText: Impetigo is characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust and can be caused by S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: Commonly seen on the chin, neck, and areas with hair.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: Frequently leads to right-sided endocarditis (tricuspid valve) and skin abscesses.

clozeText: {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is a common cause of infections associated with {{c2::prosthetic}} heart valves and hip joints.
extraNote: It produces a biofilm (slime layer) that allows it to adhere to plastic and metal surfaces.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in {{c2::young women}}.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. epidermidis by being resistant to novobiocin.

clozeText: In the laboratory, {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is sensitive to novobiocin, while {{c2::S. saprophyticus}} is resistant.
extraNote: Novobiocin resistance is the standard test to identify S. saprophyticus in urine cultures.

clozeText: S. aureus can be identified for epidemiologic purposes via {{c1::phage typing}}, which utilizes surface receptors including {{c2::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: Bacteriophages bind to specific receptors to infect the bacterial strain.

clozeText: Diabetes and the presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}} (e.g., sutures, catheters) are major predisposing factors for {{c2::S. aureus}} infections.
extraNote: Foreign bodies provide a surface for colonization and reduce the number of bacteria needed to initiate an infection.

clozeText: Vibrio cholerae is a {{c1::Gram-negative::stain}}, {{c2::comma-shaped::morphology}} rod.
extraNote: Its morphology is often described as a 'curved rod' and it possesses a single polar flagellum.

clozeText: V. cholerae is distinguished from the Enterobacteriaceae family (like E. coli) because it is {{c1::oxidase::biochemical test}} positive.
extraNote: All Vibrio species are oxidase positive, which is a key laboratory differentiator from other Gram-negative enteric rods.

clozeText: The classic motility of V. cholerae on darkfield microscopy is described as "{{c1::shooting star::description}}" motility.
extraNote: This rapid motility is due to its single polar flagellum.

clozeText: V. cholerae grows on {{c1::TCBS (Thiosulfate Citrate Bile salts Sucrose)::agar name}} agar, producing {{c2::yellow::color}} colonies.
extraNote: The yellow color indicates sucrose fermentation, which helps differentiate V. cholerae from other Vibrio species.

clozeText: V. cholerae is highly sensitive to {{c1::stomach acid::environment}}, meaning it requires a {{c2::large::magnitude}} infectious dose.
extraNote: Conditions that decrease gastric acidity (e.g., PPI use, gastrectomy) significantly lower the infectious dose required for disease.

clozeText: The selective medium TCBS used for Vibrio has an {{c1::alkaline::pH}} pH, which inhibits the growth of most other intestinal flora.
extraNote: V. cholerae is famously 'acid-labile' but 'alkali-tolerant'.

clozeText: The major virulence factor of V. cholerae is an AB exotoxin that {{c1::ADP-ribosylates::mechanism}} the {{c2::Gs alpha::target protein}} subunit.
extraNote: This leads to permanent activation of the Gs protein, locking it in the 'on' position.

clozeText: Activation of the Gs protein by cholera toxin leads to the overproduction of {{c1::cAMP::second messenger}} by adenylate cyclase.
extraNote: Increased cAMP levels in enterocytes lead to the massive secretion of electrolytes and water into the intestinal lumen.

clozeText: Cholera toxin-induced cAMP elevation opens {{c1::CFTR::channel name}} chloride channels, leading to the secretion of Cl-, Na+, and H2O.
extraNote: This is the same channel mutated in cystic fibrosis; carriers of the CF mutation may have some protection against cholera.

clozeText: The characteristic diarrhea of V. cholerae is described as "{{c1::rice-water::appearance}}" stool.
extraNote: The stool is watery and contains mucus flecks, but no blood or inflammatory cells.

clozeText: V. cholerae is a {{c1::non-invasive::pathogenesis type}} organism, meaning it does not cause mucosal inflammation or fever.
extraNote: Because it stays in the lumen and does not invade, the stool lacks white blood cells (WBCs) and blood.

clozeText: The genes for cholera toxin are encoded by the {{c1::CTX bacteriophage::genetic source}} via lysogenic conversion.
extraNote: The phage utilizes the toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP) as its receptor to enter the bacterium.

clozeText: Adherence of V. cholerae to the intestinal mucosa is mediated by the {{c1::toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP)::structure}}.
extraNote: Without this pilus, the organism cannot colonize the gut and is washed away by peristalsis.

clozeText: The primary and most essential treatment for cholera is {{c1::oral rehydration therapy (ORS)::treatment}}.
extraNote: Antibiotics (e.g., doxycycline) can shorten the duration but are secondary to aggressive fluid replacement.

clozeText: Oral rehydration salts must contain {{c1::glucose::supplement}} to facilitate the sodium-glucose cotransporter in the gut.
extraNote: The SGLT-1 transporter remains functional during cholera infection, allowing for the absorption of sodium and water even during high secretory states.

clozeText: The two main serogroups of V. cholerae that cause epidemic disease are {{c1::O1 and O139::serotypes}}.
extraNote: Other 'non-O1/non-O139' strains typically cause milder, sporadic cases of diarrhea.

clozeText: The B subunit of cholera toxin binds to the {{c1::GM1 ganglioside::receptor}} receptor on enterocytes.
extraNote: This binding allows the A (Active) subunit to enter the cell and initiate ADP-ribosylation.

clozeText: Unlike V. cholerae, the organism {{c1::Vibrio parahaemolyticus::organism}} is associated with consuming raw seafood and causes watery diarrhea.
extraNote: It is common in Japan and coastal areas and is often associated with raw oysters or sushi.

clozeText: {{c1::Vibrio vulnificus::organism}} is a halophilic Vibrio that causes severe cellulitis or sepsis, particularly in patients with {{c2::liver disease::comorbidity}}.
extraNote: Patients with cirrhosis or iron overload (hemochromatosis) are at high risk for life-threatening V. vulnificus infections after exposure to seawater.

clozeText: Vibrio species are {{c1::halophilic::environmental property}}, meaning they prefer or require saline environments for growth.
extraNote: They are commonly found in estuarine and marine environments (brackish water).

clozeText: Patients with severe cholera frequently develop metabolic {{c1::acidosis::acid-base status}} due to the loss of {{c2::bicarbonate::ion}} in the stool.
extraNote: Cholera stool also contains high concentrations of potassium (K+), leading to hypokalemia.

clozeText: The major cause of death in untreated cholera is {{c1::hypovolemic shock::complication}}.
extraNote: Fluid loss can exceed 1 liter per hour, leading to rapid cardiovascular collapse.

clozeText: The {{c1::El Tor::biotype}} biotype of V. cholerae O1 is responsible for the current (7th) pandemic and survives longer in the environment.
extraNote: It is generally more robust but causes a higher ratio of asymptomatic carriers compared to the classical biotype.

clozeText: In the laboratory, V. cholerae is known to ferment {{c1::sucrose::sugar}}, but it does NOT ferment {{c2::lactose::sugar}}.
extraNote: The sucrose fermentation is the basis for the yellow color on TCBS agar.

clozeText: Cholera is primarily transmitted via the {{c1::fecal-oral::route}} route, often through contaminated water supplies.
extraNote: Epidemics are common in areas with poor sanitation or following natural disasters.

clozeText: The cholera toxin A subunit possesses {{c1::ADP-ribosyltransferase::enzymatic activity}} activity.
extraNote: It transfers an ADP-ribose group from NAD to the Gs alpha protein.

clozeText: Detection of V. cholerae in stool can be performed using {{c1::darkfield::microscopy type}} microscopy to observe its rapid motility.
extraNote: Adding specific antiserum will stop the motility, a process known as the 'immobilization test'.

clozeText: The infectious dose for V. cholerae is approximately {{c1::10^8::number}} organisms, which is much higher than for Shigella.
extraNote: This high dose is necessary because the organism is extremely sensitive to the acidic pH of the stomach.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant {{c1::S. aureus (MRSA)}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.
extraNote: MRSA is also a significant cause of pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis, and sepsis.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the most common cause of infections in users of intravenous drugs.
extraNote: This includes endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, protecting the bacteria from oxidative killing in neutrophils.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: Hemolysis of red cells by S. aureus serves as a source of {{c1::iron}} required for bacterial growth.
extraNote: Iron is used in the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes for energy production.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::̢β-lactamase}} is encoded on plasmids in more than 90% of S. aureus strains.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades many penicillins, necessitating the use of ̢β-lactamase-resistant drugs like nafcillin.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is caused by altered {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}.
extraNote: The altered PBP, specifically PBP2a, has transpeptidase activity but does not bind ̢β-lactams.

clozeText: The {{c1::mecA}} gene on the bacterial chromosome encodes the altered PBP2a in MRSA.
extraNote: This gene is the molecular basis for methicillin resistance.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains produce this toxin.

clozeText: Full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) in S. aureus involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding its target.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major cell wall component of S. aureus that binds the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis because the Fc portion is not available to bind to receptors on macrophages and neutrophils.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of S. aureus to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the receptors for specific bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: This mechanism mimics the action of endotoxin found in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus has endotoxin-like properties and can activate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock without having true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized at any given time.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill bacteria using oxidative bursts.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis.
extraNote: These lesions often drain pus to the outside, as seen in furuncles or boils.

clozeText: {{c1::Foreign bodies}}, such as sutures and intravenous catheters, are major predisposing factors for S. aureus infection.
extraNote: These surfaces facilitate biofilm formation and bacterial persistence.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin and results in widespread desquamation in infants.
extraNote: The skin appears "rolled up" or detached.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicle and is most commonly caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: It presents as multiple small pustules, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: {{c1::Impetigo}} is characterized by vesicles that break to form a "honey-colored" crust.
extraNote: It can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is associated with superantigen activity.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major systemic predisposing factor for S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Other factors include reduced humoral immunity or low neutrophil counts.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is sensitive to {{c1::novobiocin}}, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.
extraNote: This biochemical test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: Hand contact is a primary mode of transmission for S. aureus, and {{c1::handwashing}} significantly decreases its spread.
extraNote: Hospital personnel are common carriers.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::bacterial conjunctivitis}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and septicemia.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a Gram-negative rod that is characteristically {{c1::comma or S-shaped}}.
extraNote: This morphology is often described as having a 'seagull wing' appearance when two cells are joined.

clozeText: C. jejuni displays a characteristic {{c1::corkscrew}} motility due to the presence of a single polar flagellum.
extraNote: This darting motility is a key diagnostic feature in fresh stool samples.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is uniquely {{c1::thermophilic}}, growing best at a temperature of {{c2::42}}°C.
extraNote: This adaptation reflects its primary reservoir in birds, which have higher body temperatures.

clozeText: To isolate Campylobacter, a selective medium such as {{c1::Skirrow's agar}} or Campy-BAP is used.
extraNote: These media contain antibiotics like Vancomycin, Polymyxin B, and Trimethoprim to inhibit competing flora.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a {{c1::microaerophilic}} organism, requiring low oxygen levels (5%) for growth.
extraNote: It is also capnophilic, preferring increased CO2 levels.

clozeText: The most common source of human infection with C. jejuni is the consumption of contaminated {{c1::poultry}}.
extraNote: Undercooked chicken is the classic USMLE scenario.

clozeText: Transmission of Campylobacter can occur through the consumption of {{c1::unpasteurized milk}} or contaminated water.
extraNote: Outbreaks are frequently linked to raw milk consumption on farms.

clozeText: Infected {{c1::puppies or kittens}} are a significant zoonotic source of Campylobacter, especially in domestic settings.
extraNote: This is a frequent 'distractor' or secondary hint in clinical vignettes.

clozeText: C. jejuni is a leading cause of {{c1::bloody}} diarrhea (hematochezia), especially in children and young adults.
extraNote: The diarrhea typically begins as watery but often progresses to bloody/inflammatory.

clozeText: Campylobacter infection can cause right lower quadrant pain that mimics {{c1::appendicitis::condition}}.
extraNote: This is known as 'pseudoappendicitis,' also seen with Yersinia enterocolitica.

clozeText: The most serious long-term complication of C. jejuni infection is {{c1::Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)}}.
extraNote: It is the most common antecedent infection for GBS, an ascending paralysis.

clozeText: Guillain-Barré Syndrome following Campylobacter infection is caused by {{c1::molecular mimicry}} between bacterial antigens and human nerves.
extraNote: Specifically, the bacterial lipooligosaccharide (LOS) mimics human gangliosides.

clozeText: In GBS triggered by C. jejuni, antibodies cross-react with {{c1::gangliosides (e.g., GM1)}} in the peripheral myelin.
extraNote: This leads to immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves.

clozeText: Another autoimmune complication associated with C. jejuni is {{c1::reactive arthritis}} (formerly Reiter syndrome).
extraNote: This often occurs in individuals who are HLA-B27 positive.

clozeText: Biochemically, Campylobacter jejuni is oxidase-{{c1::positive}} and catalase-{{c2::positive}}.
extraNote: Oxidase positivity distinguishes it from many other enteric Gram-negative rods (Enterobacteriaceae).

clozeText: C. jejuni can be distinguished from other Campylobacter species by its ability to {{c1::hydrolyze hippurate}}.
extraNote: C. jejuni is hippurate-positive, whereas C. coli is usually hippurate-negative.

clozeText: Unlike Helicobacter pylori, Campylobacter jejuni is urease-{{c1::negative}}.
extraNote: This is a critical biochemical differentiator between these two curved Gram-negative rods.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni causes inflammatory diarrhea by {{c1::invading}} the intestinal mucosa of the ileum and colon.
extraNote: This invasion triggers an intense inflammatory response, resulting in fecal leukocytes.

clozeText: The drug of choice for severe or persistent Campylobacter enteritis is a {{c1::macrolide (e.g., Azithromycin)}}.
extraNote: Erythromycin was historically used; fluoroquinolones are becoming less effective due to resistance.

clozeText: Campylobacter jejuni is a major cause of {{c1::fecal leukocytes}} and red blood cells in stool exams.
extraNote: Reflects the invasive, inflammatory nature of the infection.

clozeText: The primary virulence factor responsible for GBS molecular mimicry is the bacterial {{c1::lipooligosaccharide (LOS)}}.
extraNote: The LOS structure is similar to the GM1 ganglioside on human axons.

clozeText: C. jejuni is the leading cause of {{c1::bacterial}} gastroenteritis in the United States.
extraNote: It often outnumbers Salmonella and Shigella cases combined.

clozeText: Campylobacter is relatively sensitive to {{c1::gastric acid}}, so a large inoculum is typically required to cause disease.
extraNote: Conditions that decrease stomach acidity (like PPIs) may lower the infectious dose.

clozeText: Campylobacter cells possess {{c1::polar}} flagella, which are essential for navigating the thick mucus of the intestine.
extraNote: Loss of the flagellum significantly attenuates virulence.

clozeText: The incubation period for Campylobacter jejuni is typically {{c1::2 to 5}} days.
extraNote: This is longer than many preformed toxin-mediated food poisonings (e.g., S. aureus or B. cereus).

clozeText: In Gram stains of Campylobacter, the appearance of '{{c1::seagull}}' shapes is due to the attachment of two organisms at their ends.
extraNote: Useful mnemonic: Seagulls fly over 'Camp'y-lobacter.

clozeText: C. jejuni colonizes the {{c1::jejunum}} (as the name implies), ileum, and colon.
extraNote: It targets the lower small intestine and large intestine primarily.

clozeText: Bacteremia from C. jejuni is {{c1::rare}} but can occur in immunocompromised patients.
extraNote: C. fetus is much more commonly associated with systemic bacteremia than C. jejuni.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States.
extraNote: MRSA is also a leading cause of necrotizing fasciitis, pneumonia, and sepsis in immunocompetent individuals.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades {{c2::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}}.
extraNote: Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the oxidative burst (killing effect of H2O2) within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and exhibits {{c2::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron, which is recovered from hemoglobin and used for cytochrome synthesis.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess plasmids encoding {{c1::beta-lactamase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades many penicillins, necessitating the use of beta-lactamase-resistant agents like nafcillin.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in S. aureus is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) almost always produces {{c1::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}, a toxin less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: This toxin is associated with severe skin infections and necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) acquires resistance by substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in its peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This modification is carried on a transposon, typically acquired from enterococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major S. aureus cell wall protein that binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids induce the release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for Staphylococcus aureus is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic nasal carriers, which increases their risk for autoinoculation and skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections because the organism is {{c2::catalase-positive}}.
extraNote: In CGD, neutrophils cannot produce H2O2; catalase-positive organisms further deplete any residual peroxide.

clozeText: S. aureus causes septic shock via its {{c1::peptidoglycan}}, which has {{c2::endotoxin-like}} properties.
extraNote: Though it lacks true endotoxin (LPS), the peptidoglycan can activate the complement and coagulation cascades and stimulate cytokine release.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of an S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: These lesions typically undergo central necrosis and drain pus.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This includes serious conditions such as right-sided endocarditis.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to recurrent and severe infections by Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Poor glycemic control impairs neutrophil function and promotes bacterial growth.

clozeText: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} that leads to widespread epidermal desquamation.
extraNote: The toxin cleaves desmoglein in the desmosomes of the skin.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can also be caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, which increases the risk of {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by TSST-1, which acts as a superantigen.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: Both are Gram-positive cocci, but their arrangement reflects their division planes.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a coagulase-negative staph that is typically {{c2::sensitive}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: It is a common cause of infections on prosthetic heart valves and orthopedic joints.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a coagulase-negative staph that is typically {{c2::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: It is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: It is often the first organism suspected in acute hematogenous osteomyelitis.

clozeText: Epidemiologic typing of S. aureus strains can be performed using {{c1::phage typing}}, which utilizes surface receptors including teichoic acids.
extraNote: This is useful for tracking outbreaks in hospital settings.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is composed of {{c1::polysaccharide}} and is poorly immunogenic, with types {{c2::5 and 8}} being most prevalent.
extraNote: The capsule inhibits phagocytosis by host immune cells.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicles for which {{c2::S. aureus}} is the most common cause.
extraNote: It presents as small pustules on areas like the chin or neck.

clozeText: Hospital-acquired MRSA is frequently associated with {{c1::surgical-wound}} infections and cardiac {{c2::pacemaker}} site infections.
extraNote: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission in healthcare settings.

clozeText: S. aureus can be identified by its ability to cause {{c1::clotted plasma}} in a tube containing prothrombin and fibrinogen.
extraNote: This is the definitive biochemical test for differentiating it from S. epidermidis.

clozeText: Clostridium species are Gram-positive, spore-forming {{c1::obligate anaerobes}} that lack catalase and superoxide dismutase.
extraNote: Spore formation allows them to survive in oxygenated environments, but they require anaerobic conditions for vegetative growth.

clozeText: Clostridium spores can only be reliably killed by {{c1::autoclaving::method}}, which utilizes steam under pressure at 121°C.
extraNote: Standard boiling is insufficient to kill the highly resistant spores.

clozeText: On Gram stain, Clostridium tetani classically presents with a {{c1::"drumstick" or "tennis racquet"::shape}} appearance due to its terminal spores.
extraNote: This terminal spore placement is a distinguishing morphological feature of C. tetani.

clozeText: Tetanospasmin is transported from the site of the wound to the spinal cord via {{c1::retrograde axonal transport}}.
extraNote: The toxin travels through motor neurons to reach the central nervous system.

clozeText: The Clostridium tetani toxin (tetanospasmin) is a protease that cleaves {{c1::synaptobrevin::V-SNARE}}, preventing the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters.
extraNote: Cleavage of synaptobrevin prevents vesicle fusion in inhibitory interneurons.

clozeText: Clostridium tetani prevents the release of {{c1::GABA and glycine}} from Renshaw cells in the spinal cord.
extraNote: Loss of inhibition leads to overactivity of motor neurons, causing spastic paralysis.

clozeText: The classic clinical presentation of tetanus includes lockjaw (trismus), {{c1::risus sardonicus::facial grin}}, and opisthotonos.
extraNote: Opisthotonos refers to the severe backward arching of the head, neck, and spine.

clozeText: Clostridium botulinum toxin prevents the release of the excitatory neurotransmitter {{c1::acetylcholine}} at the neuromuscular junction.
extraNote: The lack of acetylcholine release results in flaccid paralysis.

clozeText: Clostridium botulinum toxin acts by cleaving {{c1::SNARE proteins}}, which are essential for neurotransmitter vesicle docking and fusion.
extraNote: Specific targets include synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, and syntaxin.

clozeText: In adults, botulism is typically caused by the ingestion of {{c1::preformed toxin::form}} from improperly canned alkaline vegetables.
extraNote: Because the toxin is preformed, symptoms appear rapidly after ingestion.

clozeText: Infant botulism (Floppy Baby Syndrome) is caused by the ingestion of {{c1::spores::form}} found in honey.
extraNote: Infants lack the mature gut flora necessary to prevent Clostridium spores from germinating into vegetative cells.

clozeText: The clinical presentation of botulism classically begins with {{c1::cranial nerve palsies::e.g., diplopia, ptosis}} before progressing to a descending flaccid paralysis.
extraNote: The 4 Ds: Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysphagia, Dyspnea.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens produces {{c1::Alpha toxin}}, which is a lecithinase (phospholipase C) that damages cell membranes.
extraNote: Lecithinase lyses erythrocytes, platelets, and endothelial cells, leading to massive tissue necrosis.

clozeText: On blood agar, Clostridium perfringens characteristically produces a {{c1::double zone of hemolysis}}.
extraNote: The inner zone is due to theta toxin (complete hemolysis), and the outer zone is due to alpha toxin (partial hemolysis).

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens is the most common cause of {{c1::myonecrosis::gas gangrene}}, which is characterized by crepitus on physical exam.
extraNote: Crepitus is the crackling sound caused by gas production in the infected tissue.

clozeText: Clostridium perfringens food poisoning is caused by an enterotoxin and is associated with a {{c1::late onset::timing}} (8-22 hours) of watery diarrhea.
extraNote: The toxin is produced during sporulation in the gut, rather than being preformed in the food.

clozeText: The most commonly associated antibiotic that predisposes patients to Clostridium difficile infection is {{c1::clindamycin}}.
extraNote: Other common triggers include ampicillin, cephalosporins, and fluoroquinolones.

clozeText: Clostridium difficile Toxin A is an enterotoxin that damages the {{c1::brush border}} of the intestinal mucosa, leading to watery diarrhea.
extraNote: Toxin A attracts neutrophils and induces an inflammatory response.

clozeText: Clostridium difficile Toxin B is a cytotoxin that causes {{c1::actin depolymerization}}, leading to cell death and pseudomembrane formation.
extraNote: This disrupts the cytoskeleton and tight junctions of the colonic epithelial cells.

clozeText: The diagnosis of Clostridium difficile is usually confirmed by detecting the {{c1::toxin B gene (PCR) or toxin antigens}} in the stool.
extraNote: Culture is not usually performed for diagnosis because C. difficile can be part of the normal flora in some individuals.

clozeText: First-line treatment for an initial episode of Clostridium difficile infection includes {{c1::fidaxomicin}} or oral vancomycin.
extraNote: Metronidazole is no longer considered first-line for non-severe C. difficile in many guidelines.

clozeText: Severe Clostridium difficile infection can lead to {{c1::pseudomembranous colitis}}, characterized by yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa.
extraNote: On histology, these plaques appear as a 'volcano' lesion of fibrin and inflammatory debris.

clozeText: Clostridium septicum is highly associated with underlying {{c1::colon cancer::malignancy}} if it causes spontaneous gas gangrene.
extraNote: Bacteremia with C. septicum should prompt an evaluation for occult colonic malignancy (e.g., colonoscopy).

clozeText: Botulinum toxin is {{c1::heat-labile::stability}}, meaning that boiling food before consumption can prevent botulism.
extraNote: In contrast, the spores are heat-stable and require autoclaving to kill.

clozeText: Active immunity against tetanus is provided by the {{c1::tetanus toxoid}} vaccine, which is often combined with diphtheria and pertussis (DTaP).
extraNote: The vaccine contains an inactivated toxin (toxoid), not the bacteria itself.

clozeText: Clostridium tetani specifically inhibits {{c1::Renshaw cells::cell type}} in the spinal cord, which are inhibitory interneurons.
extraNote: This results in the loss of glycine/GABA mediated relaxation of muscles.

clozeText: The classic triad of symptoms for botulism includes symmetric descending paralysis, a normal sensorium, and the {{c1::absence of fever}}.
extraNote: The absence of fever helps distinguish toxin-mediated botulism from bacterial meningitis or other infections.

clozeText: Recurrent Clostridium difficile infections that do not respond to antibiotics may be effectively treated with a {{c1::fecal microbiota transplant}}.
extraNote: FMT restores the normal gut flora that competes with and inhibits C. difficile.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} (MRSA) is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States and is also a frequent cause of pneumonia and necrotizing fasciitis.
extraNote: In addition to skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs), S. aureus is a leading cause of infections in intravenous drug users.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas streptococci do not.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, allowing bacteria to survive oxidative killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci are arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters::shape}}, whereas streptococci are found in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive cocci and nonmotile; neither forms spores.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron, which is necessary for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes used in energy production.

clozeText: The lesions of {{c1::impetigo}} are characterized as crops of vesicles with a "honey-colored" crust.
extraNote: Impetigo is caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is caused by genes called {{c1::mecA::gene}} on the bacterial chromosome.
extraNote: The mecA gene encodes altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), specifically PBP2a.

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein {{c1::PBP2a}} in MRSA can perform transpeptidation but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This mechanism renders β-lactamase–resistant penicillins, such as nafcillin, ineffective.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) typically produces {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a factor less commonly found in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is USA300.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) carries genes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This substitution is encoded by a transposon on a plasmid, originally found in enterococci.

clozeText: S. aureus virulence factor {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils.
extraNote: Protein A is found on the surface of S. aureus but is absent in coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids::Polymer}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} induce the release of IL-1 and TNF from macrophages, which can trigger septic shock.
extraNote: This pathway is similar to the mechanism by which endotoxin triggers shock in gram-negative infections.

clozeText: S. aureus has a {{c1::polysaccharide capsule::structure}} with 11 serotypes, of which types 5 and 8 cause 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus possesses {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, allowing it to activate complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus causes clinical findings of septic shock despite being gram-positive and lacking true endotoxin.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill the bacteria.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the oxidative burst required to kill catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately 5% of women, which predisposes them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome::syndrome}}.
extraNote: This syndrome is caused by a toxin acting as a superantigen.

clozeText: The typical lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Abscesses like furuncles and boils are classic presentations; however, organisms can also disseminate via the bloodstream.

clozeText: Important predisposing factors to S. aureus infection include {{c1::foreign bodies}} such as sutures and intravenous catheters.
extraNote: These provide a surface for biofilm formation and protect the bacteria from the immune system.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is distinguished from Staphylococcus saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: Both are coagulase-negative staphylococci, but S. epidermidis is a major part of the normal skin flora.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a frequent cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and prosthetic hip joints.
extraNote: Its ability to produce biofilms on plastic and metal surfaces is a key virulence trait.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is characterized by being {{c1::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: In clinical labs, the novobiocin disk test is used to differentiate it from S. epidermidis.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young women.
extraNote: It is second only to E. coli as a cause of community-acquired UTIs in this demographic.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus and presents with desquamated skin.
extraNote: It primarily affects infants and young children; the toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}}, an infection of the bone, often following hematogenous spread.
extraNote: It is the most common cause of osteomyelitis across most patient populations.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains contain {{c1::plasmids}} that encode β-lactamase, rendering them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: For these strains, β-lactamase–resistant penicillins like nafcillin are the drugs of choice.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::food poisoning}} through the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins.
extraNote: The onset is rapid (1-6 hours) and is characterized by severe vomiting and diarrhea.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum is a thin, motile {{c1::spirochete::morphology}} that cannot be seen on a standard Gram stain.
extraNote: Its cell wall is too thin to take up Gram stain; it is visualized using dark-field microscopy or silver stains.

clozeText: The primary method for direct visualization of Treponema pallidum from a chancre is {{c1::dark-field microscopy}}.
extraNote: Spirochetes appear as bright, coiled organisms against a dark background.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum cannot be grown on artificial media and must be maintained in {{c1::rabbit testes::animal model}}.
extraNote: It is an obligate intracellular pathogen with a slow doubling time.

clozeText: The fundamental pathological lesion in all stages of syphilis is {{c1::endarteritis obliterans::vascular pathology}}.
extraNote: This refers to the inflammation and narrowing of small blood vessels, often surrounded by plasma cells.

clozeText: Primary syphilis is characterized by a {{c1::painless::pain level}} chancre at the site of inoculation.
extraNote: The chancre is highly infectious and usually heals spontaneously within 3 to 6 weeks.

clozeText: Secondary syphilis typically presents with a maculopapular rash that involves the {{c1::palms and soles::specific location}}.
extraNote: This distribution is high-yield, as few other conditions (like Rickettsia rickettsii or Coxsackievirus A) affect these areas.

clozeText: The smooth, moist, flat-topped lesions found in the anogenital region during secondary syphilis are called {{c1::condylomata lata}}.
extraNote: These must be distinguished from condylomata acuminata (HPV), which are typically cauliflower-like and wart-like.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis is characterized by the formation of {{c1::gummas::lesion type}}, which are chronic granulomatous lesions.
extraNote: Gummas can occur in the skin, bone, or internal organs like the liver.

clozeText: Cardiovascular syphilis involves the destruction of the {{c1::vasa vasorum::structure}} of the ascending aorta.
extraNote: This leads to medial necrosis, aortic aneurysm, and a 'tree-bark' appearance of the aortic intima.

clozeText: Neurosyphilis involving the dorsal columns of the spinal cord is known as {{c1::tabes dorsalis}}.
extraNote: It results in loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and a positive Romberg sign.

clozeText: The {{c1::Argyll Robertson::eponym}} pupil constricts during accommodation but does not react to light.
extraNote: Also known as the 'prostitute's pupil,' it is highly specific for neurosyphilis.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis can present early with {{c1::snuffles::symptom}}, which is a highly infectious, bloody nasal discharge.
extraNote: This occurs within the first few months of life.

clozeText: Bowing of the tibias in congenital syphilis is referred to as {{c1::saber shins}}.
extraNote: This is a late manifestation of congenital syphilis.

clozeText: Hutchinson's triad of congenital syphilis includes interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, and {{c1::Hutchinson teeth::dental finding}}.
extraNote: Hutchinson teeth are characterized by notched, widely spaced incisors.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis may lead to molars with multiple tiny cusps, known as {{c1::mulberry molars}}.
extraNote: This is a deformity of the first permanent molars.

clozeText: The VDRL and RPR tests detect antibodies against {{c1::cardiolipin::antigen}}.
extraNote: Cardiolipin is a beef heart extract; these are 'non-treponemal' screening tests.

clozeText: The specific confirmatory test for syphilis after a positive screening test is the {{c1::FTA-ABS::acronym}} test.
extraNote: Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption test remains positive for life even after treatment.

clozeText: A false-positive VDRL result is commonly associated with {{c1::Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)::disease}}.
extraNote: Other causes include viral infections (EBV, Hepatitis), leprosy, and IV drug use.

clozeText: The drug of choice for all stages of syphilis is {{c1::Penicillin G::antibiotic}}.
extraNote: For tertiary syphilis or neurosyphilis, IV Penicillin G is required.

clozeText: The acute febrile reaction occurring within 24 hours of starting penicillin for syphilis is the {{c1::Jarisch-Herxheimer}} reaction.
extraNote: It is caused by the release of endotoxin-like pyrogens from dying spirochetes.

clozeText: In a pregnant patient with syphilis and a penicillin allergy, the management is {{c1::desensitization}}.
extraNote: Penicillin is the only effective treatment to prevent congenital syphilis; other options like doxycycline are contraindicated or less effective.

clozeText: Tabes dorsalis results in a {{c1::broad-based::gait description}} ataxia and a positive Romberg sign.
extraNote: The ataxia is sensory, not cerebellar, due to loss of dorsal column input.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum's corkscrew motility is facilitated by {{c1::endoflagella::structure}} located in the periplasmic space.
extraNote: Also called axial filaments, these allow the organism to move through viscous media.

clozeText: The saddle nose deformity in congenital syphilis is caused by destruction of the {{c1::nasal cartilage}}.
extraNote: It is a late manifestation of congenital syphilis.

clozeText: Sensorineural deafness in congenital syphilis is caused by damage to the {{c1::eighth::cranial nerve number}} cranial nerve.
extraNote: This is a component of Hutchinson's triad.

clozeText: Aortic aneurysm in tertiary syphilis most commonly affects the {{c1::ascending::part of aorta}} aorta.
extraNote: This leads to aortic valve insufficiency and heart failure.

clozeText: Treatment of neurosyphilis requires high doses of {{c1::intravenous}} Penicillin G for 10–14 days.
extraNote: Standard IM benzathine penicillin does not reach sufficient CSF concentrations.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum is a {{c1::microaerophilic::oxygen requirement}} organism.
extraNote: It is extremely sensitive to oxygen toxicity and heat.

clozeText: Primary syphilis is characterized by a {{c1::painless chancre::lesion type}} at the site of inoculation, often accompanied by painless regional lymphadenopathy.
extraNote: The chancre typically appears 3 weeks after infection and heals spontaneously within 3 to 6 weeks.

clozeText: Secondary syphilis classically presents with a maculopapular rash that involves the {{c1::palms and soles::specific body parts}}.
extraNote: This rash is often accompanied by lymphadenopathy, fever, and malaise.

clozeText: {{c1::Condyloma lata}} are smooth, flat, moist, wart-like lesions found in the anogenital region during secondary syphilis.
extraNote: These lesions are highly infectious and should be distinguished from the cauliflower-like Condyloma acuminata caused by HPV.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis is characterized by {{c1::gummas::lesion type}}, which are chronic granulomas that can undergo central necrosis and affect skin, bone, or organs.
extraNote: Gummas are a result of a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to the spirochetes.

clozeText: The {{c1::Argyll Robertson}} pupil, seen in tertiary syphilis, constricts with accommodation but does not react to light.
extraNote: This is also known as the 'Prostitute's Pupil' and is caused by damage to the pretectal nuclei.

clozeText: Neurosyphilis can cause {{c1::tabes dorsalis}}, which involves the degeneration of the posterior (dorsal) columns of the spinal cord.
extraNote: Patients present with impaired proprioception, loss of vibration sense, and a positive Romberg sign.

clozeText: Treponema pallidum is a {{c1::spirochete}} and cannot be cultured on standard agar; it is typically visualized using darkfield microscopy.
extraNote: Darkfield microscopy shows motile, spiral-shaped organisms directly from a primary chancre.

clozeText: Syphilitic aortitis is caused by the destruction of the {{c1::vasa vasorum::blood vessel}}, leading to dilation of the aortic root and a 'tree-bark' appearance.
extraNote: This destruction can lead to aortic aneurysm or aortic valve insufficiency.

clozeText: The screening test for syphilis is usually a non-treponemal test such as {{c1::VDRL or RPR}}.
extraNote: These tests detect antibodies against cardiolipin and are used for screening and monitoring treatment response.

clozeText: VDRL tests detect antibodies against {{c1::cardiolipin}}, which can lead to false positives in patients with SLE, leprosy, or IV drug use.
extraNote: The mnemonic for VDRL false positives is 'VDRL': Viruses, Drugs, Rheumatic fever, Lupus/Leprosy.

clozeText: The confirmatory test for syphilis, which remains positive for life even after treatment, is the {{c1::FTA-ABS::specific test}}.
extraNote: The FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) test detects specific antibodies against T. pallidum.

clozeText: The drug of choice for all stages of syphilis is {{c1::Penicillin G}}.
extraNote: For primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis, a single IM dose of benzathine penicillin G is typically used.

clozeText: The {{c1::Jarisch-Herxheimer}} reaction is a systemic inflammatory response (fever, chills) that occurs shortly after starting penicillin for syphilis.
extraNote: It is caused by the rapid release of lipoproteins (endotoxin-like) from dying spirochetes.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis can lead to {{c1::Hutchinson teeth::finding}}, which are notched, peg-shaped permanent incisors.
extraNote: Hutchinson teeth are part of the classic 'Hutchinson triad' along with interstitial keratitis and CN VIII deafness.

clozeText: {{c1::Mulberry molars::finding}} are a sign of congenital syphilis characterized by first molars with multiple tiny cusps.
extraNote: This is a classic dental deformity seen in patients with congenital syphilis.

clozeText: {{c1::Saber shins}} are a skeletal manifestation of congenital syphilis resulting from chronic periostitis and bowing of the tibia.
extraNote: This bowing of the shin bone is a classic late finding in congenital syphilis.

clozeText: A skeletal deformity seen in congenital syphilis involving the collapse of the nasal bridge is called {{c1::saddle nose}}.
extraNote: This occurs due to destruction of the nasal cartilage by the infection.

clozeText: Neurosyphilis must be evaluated using a {{c1::lumbar puncture}} to perform a VDRL test on the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
extraNote: A positive CSF-VDRL is highly specific for neurosyphilis.

clozeText: The Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is not an allergic reaction; it is mediated by {{c1::cytokines}} released in response to spirochete lysis.
extraNote: Treatment is supportive (NSAIDs, fluids) and the reaction typically resolves within 24 hours.

clozeText: In primary syphilis, the chancre heals spontaneously within {{c1::3 to 6 weeks}} even without antibiotic treatment.
extraNote: The disappearance of the lesion does not mean the infection is cured; it progresses to the latent stage.

clozeText: Secondary syphilis symptoms appear {{c1::weeks to months}} after the initial chancre has healed.
extraNote: Secondary syphilis represents the systemic dissemination of the spirochetes.

clozeText: {{c1::Broad-based gait}} and a positive Romberg sign are clinical features of tabes dorsalis due to loss of sensory input from the lower limbs.
extraNote: This is a hallmark of sensory ataxia in neurosyphilis.

clozeText: Tertiary syphilis typically manifests {{c1::years or decades}} after the initial untreated infection.
extraNote: Approximately one-third of untreated patients will develop tertiary syphilis features.

clozeText: To treat neurosyphilis, the preferred regimen is {{c1::intravenous (IV)}} Penicillin G for 10-14 days.
extraNote: IV administration is necessary to achieve adequate bactericidal levels in the CNS.

clozeText: If a pregnant woman is allergic to penicillin and has syphilis, the recommended management is {{c1::penicillin desensitization}}.
extraNote: Penicillin is the only effective treatment for preventing vertical transmission to the fetus.

clozeText: Unlike the lesions of HPV (Condyloma acuminata), the lesions of secondary syphilis (Condyloma lata) are {{c1::smooth/flat::morphology}}.
extraNote: Condyloma lata are rich in spirochetes and are extremely infectious.

clozeText: Congenital syphilis can lead to sensorineural hearing loss due to inflammatory damage to cranial nerve {{c1::VIII (8)}}.
extraNote: This is a component of Hutchinson's triad and usually presents in late childhood.

clozeText: The non-treponemal tests (VDRL/RPR) are useful for {{c1::monitoring response to treatment::utility}} because their titers decrease with successful therapy.
extraNote: A fourfold drop in titer is typically used to define a successful response to treatment.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis is an {{c1::obligate intracellular}} organism because it cannot synthesize its own ATP.
extraNote: It is often called an 'energy parasite' for this reason.

clozeText: The {{c1::Elementary body::EB or RB?}} is the small, dense, infectious form of Chlamydia trachomatis that enters the cell via endocytosis.
extraNote: Think 'E' for Enters and 'E' for Elementary.

clozeText: The {{c1::Reticulate body::EB or RB?}} is the metabolically active, replicating form of Chlamydia trachomatis seen inside host cells.
extraNote: Think 'R' for Replicates and 'R' for Reticulate. It replicates via binary fission.

clozeText: Chlamydia species lack {{c1::muramic acid}} in their peptidoglycan cell wall, making β-lactam antibiotics relatively ineffective.
extraNote: This is a classic 'factoid'—though they have genes for peptidoglycan synthesis, the lack of muramic acid is the key board-tested feature.

clozeText: C. trachomatis cytoplasmic inclusions can be visualized using {{c1::Giemsa}} or fluorescent-antibody-stained smears.
extraNote: They are not seen on standard Gram stain because they are intracellular and lack a typical cell wall.

clozeText: Serotypes {{c1::A, B, and C}} of C. trachomatis are associated with chronic infection and cause follicular conjunctivitis and blindness.
extraNote: Mnemonic: ABC = Africa, Blindness, Chronic.

clozeText: Serotypes {{c1::D–K}} of C. trachomatis cause urethritis, PID, ectopic pregnancy, and neonatal pneumonia.
extraNote: This is the most common bacterial STI in the United States.

clozeText: Serotypes {{c1::L1, L2, and L3}} cause lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV).
extraNote: LGV is characterized by small, painless ulcers followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

clozeText: The gold standard for diagnosing a Chlamydia trachomatis infection is the {{c1::Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)}}.
extraNote: NAAT can be performed on vaginal swabs or 'first-catch' urine.

clozeText: Neonatal conjunctivitis caused by C. trachomatis typically appears {{c1::1–2 weeks}} after birth.
extraNote: Contrast this with N. gonorrhoeae conjunctivitis, which appears much earlier (2–5 days).

clozeText: Chlamydial neonatal pneumonia is characterized by a distinctive {{c1::staccato cough}} and peripheral eosinophilia.
extraNote: The infant is usually afebrile.

clozeText: Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome), characterized by the triad of uveitis, urethritis, and arthritis, is most commonly a late sequela of {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}} infection.
extraNote: Associated with the HLA-B27 genotype.

clozeText: The recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated chlamydial urethritis is {{c1::Azithromycin::1 dose}} or Doxycycline.
extraNote: Azithromycin is preferred because it is a single dose, improving compliance.

clozeText: In patients with Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) caused by C. trachomatis, infection can spread to the liver capsule, causing {{c1::Fitz-Hugh-Curtis}} syndrome.
extraNote: Presents as 'violin-string' adhesions between the liver capsule and the peritoneal wall.

clozeText: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) often presents with the {{c1::groove sign}}, where the inguinal ligament divides matted painful lymph nodes.
extraNote: Caused by serotypes L1-L3.

clozeText: C. trachomatis {{c1::urethritis}} is often 'silent' or asymptomatic, especially in women, leading to undiagnosed PID.
extraNote: This is why screening is recommended for all sexually active women under 25.

clozeText: Unlike most bacteria, Chlamydia cannot be grown on {{c1::agar}} plates because they require living host cells to replicate.
extraNote: They are grown in cell cultures (e.g., McCoy cells).

clozeText: If a patient is diagnosed with Gonorrhea, they should also be empirically treated for {{c1::Chlamydia}} due to high rates of co-infection.
extraNote: Standard practice is Ceftriaxone (for Gonorrhea) + Doxycycline/Azithromycin (for Chlamydia).

clozeText: The primary cause of scarring and blindness in Trachoma is repeated infection leading to {{c1::eyelid scarring}} and inward-turning eyelashes (trichiasis).
extraNote: The eyelashes eventually abrade the cornea, leading to opacification.

clozeText: Treatment for neonatal Chlamydial pneumonia or conjunctivitis requires oral {{c1::Erythromycin}}.
extraNote: Topical drops are insufficient for Chlamydia; systemic treatment is required to prevent pneumonia.

clozeText: C. trachomatis causes a {{c1::non-gonococcal}} urethritis characterized by clear, watery discharge.
extraNote: N. gonorrhoeae typically produces a thick, purulent discharge.

clozeText: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) increases the risk for {{c1::ectopic pregnancy}} and infertility due to fallopian tube scarring.
extraNote: Chronic inflammation leads to salpingitis.

clozeText: LGV begins with a {{c1::painless}} primary lesion that often heals quickly and may go unnoticed.
extraNote: The subsequent lymphadenopathy is what typically brings the patient to the clinic.

clozeText: The extracellular form (EB) is metabolically {{c1::inactive::active or inactive?}}.
extraNote: It only becomes active once it transforms into a Reticulate Body (RB) inside the host cell.

clozeText: Chlamydia species are {{c1::Gram-negative}} in structure (having an inner and outer membrane) but do not stain well with Gram stain.
extraNote: This is due to the lack of peptidoglycan/muramic acid.

clozeText: Azithromycin works against Chlamydia by inhibiting the {{c1::50S}} ribosomal subunit.
extraNote: It is a macrolide antibiotic.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis enters host cells primarily through the process of {{c1::receptor-mediated endocytosis}}.
extraNote: The EB triggers its own uptake by the cell.

clozeText: The differential diagnosis for a painful inguinal bubo includes LGV and {{c1::Haemophilus ducreyi}} (Chancroid).
extraNote: However, LGV starts with a painless ulcer, whereas Chancroid starts with a painful ulcer.

clozeText: The {{c1::elementary body}} is the small, infectious form of Chlamydia trachomatis that is metabolically inactive and extracellular.
extraNote: It enters the host cell via endocytosis. Think 'E' for Elementary and 'E' for Enters/Extracellular.

clozeText: The {{c1::reticulate body}} is the metabolically active, replicating form of Chlamydia trachomatis found within intracellular inclusions.
extraNote: It replicates via binary fission within the host cell vacuole. Think 'R' for Reticulate and 'R' for Replicates.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis cannot be visualized on Gram stain because its cell wall lacks {{c1::muramic acid::specific component}}.
extraNote: While it has a thin peptidoglycan layer, the lack of classic muramic acid makes it poorly visible on standard Gram stains.

clozeText: The classic stain used to identify Chlamydia cytoplasmic inclusion bodies (reticulate bodies) is the {{c1::Giemsa}} stain.
extraNote: Inclusions can also be visualized using fluorescent-antibody staining.

clozeText: Serotypes {{c1::A, B, and C}} of Chlamydia trachomatis are the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide (Trachoma).
extraNote: Mnemonic: ABC = Africa, Blindness, Chronic infection.

clozeText: Serotypes {{c1::D-K}} of Chlamydia trachomatis cause the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the US and neonatal conjunctivitis.
extraNote: These serotypes are also associated with non-gonococcal urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease.

clozeText: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes {{c1::L1, L2, and L3}}.
extraNote: LGV is characterized by a painless primary ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.

clozeText: The painful, swollen inguinal lymph nodes characteristic of Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) are called {{c1::buboes}}.
extraNote: The 'groove sign' may be seen when the inguinal ligament divides the enlarged nodes.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis is described as an {{c1::obligate intracellular}} pathogen because it cannot synthesize its own ATP.
extraNote: It is an 'energy parasite' that uses an ATP/ADP translocator to steal host energy.

clozeText: The diagnostic gold standard for Chlamydia trachomatis infection is {{c1::NAAT::acronym}}.
extraNote: Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT) can be performed on urine or vaginal swabs with high sensitivity.

clozeText: Neonatal conjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis typically presents {{c1::5–14 days}} after delivery.
extraNote: In contrast, Neisseria gonorrhoeae conjunctivitis presents earlier (2-5 days), and chemical conjunctivitis presents within 24 hours.

clozeText: Infants infected with Chlamydia trachomatis during birth may develop a pneumonia characterized by a {{c1::staccato}} cough.
extraNote: Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation and interstitial infiltrates; peripheral eosinophilia is common.

clozeText: Inflammation of the liver capsule following pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is known as {{c1::Fitz-Hugh-Curtis}} syndrome.
extraNote: It results in 'violin-string' adhesions between the liver capsule and the parietal peritoneum.

clozeText: Reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter syndrome) is a post-Chlamydia complication associated with the {{c1::HLA-B27}} genetic marker.
extraNote: Classically presents as: 'Can't see (uveitis), can't pee (urethritis), can't climb a tree (arthritis).'

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Chlamydia trachomatis in a non-pregnant adult is {{c1::Doxycycline}} for 7 days or a single dose of Azithromycin.
extraNote: Doxycycline is preferred for LGV and most cases of urethritis/cervicitis according to updated guidelines.

clozeText: Chlamydia-induced blindness in Trachoma is caused by chronic inflammation leading to {{c1::trichiasis::condition}}, where eyelashes turn inward and abrade the cornea.
extraNote: This leads to corneal scarring and eventual opacification.

clozeText: To prevent neonatal ophthalmia, all newborns receive erythromycin ointment, which is primarily effective against {{c1::Neisseria gonorrhoeae}}.
extraNote: Prophylaxis is less effective against Chlamydia; oral erythromycin is required if Chlamydial conjunctivitis develops.

clozeText: In males, Chlamydia trachomatis is the leading cause of {{c1::non-gonococcal}} urethritis.
extraNote: It usually presents with a clear or mucoid discharge, distinguishing it from the purulent discharge of Gonorrhea.

clozeText: The {{c1::groove sign}} refers to the depression seen in LGV where the inguinal ligament separates inflamed superficial and deep inguinal lymph nodes.
extraNote: This is a classic finding in advanced Lymphogranuloma venereum.

clozeText: When treating suspected Chlamydia urethritis, patients are often empirically treated for Gonorrhea with {{c1::Ceftriaxone}}.
extraNote: Co-infection is frequent, so dual therapy (Ceftriaxone + Doxycycline) is standard empirical management.

clozeText: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes D-K can cause {{c1::follicular}} conjunctivitis in adults, characterized by lymphoid nodules in the conjunctiva.
extraNote: This is often secondary to self-inoculation from genital secretions.

clozeText: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) caused by Chlamydia often leads to {{c1::ectopic pregnancy}} or infertility due to fallopian tube scarring.
extraNote: Scarring (salpingitis) obstructs the passage of the ovum.

clozeText: The primary mechanism of action for Azithromycin in treating Chlamydia is the inhibition of the {{c1::50S}} ribosomal subunit.
extraNote: It prevents protein synthesis by inhibiting translocation.

clozeText: Doxycycline treats Chlamydia by binding to the {{c1::30S}} ribosomal subunit, preventing the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA.
extraNote: It is a bacteriostatic tetracycline antibiotic.
