clozeText: The material aspirated from an amebic liver abscess is classically described as {{c1::anchovy paste}}.
extraNote: This 'pus' is actually necrotic liver tissue and is typically odorless and sterile (no bacteria or trophozoites inside the center).

clozeText: Amebic liver abscesses are most commonly located in the {{c1::right}} lobe of the liver.
extraNote: This is due to the bulk of portal blood flow being directed to the right lobe.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating invasive Entamoeba histolytica (e.g., dysentery or liver abscess) is {{c1::metronidazole::class}} or tinidazole.
extraNote: These must always be followed by a luminal amebicide to eliminate remaining cysts.

clozeText: Luminal agents used to treat asymptomatic colonization or following metronidazole therapy for E. histolytica include {{c1::paromomycin}} or {{c2::iodoquinol}}.
extraNote: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that is poorly absorbed from the GI tract.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites kill host cells by inserting {{c1::amoebapores::pore-forming proteins}} into the target cell membrane.
extraNote: This leads to ion flux and eventual cell lysis or apoptosis.

clozeText: Transmission of Entamoeba histolytica is primarily via the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route, often through contaminated water.
extraNote: It is also recognized as a sexually transmitted infection in men who have sex with men (MSM).

clozeText: Excystation of Entamoeba histolytica occurs in the {{c1::small intestine}}, where one cyst releases four trophozoites.
extraNote: The alkalinity of the small intestine triggers this process.

clozeText: For diagnosing extra-intestinal amebiasis, {{c1::serology (EIA/ELISA)}} is highly sensitive, as stool O&P is often negative.
extraNote: Antibodies are present in over 90% of patients with amebic liver abscess.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica must be differentiated from the morphologically identical but non-pathogenic {{c1::Entamoeba dispar}}.
extraNote: E. dispar lacks the Gal/GalNAc lectin and the ability to cause invasive disease.

clozeText: A common complication of severe amebic colitis is {{c1::toxic megacolon}}, similar to that seen in ulcerative colitis.
extraNote: Perforation and peritonitis can also occur.

clozeText: Stool examination for Entamoeba histolytica should include at least {{c1::three}} samples to increase diagnostic sensitivity.
extraNote: Stool antigen tests are now preferred over microscopy due to higher specificity.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites secrete {{c1::cysteine proteases}} that degrade the extracellular matrix and allow tissue invasion.
extraNote: These proteases digest collagen and elastin, facilitating the formation of flask-shaped ulcers.

clozeText: In the liver, Entamoeba histolytica causes {{c1::liquefactive}} necrosis.
extraNote: The lack of inflammatory cells in the center of the 'abscess' results in the characteristic pasty consistency.

clozeText: The incubation period for Entamoeba histolytica infection usually ranges from {{c1::2 to 4::time range}} weeks.
extraNote: Symptoms can range from mild diarrhea to fulminant dysentery.

clozeText: Unlike pyogenic liver abscesses, amebic liver abscesses rarely present with {{c1::jaundice}}.
extraNote: Fever and RUQ pain are the most common presenting symptoms.

clozeText: The non-pathogenic commensal {{c1::Entamoeba coli}} can be distinguished from E. histolytica because its mature cysts have {{c2::8}} nuclei.
extraNote: E. coli cysts also have splintered ends on their chromatoid bodies.

clozeText: Diagnosis of an amebic liver abscess is often supported by an ultrasound showing a {{c1::hypoechoic}} round lesion.
extraNote: The lesion is typically well-circumscribed and lacks a prominent wall.

clozeText: In Entamoeba histolytica infection, the presence of blood in the stool (dysentery) is caused by trophozoites invading the {{c1::lamina propria}}.
extraNote: Damage to the vascularized layers of the gut leads to hematochezia.

clozeText: The reservoir for Entamoeba histolytica is exclusively {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: There are no significant animal reservoirs for this parasite.

clozeText: Chlorination of water may not be sufficient to kill Entamoeba histolytica {{c1::cysts}}; water must be {{c2::boiled::method}} or filtered.
extraNote: Standard chlorination levels in municipal water are often inadequate for cyst inactivation.

clozeText: An ameboma is a(n) {{c1::granulomatous mass::lesion type}} that can form in the colon as a result of chronic E. histolytica infection.
extraNote: It can be mistaken for colonic adenocarcinoma on imaging.

clozeText: {{c1::Flask-shaped}} ulcers are the characteristic histopathological finding in the colon of patients with intestinal Entamoeba histolytica infection.
extraNote: These ulcers have a narrow neck and broad base, resulting from the parasite's lateral spread once it breaches the muscularis mucosae.

clozeText: The liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica is classically described as containing "{{c1::anchovy paste::texture}}" material.
extraNote: The abscess contains reddish-brown liquefied liver tissue and debris, but lacks a significant neutrophil response (sterile pus).

clozeText: On microscopic examination of stool, the presence of trophozoites with {{c1::engulfed RBCs::finding}} (erythrophagocytosis) is pathognomonic for E. histolytica.
extraNote: This feature distinguishes pathogenic E. histolytica from the morphologically identical but non-pathogenic E. dispar.

clozeText: The infectious stage of Entamoeba histolytica is the {{c1::cyst}}, which is resistant to environmental stressors like gastric acid.
extraNote: Transmission occurs through ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food (fecal-oral route).

clozeText: The non-infectious, motile stage of Entamoeba histolytica found in the colon and in diarrheal stools is the {{c1::trophozoite}}.
extraNote: Trophozoites are the invasive form that causes tissue destruction and can travel to extraintestinal sites.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica cysts are characterized by having a maximum of {{c1::4::number}} nuclei.
extraNote: This is a key diagnostic feature in stool O&P (Ova and Parasites) exams.

clozeText: Intestinal amebiasis typically presents as {{c1::bloody::type}} diarrhea, also known as amebic dysentery.
extraNote: The blood results from tissue invasion and ulceration of the colonic mucosa.

clozeText: The most common extraintestinal site for Entamoeba histolytica infection is the {{c1::liver}}, where it causes abscess formation.
extraNote: The parasites reach the liver via the portal venous system after penetrating the bowel wall.

clozeText: Treatment for invasive amebiasis should begin with {{c1::Metronidazole::drug class}} or Tinidazole to target the trophozoites in the tissue.
extraNote: Always follow tissue amebicides with a luminal amebicide to prevent recurrence and carrier state.

clozeText: To eliminate the intraluminal carrier state of E. histolytica, a luminal agent such as {{c1::Paromomycin::drug}} or Iodoquinol must be used.
extraNote: Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside that is not absorbed in the GI tract, making it ideal for intraluminal parasites.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica uses a {{c1::galactose-inhibitable adherence lectin::protein}} to bind to and kill colonic epithelial cells.
extraNote: This lectin mediates the attachment and subsequent contact-dependent killing (trogocytosis) of host cells.

clozeText: In contrast to pyogenic liver abscesses, amebic liver abscesses are usually {{c1::solitary}} and located in the right lobe.
extraNote: Pyogenic abscesses (e.g., from E. coli or S. aureus) are more frequently multiple and seen in older patients or post-surgery.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica is morphologically identical to the non-pathogenic species {{c1::Entamoeba dispar::species}}, which does not exhibit erythrophagocytosis.
extraNote: Because of this, stool antigen tests or PCR are preferred over microscopy for definitive diagnosis.

clozeText: The transmission of Entamoeba histolytica is primarily via the {{c1::fecal-oral::route}} route, often through contaminated water in endemic areas.
extraNote: Cysts can survive in the environment for weeks; boiling water is required to kill them.

clozeText: Amebic liver abscesses typically present with {{c1::right upper quadrant::location}} pain, fever, and sometimes referred pain to the right shoulder.
extraNote: Jaundice is uncommon unless the abscess is very large or obstructing bile ducts.

clozeText: In the small intestine, {{c1::excystation}} occurs, where one cyst releases trophozoites that subsequently divide to form eight organisms.
extraNote: The released trophozoites then migrate to the large intestine to colonize the cecum and colon.

clozeText: Stool {{c1::Antigen::test type}} assays (EIA) are more sensitive and specific than microscopy for differentiating E. histolytica from commensal amoebas.
extraNote: Microscopy often misses the organism or fails to distinguish species (sensitivity is only ~60%).

clozeText: Metronidazole is effective against Entamoeba because it is reduced to {{c1::toxic free radicals::mechanism}} in anaerobic environments by ferredoxin.
extraNote: These radicals damage the parasite's DNA and proteins, leading to cell death.

clozeText: The "anchovy paste" material in an amebic liver abscess consists of liquefied hepatocytes and is typically {{c1::sterile::bacterial status}}.
extraNote: Drainage is rarely necessary unless the abscess is at risk of rupture or the diagnosis is uncertain.

clozeText: {{c1::Iodoquinol::drug}} is an alternative luminal amebicide used to treat asymptomatic cyst passers or as follow-up after metronidazole.
extraNote: It is an 8-hydroxyquinoline derivative with poor systemic absorption.

clozeText: Risk factors for amebiasis in developed countries include travelers to endemic areas, institutionalized individuals, and {{c1::men who have sex with men (MSM)::population}}.
extraNote: In the MSM population, transmission occurs through oral-anal contact.

clozeText: A serious but rare complication of intestinal amebiasis that presents with severe abdominal distension and systemic toxicity is {{c1::toxic megacolon}}.
extraNote: This is a medical emergency and may require surgical intervention/colectomy.

clozeText: Chronic intestinal amebiasis can occasionally be misdiagnosed as {{c1::Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)::condition}} because both present with bloody stools and ulcers.
extraNote: Mistakenly giving corticosteroids for suspected IBD can lead to perforation in a patient with amebiasis.

clozeText: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites move and feed using {{c1::pseudopodia::structure}}.
extraNote: The name 'histolytica' refers to the organism's ability to lyse host tissues (histo = tissue, lytic = dissolving).

clozeText: During {{c1::encystation}}, trophozoites transform into cysts in the lumen of the large intestine before being passed in feces.
extraNote: Encystation is triggered by the dehydration of feces as they move through the distal colon.

clozeText: Imaging (CT or MRI) of an amebic liver abscess often shows a well-circumscribed {{c1::hypodense}} lesion with a peripheral enhancing rim.
extraNote: Ultrasound is often the first-line imaging modality due to lower cost and accessibility.

clozeText: Paromomycin acts by binding to the {{c1::30S::ribosomal subunit}} of the parasite to inhibit protein synthesis.
extraNote: It belongs to the aminoglycoside family but is used for its local effect in the gut lumen.

clozeText: {{c1::Cysteine proteinases::enzyme}} are virulence factors secreted by E. histolytica that degrade the extracellular matrix, facilitating tissue invasion.
extraNote: These enzymes help the parasite penetrate the protective mucus layer and the epithelial barrier of the colon.

clozeText: The definitive host for {{c1::Echinococcus granulosus}} is the dog, whereas the intermediate host is usually sheep.
extraNote: Humans are accidental intermediate hosts who ingest eggs from dog feces.

clozeText: Humans become infected with Echinococcus by ingesting {{c1::eggs::stage}} found in dog feces.
extraNote: Ingesting the cysts found in meat (like sheep liver) does not infect humans; only the eggs are infectious to intermediate hosts.

clozeText: In the human gut, Echinococcus eggs hatch into {{c1::oncospheres::larval stage}}, which then penetrate the intestinal wall to enter the portal circulation.
extraNote: This migration is why the liver is the most common site of infection.

clozeText: The most common site of hydatid cyst formation in Echinococcus granulosus infection is the {{c1::liver}} (approximately 70% of cases).
extraNote: The second most common site is the lungs.

clozeText: A characteristic CT finding for Echinococcus granulosus is a cyst with {{c1::eggshell calcification::imaging finding}}.
extraNote: This represents mineralization of the cyst wall and is highly suggestive of hydatid disease.

clozeText: Spontaneous or surgical rupture of an Echinococcus cyst can cause {{c1::anaphylaxis}} due to the high antigenicity of the cyst fluid.
extraNote: Release of cyst contents can also lead to the seeding of secondary cysts throughout the peritoneal cavity.

clozeText: Within a hydatid cyst, {{c1::protoscolices::structure}} and daughter cysts accumulate to form what is known as 'hydatid sand'.
extraNote: Each protoscolex has the potential to develop into an adult worm if ingested by a definitive host.

clozeText: The surgical technique used for hydatid cysts is abbreviated as {{c1::PAIR::acronym}}, standing for Puncture, Aspirate, Inject, and Re-aspirate.
extraNote: A scolicidal agent is injected to kill the organisms before the cyst is fully removed.

clozeText: Before the surgical removal of a hydatid cyst, {{c1::hypertonic saline::substance}} (or ethanol) is injected to kill the protoscolices.
extraNote: This reduces the risk of anaphylaxis and secondary seeding if the cyst leaks.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating Echinococcus granulosus, often used as an adjunct to surgery, is {{c1::albendazole}}.
extraNote: Albendazole inhibits microtubule synthesis in the parasite.

clozeText: {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}} is the species responsible for alveolar hydatid disease, which mimics a slow-growing liver tumor.
extraNote: It is much more aggressive than E. granulosus because it grows invasively and lacks a thick laminated membrane.

clozeText: The definitive hosts for Echinococcus multilocularis are usually {{c1::foxes}}, and the intermediate hosts are rodents.
extraNote: Humans are accidental intermediate hosts, often infected by contact with fox or dog feces in endemic areas like the Northern Hemisphere.

clozeText: Adult Echinococcus worms are remarkably {{c1::small::size}}, typically only 3 to 6 mm long with only three proglottids.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from other tapeworms like Taenia solium which can be meters long.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus cysts are typically {{c1::unilocular::structure}}, meaning they consist of a single, large fluid-filled cavity.
extraNote: In contrast, E. multilocularis cysts are multilocular and lack a clear boundary, resembling a malignancy.

clozeText: Echinococcus cysts are often found in individuals from regions associated with {{c1::sheep raising}}.
extraNote: Endemic areas include the Mediterranean, South America, and the Middle East.

clozeText: On microscopic examination of hydatid fluid, the presence of diagnostic {{c1::hooklets}} confirms Echinococcus infection.
extraNote: These hooklets are part of the scolex of the future adult worm.

clozeText: Echinococcus multilocularis infection frequently presents as a liver mass with {{c1::central necrosis}}.
extraNote: The invasive nature and lack of a capsule make surgical resection difficult compared to E. granulosus.

clozeText: Laboratory findings in Echinococcus infection may include {{c1::eosinophilia}}, although this is often absent unless the cyst leaks.
extraNote: Serum IgE levels may also be elevated during a leak or rupture.

clozeText: Diagnosis of Echinococcus is primarily performed via {{c1::imaging::modality}} (US/CT) supported by serology (ELISA/Western blot).
extraNote: Diagnostic aspiration is generally avoided unless using the PAIR technique due to the risk of anaphylaxis.

clozeText: Definitive hosts (dogs) become infected by ingesting {{c1::hydatid cysts}} found in the organs of intermediate hosts.
extraNote: This cycle is maintained in nature through the consumption of infected offal by canines.

clozeText: The {{c1::proglottid::segment}} of the adult Echinococcus worm contains the eggs that are eventually shed in dog feces.
extraNote: The adult worm consists of a scolex, a neck, and three proglottids (one immature, one mature, and one gravid).

clozeText: In the life cycle of Echinococcus, the {{c1::embryonated egg::infectious stage}} is the stage that is infectious to the intermediate host (sheep or humans).
extraNote: The egg contains the hexacanth embryo (oncosphere).

clozeText: The {{c1::laminated membrane::structure}} is a thick, acellular protective layer of a hydatid cyst that is absent in E. multilocularis.
extraNote: The presence of this membrane in E. granulosus allows for the formation of a distinct, well-circumscribed cyst.

clozeText: Hydatid disease in the lungs usually presents with {{c1::cough and chest pain::symptoms}}.
extraNote: Rupture into a bronchus can cause the patient to expectorate 'salty' fluid and membrane fragments.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus is often referred to as the {{c1::dog tapeworm}}.
extraNote: This differentiates it from Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) and Taenia solium (pork tapeworm).

clozeText: The primary risk factor for humans acquiring Echinococcus is {{c1::close contact with dogs}} in endemic rural areas.
extraNote: Eggs can stick to the dog's fur and be transferred to the human's mouth via hands.

clozeText: Metastatic spread of {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}} to the lungs and brain can occur in advanced alveolar hydatid disease.
extraNote: It behaves much like a malignant tumor with the ability to metastasize hematogenously.

clozeText: The 'Casoni test' is an older {{c1::skin test::diagnostic method}} for Echinococcus that is largely replaced by serology and imaging.
extraNote: It involved injecting hydatid fluid intradermally and looking for a wheal-and-flare reaction.

clozeText: {{c1::Echinococcus granulosus}} is the primary cestode responsible for cystic echinococcosis, characterized by slow-growing, unilocular cysts.
extraNote: The liver is the most common organ involved (approx. 66% of cases).

clozeText: The {{c1::dog}} is the definitive host for Echinococcus granulosus, harboring the adult tapeworm in its intestine.
extraNote: Humans are accidental intermediate hosts.

clozeText: Humans acquire Echinococcus infection through the ingestion of {{c1::eggs::form}} shed in the feces of the definitive host.
extraNote: Ingestion often occurs via contaminated food, water, or direct contact with dogs.

clozeText: The {{c1::sheep}} is the most common natural intermediate host in the Echinococcus granulosus lifecycle.
extraNote: Intermediate hosts harbor the hydatid cysts.

clozeText: On CT imaging, the presence of {{c1::eggshell calcification}} in a hepatic cyst is highly suggestive of Echinococcus granulosus.
extraNote: This represents calcification of the cyst wall.

clozeText: A feared complication of hydatid cyst rupture is {{c1::anaphylaxis}} due to the release of highly antigenic cyst fluid.
extraNote: Immediate treatment with epinephrine is required if rupture occurs during a procedure.

clozeText: {{c1::Echinococcus multilocularis}} causes alveolar echinococcosis, which mimics a malignant liver tumor due to its infiltrative growth.
extraNote: Unlike E. granulosus, it lacks a limiting membrane.

clozeText: The drug of choice for the medical management of Echinococcus cysts is {{c1::albendazole}}.
extraNote: It is often used as an adjunct to surgery or the PAIR procedure.

clozeText: The PAIR procedure stands for Puncture, {{c1::Aspiration}}, Injection, and Re-aspiration.
extraNote: It is used for unilocular cysts that are not easily accessible by surgery.

clozeText: During the PAIR procedure, a {{c1::scolicidal}} agent such as ethanol or hypertonic saline is injected into the cyst.
extraNote: This is done to kill the germinal layer and prevent seeding.

clozeText: Aspiration of a hydatid cyst for diagnosis is generally {{c1::avoided::encouraged or avoided?}} because of the risk of leakage and anaphylaxis.
extraNote: Imaging and serology are the preferred diagnostic modalities.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of hydatid cyst fluid reveals {{c1::hydatid sand}}, which consists of liberated protoscolices and hooklets.
extraNote: This finding is pathognomonic if fluid is obtained.

clozeText: {{c1::Eosinophilia}} is present in only about 20-25% of patients with Echinococcus and is usually only seen if the cyst leaks.
extraNote: A normal eosinophil count does not rule out the disease.

clozeText: {{c1::Serology (ELISA/Immunoblot)}} is the initial screening test of choice for detecting antibodies against Echinococcus antigens.
extraNote: Sensitivity varies by cyst location; liver cysts are more likely to have positive serology than lung cysts.

clozeText: In the Echinococcus lifecycle, the {{c1::oncosphere}} larva hatches in the duodenum and penetrates the intestinal wall to enter the portal circulation.
extraNote: This explains why the liver is the most common primary site.

clozeText: The definitive host for Echinococcus multilocularis is the {{c1::fox}}.
extraNote: Rodents typically serve as the intermediate host in this cycle.

clozeText: The inner {{c1::germinal layer}} of a hydatid cyst is responsible for the asexual production of protoscolices.
extraNote: Damage to this layer is the goal of scolicidal therapy.

clozeText: {{c1::Daughter cysts}} within a larger 'mother' cyst are a characteristic finding of Echinococcus granulosus on ultrasound.
extraNote: This provides a 'cyst-within-a-cyst' appearance.

clozeText: Secondary {{c1::peritoneal}} echinococcosis can occur if a hepatic hydatid cyst ruptures into the abdominal cavity.
extraNote: This leads to the formation of multiple new cysts throughout the peritoneum.

clozeText: If a hydatid cyst is found in the {{c1::lung::organ}}, it may present with cough, chest pain, and hemoptysis.
extraNote: Lung cysts are less likely to calcify than liver cysts.

clozeText: The mechanism of action for albendazole in treating Echinococcus is the inhibition of {{c1::microtubule}} synthesis.
extraNote: It binds to beta-tubulin, leading to glucose depletion and death of the parasite.

clozeText: Alveolar echinococcosis (E. multilocularis) most commonly involves the {{c1::liver}}, but frequently metastasizes to the lungs and brain.
extraNote: It behaves much like a slow-growing carcinoma.

clozeText: Surgery is the treatment of choice for {{c1::large or complex}} hydatid cysts that carry a high risk of spontaneous rupture.
extraNote: Pre-operative albendazole is given to reduce cyst pressure and viability.

clozeText: For a patient with a suspected hydatid cyst, {{c1::epinephrine}} should be readily available during any invasive procedure to manage potential anaphylaxis.
extraNote: Standard precaution for PAIR or surgical removal.

clozeText: Echinococcus granulosus belongs to the class {{c1::Cestoda}} (tapeworms).
extraNote: They are characterized by a scolex (head) and proglottids (segments).

clozeText: Echinococcus cysts are often {{c1::asymptomatic}} for many years, only becoming symptomatic when they exert a mass effect on adjacent structures.
extraNote: Incubation can last 5 to 20 years.

clozeText: The presence of a {{c1::water-lily sign}} on imaging indicates a ruptured hydatid cyst where the endocyst membranes float in the remaining fluid.
extraNote: This is a classic radiologic sign.

clozeText: In areas where Echinococcus is endemic, prevention focuses on {{c1::preventing dogs from eating raw sheep offal}}.
extraNote: Offal often contains the hydatid cysts that complete the cycle in dogs.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are a group of fungi that require {{c1::keratin}} for growth, restricting their infection to the skin, hair, and nails.
extraNote: They utilize keratinase to break down structural proteins in the stratum corneum.

clozeText: The definitive diagnostic test for dermatophytosis involves visualizing {{c1::branching septate hyphae}} on a KOH preparation of skin scrapings.
extraNote: KOH (potassium hydroxide) dissolves keratin, making the fungal elements more visible under microscopy.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Microsporum}} is known for producing many spindle-shaped, multicellular, thick-walled macroconidia.
extraNote: Microsporum primarily infects the hair and skin, but rarely the nails.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Trichophyton}} is characterized by the production of numerous microconidia and rare, thin-walled, pencil-shaped macroconidia.
extraNote: Trichophyton can infect hair, skin, and nails.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Epidermophyton}} is unique because it produces no microconidia and has club-shaped macroconidia.
extraNote: Epidermophyton floccosum only infects skin and nails, never hair.

clozeText: A positive Wood's lamp test (bright green fluorescence) typically indicates an infection by certain species of {{c1::Microsporum}}.
extraNote: Tinea capitis caused by Microsporum canis or audouinii fluoresces, whereas Trichophyton tonsurans usually does not.

clozeText: The most common cause of Tinea capitis in the United States is {{c1::Trichophyton tonsurans}}.
extraNote: It often presents with 'black dots' where the hair shafts have broken off at the scalp surface.

clozeText: Oral {{c1::Griseofulvin}} is the first-line treatment for Tinea capitis because it accumulates in keratin precursor cells.
extraNote: Mechanism: Interferes with microtubule function, thereby inhibiting mitosis.

clozeText: For the treatment of onychomycosis (Tinea unguium), the drug of choice is oral {{c1::Terbinafine}}.
extraNote: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase, leading to a buildup of toxic squalene and ergosterol deficiency.

clozeText: Tinea corporis typically presents as an {{c1::annular (ring-shaped)}} lesion with central clearing and a scaly, erythematous border.
extraNote: Commonly known as 'ringworm' despite being a fungal infection.

clozeText: Dermatophytes are classified based on their natural habitat into geophilic, zoophilic, and {{c1::anthropophilic}} types.
extraNote: Anthropophilic species (e.g., T. rubrum) are transmitted from person to person and often cause chronic, less inflammatory infections.

clozeText: The standard fungal culture medium used to grow dermatophytes is {{c1::Sabouraud agar}}.
extraNote: It has a low pH and often contains antibiotics to inhibit bacterial overgrowth.

clozeText: A highly inflammatory, boggy, purulent mass on the scalp resulting from an exaggerated immune response to a dermatophyte is called a {{c1::kerion}}.
extraNote: Often seen with zoophilic dermatophytes like Trichophyton mentagrophytes.

clozeText: Tinea cruris, commonly known as 'jock itch,' usually spares the {{c1::scrotum}}, which helps distinguish it from Candidiasis.
extraNote: Candida infections typically involve the scrotum and present with satellite lesions.

clozeText: The dermatophytid (or 'id') reaction is a secondary eruption of sterile vesicles at a distant site caused by {{c1::hypersensitivity}} to fungal antigens.
extraNote: No fungal elements are found in the 'id' reaction site itself.

clozeText: Tinea pedis 'moccasin type' is most frequently caused by the organism {{c1::Trichophyton rubrum}}.
extraNote: It presents as chronic scaling and thickening of the soles.

clozeText: The primary virulence factor allowing dermatophytes to invade the stratum corneum is the enzyme {{c1::keratinase}}.
extraNote: This protease digests the tough fibrous protein keratin found in skin appendages.

clozeText: Infection of the hair shaft where fungal elements are found *inside* the shaft is termed {{c1::endothrix}}.
extraNote: Trichophyton tonsurans is a classic cause of endothrix infection.

clozeText: Infection of the hair shaft where fungal spores form a sheath *around* the outside of the shaft is termed {{c1::ectothrix}}.
extraNote: Microsporum species are classic examples of ectothrix infection.

clozeText: The drug Terbinafine works by inhibiting the enzyme {{c1::squalene epoxidase}}.
extraNote: This is a key step in the biosynthesis of ergosterol, the fungal cell membrane component.

clozeText: Dermatophyte infections of the nails are medically referred to as {{c1::Tinea unguium::Tinea name}} or onychomycosis.
extraNote: Usually requires systemic rather than topical treatment for efficacy.

clozeText: Tinea barbae is a dermatophyte infection involving the {{c1::beard area}} of the face and neck.
extraNote: Often contracted from animals (zoophilic species).

clozeText: Unlike dermatophytes, {{c1::Malassezia furfur}} (Tinea versicolor) requires lipids for growth and shows a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH.
extraNote: Malassezia is not a dermatophyte, though the name 'Tinea versicolor' is traditionally used.

clozeText: Favus is a severe form of Tinea capitis characterized by the formation of yellow, cup-shaped crusts called {{c1::scutula}}.
extraNote: Usually caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii.

clozeText: Topical azoles, such as clotrimazole, treat dermatophytosis by inhibiting {{c1::14-alpha-demethylase}}.
extraNote: This prevents the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol.

clozeText: Dermatophytes typically do not invade deeper tissues because their growth is inhibited by {{c1::serum}} and body temperature.
extraNote: They are restricted to the non-living keratinized layers of the skin.

clozeText: The transmission of {{c1::Microsporum canis}} usually occurs through contact with infected cats or dogs.
extraNote: This is a common zoophilic source of ringworm in children.

clozeText: Dermatophytes can be identified by their macroconidial shape; Epidermophyton has {{c1::club-shaped}} macroconidia.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from the spindle-shaped Microsporum or pencil-shaped Trichophyton.

clozeText: Dermatophytes require {{c1::keratin}} for growth, which explains why they are restricted to non-viable cornified layers of the skin, hair, and nails.
extraNote: They produce keratinase to digest this protein as their primary nutrient source.

clozeText: On a KOH preparation of skin scrapings, dermatophyte infections typically show {{c1::branching septate hyphae::microscopic finding}}.
extraNote: This differentiates them from Malassezia furfur, which shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Microsporum}} is characterized by the ability of certain species to fluoresce bright green under a Wood’s lamp.
extraNote: Trichophyton species typically do not fluoresce.

clozeText: {{c1::Trichophyton rubrum}} is the most common global cause of tinea pedis, tinea cruris, and onychomycosis.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of chronic, non-inflammatory infections.

clozeText: The clinical syndrome {{c1::tinea corporis}} presents as annular, erythematous scaling lesions with {{c2::central clearing}}.
extraNote: Also known as 'ringworm,' the active border contains the highest density of hyphae.

clozeText: {{c1::Tinea capitis}} often presents with circular patches of alopecia and is frequently accompanied by regional {{c2::lymphadenopathy}}.
extraNote: It is most common in children and can be highly contagious.

clozeText: A {{c1::kerion}} is a severe, inflammatory, boggy mass on the scalp caused by a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to a fungal infection.
extraNote: It may mimic a bacterial abscess but requires antifungal therapy rather than just antibiotics.

clozeText: {{c1::Onychomycosis::condition}} is a fungal infection of the nails that often requires oral therapy because topical agents cannot penetrate the nail bed effectively.
extraNote: It is also known as Tinea unguium.

clozeText: The first-line oral treatment for Tinea capitis in children, specifically for Microsporum, is {{c1::Griseofulvin}}.
extraNote: Terbinafine is also used, but Griseofulvin has the longest history of use for this indication.

clozeText: The mechanism of action for {{c1::Terbinafine}} is the inhibition of the enzyme {{c2::squalene epoxidase}}.
extraNote: This leads to an accumulation of squalene, which is toxic to the fungal cell.

clozeText: Inhibition of squalene epoxidase by terbinafine prevents the synthesis of {{c1::ergosterol}}, an essential component of the fungal cell membrane.
extraNote: This mechanism is fungicidal for dermatophytes.

clozeText: {{c1::Griseofulvin}} acts by interfering with {{c2::microtubule}} function, thereby inhibiting fungal mitosis.
extraNote: It deposits in keratin precursor cells, making them resistant to fungal invasion.

clozeText: Unlike dermatophytes, which are septate, Tinea versicolor is caused by {{c1::Malassezia furfur}} and typically presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented patches.
extraNote: Malassezia is a yeast-like fungus, not a true dermatophyte.

clozeText: Azole antifungals, such as Itraconazole, treat dermatophytes by inhibiting the enzyme {{c1::14-α-demethylase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme is a cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for converting lanosterol to ergosterol.

clozeText: The three genera of dermatophytes are {{c1::Microsporum}}, {{c2::Trichophyton}}, and {{c3::Epidermophyton}}.
extraNote: They are categorized based on their macroconidia and microconidia morphology.

clozeText: In contrast to the honey-colored crusts of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} impetigo, dermatophyte lesions are usually dry and scaly.
extraNote: Staph aureus is a common bacterial differential for skin lesions mentioned in Step 1.

clozeText: {{c1::Tinea pedis::syndrome}} can present in a 'moccasin' distribution, characterized by chronic scaling and thickening of the soles.
extraNote: It is often associated with Tinea manuum (two feet, one hand syndrome).

clozeText: Transmission of {{c1::Microsporum canis}} is typically associated with exposure to {{c2::infected pets (cats/dogs)}}.
extraNote: This is an example of a zoophilic dermatophyte transmission.

clozeText: The genus {{c1::Epidermophyton}} is distinguished by its lack of {{c2::microconidia}} and the presence of smooth-walled, club-shaped macroconidia.
extraNote: Epidermophyton floccosum is the only species in this genus that causes human disease.

clozeText: Oral Griseofulvin is a significant inducer of the {{c1::Cytochrome P450}} system.
extraNote: This can lead to decreased levels of drugs like warfarin or oral contraceptives.

clozeText: The most sensitive diagnostic test for confirming onychomycosis is a {{c1::PAS (Periodic Acid-Schiff)}} stain of nail clippings.
extraNote: It highlights the fungal polysaccharides in the nail plate.

clozeText: {{c1::Tinea cruris}} typically spares the {{c2::scrotum}}, which helps distinguish it from cutaneous Candidiasis.
extraNote: Candidiasis usually involves the scrotum and presents with satellite lesions.

clozeText: Topical {{c1::Nystatin}} is effective against Candida but has no activity against {{c2::dermatophytes}}.
extraNote: Nystatin binds to ergosterol to form pores; dermatophytes are innately resistant.

clozeText: An {{c1::id reaction::term}} refers to a secondary skin eruption that occurs at a distant site due to hypersensitivity to a primary dermatophyte infection.
extraNote: The 'id' site is sterile and does not contain fungi.

clozeText: {{c1::Sabouraud}} agar is the specialized medium used for the laboratory culture of dermatophytes.
extraNote: It has a low pH to inhibit bacterial growth.

clozeText: Dermatophytes use the enzyme {{c1::keratinase}} as a virulence factor to penetrate host tissue.
extraNote: Because they cannot survive at 37°C or in the presence of serum, they remain superficial.

clozeText: Dermatophyte infections of the beard area are known as {{c1::Tinea barbae}}.
extraNote: It is often seen in agricultural workers in contact with cattle.

clozeText: Unlike the abscesses caused by Staphylococcus aureus which involve {{c1::central necrosis}} and pus, dermatophyte infections are confined to the {{c2::stratum corneum}}.
extraNote: Dermatophytes do not typically invade deeper tissues unless the patient is severely immunocompromised.

clozeText: {{c1::Malassezia furfur::Organism}} is the causative agent of Pityriasis (Tinea) versicolor, a superficial fungal infection of the skin.
extraNote: It is a lipophilic yeast that is part of the normal human skin flora, typically found in areas with high sebum production.

clozeText: On KOH preparation of skin scrapings, Malassezia furfur exhibits a characteristic {{c1::"spaghetti and meatballs"::microscopic appearance}}.
extraNote: This appearance is created by a combination of short, curved hyphae (spaghetti) and clusters of round yeast cells (meatballs).

clozeText: Malassezia furfur produces {{c1::azelaic acid}}, which inhibits the enzyme {{c2::tyrosinase}} to cause hypopigmentation in Tinea versicolor.
extraNote: Tyrosinase is essential for melanin production; its inhibition leads to the characteristic pale patches on darker skin.

clozeText: To culture Malassezia furfur, the medium must be supplemented with {{c1::lipids::macronutrient}} (e.g., olive oil) because the organism is lipophilic.
extraNote: Standard Sabouraud agar does not support its growth without the addition of long-chain fatty acids.

clozeText: Under a Wood’s lamp, lesions of Tinea versicolor may show a {{c1::coppery-orange::color}} or yellowish fluorescence.
extraNote: This is a quick bedside diagnostic tool, though the fluorescence is not always present in all cases.

clozeText: Neonates receiving {{c1::total parenteral nutrition (TPN)}} via central venous catheters are at risk for {{c2::Malassezia furfur}} fungemia.
extraNote: The fungus thrives in the lipid-rich emulsions of the TPN and colonizes the catheter surface.

clozeText: In addition to Tinea versicolor, Malassezia furfur is associated with {{c1::seborrheic dermatitis}}, especially in patients with HIV or Parkinson's disease.
extraNote: Seborrheic dermatitis presents as greasy scales in 'seborrheic' areas like the scalp (dandruff) and nasolabial folds.

clozeText: The hypopigmented patches of Tinea versicolor are most commonly found on the {{c1::trunk (back and chest)}}.
extraNote: These areas have a high density of sebaceous glands, providing the lipids necessary for the organism's growth.

clozeText: First-line topical treatment for Tinea versicolor includes {{c1::selenium sulfide}} lotion or topical azoles (e.g., ketoconazole).
extraNote: Selenium sulfide works by promoting the shedding of the stratum corneum and acting as a mild antifungal.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur yeast cells typically exhibit {{c1::unipolar::pattern}} budding with a prominent {{c2::bud scar (collarette)}}.
extraNote: The collarette is a characteristic rim seen where the daughter cell has pinched off from the mother cell.

clozeText: Tinea versicolor is more common in {{c1::hot and humid::climate}} environments, which promote fungal overgrowth.
extraNote: Increased sweating (hyperhidrosis) and lipid production in these climates facilitate the transition from yeast to pathogenic hyphal forms.

clozeText: The hyphae of Malassezia furfur in clinical specimens are described as {{c1::short, thick, and non-branching}}.
extraNote: These represent the mold-like phase induced by environmental triggers (heat/moisture).

clozeText: In Tinea versicolor, Malassezia furfur is restricted to the {{c1::stratum corneum::skin layer}}, the outermost layer of the epidermis.
extraNote: As a superficial mycosis, it does not penetrate into the deeper dermis or cause systemic inflammation in healthy hosts.

clozeText: The hyperpigmentation occasionally seen in Malassezia furfur infections is thought to be caused by {{c1::increased melanosome size}} and an inflammatory response.
extraNote: The organism can present as either hypo- or hyperpigmented, hence the name 'versicolor'.

clozeText: In neonates with Malassezia fungemia, the primary management step is {{c1::discontinuation of lipid infusions}} and removal of the contaminated catheter.
extraNote: Antifungal therapy (e.g., Amphotericin B) may be used, but removing the lipid source is critical.

clozeText: Unlike dermatophytes, Malassezia furfur is a {{c1::yeast::fungal type}}, not a mold (monomorphic filamentous fungus).
extraNote: While it can form hyphae (dimorphism), its primary state in the environment and flora is as a yeast.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur belongs to the phylum {{c1::Basidiomycota}}.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from many other pathogenic fungi (like Candida or Dermatophytes) which are Ascomycota.

clozeText: The scaling in Tinea versicolor is often described as {{c1::furfuraceous::texture}} (fine, bran-like scales).
extraNote: Scraping the lesion with a glass slide or scalpel easily produces these fine scales for KOH testing.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur can cause {{c1::folliculitis::condition}}, an infection of the hair follicles that presents as itchy papulopustules on the back.
extraNote: This is often confused with bacterial acne but does not respond to typical acne medications.

clozeText: Systemic treatment for Tinea versicolor, if needed, usually involves {{c1::oral azoles}} like fluconazole or itraconazole.
extraNote: Oral terbinafine is notably ineffective for Tinea versicolor, unlike its use in dermatophyte infections.

clozeText: The pathogenesis of Tinea versicolor involves the transition of Malassezia from a {{c1::commensal yeast}} to an {{c2::opportunistic hyphal}} form.
extraNote: Factors like immunosuppression, high cortisol, or high humidity trigger this transition.

clozeText: The term "Pityriasis" in Pityriasis versicolor refers to the {{c1::fine scales::physical feature}} associated with the rash.
extraNote: The scales are most visible when the skin is stretched or scraped.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur remains on the surface of the skin because it is {{c1::keratinophilic::affinity}} and utilizes skin oils.
extraNote: It lacks the ability to invade living tissue in immunocompetent hosts, keeping the infection superficial.

clozeText: Pityriasis versicolor patches {{c1::do not::do/do not}} tan when exposed to sunlight.
extraNote: This makes the lesions more prominent in the summer months against the background of tanned, healthy skin.

clozeText: Malassezia species are unique among yeasts for having a {{c1::thick, multilayered cell wall}} that is rich in lipids.
extraNote: This wall provides resistance to environmental stressors and assists in immune evasion.

clozeText: In clinical diagnosis, the {{c1::"Cigarette paper" sign}} refers to the fine wrinkling of the skin seen when scaling occurs in Tinea versicolor.
extraNote: It is a subtle clinical sign that indicates involvement of the stratum corneum.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::lipase::enzyme}} is produced by Malassezia furfur to break down skin triglycerides into free fatty acids.
extraNote: These fatty acids are then utilized by the fungus for energy and can also contribute to skin irritation.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur is often differentiated from Malassezia globosa, with {{c1::M. globosa}} being the most common species associated with Tinea versicolor globally.
extraNote: However, for USMLE Step 1, 'M. furfur' is the historical and frequently tested name for the complex.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur causes {{c1::Pityriasis (Tinea) versicolor::disease}}, a superficial fungal infection of the skin.
extraNote: This presents as hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches, typically on the trunk and back.

clozeText: On KOH preparation, Malassezia furfur displays a classic {{c1::spaghetti and meatballs::morphology}} appearance.
extraNote: This refers to the combination of short, curved hyphae and round yeast cells.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur is a {{c1::lipophilic::metabolism}} fungus, meaning it requires lipids for growth.
extraNote: In the laboratory, this is often achieved by adding an olive oil overlay to the culture medium.

clozeText: The hypopigmentation in Pityriasis versicolor is caused by {{c1::azelaic acid::molecule}}, which inhibits tyrosinase.
extraNote: Tyrosinase is a key enzyme in melanin synthesis; its inhibition leads to lightened skin patches.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur is part of the {{c1::normal skin flora::origin}} and is normally found in the stratum corneum.
extraNote: It only becomes pathogenic under specific conditions like heat, humidity, or immunosuppression.

clozeText: Neonates receiving {{c1::Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)::treatment}} are at high risk for Malassezia furfur fungemia.
extraNote: TPN contains lipid emulsions (long-chain fatty acids) which promote the growth of this lipophilic yeast in catheters.

clozeText: Under a Wood's lamp, lesions of Pityriasis versicolor show a {{c1::yellow-gold::color}} fluorescence.
extraNote: This is a quick bedside diagnostic tool used to differentiate it from other skin conditions like vitiligo (which shows no fluorescence).

clozeText: First-line topical treatment for Pityriasis versicolor includes {{c1::selenium sulfide::drug}} (Selsun Blue).
extraNote: Topical azoles (like ketoconazole) are also frequently used for localized infections.

clozeText: Malassezia species are associated with {{c1::seborrheic dermatitis::disease}}, which presents as greasy scales on the scalp or face.
extraNote: Commonly known as dandruff in adults and 'cradle cap' in infants.

clozeText: The "spaghetti" part of the microscopic appearance of M. furfur consists of {{c1::short, curved hyphae::structure}}.
extraNote: The 'meatballs' are the thick-walled round yeast cells.

clozeText: Pityriasis versicolor lesions typically fail to {{c1::tan::action}} when exposed to sunlight.
extraNote: This makes the hypopigmented patches more prominent in the summer months.

clozeText: The fungal cells of Malassezia furfur remain confined to the {{c1::stratum corneum::skin layer}} of the epidermis.
extraNote: It is a strictly superficial mycosis and does not invade deeper tissues unless systemic fungemia occurs.

clozeText: Severe or refractory cases of Pityriasis versicolor may require {{c1::oral itraconazole::drug}} or fluconazole.
extraNote: Oral ketoconazole is less preferred now due to its side effect profile (e.g., hepatotoxicity).

clozeText: Malassezia furfur fungemia in catheterized patients is often associated with the infusion of {{c1::lipid emulsions::nutrient}}.
extraNote: The yeast colonizes the catheter surface where it thrives on the high-fat environment of the TPN.

clozeText: Seborrheic dermatitis associated with Malassezia is particularly common in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS::condition}} or Parkinson's disease.
extraNote: These populations show higher rates of severe, inflammatory skin involvement.

clozeText: The mechanism of hyperpigmentation in M. furfur infection involves the {{c1::inflammatory response::mechanism}} or enlargement of melanosomes.
extraNote: While hypopigmentation is due to acid-induced tyrosinase inhibition, hyperpigmentation is less well understood but linked to inflammation.

clozeText: In laboratory culture, M. furfur requires specific supplementation with {{c1::long-chain fatty acids::requirement}} for survival.
extraNote: Dixon's agar or Sabouraud's agar with olive oil are standard choices.

clozeText: The term "versicolor" refers to the {{c1::variable colors::meaning}} (pink, brown, or white) that the skin patches can take.
extraNote: The presentation varies based on the patient's baseline skin tone and recent sun exposure.

clozeText: M. furfur is a {{c1::dimorphic::classification}} fungus, although it is often described simply as a yeast-like organism.
extraNote: It can exist in both yeast and mycelial forms, though both are typically seen together on KOH from skin scrapings.

clozeText: Tinea versicolor is more common in {{c1::hot and humid::environment}} climates.
extraNote: Excessive sweating and high moisture levels promote the conversion of the yeast to the pathogenic hyphal form.

clozeText: The diagnosis of M. furfur infection is primarily {{c1::clinical and microscopic::method}} rather than by culture.
extraNote: Culture is difficult due to the specialized lipid requirements and is usually unnecessary given the classic KOH findings.

clozeText: Differential diagnosis for hypopigmented Pityriasis versicolor often includes {{c1::vitiligo::disease}} and pityriasis alba.
extraNote: Vitiligo is an autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, whereas Pityriasis versicolor is an infectious inhibition of melanin synthesis.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur-related fungemia should be suspected when a neonate on TPN has {{c1::negative blood cultures::finding}} on standard media.
extraNote: Standard blood culture media may not contain the necessary lipids for Malassezia growth; specialized lipid-enriched media is needed.

clozeText: {{c1::Ketoconazole shampoo::treatment}} is a common treatment for seborrheic dermatitis caused by Malassezia.
extraNote: It works by reducing the fungal load on the scalp.

clozeText: The round cells seen in M. furfur KOH preps are often described as having a {{c1::collarette::structure}} from which daughter cells bud.
extraNote: This 'phialide' structure is a characteristic feature of the genus Malassezia.

clozeText: Malassezia furfur belongs to the phylum {{c1::Basidiomycota::classification}}.
extraNote: This is unique as most other common dermatological fungi belong to Ascomycota.

clozeText: Pityriasis versicolor is {{c1::not::(is/is not)}} contagious.
extraNote: Because it is caused by an overgrowth of normal skin flora rather than transmission from another person.

clozeText: In the presence of infection, the yeast form of Malassezia transforms into the {{c1::hyphal::form}} form.
extraNote: The hyphal form is associated with tissue invasion in the stratum corneum and clinical disease.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is a {{c1::dimorphic}} fungus, existing as a mold in nature and a yeast in human tissue.
extraNote: Thermal dimorphism is a classic feature of systemic and subcutaneous mycoses.

clozeText: At 25°C (room temperature), Sporothrix schenckii grows as a mold with branching hyphae and {{c1::daisy-like::arrangement}} conidia.
extraNote: The conidia are often described as 'rosette-like' or forming a daisy-wheel pattern at the tips of conidiophores.

clozeText: At 37°C (body temperature), Sporothrix schenckii grows as a yeast characterized by {{c1::cigar-shaped}} cells.
extraNote: In contrast to many other fungi that appear round/oval, these elongated 'cigar' shapes are highly diagnostic.

clozeText: The classic clinical presentation of Sporothrix infection is known as {{c1::Rose gardener's}} disease.
extraNote: It is associated with traumatic inoculation by thorns, splinters, or sphagnum moss.

clozeText: Transmission of Sporothrix schenckii typically occurs via {{c1::traumatic inoculation}} into the skin.
extraNote: Common sources include decaying vegetation, rose bushes, and mulch.

clozeText: In lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis, a primary nodule forms at the site of entry and is followed by {{c1::ascending lymphangitis}}.
extraNote: This presents as a chain of secondary nodules along the lymphatic drainage pathway.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is {{c1::itraconazole}}.
extraNote: Treatment usually lasts 3 to 6 months.

clozeText: A historical high-yield treatment for cutaneous sporotrichosis, though rarely used now, is {{c1::Potassium iodide (SSKI)}}.
extraNote: Potassium iodide is administered in milk or juice to mask the taste.

clozeText: Histopathology of sporotrichosis may reveal {{c1::asteroid bodies}}, which consist of yeast cells surrounded by eosinophilic radiates.
extraNote: This is known as the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon.

clozeText: Unlike most other fungi, Sporothrix is often difficult to see on H&E or silver stain; therefore, {{c1::culture}} is the gold standard for diagnosis.
extraNote: Fungal culture from biopsied tissue or pus is the most sensitive method.

clozeText: The {{c1::splendore-hoeppli}} phenomenon describes the eosinophilic material (antigen-antibody complexes) seen around Sporothrix yeast in tissue.
extraNote: It is a non-specific but characteristic histological finding.

clozeText: Pulmonary sporotrichosis is most commonly seen in patients with {{c1::alcoholism::comorbidity}} who inhale the spores.
extraNote: It often presents similarly to tuberculosis (cavitary lesions in the upper lobes).

clozeText: The differential diagnosis for sporotrichoid (linear) spread of nodules includes {{c1::Nocardia brasiliensis::Bacteria}} and Mycobacterium marinum.
extraNote: Nocardia is partially acid-fast, and M. marinum is associated with fish tanks.

clozeText: In Brazil, a significant number of Sporothrix cases are transmitted by {{c1::cats}}.
extraNote: This is specifically associated with Sporothrix brasiliensis, a more virulent species.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii belongs to the category of {{c1::subcutaneous}} mycoses.
extraNote: These infections involve the dermis, subcutaneous tissues, and adjacent lymphatics.

clozeText: Disseminated sporotrichosis is usually seen in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS::immunocompromise}}.
extraNote: It can involve the joints, bones, and meninges.

clozeText: For disseminated or meningeal sporotrichosis, the initial treatment of choice is {{c1::amphotericin B}}.
extraNote: This is followed by long-term suppression with itraconazole.

clozeText: The initial nodule in sporotrichosis is typically {{c1::painless}} but eventually ulcerates and discharges pus.
extraNote: The lack of initial pain often delays patients seeking medical attention.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii utilizes {{c1::melanin::pigment}} as a virulence factor to protect against oxidative stress and UV radiation.
extraNote: Melanized fungi are often more resistant to host immune responses.

clozeText: Culture of Sporothrix on {{c1::Sabouraud}} agar at 25°C typically results in moist, wrinkled colonies that turn black/brown over time.
extraNote: The darkening is due to the production of melanin in the conidia.

clozeText: The cell wall of Sporothrix contains {{c1::rhamnomannans}}, which are antigenic markers used in some experimental diagnostic assays.
extraNote: These cell wall components are key targets for the immune system.

clozeText: Sporotrichoid spread refers to nodules following the path of {{c1::lymphatic vessels}}.
extraNote: This is a key physical exam finding for subcutaneous fungal infections.

clozeText: The conversion from mold to yeast form in Sporothrix is triggered by a temperature of {{c1::37}}°C.
extraNote: This shift is essential for the organism to establish infection in the host.

clozeText: Extracutaneous sporotrichosis most commonly affects the {{c1::joints::location}}, specifically the knees, elbows, and wrists.
extraNote: This is often termed 'sporotrichoid arthritis'.

clozeText: The conidia of Sporothrix are produced by specialized hyphae called {{c1::conidiophores}}.
extraNote: They are attached by very thin stalks, giving them the rosette appearance.

clozeText: Fixed cutaneous sporotrichosis differs from the lymphocutaneous form because it {{c1::does not spread}} via the lymphatics.
extraNote: It remains as a single lesion at the site of inoculation, often seen in endemic areas with high host immunity.

clozeText: Sporothrix is found worldwide but is most prevalent in {{c1::temperate and tropical}} regions.
extraNote: Mexico, South Africa, and Japan are notable endemic zones.

clozeText: The most common laboratory-acquired fungal infection is often cited as {{c1::sporotrichosis}}.
extraNote: Researchers must use caution when handling cultures with aerosolized conidia.

clozeText: {{c1::Sporothrix schenckii}} is a thermally {{c2::dimorphic::property}} fungus that causes "rose gardener's disease."
extraNote: It exists as a mold in the environment and a yeast in the human body (37°C).

clozeText: In its mold form (25°C), Sporothrix schenckii is characterized by {{c1::septate hyphae}} with {{c2::daisy-like::arrangement}} conidia.
extraNote: This branching, flower-like appearance is a classic diagnostic clue on culture.

clozeText: In its yeast form (37°C), Sporothrix schenckii is famously described as being {{c1::cigar-shaped}}.
extraNote: The yeast are pleomorphic, appearing as oval or elongated buds.

clozeText: The most common route of transmission for Sporothrix schenckii is {{c1::traumatic inoculation}} of soil, moss, or decaying vegetation.
extraNote: Typical scenarios involve rose thorns, splinters, or sphagnum moss.

clozeText: The classic clinical presentation of {{c1::lymphocutaneous::type}} sporotrichosis involves a primary nodule that eventually ulcerates and follows {{c2::lymphatic::direction}} drainage.
extraNote: This results in a linear chain of nodules along the arm or leg.

clozeText: {{c1::Sporotrichoid spread}} is the term for the proximal progression of subcutaneous nodules along lymphatic channels.
extraNote: Differential diagnosis includes Nocardia, Mycobacterium marinum, and Leishmania.

clozeText: Besides rose thorns, exposure to {{c1::sphagnum moss}} is a high-yield risk factor for acquiring Sporothrix schenckii.
extraNote: It is often found in soil and mulch used by florists and gardeners.

clozeText: The histological finding of a yeast cell surrounded by eosinophilic, radiating intensely stained material is known as an {{c1::asteroid body}}.
extraNote: This represents the Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon (antigen-antibody complexes).

clozeText: While rare, {{c1::pulmonary::organ}} sporotrichosis can occur via {{c2::inhalation::route}}, particularly in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or alcoholism.
extraNote: It typically presents as cavitary lesions similar to tuberculosis.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating localized lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis is {{c1::Itraconazole}}.
extraNote: Treatment is typically continued for 3 to 6 months.

clozeText: An older, historical treatment for cutaneous sporotrichosis that is still tested is {{c1::Potassium iodide (SSKI)}}.
extraNote: It is administered as a saturated solution; side effects include parotitis and a metallic taste.

clozeText: For disseminated or life-threatening Sporothrix schenckii infections, the treatment of choice is {{c1::Amphotericin B}}.
extraNote: Once stabilized, patients are often transitioned to oral Itraconazole.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is a {{c1::subcutaneous::category}} mycosis, meaning it primarily affects the dermis and underlying tissues.
extraNote: Unlike superficial mycoses, it often involves the lymphatic system.

clozeText: {{c1::Alcoholism}} and immunosuppression are significant risk factors for the {{c2::disseminated::clinical form}} form of sporotrichosis.
extraNote: Dissemination can involve the joints (arthritis) and the central nervous system.

clozeText: In Brazil, a significant number of Sporothrix infections are transmitted via {{c1::cat scratches::vector}}.
extraNote: This is specifically associated with the species Sporothrix brasiliensis.

clozeText: Biopsy of a Sporothrix lesion typically reveals a {{c1::mixed pyogenic and granulomatous}} inflammatory response.
extraNote: This combination is a hallmark of many deep fungal and certain bacterial infections (like Nocardia).

clozeText: The definitive gold standard for the diagnosis of sporotrichosis is {{c1::culture}} of tissue or aspirated pus.
extraNote: The dimorphism must be demonstrated by growing it at two different temperatures.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii yeast are typically {{c1::4-6}} micrometers in size.
extraNote: They are much smaller than the spherules of Coccidioides.

clozeText: The {{c1::fixed cutaneous::variant}} form of sporotrichosis presents as a single ulcerated or non-ulcerated lesion without lymphatic spread.
extraNote: This form is more common in endemic areas where people have partial immunity.

clozeText: The {{c1::Splendore-Hoeppli}} phenomenon describes the eosinophilic material surrounding the yeast in an asteroid body.
extraNote: It is not pathognomonic but strongly suggestive in the correct clinical context.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii infection can be differentiated from {{c1::Mycobacterium marinum}} because the latter is usually associated with {{c2::fish tanks::source}} or salt water.
extraNote: Both cause sporotrichoid spread of nodules.

clozeText: Unlike {{c1::Nocardia}}, which is a branching Gram-positive {{c2::aerobic::oxygen requirement}} rod, Sporothrix is a fungus.
extraNote: They both cause similar linear skin nodules and require special stains for identification.

clozeText: The yeast form of Sporothrix is often difficult to see on standard H&E stains and requires {{c1::PAS::stain}} or {{c2::GMS::stain}} silver stains.
extraNote: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) and Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stains highlight fungal cell walls.

clozeText: Involvement of the {{c1::joints::location}} (osteoarticular sporotrichosis) is the most common manifestation of disseminated disease in non-HIV patients.
extraNote: It often presents as a chronic monoarthritis.

clozeText: Potassium iodide (SSKI) is thought to work by {{c1::promoting the lysis}} of fungal cells through immune modulation.
extraNote: It does not have direct antifungal activity in vitro.

clozeText: Wait time for Sporothrix {{c1::culture}} growth is usually {{c2::2-5::days}} days.
extraNote: Rapid growth compared to other systemic fungi like Histoplasma.

clozeText: Sporothrix schenckii is found worldwide but is most prevalent in {{c1::temperate and tropical}} regions.
extraNote: Endemic areas include Mexico, South Africa, and parts of South America.

clozeText: The {{c1::conidiophore}} of Sporothrix schenckii bears the conidia in a characteristic daisy-petal cluster.
extraNote: Identification of this microscopic structure confirms the mold phase.

clozeText: Histoplasma capsulatum is a {{c1::dimorphic::thermal category}} fungus, existing as a mold in the environment and a yeast in the body.
extraNote: Mold in the cold (25°C), yeast in the heat (37°C).

clozeText: Histoplasma is endemic to the {{c1::Mississippi and Ohio::Geographic region}} River Valleys in the United States.
extraNote: Commonly tested in patients presenting with pulmonary symptoms after traveling to the Central/Eastern US.

clozeText: Transmission of Histoplasma occurs via inhalation of spores found in soil contaminated with {{c1::bird or bat}} droppings.
extraNote: Often associated with cleaning chicken coops or spelunking (bat guano in caves).

clozeText: Inside the host, Histoplasma yeast are characteristically found within {{c1::macrophages::cell type}}.
extraNote: They are intracellular parasites of the reticuloendothelial system.

clozeText: Histoplasma yeast are {{c1::smaller::smaller/larger}} than red blood cells, typically measuring 2-4 μm.
extraNote: In contrast, Blastomyces is roughly the same size as an RBC, and Coccidioides (spherules) is much larger.

clozeText: The mold form of Histoplasma produces characteristic {{c1::tuberculate macroconidia::specific structure}} with spike-like protrusions.
extraNote: These are the diagnostic structures seen on culture at 25°C.

clozeText: Histoplasma survives within phagocytes by secreting proteins that {{c1::increase::increase/decrease}} the pH of the phagolysosome.
extraNote: Neutralizing the acidic environment prevents lysosomal enzyme activity.

clozeText: In the lungs, Histoplasma causes the formation of {{c1::granulomas}} that may eventually calcify.
extraNote: Presents similarly to tuberculosis on chest X-ray with hilar lymphadenopathy and calcifications.

clozeText: Disseminated histoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients often presents with {{c1::hepatosplenomegaly::organ sign}}.
extraNote: The fungus targets the reticuloendothelial system, including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

clozeText: A high-yield physical exam finding in disseminated histoplasmosis is the presence of {{c1::palatal or tongue ulcers}}.
extraNote: Painful mucosal ulcers are a classic sign of dissemination in HIV-positive patients.

clozeText: In patients with AIDS, Histoplasma dissemination typically occurs when the CD4 count is less than {{c1::150::number}} cells/mm³.
extraNote: This is a key threshold for opportunistic fungal infections in HIV management.

clozeText: The most sensitive rapid diagnostic test for disseminated histoplasmosis is the {{c1::urinary antigen::test type}} assay.
extraNote: Can also be detected in the serum; more rapid than culture which can take weeks.

clozeText: Histoplasma yeast can be visualized in tissue using {{c1::Gomori methenamine silver (GMS)}} or PAS stains.
extraNote: Silver stains help distinguish the small yeast from other intracellular structures.

clozeText: The drug of choice for severe or disseminated histoplasmosis is {{c1::Amphotericin B}}.
extraNote: Once stabilized, patients are often switched to long-term azole therapy.

clozeText: For mild to moderate pulmonary histoplasmosis, the treatment of choice is {{c1::Itraconazole}}.
extraNote: Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis by targeting 14-alpha-demethylase.

clozeText: Histoplasma yeast are described as having {{c1::narrow-based::budding style}} budding.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from Blastomyces, which has broad-based budding.

clozeText: A rare but serious complication of Histoplasma infection is {{c1::fibrosing mediastinitis}}, causing compression of the SVC or bronchi.
extraNote: It is an abnormal fibroinflammatory response to the fungus.

clozeText: Chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis typically occurs in patients with underlying {{c1::COPD::disease}} and presents with cavitary lesions.
extraNote: It mimics secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis.

clozeText: Histoplasma yeast can cause {{c1::pancytopenia::hematologic finding}} if it disseminates to the bone marrow.
extraNote: Commonly seen in advanced HIV/AIDS patients.

clozeText: Histoplasma utilizes {{c1::siderophores}} to acquire iron from the host environment, which is essential for its growth.
extraNote: Iron acquisition is a critical virulence factor in intracellular fungi.

clozeText: Unlike Coccidioides, Histoplasma yeast do {{c1::not}} have a capsule.
extraNote: The name 'capsulatum' is a misnomer based on the halo seen on early Histoplasma slides (which was an artifact).

clozeText: Protection against Histoplasma requires a {{c1::Th1}} cell-mediated immune response and macrophage activation.
extraNote: IL-12 and IFN-gamma are essential for controlling the infection.

clozeText: Reactive skin nodules known as {{c1::erythema nodosum}} can occur during acute histoplasmosis as an immune-mediated response.
extraNote: This is a sign of good cell-mediated immunity.

clozeText: Histoplasma adheres to macrophages via the {{c1::Hsp60::surface protein}} protein binding to CD11/CD18 receptors.
extraNote: Heat shock proteins play roles in both stress response and host cell adherence.

clozeText: Histoplasma capsulatum var. {{c1::duboisii}} is the variant found primarily in Africa, causing more skin and bone lesions.
extraNote: The standard capsulatum variant is more common in the Americas.

clozeText: Primary pulmonary histoplasmosis often presents with incidental {{c1::calcified splenic granulomas}} years after the initial infection.
extraNote: Frequently seen as 'buckshot calcifications' on abdominal imaging.

clozeText: The yeast form of Histoplasma resides within the {{c1::phagosome}} of the macrophage.
extraNote: It prevents phagosome-lysosome fusion or modulates the internal environment to survive.

clozeText: Culture of Histoplasma on {{c1::Sabouraud}} agar at 25°C will reveal white or brownish hyphae.
extraNote: Sabouraud agar is the classic media for fungal isolation.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas no streptococci do.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into O2 and H2O, which helps the bacteria survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) primarily by its production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase is an enzyme that activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then catalyzes the formation of a fibrin clot.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the immunoglobulin from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: MRSA strains are resistant to methicillin and nafcillin due to alterations in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}, encoded by the {{c2::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: The most important of these is PBP2a, which performs transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: The specific substitution in the peptidoglycan of vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) is {{c1::D-lactate::amino acid derivative}} for {{c2::D-alanine}}.
extraNote: This modification is encoded by the same cassette of genes found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate adherence to {{c2::mucosal cells}}.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in S. aureus play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}} from macrophages.
extraNote: S. aureus can cause findings of septic shock despite not possessing true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Abscesses are the classic lesion; common examples include furuncles and boils.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::30}}% of people are chronic carriers of S. aureus, with the {{c2::nose (nares)}} being the primary site of colonization.
extraNote: Colonization in the nose increases the risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the respiratory burst to kill catalase-positive organisms effectively.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: MRSA is specifically highlighted as an important pathogen in this population.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}} and produce {{c2::beta-hemolysis}}.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the source of iron (from hemoglobin) required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: {{c1::Impetigo}} is characterized by crops of vesicles that develop into a {{c2::honey-colored}} crust, caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: This is a common skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI).

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus, resulting in widespread desquamation.
extraNote: This syndrome is most common in infants and young children.

clozeText: Almost all strains of {{c1::community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA)}} produce the {{c2::P-V leukocidin}} toxin.
extraNote: Relatively few strains of healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA) produce this toxin.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately 5% of women, predisposing them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen exotoxin (TSST-1).

clozeText: S. epidermidis is generally {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains possess plasmids encoding {{c2::beta-lactamase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins like penicillin G; nafcillin is used for these penicillin-resistant strains.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for S. aureus in the hospital setting is {{c1::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Handwashing is the most effective way to decrease transmission among hospital personnel and patients.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: Compromised immune status and poor vascularization contribute to increased infection risk.

clozeText: S. aureus peptidoglycan has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, allowing it to activate the {{c2::complement}} and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock without having LPS.

clozeText: The microcapsule of S. aureus is considered {{c1::poorly}} immunogenic, which has hindered the production of an effective vaccine.
extraNote: There are 11 serotypes based on capsular polysaccharide, with types 5 and 8 causing 85% of infections.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: This morphology contrasts with streptococci, which typically appear in chains.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, which presents as small pustules on hair follicles.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of other skin infections like cellulitis.

clozeText: {{c1::Foreign bodies::Sutures/Catheters}} are important predisposing factors for infection by S. aureus.
extraNote: These materials allow the bacteria to evade the immune system and form biofilms.

clozeText: S. aureus causes several toxin-mediated diseases, including {{c1::food poisoning}}, toxic shock syndrome, and {{c2::scalded skin syndrome}}.
extraNote: Food poisoning is typically caused by the ingestion of preformed enterotoxin.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the normal {{c1::skin}} flora but frequently causes infections of {{c2::prosthetic heart valves}} and joints.
extraNote: Its ability to produce biofilms on plastic surfaces is a key virulence factor.

clozeText: Coccidioides is a {{c1::thermally dimorphic::dimorphism type}} fungus, existing as mold in the soil and spherules in tissue.
extraNote: Unlike many other dimorphic fungi, Coccidioides forms spherules containing endospores rather than yeast cells in human tissue.

clozeText: In the environment, Coccidioides forms {{c1::barrel-shaped::shape}} arthroconidia that are easily aerosolized.
extraNote: These arthroconidia are highly infectious and represent a major laboratory safety hazard.

clozeText: Coccidioides is endemic to the {{c1::Southwestern United States::geographic region}}, specifically the San Joaquin Valley of California.
extraNote: It is also found in Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Central/South America.

clozeText: Natural events such as {{c1::earthquakes::disaster type}} or dust storms increase the incidence of Coccidioidomycosis by aerosolizing soil.
extraNote: The Northridge earthquake in 1994 is a classic USMLE example of a spike in cases.

clozeText: Inside the lungs, arthroconidia transform into {{c1::spherules::structure name}} which enlarge and divide internally.
extraNote: The spherules are much larger than red blood cells (up to 60-100 micrometers).

clozeText: Each spherule matures and ruptures, releasing hundreds of {{c1::endospores::released unit}} into the surrounding tissue.
extraNote: Each endospore can then develop into a new spherule, propagating the infection.

clozeText: The clinical syndrome "Valley Fever" consists of a triad of fever, arthralgia, and {{c1::erythema nodosum::skin finding}}.
extraNote: Erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins) is a sign of a robust T-cell response and a good prognosis.

clozeText: Desert Rheumatism refers to the {{c1::arthralgia::symptom}} associated with primary Coccidioidomycosis.
extraNote: This typically affects the knees and ankles.

clozeText: Coccidioides spherules are unique because they are {{c1::larger than::comparison}} a typical red blood cell.
extraNote: This size difference is a key histological feature distinguishing them from Histoplasma or Blastomyces.

clozeText: The risk of disseminated Coccidioidomycosis is highest in {{c1::third-trimester pregnancy::patient group}} due to increased estrogen levels.
extraNote: Coccidioides has estrogen receptors that stimulate its growth and transition.

clozeText: Dissemination of Coccidioides commonly occurs to the {{c1::meninges::organ system}}, skin, and bones.
extraNote: Coccidioidal meningitis is a chronic, life-threatening complication.

clozeText: Ethnic groups at significantly higher risk for disseminated Coccidioides include {{c1::Filipino::ethnicity 1}} and African American populations.
extraNote: Genetic factors related to HLA types and cytokine profiles may play a role.

clozeText: On chest X-ray, chronic Coccidioidomycosis may present as {{c1::thin-walled cavities::radiological finding}}.
extraNote: These cavities can sometimes result in hemoptysis or pneumothorax.

clozeText: The {{c1::complement fixation::test name}} test measures IgG antibodies and is used to monitor the progression of Coccidioidomycosis.
extraNote: A rising titer indicates worsening disease or dissemination.

clozeText: Initial infection with Coccidioides is often detected via {{c1::tube precipitin::test name}} tests which measure IgM antibodies.
extraNote: IgM appears early in the course of the infection.

clozeText: For mild to moderate pulmonary Coccidioidomycosis, the treatment of choice is {{c1::Itraconazole::drug name}} or Fluconazole.
extraNote: Azoles inhibit the synthesis of ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane.

clozeText: Severe or disseminated Coccidioidomycosis is treated with {{c1::Amphotericin B::drug name}}.
extraNote: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol to form pores in the fungal membrane.

clozeText: Patients with Coccidioidal meningitis often require lifelong treatment with {{c1::Fluconazole::drug name}}.
extraNote: Fluconazole has excellent CNS penetration, making it the preferred maintenance therapy for meningitis.

clozeText: Coccidioides thrives in {{c1::alkaline::pH type}} soil with high salt content in semi-arid climates.
extraNote: The fungus remains dormant during dry spells and blooms after rainfall.

clozeText: A positive coccidioidin skin test indicates a {{c1::Type IV::hypersensitivity type}} hypersensitivity reaction.
extraNote: A positive test shows previous exposure and intact cell-mediated immunity.

clozeText: The primary defense against Coccidioides infection is {{c1::cell-mediated::immunity type}} immunity.
extraNote: T-cells and macrophages are required to contain the endospores within granulomas.

clozeText: Biopsy of a Coccidioides lesion typically shows {{c1::granulomatous::inflammation type}} inflammation.
extraNote: The immune system attempts to wall off the spherules, leading to granuloma formation.

clozeText: The two main species of Coccidioides are C. immitis and {{c1::C. posadasii::species name}}.
extraNote: C. immitis is primarily found in California, while C. posadasii is found elsewhere.
