clozeText: Secondary prophylaxis for Cryptococcus in HIV patients is generally discontinued when the CD4 count is > {{c1::100}} for at least {{c2::6::number}} months.
extraNote: Reconstitution of the immune system via HAART is essential for long-term management.

clozeText: Cryptococcal meningitis characteristically presents with a {{c1::low::high/low}} glucose and {{c2::high::high/low}} protein in the CSF.
extraNote: This profile is typical of fungal and bacterial meningitides.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::phenoloxidase}} is required by Cryptococcus to synthesize melanin from catecholamines.
extraNote: This may explain the organism's high affinity for the central nervous system, which is rich in catecholamines.

clozeText: Cryptococcal infection is considered an {{c1::AIDS-defining}} illness.
extraNote: In a patient with unknown HIV status, a positive Cryptococcus test necessitates HIV screening.

clozeText: In addition to meningitis and pneumonia, Cryptococcus can cause skin lesions that resemble {{c1::molluscum contagiosum}}.
extraNote: Disseminated cryptococcosis can present with umbilicated papules in immunocompromised hosts.

clozeText: When performing a lumbar puncture for suspected cryptococcal meningitis, the {{c1::opening pressure}} is usually significantly elevated.
extraNote: Pressures >200 mm H2O are common and diagnostic of increased ICP.

clozeText: The yeast form of Cryptococcus neoformans usually measures {{c1::5–10}} μm in diameter.
extraNote: The wide variation in size and the presence of the capsule are distinctive in microscopic exams.

clozeText: Candida albicans is unique among dimorphic fungi because it forms {{c1::germ tubes::structure}} (hyphae) at 37°C and {{c2::pseudohyphae::structure}} and yeast at 20°C.
extraNote: Mnemonic: 'Yeast in the heat, mold in the cold' is reversed for Candida compared to other systemic mycoses.

clozeText: Incubating Candida albicans in {{c1::animal serum::substance}} at 37°C for 3 hours is used to identify germ tubes.
extraNote: Germ tube formation is a classic diagnostic test for Candida albicans specifically.

clozeText: Candida albicans typically stains {{c1::Gram-positive::stain type}} although it is a fungus.
extraNote: Yeast cells are much larger than bacterial cocci, even though they share the same purple color on Gram stain.

clozeText: The fungal culture medium typically used to grow Candida is {{c1::Sabouraud dextrose agar::medium}}.
extraNote: Candida grows as smooth, white, creamy colonies with a distinct 'yeasty' odor.

clozeText: {{c1::T cells::cell type}} are essential for preventing mucocutaneous (superficial) Candida infections.
extraNote: This is why patients with HIV/AIDS (low T cells) often present with oral thrush or esophagitis.

clozeText: {{c1::Neutrophils::cell type}} are the primary defense against disseminated or systemic Candida infections.
extraNote: Patients with neutropenia (e.g., following chemotherapy) are at high risk for life-threatening candidemia.

clozeText: Oral thrush is characterized by white plaques on the tongue and oropharynx that {{c1::can::can/cannot}} be easily scraped off.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), which cannot be scraped off.

clozeText: Candida {{c1::esophagitis::condition}} is an AIDS-defining illness often occurring when CD4 counts drop below 200.
extraNote: Patients typically present with odynophagia (painful swallowing).

clozeText: Vaginal candidiasis presents with a thick 'cottage cheese' discharge and a vaginal pH that is typically {{c1::normal (<4.5)::pH value}}.
extraNote: This helps differentiate it from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, where pH is usually >4.5.

clozeText: A common skin manifestation of Candida in infants is {{c1::diaper rash::condition}}, which is identified by erythematous patches with {{c2::satellite lesions::classic sign}}.
extraNote: Satellite lesions are small red macules or pustules located outside the main area of redness.

clozeText: Candida albicans is a significant cause of endocarditis in {{c1::intravenous drug users::population}}, frequently involving the {{c2::tricuspid::heart valve}} valve.
extraNote: Fungal endocarditis often produces large vegetations that can embolize to the peripheries.

clozeText: The use of {{c1::broad-spectrum antibiotics::medication class}} is a major risk factor for Candida overgrowth because it reduces the competing normal bacterial flora.
extraNote: This often leads to oral thrush or vaginal candidiasis.

clozeText: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is associated with defects in the {{c1::AIRE::gene}} gene or the {{c2::STAT1::pathway}} signaling pathway.
extraNote: These patients suffer from persistent non-invasive Candida infections of the skin, nails, and mucous membranes.

clozeText: In the presence of {{c1::KOH (Potassium hydroxide)::reagent}}, Candida skin scrapings reveal pseudohyphae and budding yeasts.
extraNote: KOH dissolves skin cells (keratinocytes) but leaves the fungal cell walls intact for visualization.

clozeText: {{c1::Nystatin::medication}} is the preferred topical treatment for oral thrush, often administered as a 'swish and swallow' solution.
extraNote: Nystatin works by binding to ergosterol and forming pores in the fungal cell membrane.

clozeText: For systemic, life-threatening candidemia, {{c1::Amphotericin B::medication}} or {{c2::Echinocandins::medication class}} (like Caspofungin) are used for initial therapy.
extraNote: Echinocandins inhibit the synthesis of beta-glucan in the cell wall.

clozeText: Candida albicans is {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}-positive, which explains why patients with {{c2::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)::condition}} are at increased risk.
extraNote: CGD patients lack NADPH oxidase, preventing them from producing H2O2 to overcome catalase-producing organisms.

clozeText: In cornmeal agar, Candida albicans forms thick-walled terminal structures called {{c1::chlamydospores::structure}}.
extraNote: Chlamydospores are a classic morphological identifier in laboratory diagnostic settings.

clozeText: A high {{c1::estrogen::hormone}} state (e.g., pregnancy or OCP use) increases the risk of vaginal candidiasis by increasing glycogen content in the vaginal mucosa.
extraNote: Increased glycogen provides more nutrients for Candida to thrive.

clozeText: Candida overgrowth in the mouth can be a side effect of using {{c1::inhaled corticosteroids::medication class}}.
extraNote: Patients are advised to rinse their mouth after using inhalers to prevent thrush.

clozeText: {{c1::Fluconazole::drug name}} is the standard oral treatment for localized vulvovaginal candidiasis.
extraNote: It inhibits the enzyme 14-alpha-demethylase, preventing the synthesis of ergosterol.

clozeText: Candida infection of the intertriginous skin folds (e.g., under the breast or in the groin) is known as {{c1::intertrigo::condition}}.
extraNote: It typically presents as a red, macerated rash with satellite pustules.

clozeText: The cell wall component of Candida that can be used as a serum marker for invasive disease is {{c1::1,3-beta-D-glucan::biomarker}}.
extraNote: The Fungitell assay detects this component in the blood.

clozeText: Candida albicans can form {{c1::biofilms::structure}} on prosthetic devices and central venous catheters, making the infection difficult to clear.
extraNote: Biofilms protect the organism from the host immune response and antifungal drugs.

clozeText: In patients with {{c1::Diabetes Mellitus::condition}}, glycosuria and high skin glucose levels predispose to both vaginal and cutaneous Candida infections.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function, further increasing risk.

clozeText: Candida parapsilosis is a species frequently associated with infections of {{c1::vascular catheters::device type}} and parenteral nutrition.
extraNote: While C. albicans is most common, other species like C. parapsilosis and C. glabrata are medically significant.

clozeText: The presence of Candida in a {{c1::blood culture::test type}} is never considered a contaminant and always indicates a serious infection.
extraNote: Candidemia requires prompt treatment and usually removal of any suspect intravenous lines.

clozeText: Candida albicans undergoes {{c1::phenotypic switching::process}}, allowing it to change its morphology and surface antigens to adapt to different host environments.
extraNote: This contributes to its success as both a commensal and a pathogen.

clozeText: Candida albicans is dimorphic, forming {{c1::pseudohyphae}} and budding yeasts at 20°C (cold).
extraNote: Unlike most fungi, Candida is 'opposite' in its dimorphism: it forms germ tubes in the heat (37°C).

clozeText: At 37°C (warm), Candida albicans forms {{c1::germ tubes::morphology}}, which are true hyphae.
extraNote: Germ tube formation in serum is a rapid diagnostic test for C. albicans.

clozeText: Candida albicans is {{c1::catalase}}-positive, making patients with Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) highly susceptible to infection.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in NADPH oxidase, leading to failure to clear catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: Oral thrush caused by Candida {{c1::can::can/cannot}} be scraped off the mucosa.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Oral Hairy Leukoplakia (EBV), which cannot be scraped off.

clozeText: Vulvovaginal candidiasis typically presents with a 'cottage cheese' discharge and a vaginal pH that is {{c1::normal::normal/elevated}} (< 4.5).
extraNote: The pH remains normal (<4.5), unlike Trichomoniasis or Bacterial Vaginosis where pH is >4.5.

clozeText: Superficial Candida infections (e.g., thrush) are prevented by {{c1::T-cells}}, whereas disseminated infections are prevented by {{c2::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: This explains why HIV patients get thrush (low T-cells) and neutropenic patients get candidemia.

clozeText: Esophageal candidiasis is an {{c1::AIDS-defining}} illness, typically occurring when the CD4 count is < 200.
extraNote: Presents with odynophagia (painful swallowing).

clozeText: Candida endocarditis is most commonly seen in {{c1::intravenous drug users (IVDU)}} and often affects the {{c2::tricuspid}} valve.
extraNote: It is a common cause of fungal endocarditis and may require surgical valve replacement.

clozeText: In infants, Candida albicans causes a diaper rash characterized by a red rash with {{c1::satellite lesions}}.
extraNote: Satellite lesions are small red papules or pustules located just beyond the main border of the rash.

clozeText: The treatment for mild oral thrush or vaginal candidiasis is often {{c1::Nystatin}} (topical) or {{c2::Fluconazole}} (oral).
extraNote: Nystatin uses a 'swish and spit' method for oral lesions.

clozeText: Severe or systemic Candida infections are treated with {{c1::Amphotericin B}} or {{c2::Echinocandins::drug class}} (e.g., Caspofungin).
extraNote: Echinocandins inhibit the synthesis of beta-glucan in the fungal cell wall.

clozeText: Candida albicans can form {{c1::chlamydospores}} on cornmeal agar.
extraNote: These are thick-walled resting spores used for laboratory identification.

clozeText: Azole antifungals (like Fluconazole) work by inhibiting the enzyme {{c1::14-α-demethylase}}, which prevents ergosterol synthesis.
extraNote: This enzyme is part of the P450 system.

clozeText: Amphotericin B and Nystatin work by binding directly to {{c1::ergosterol}} in the fungal cell membrane.
extraNote: This creates pores that cause leakage of electrolytes and cell death.

clozeText: {{c1::Chronic Mucocutaneous Candidiasis}} is a genetic condition involving T-cell dysfunction (often AIRE gene) leading to persistent skin/nail infections.
extraNote: Associated with endocrine abnormalities like hypoparathyroidism.

clozeText: Risk factors for vaginal candidiasis include recent {{c1::antibiotic use}}, pregnancy, and uncontrolled diabetes.
extraNote: Antibiotics (especially broad-spectrum) decrease the Lactobacillus population, allowing Candida overgrowth.

clozeText: Candida is a common cause of {{c1::intertrigo}}, an inflammatory condition of skin folds (e.g., under the breasts or in the groin).
extraNote: The moist, warm environment of skin folds promotes fungal growth.

clozeText: Systemic candidiasis (candidemia) can lead to fungal {{c1::endophthalmitis}}, requiring a dilated eye exam for all patients with positive blood cultures.
extraNote: Early detection prevents permanent vision loss.

clozeText: In the laboratory, Candida is grown on {{c1::Sabouraud::Agar}} dextrose agar.
extraNote: The low pH of this agar inhibits bacterial growth while favoring fungi.

clozeText: The echinocandin class (e.g., micafungin) inhibits the synthesis of {{c1::β-glucan}}, a critical component of the fungal cell wall.
extraNote: This is often the first-line treatment for candidemia in stable patients.

clozeText: Candida albicans is considered {{c1::normal flora}} of the skin, mouth, GI tract, and vagina.
extraNote: Infection is usually endogenous, arising from overgrowth of the patient's own flora.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of Candida using a {{c1::KOH}} prep reveals budding yeast and pseudohyphae.
extraNote: Potassium hydroxide (KOH) dissolves epithelial cells, making the fungal elements easier to see.

clozeText: A patient with {{c1::Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)}} or central venous catheters is at high risk for healthcare-associated candidemia.
extraNote: Candida can colonize catheters and form biofilms.

clozeText: {{c1::Neutropenia}} is the single most important risk factor for the development of disseminated/visceral candidiasis.
extraNote: Without neutrophils, the fungus can invade the bloodstream and organs like the liver and spleen.

clozeText: Oral candidiasis in an adult without known risk factors should prompt testing for {{c1::HIV/AIDS}}.
extraNote: It is often the first clinical sign of immunosuppression.

clozeText: Flucytosine is often used in combination with {{c1::Amphotericin B}} to treat severe systemic Candida infections.
extraNote: Flucytosine inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis.

clozeText: Right-sided endocarditis in an IV drug user with large vegetations on the tricuspid valve suggests {{c1::Candida albicans}} (or S. aureus).
extraNote: Fungal vegetations tend to be larger than bacterial ones.

clozeText: The primary mechanism of resistance to azoles in Candida is via {{c1::efflux pumps}} or mutations in the target enzyme.
extraNote: This is a significant concern in species like C. glabrata and C. auris.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas no streptococci do.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, serving as a virulence factor that helps bacteria survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike most other staphylococci, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β (beta)}} hemolysis.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides a source of iron, which is recovered and utilized in the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes for energy production.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions for cell wall synthesis but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: In the United States, {{c1::MRSA}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses.
extraNote: It is also a significant cause of pneumonia, necrotizing fasciitis, and sepsis in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised patients.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This include endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of developing skin infections.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This mechanism is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci and is often carried on a transposon within a plasmid.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also function as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which trigger the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mimics the action of Gram-negative endotoxin, although S. aureus does not possess true endotoxin.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus causes disease both through pyogenic inflammation and toxin production.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}.
extraNote: This toxin is much less common in healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA).

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the respiratory burst necessary to kill catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::peptidoglycan}} has endotoxin-like properties, stimulating macrophages and activating the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains the clinical findings of shock in the absence of traditional Gram-negative LPS.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is characterized by widespread desquamation of the skin, often in infants.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is differentiated from Staphylococcus saprophyticus by its sensitivity to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections on {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and often gains access during surgery or through catheters.

clozeText: The {{c1::USA300}} strain is the most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States.
extraNote: It is associated with both skin infections and severe necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: S. aureus produces {{c1::β-lactamase}}, an enzyme that degrades many penicillins; it is encoded by {{c2::plasmids}} in >90% of strains.
extraNote: This necessitates the use of β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin or oxacillin.

clozeText: Staphylococcal impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles.
extraNote: Clinical presentation includes multiple small pustules, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: S. aureus is a significant cause of {{c1::food poisoning}}, which is mediated by a preformed toxin.
extraNote: The clinical course is typically rapid in onset and characterized by vomiting.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is poorly {{c1::immunogenic}}, which has made development of an effective vaccine difficult.
extraNote: There are 11 serotypes, but types 5 and 8 cause the majority of infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: Other factors include reduced humoral immunity (low antibodies/complement) and neutrophil defects.

clozeText: S. aureus can be found in the {{c1::vagina}} of approximately 5% of women, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is associated with superantigen production during tampon use or wound infections.

clozeText: In the laboratory, the formation of a {{c1::fibrin clot}} in a tube of plasma indicates a positive result for S. aureus.
extraNote: This is the definitive biochemical test for differentiating S. aureus from coagulase-negative species.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans is a heavily {{c1::encapsulated}} yeast that is not dimorphic.
extraNote: Unlike many other systemic fungi, it exists only as a yeast (monomorphic).

clozeText: The primary reservoir for Cryptococcus neoformans is {{c1::pigeon droppings::animal vector}}.
extraNote: Infection is acquired via inhalation into the lungs.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans capsule is composed of {{c1::glucuronoxylomannan}}, which is the major virulence factor.
extraNote: The polysaccharide capsule inhibits phagocytosis and leukocyte migration.

clozeText: On microscopy, Cryptococcus neoformans is characterized by {{c1::narrow-based::budding style}} budding.
extraNote: This helps distinguish it from Blastomyces, which has broad-based budding.

clozeText: {{c1::India ink}} stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows yeast with a clear halo against a dark background.
extraNote: The halo represents the thick, non-staining polysaccharide capsule.

clozeText: {{c1::Mucicarmine}} stain can be used to specifically identify the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans by staining it red.
extraNote: It is a tissue stain useful in pathology specimens.

clozeText: The most sensitive test for cryptococcal meningitis is the {{c1::latex agglutination}} test, which detects the capsular polysaccharide antigen.
extraNote: This test is more sensitive and specific than India ink.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans is {{c1::urease::biochemical test}} positive.
extraNote: This is a key biochemical differentiator from many other yeasts.

clozeText: Cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS patients typically occurs when the CD4 count is less than {{c1::100}} cells/mm³.
extraNote: It is a major AIDS-defining illness.

clozeText: Brain MRI of a patient with Cryptococcus may show {{c1::soap bubble::imaging finding}} lesions in the basal ganglia.
extraNote: These represent gelatinous pseudocysts caused by the expansion of perivascular (Virchow-Robin) spaces.

clozeText: The standard induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis is {{c1::Amphotericin B}} plus {{c2::Flucytosine}}.
extraNote: This combination is used for initial aggressive therapy (usually 2 weeks).

clozeText: Following induction therapy, patients with cryptococcal meningitis require long-term maintenance with {{c1::Fluconazole}}.
extraNote: Maintenance prevents relapse in immunocompromised patients.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans produces the enzyme {{c1::phenyloxidase}}, which produces melanin as a virulence factor.
extraNote: Melanin protects the fungus from oxidative stress within the host.

clozeText: In patients with cryptococcal meningitis, lumbar puncture often reveals significantly {{c1::increased}} opening pressure.
extraNote: Serial lumbar punctures may be necessary to manage intracranial pressure.

clozeText: Disseminated Cryptococcus in immunocompromised patients can cause skin lesions that resemble {{c1::molluscum contagiosum}}.
extraNote: These present as umbilicated papules.

clozeText: The mechanism of {{c1::Flucytosine}} involves conversion to 5-fluorouracil, which inhibits DNA and RNA synthesis.
extraNote: Its primary toxicity is bone marrow suppression.

clozeText: Amphotericin B works by binding to {{c1::ergosterol}} and forming pores in the fungal cell membrane.
extraNote: The major side effect is nephrotoxicity.

clozeText: Fluconazole inhibits the enzyme {{c1::14-alpha-demethylase::specific enzyme}}, preventing the conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol.
extraNote: It is a member of the azole class of antifungals.

clozeText: The clear areas surrounding yeast cells in a {{c1::GMS (Grocott-Gomori Methenamine Silver)}} stain help visualize Cryptococcus in tissue.
extraNote: PAS (Periodic acid-Schiff) is also commonly used.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans primarily enters the body via the {{c1::respiratory}} tract.
extraNote: Lung infection can be asymptomatic or cause pneumonia before spreading to the CNS.

clozeText: Cryptococcus neoformans grows on {{c1::Sabouraud::agar type}} agar.
extraNote: It forms creamy, mucoid colonies due to the abundant capsule.

clozeText: A common complication of cryptococcal meningitis that results in permanent neurological damage is {{c1::hydrocephalus}}.
extraNote: It is usually communicating hydrocephalus due to decreased resorption of CSF by arachnoid granulations.

clozeText: While C. neoformans is found worldwide in bird droppings, {{c1::Cryptococcus gattii}} is associated with Eucalyptus trees and can infect immunocompetent hosts.
extraNote: C. gattii is an important differential for Cryptococcus in the Pacific Northwest.

clozeText: In the CNS, Cryptococcus has a predilection for the {{c1::Virchow-Robin}} spaces.
extraNote: Expansion of these spaces by fungal polysaccharide leads to the soap bubble appearance.

clozeText: High doses of {{c1::corticosteroids}} are a significant risk factor for disseminated cryptococcosis.
extraNote: Steroids impair cell-mediated immunity required to contain the fungus.

clozeText: Unlike most other fungi, Cryptococcus is considered {{c1::monomorphic}} because it lacks a mold phase.
extraNote: It is always found as a yeast at both environmental and body temperatures.

clozeText: Detection of cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) in the {{c1::serum}} can be a screening tool in AIDS patients with low CD4 counts.
extraNote: Positive serum CrAg often precedes clinical meningitis.

clozeText: Pulmonary cryptococcosis may present on a chest X-ray as solitary or multiple {{c1::nodules}}.
extraNote: It may be misdiagnosed as malignancy in non-HIV patients.

clozeText: Adenoviruses have a {{c1::double-stranded (dsDNA)}} genome that is {{c2::linear::shape}} in structure.
extraNote: Unlike many other DNA viruses, Adenovirus is not circular.

clozeText: Adenoviruses are described as {{c1::naked::envelope?}} and possess an {{c2::icosahedral}} nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Lack of an envelope makes them resistant to detergents and environmental degradation.

clozeText: The attachment of Adenoviruses to host cells is mediated by {{c1::penton fibers::structure}} that project from the icosahedral vertices.
extraNote: These fibers act as hemagglutinins and are essential for viral entry.

clozeText: The primary cellular receptor for most Adenoviruses is the {{c1::CAR (Coxsackievirus and Adenovirus Receptor)}}.
extraNote: Understanding the receptor helps explain the viral tropism for various epithelial surfaces.

clozeText: Adenovirus is a common cause of {{c1::pharyngoconjunctival fever}}, which typically presents with the triad of fever, pharyngitis, and conjunctivitis.
extraNote: Outbreaks are frequently associated with swimming pools or summer camps.

clozeText: Adenovirus serotypes {{c1::4 and 7}} are high-yield causes of severe pneumonia among {{c2::military recruits}}.
extraNote: A live, non-attenuated oral vaccine is administered to this specific population to prevent outbreaks.

clozeText: Adenovirus serotypes {{c1::40 and 41}} are specifically associated with {{c2::infantile gastroenteritis}}.
extraNote: They are the second most common cause of viral diarrhea in children after Rotavirus.

clozeText: In children, Adenovirus is a leading cause of {{c1::acute hemorrhagic cystitis}}, characterized by gross hematuria.
extraNote: This condition is self-limiting but can be alarming due to the presence of blood in the urine.

clozeText: Adenovirus can cause {{c1::epidemic keratoconjunctivitis}} (also known as 'shipyard eye'), which is highly contagious and often associated with ophthalmic clinics.
extraNote: Transmission usually occurs via contaminated medical instruments or hands.

clozeText: The characteristic histological finding in Adenovirus-infected cells is the presence of large, basophilic {{c1::intranuclear inclusion bodies}} (often called 'smudge cells').
extraNote: Replication occurs in the nucleus, leading to these characteristic densly staining areas.

clozeText: Adenovirus is known to cause {{c1::Peyer's patch}} hypertrophy, which can lead to {{c2::intussusception::complication}} in young children.
extraNote: The enlarged lymphoid tissue acts as a lead point for the telescoping of the bowel.

clozeText: The Adenovirus {{c1::E1A}} protein promotes viral replication by binding and inactivating the {{c2::Rb (Retinoblastoma)}} tumor suppressor protein.
extraNote: This releases E2F transcription factors, pushing the cell into S-phase.

clozeText: The Adenovirus {{c1::E1B}} protein promotes viral replication by binding and inactivating the {{c2::p53}} tumor suppressor protein.
extraNote: This prevents apoptosis and allows the cell to continue producing viral progeny.

clozeText: Adenovirus can remain latent in {{c1::adenoids}} and {{c2::tonsils}}, which may lead to shedding in the stool for months after infection.
extraNote: The virus was originally isolated from adenoid tissue, giving it its name.

clozeText: The Adenovirus vaccine used for military recruits is a {{c1::live, non-attenuated}} oral capsule.
extraNote: It is administered orally so it replicates in the gut rather than the respiratory tract, providing immunity without causing disease.

clozeText: The {{c1::penton base}} of the Adenovirus capsid is directly toxic to host cells and can inhibit host {{c2::protein synthesis}}.
extraNote: This contributes to the rapid cytopathic effect seen in cell culture.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating severe Adenovirus infections in immunocompromised patients is {{c1::cidofovir}}.
extraNote: Cidofovir is a cytosine analog that inhibits the viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: Adenoviruses are transmitted via {{c1::respiratory droplets}}, {{c2::fecal-oral}} route, and direct inoculation from fomites.
extraNote: High stability outside the body allows it to survive on towels and medical equipment.

clozeText: Adenovirus is a major cause of viral {{c1::conjunctivitis}}, typically described as {{c2::follicular::type}} in appearance.
extraNote: Follicular conjunctivitis is characterized by small, pale bumps on the palpebral conjunctiva.

clozeText: Adenovirus encodes its own {{c1::DNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} to replicate its linear genome.
extraNote: This makes the virus independent of the host cell's DNA synthesis machinery once the cell enters S-phase.

clozeText: In stool samples from infants with diarrhea, Adenovirus (types 40/41) is typically diagnosed using {{c1::Enzyme Immunoassay (EIA)}} or PCR.
extraNote: Serotypes 40/41 do not grow well in standard cell culture, unlike respiratory serotypes.

clozeText: Adenoviral {{c1::VA RNAs}} are small RNA molecules that inhibit the host's {{c2::interferon}} response.
extraNote: They specifically block the action of Protein Kinase R (PKR), preventing the shutdown of protein synthesis.

clozeText: Adenoviruses have been modified for use in {{c1::gene therapy}} as vectors to deliver therapeutic genes into host cells.
extraNote: They are useful because they can infect both dividing and non-dividing cells.

clozeText: The gross hematuria seen in Adenovirus-associated {{c1::hemorrhagic cystitis}} is most common in {{c2::young boys}}.
extraNote: It is a self-limiting condition that resolves within a week.

clozeText: In the respiratory tract, Adenovirus causes {{c1::non-purulent}} pharyngitis that is difficult to distinguish from Group A Strep clinically.
extraNote: A negative rapid strep test and negative culture often point toward Adenovirus.

clozeText: Adenoviruses enter cells through {{c1::receptor-mediated endocytosis}}.
extraNote: After binding to CAR, the virus is internalized into clathrin-coated pits.

clozeText: The protein shell of Adenovirus is composed of {{c1::252}} capsomeres, consisting of 240 {{c2::hexons}} and 12 pentons.
extraNote: Hexons make up the majority of the capsid face.

clozeText: Adenovirus gastroenteritis is characterized by {{c1::non-bloody}} diarrhea and usually lacks the severe dehydration seen with Rotavirus.
extraNote: The clinical course is generally milder and more prolonged (7-8 days).

clozeText: Adenoviruses possess a {{c1::linear::shape}} double-stranded DNA genome.
extraNote: They are unique among DNA viruses for having a linear genome without an envelope.

clozeText: Adenoviruses are {{c1::non-enveloped (naked)}} viruses, which makes them resistant to detergents and gastrointestinal conditions.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are generally more fragile and susceptible to bile and acid.

clozeText: The {{c1::fiber proteins}} protruding from the penton bases of Adenoviruses mediate attachment to host cell receptors.
extraNote: These fibers are toxic to human cells and are used for serotyping.

clozeText: Adenovirus is a classic cause of {{c1::pharyngoconjunctival fever}}, characterized by fever, sore throat, and red eyes.
extraNote: Outbreaks are frequently linked to poorly chlorinated swimming pools.

clozeText: Adenovirus types {{c1::4 and 7}} are the primary causes of acute respiratory disease (ARD) in {{c2::military recruits}}.
extraNote: A live, oral, non-attenuated vaccine is administered only to military populations to prevent these outbreaks.

clozeText: Acute {{c1::hemorrhagic cystitis}}, presenting with gross hematuria and dysuria in a child, is commonly caused by Adenovirus types {{c2::11 and 21}}.
extraNote: It is usually self-limiting and must be differentiated from bacterial causes like E. coli.

clozeText: Adenovirus types {{c1::40 and 41}} are significant causes of {{c2::infantile gastroenteritis}}.
extraNote: Unlike Rotavirus, Adenovirus gastroenteritis occurs year-round.

clozeText: Adenovirus can cause {{c1::epidemic keratoconjunctivitis::condition}}, also known as 'shipyard eye,' often associated with contaminated ophthalmic instruments.
extraNote: Type 8 is the most common serotype associated with this severe form of conjunctivitis.

clozeText: Microscopic examination of Adenovirus-infected cells reveals characteristic {{c1::basophilic intranuclear::description}} inclusion bodies.
extraNote: Because it is a DNA virus (except Poxvirus), replication and assembly occur in the nucleus.

clozeText: In immunocompromised patients (e.g., transplant recipients), severe Adenovirus infection may be treated with {{c1::cidofovir}}.
extraNote: Cidofovir acts by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: The Adenovirus {{c1::E1A}} protein promotes cell cycle progression by binding and inactivating the {{c2::Rb (retinoblastoma)}} protein.
extraNote: This mechanism allows the virus to force the host cell into the S phase for replication.

clozeText: The Adenovirus {{c1::E1B}} protein interferes with apoptosis by binding and inactivating the {{c2::p53}} tumor suppressor protein.
extraNote: Inactivation of p53 and Rb contributes to the oncogenic potential of Adenoviruses in animal models.

clozeText: Adenoviruses can remain latent in {{c1::lymphoid tissue::location}} such as the adenoids and tonsils.
extraNote: The virus name is actually derived from its initial isolation from adenoid tissue.

clozeText: Adenovirus-induced inflammation of {{c1::Peyer's patches}} in the terminal ileum can serve as a lead point for {{c2::intussusception}}.
extraNote: This is a surgical emergency where one segment of the bowel telescopes into another.

clozeText: Adenoviruses utilize the {{c1::CAR (Coxsackie-Adenovirus Receptor)}} to gain entry into host cells.
extraNote: This receptor is shared with Coxsackie B viruses.

clozeText: To evade the immune system, Adenoviruses produce {{c1::VA (virus-associated) RNAs}} that inhibit the action of {{c2::interferon::cytokine}}.
extraNote: Specifically, these RNAs prevent the activation of protein kinase R (PKR).

clozeText: Adenovirus infection is a common cause of {{c1::viral pneumonia::condition}} in children, especially those under the age of 2.
extraNote: It often follows an upper respiratory infection and can be life-threatening in neonates.

clozeText: The Adenovirus vaccine is a {{c1::live, non-attenuated}} virus delivered in an enteric-coated capsule.
extraNote: The enteric coating ensures the virus bypasses the respiratory tract to reach the gut, where it causes an asymptomatic, immunizing infection.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Adenoviruses includes {{c1::respiratory droplets}}, {{c2::fecal-oral}} spread, and direct contact.
extraNote: Fecal-oral transmission is common in daycare settings.

clozeText: Adenoviruses are popular vectors for {{c1::gene therapy}} because they can infect both dividing and non-dividing cells.
extraNote: However, their high immunogenicity can sometimes limit their clinical use.

clozeText: Unlike many other respiratory viruses, Adenovirus infections are not strictly seasonal and can occur {{c1::year-round}}.
extraNote: This contrasts with Influenza (winter) or RSV (winter).

clozeText: Adenoviruses reduce host immune detection by inhibiting the cell surface expression of {{c1::MHC class I}}.
extraNote: This prevents CD8+ T-cells from recognizing and killing the infected cells.

clozeText: In the laboratory, Adenoviruses can be identified by {{c1::PCR::test name}}, which is the fastest and most sensitive diagnostic method.
extraNote: Viral culture showing cytopathic effects (CPE) is also possible but takes longer.

clozeText: Adenovirus types {{c1::1, 2, and 5}} are most frequently associated with endemic {{c2::upper respiratory infections}} in young children.
extraNote: Most children have antibodies to these serotypes by age 5.

clozeText: Adenovirus can cause {{c1::meningoencephalitis}}, particularly in immunocompromised hosts.
extraNote: It should be part of the differential for viral CNS infections in transplant patients.

clozeText: The Adenovirus capsid has {{c1::icosahedral::symmetry}} symmetry.
extraNote: It is composed of 252 capsomeres (hexons and pentons).

clozeText: One of the complications of Adenoviral keratitis is the formation of {{c1::subepithelial opacities}} in the cornea.
extraNote: These can persist for weeks or months after the acute infection has resolved.

clozeText: Because Adenoviruses are {{c1::naked (non-enveloped)}}, they are highly resistant to {{c2::hand sanitizers (alcohol-based)}} and require handwashing or bleach for disinfection.
extraNote: Alcohol disrupts lipid membranes, which naked viruses lack.

clozeText: Papillomaviruses possess a {{c1::circular::shape}} double-stranded DNA genome.
extraNote: The genome is approximately 8 kb in size and replicates in the host cell nucleus.

clozeText: Human Papillomavirus (HPV) is a {{c1::non-enveloped::envelope status}} virus, which contributes to its environmental stability.
extraNote: Naked viruses are generally more resistant to detergents and heat compared to enveloped viruses.

clozeText: The HPV oncoprotein {{c1::E6::protein}} promotes the degradation of the tumor suppressor p53.
extraNote: E6 recruits E6-AP (ubiquitin ligase) to target p53 for proteasomal degradation, preventing apoptosis.

clozeText: The HPV oncoprotein {{c1::E7::protein}} binds to and inactivates the tumor suppressor protein Rb.
extraNote: By inactivating Rb, E7 releases the E2F transcription factor, which pushes the cell into the S-phase of the cell cycle.

clozeText: HPV types {{c1::16 and 18::types}} are the most high-risk strains associated with cervical and anal squamous cell carcinoma.
extraNote: These types account for approximately 70% of all cervical cancer cases worldwide.

clozeText: HPV types {{c1::6 and 11::types}} are low-risk strains that primarily cause condyloma acuminata (genital warts).
extraNote: These types are also the primary cause of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (Laryngeal papillomas).

clozeText: The histologic hallmark of an HPV-infected cell is the {{c1::koilocyte::cell type}}, characterized by a perinuclear halo and wrinkled nucleus.
extraNote: Koilocytosis is a sign of squamous epithelial cell infection and is seen on Pap smears and biopsies.

clozeText: HPV initially infects cells in the {{c1::basal::epithelial layer}} layer of the stratified squamous epithelium.
extraNote: The virus enters through micro-abrasions in the skin or mucous membranes.

clozeText: The HPV vaccine (Gardasil) is composed of virus-like particles (VLPs) made of the {{c1::L1::protein}} capsid protein.
extraNote: The L1 protein is the major capsid protein that self-assembles into empty shells to induce a neutralizing antibody response.

clozeText: In high-risk HPV infections leading to cancer, the viral genome typically {{c1::integrates::genomic event}} into the host chromosome.
extraNote: Integration often disrupts the E2 gene, leading to the overexpression of the E6 and E7 oncoproteins.

clozeText: The {{c1::E2::protein}} viral protein normally functions to regulate and repress the expression of E6 and E7.
extraNote: When E2 is disrupted during integration, the loss of its inhibitory effect allows uncontrolled production of E6 and E7.

clozeText: Application of {{c1::acetic acid::chemical}} to the cervix during a colposcopy causes HPV-infected areas to turn white.
extraNote: This is known as 'acetowhite' change and helps clinicians identify areas for biopsy.

clozeText: Cutaneous warts, such as verruca vulgaris, are most commonly associated with HPV types {{c1::1 through 4::types}}.
extraNote: Types 1 and 2 are particularly common for plantar and common skin warts respectively.

clozeText: HPV type {{c1::16::type}} is the strain most frequently implicated in HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma.
extraNote: Incidence of HPV-positive head and neck cancers has risen significantly in recent decades.

clozeText: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis in children is usually acquired during birth via {{c1::vertical transmission::mode}}.
extraNote: Mothers with active genital warts (HPV 6 or 11) can transmit the virus to the neonate's larynx during delivery.

clozeText: In the cell cycle, the p53 protein normally induces {{c1::p21::inhibitor}}, which inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
extraNote: E6-mediated degradation of p53 prevents this checkpoint, leading to unregulated cell division.

clozeText: Koilocytes are typically found in the {{c1::superficial::epithelial layer}} layers of the squamous epithelium during active viral shedding.
extraNote: While the virus infects the basal layer, full assembly and shedding occur as cells differentiate and move toward the surface.

clozeText: Low-risk HPV types (6 and 11) generally maintain their DNA as {{c1::episomes::genomic form}} rather than integrating into host DNA.
extraNote: Because they don't integrate, the E2 gene remains intact, keeping E6 and E7 levels low.

clozeText: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis is a rare genetic condition that predisposes patients to widespread infection with {{c1::betapapillomaviruses::category}}.
extraNote: This condition often leads to the development of non-melanoma skin cancers.

clozeText: HPV-induced cervical cancer is staged using the {{c1::CIN (Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia)::system}} system based on the depth of epithelial involvement.
extraNote: CIN 1 involves the lower 1/3, CIN 2 involves 2/3, and CIN 3 is carcinoma in situ.

clozeText: HPV type {{c1::18::type}} is specifically known for its association with cervical adenocarcinoma.
extraNote: While type 16 is more common in squamous cell carcinoma, type 18 has a stronger relative association with the glandular variant.

clozeText: Immunocompromised patients, especially those with {{c1::HIV/AIDS::condition}}, have a much higher risk of HPV-related anal cancer.
extraNote: Lack of T-cell mediated immunity allows for persistent high-risk HPV infection.

clozeText: The HPV genome encodes {{c1::early (E)::gene group}} genes for replication and transformation and late (L) genes for structural proteins.
extraNote: E1 through E7 are involved in viral DNA replication and host cell control.

clozeText: The main host cell enzyme utilized for HPV DNA replication is {{c1::DNA polymerase delta::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Like most DNA viruses (except Poxvirus), HPV relies on host machinery in the nucleus for replication.

clozeText: The E6 protein's degradation of p53 results in the failure of {{c1::G1/S::cell cycle checkpoint}} checkpoint control.
extraNote: This allows cells with DNA damage to continue dividing, increasing the risk of malignancy.

clozeText: Gardasil-9 is a {{c1::9-valent::valence}} vaccine covering types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.
extraNote: It targets both the most common causes of warts and the most common causes of cervical cancer.

clozeText: The physical appearance of Condyloma acuminatum is often described as {{c1::cauliflower-like::description}}.
extraNote: These are flesh-colored, exophytic papules found in the anogenital region.

clozeText: Papillomaviruses have an {{c1::icosahedral::symmetry}} capsid symmetry.
extraNote: This is a 20-sided geometric shape common among many DNA viruses.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas streptococci do not.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from neutrophil killing.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: This arrangement is due to the plane of cell division in the organism.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike most other staphylococci, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and causes hemolysis.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene on the bacterial chromosome.
extraNote: This gene encodes for an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA, known as {{c1::PBP2a}}, has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.
extraNote: PBP2a still performs its transpeptidase function but does not bind penicillins effectively.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) typically produces {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, whereas relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains do.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is an exotoxin that can cause necrotizing skin infections and pneumonia.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate::molecule}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This change is encoded by a cassette of genes often acquired from enterococci via transposons.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} acts as a virulence factor by binding the {{c1::Fc::region}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis because the Fc receptor on neutrophils cannot bind the antibody.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers in the cell wall that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release {{c1::IL-1::cytokine}} and TNF.
extraNote: This mimics the action of endotoxin found in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers at any given time.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess::collection of pus}}.
extraNote: Abscesses undergo central necrosis and often require drainage.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to recurrent S. aureus infections due to defective neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the NADPH oxidase system, making them susceptible to catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::epidermidis::species}} is a common member of the skin flora that frequently infects prosthetic heart valves and hips.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and sensitive to novobiocin.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections and is distinguished from S. epidermidis by being {{c1::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: Novobiocin resistance is a key lab differentiator for coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is at high risk for endocarditis, often involving the tricuspid valve.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is linked to S. aureus colonization in the {{c1::vagina}}, which occurs in about 5% of women.
extraNote: TSS involves the production of a superantigen toxin (TSST-1).

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus that results in widespread desquamation.
extraNote: This condition is most commonly seen in infants and young children.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts::physical finding}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection.

clozeText: The majority (90%) of S. aureus strains are resistant to penicillin G because they possess {{c1::beta-lactamase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Beta-lactamase is typically encoded on a plasmid.

clozeText: The drug of choice for non-MRSA S. aureus infections is a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin such as {{c1::nafcillin::drug name}}.
extraNote: Oxacillin or dicloxacillin are alternative choices.

clozeText: S. aureus recovers {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin to utilize in the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: The bacteria produce hemolysins to lyse red blood cells and access the iron source.

clozeText: Peptidoglycan in S. aureus has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, stimulating cytokines and the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus can cause septic shock without possessing true LPS (endotoxin).

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It typically presents in children with fever, strawberry tongue, and desquamating rash.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection involving small pustules on hair follicles.
extraNote: This often occurs in areas of friction or shaving.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule exists in 11 serotypes, but types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the vast majority (85%) of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: {{c1::Phage typing}} of S. aureus strains is possible because surface teichoic acids serve as receptors for specific bacteriophages.
extraNote: This is primarily used for epidemiologic investigation of hospital outbreaks.

clozeText: The Polyomavirus genome consists of {{c1::circular dsDNA}}.
extraNote: This is similar to Papillomaviruses, though Polyomaviruses are smaller (~5 kb).

clozeText: Polyomaviruses are described as {{c1::naked (non-enveloped)}} viruses with an icosahedral capsid.
extraNote: Being non-enveloped makes them relatively resistant to environmental degradation.

clozeText: The JC virus (JCV) is the causative agent of {{c1::Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)}}.
extraNote: PML is a severe demyelinating disease of the central nervous system.

clozeText: In PML, the JC virus infects and kills {{c1::oligodendrocytes::cell type}}.
extraNote: This leads to multifocal areas of demyelination throughout the brain.

clozeText: The BK virus is primarily associated with {{c1::hemorrhagic cystitis}} in bone marrow transplant patients.
extraNote: Presentation includes gross hematuria and dysuria.

clozeText: In renal transplant patients, BK virus reactivation leads to {{c1::nephropathy}} and ureteral stenosis.
extraNote: It is a major cause of graft failure in kidney transplant recipients.

clozeText: On MRI, PML typically presents as {{c1::non-enhancing}} white matter lesions.
extraNote: This helps differentiate it from CNS toxoplasmosis or primary CNS lymphoma, which often show ring enhancement.

clozeText: The diagnosis of JC virus infection in the CNS is usually confirmed by {{c1::PCR}} of the cerebrospinal fluid.
extraNote: Detection of JCV DNA in the CSF is highly specific for PML.

clozeText: Polyomavirus {{c1::Large T-antigen}} promotes cell cycle progression by inhibiting the tumor suppressors p53 and Rb.
extraNote: This is the primary mechanism for transformation and viral genome replication.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::decoy cells}} (cells with enlarged nuclei and intranuclear inclusions) in the urine is suggestive of BK virus reactivation.
extraNote: These are often found in the urine sediment of transplant patients.

clozeText: Polyomaviruses replicate their genome within the host cell's {{c1::nucleus}}.
extraNote: They utilize the host's DNA polymerase for replication.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::natalizumab}} (used for Multiple Sclerosis) is associated with an increased risk of PML due to reactivation of the JC virus.
extraNote: Patients are screened for JCV antibodies before and during treatment.

clozeText: PML is most commonly seen in AIDS patients with a CD4 count less than {{c1::200::number}} cells/mm³.
extraNote: It is considered an AIDS-defining illness.

clozeText: {{c1::Merkel cell polyomavirus}} is associated with a highly aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin.
extraNote: The virus is integrated into the host genome in Merkel cell carcinoma cases.

clozeText: BK virus remains latent in the {{c1::kidney (renal tubule cells)}} after primary infection.
extraNote: Reactivation occurs during periods of significant immunosuppression.

clozeText: JC virus remains latent in the kidneys, {{c1::lymphoid tissue::organ}}, and B cells.
extraNote: Immunosuppression allows the virus to cross the blood-brain barrier.

clozeText: The {{c1::Small T-antigen}} of Polyomaviruses functions by inhibiting Protein Phosphatase 2A (PP2A).
extraNote: This helps stimulate MAP kinase pathways to promote cell growth.

clozeText: The capsid of Polyomaviruses is composed of three proteins: {{c1::VP1, VP2, and VP3}}.
extraNote: VP1 is the major capsid protein responsible for host cell attachment.

clozeText: Primary infection with Polyomaviruses usually occurs via the {{c1::respiratory}} route during childhood.
extraNote: Most individuals are seropositive by adulthood.

clozeText: The {{c1::SV40::Virus name}} virus is a simian polyomavirus that was a known contaminant of early Salk polio vaccines.
extraNote: It was studied extensively for its ability to induce tumors in rodents.

clozeText: The primary treatment for PML in HIV-infected patients is {{c1::immune reconstitution}} (e.g., via HAART).
extraNote: There are no effective direct antiviral medications for JCV.

clozeText: Polyomavirus early genes encode for proteins involved in {{c1::replication and transformation}}.
extraNote: Late genes encode for structural capsid proteins.

clozeText: Hemorrhagic cystitis from BK virus is a classic complication in patients receiving {{c1::cyclophosphamide}} or undergoing bone marrow transplantation.
extraNote: It must be differentiated from chemical cystitis caused by acrolein.

clozeText: Clinical symptoms of PML include focal deficits such as {{c1::aphasia::language deficit}}, hemiparesis, and visual field defects.
extraNote: The progression is typically subacute and fatal if the immune system is not restored.

clozeText: Unlike Herpesviruses, Polyomaviruses do not have a {{c1::viral DNA polymerase}} and must rely on host machinery.
extraNote: This is why they must force the host cell into S-phase using T-antigens.

clozeText: The Polyomavirus genome is divided into three regions: the Early region, the Late region, and the {{c1::Noncoding Control Region (NCCR)}}.
extraNote: The NCCR contains the origin of replication and promoter elements.

clozeText: The 'B' in BK virus stands for the {{c1::initials of the patient}} from whom the virus was first isolated.
extraNote: Similarly, JC stands for the initials of the patient with PML.

clozeText: Merkel cell carcinoma typically presents as a painless, {{c1::flesh-colored or bluish-red}} nodule on sun-exposed skin.
extraNote: It is often mistaken for a cyst or insect bite initially.

clozeText: Polyomaviruses possess a {{c1::double-stranded DNA::nucleic acid type}} genome.
extraNote: The genome is circular and relatively small (~5 kbp).

clozeText: The shape of the Polyomavirus genome is {{c1::circular}}.
extraNote: Like Papillomaviruses, they belong to the formerly grouped 'Papovavirus' family due to shared dsDNA circular genomes.

clozeText: Polyomaviruses are {{c1::naked::enveloped or naked?}} viruses.
extraNote: Naked viruses are generally more resistant to environmental conditions than enveloped viruses.

clozeText: JC virus causes {{c1::Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)::disease name}}.
extraNote: PML is a severe demyelinating disease of the central nervous system.

clozeText: JC virus primarily infects and destroys {{c1::oligodendrocytes::cell type}} in the CNS.
extraNote: Destruction of these cells leads to the characteristic demyelination seen in PML.

clozeText: PML lesions on MRI typically appear as {{c1::non-enhancing::enhancing or non-enhancing?}} white matter lesions.
extraNote: This helps distinguish PML from CNS Toxoplasmosis or Primary CNS Lymphoma, which usually show ring-enhancement.

clozeText: PML typically manifests in HIV patients when the CD4 count drops below {{c1::200::threshold}} cells/mm³.
extraNote: It is an AIDS-defining illness reflecting profound immunosuppression.

clozeText: The BK virus is most notorious for causing {{c1::nephropathy::organ pathology}} in renal transplant patients.
extraNote: It is a major cause of graft failure in the post-transplant period.

clozeText: In bone marrow transplant recipients, BK virus commonly causes {{c1::hemorrhagic cystitis}}.
extraNote: Patients present with hematuria and dysuria due to viral reactivation in the bladder.

clozeText: The classic cytopathologic finding in the urine of a patient with BK virus is {{c1::decoy cells}}.
extraNote: Decoy cells have enlarged nuclei with dark basophilic intranuclear inclusions, resembling carcinoma cells.

clozeText: Both JC and BK viruses establish latency in the {{c1::kidneys}}.
extraNote: They remain asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts and reactivate only during immunosuppression.

clozeText: JC virus uses the {{c1::5-HT2A (serotonin)::receptor name}} receptor to enter host cells.
extraNote: This specific receptor profile contributes to its CNS tropism.

clozeText: The primary treatment for JC virus/PML in AIDS patients is {{c1::Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)::treatment}}.
extraNote: Immune reconstitution is the only effective way to stop the progression of the virus.

clozeText: Management of BK nephropathy in renal transplant patients usually involves {{c1::decreasing}} the dose of immunosuppressive drugs.
extraNote: Allowing the host's immune system to recover slightly helps control the viral replication.

clozeText: Merkel cell virus (MCV) is a polyomavirus associated with {{c1::Merkel cell carcinoma}}.
extraNote: This is an aggressive form of skin cancer occurring mostly in the elderly or immunocompromised.

clozeText: The MRI findings in PML typically lack {{c1::mass effect}}.
extraNote: The absence of mass effect helps differentiate it from tumors or abscesses.

clozeText: Polyomaviruses replicate their DNA in the {{c1::nucleus}} of the host cell.
extraNote: They utilize the host's DNA polymerase for replication.

clozeText: The {{c1::Large T-antigen}} is a polyomavirus protein that promotes cell cycle entry by inhibiting p53 and Rb.
extraNote: This protein is essential for viral replication and can drive oncogenesis.

clozeText: BK virus-induced {{c1::ureteral stenosis}} can lead to obstructive uropathy in kidney transplant recipients.
extraNote: The inflammation and scarring from viral replication can narrow the ureter.

clozeText: PML typically involves the {{c1::subcortical}} white matter.
extraNote: Lesions are often multifocal and start in the posterior regions of the brain.

clozeText: Diagnosis of PML is often confirmed by detecting JC virus DNA in the {{c1::CSF::fluid}} via PCR.
extraNote: Brain biopsy is the gold standard but PCR is preferred as it is less invasive.

clozeText: JC virus can also establish latency in {{c1::B-lymphocytes}}.
extraNote: The virus can be carried to the CNS within these cells during reactivation.

clozeText: Common clinical presentations of PML include ataxia, hemiparesis, and {{c1::visual field defects::symptom}}.
extraNote: Neurological deficits are progressive and vary based on the location of the lesions.

clozeText: The {{c1::SV40}} virus is a simian polyomavirus that historically contaminated early batches of the Polio vaccine.
extraNote: While it can transform human cells in vitro, it has not been proven to cause human cancer.

clozeText: On histology, cells infected with polyomaviruses show large, basophilic {{c1::intranuclear}} inclusions.
extraNote: These inclusions represent the site of viral assembly in the nucleus.

clozeText: Unlike BK virus, JC virus reactivation rarely causes {{c1::renal::organ}} disease.
extraNote: JC is almost exclusively associated with CNS pathology during reactivation.

clozeText: Cidofovir is an antiviral occasionally used for {{c1::BK virus}} infections, although its efficacy is not well-established.
extraNote: It is a nucleotide analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: The JC virus is named after the initials of a patient with {{c1::Hodgkin lymphoma}} from whom it was first isolated.
extraNote: Historical context: Polyomaviruses were named after their ability to cause 'many tumors' in laboratory animals.

clozeText: Poxviruses are unique among DNA viruses because they replicate entirely within the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus; Poxviruses must provide their own enzymes for transcription and replication to bypass this.

clozeText: Because they replicate in the cytoplasm, Poxviruses must carry a pre-packaged {{c1::DNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} to synthesize mRNA.
extraNote: Host RNA polymerase is sequestered in the nucleus, necessitating the virus to carry its own.

clozeText: The genome of Poxviruses is composed of {{c1::double-stranded linear::DNA type}} DNA.
extraNote: It is a large genome, typically 130-230 kb, encoding roughly 200 proteins.

clozeText: Smallpox (Variola) is characterized by skin lesions that are {{c1::synchronous::stage similarity}}, meaning all lesions are at the same stage of development.
extraNote: This is a key clinical differentiator from Varicella (Chickenpox), which presents with lesions in various stages (asynchronous).

clozeText: The intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies seen in cells infected with Variola virus are known as {{c1::Guarnieri bodies}}.
extraNote: These represent the 'viral factories' where replication and assembly occur.

clozeText: Molluscum contagiosum virus causes flesh-colored, {{c1::umbilicated}} papules with a central dimple.
extraNote: These lesions are commonly seen in children or as a sexually transmitted infection in adults.

clozeText: The eosinophilic, large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies characteristic of Molluscum contagiosum are called {{c1::Henderson-Paterson}} bodies.
extraNote: These are found within the keratinocytes of the papules.

clozeText: Under electron microscopy, Poxviruses exhibit a distinct {{c1::brick-shaped::morphology}} appearance.
extraNote: They possess a complex structure with a core and lateral bodies, unlike simple icosahedral viruses.

clozeText: Poxviruses are the {{c1::largest::size}} viruses that infect humans, often visible under a light microscope.
extraNote: They measure approximately 250 x 350 nm.

clozeText: Smallpox was eradicated worldwide by 1980, primarily because the virus has no {{c1::animal reservoir}}.
extraNote: Only humans are infected by Variola, making vaccination campaigns highly effective for elimination.

clozeText: The Smallpox vaccine is a {{c1::live attenuated::vaccine type}} vaccine containing the Vaccinia virus.
extraNote: Vaccinia virus provides cross-immunity against Variola (Smallpox).

clozeText: The rash in Smallpox follows a {{c1::centrifugal}} distribution, being most dense on the face and extremities.
extraNote: In contrast, Chickenpox (Varicella) has a centripetal distribution, primarily affecting the trunk.

clozeText: Unlike Chickenpox, the lesions of Smallpox frequently involve the {{c1::palms and soles}}.
extraNote: This is a high-yield clinical pearl for differentiating viral exanthems.

clozeText: {{c1::Monkeypox}} is a zoonotic poxvirus that is clinically distinguished from Smallpox by the presence of prominent lymphadenopathy.
extraNote: It is transmitted via contact with infected animals (e.g., rodents, primates).

clozeText: The {{c1::Orf}} virus is a poxvirus transmitted to humans through contact with infected sheep or goats, typically causing a single granulomatous lesion.
extraNote: Also known as contagious pustular dermatitis.

clozeText: Smallpox eradication was possible because the Variola virus exists as a {{c1::single::number}} serotype.
extraNote: This meant the vaccine was effective against all circulating strains.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Cidofovir}} can be used to treat severe poxvirus infections by inhibiting the viral DNA polymerase.
extraNote: It is a nucleotide analog (cytosine analog).

clozeText: Poxviruses possess {{c1::complex}} symmetry, which is neither purely icosahedral nor helical.
extraNote: The virus contains a biconcave core and two lateral bodies.

clozeText: Human transmission of Smallpox (Variola) occurs primarily through {{c1::respiratory droplets}}.
extraNote: Fomites (contaminated clothing/bedding) were also a significant route of transmission.

clozeText: The first vaccine ever developed was by {{c1::Edward Jenner}}, who used Cowpox to protect against Smallpox.
extraNote: He noticed milkmaids were often immune to smallpox after being exposed to cowpox.

clozeText: Poxviruses are {{c1::enveloped}} viruses, but they are unusually stable in the environment.
extraNote: Most enveloped viruses are fragile, but poxviruses can survive for long periods in crusts or fomites.

clozeText: During replication, Poxviruses encode their own {{c1::DNA-dependent DNA polymerase}} to replicate their genome in the cytoplasm.
extraNote: They also encode enzymes for polyadenylation and capping of mRNA.

clozeText: In adults, Molluscum contagiosum is often seen as a {{c1::sexually transmitted}} infection with lesions in the genital region.
extraNote: In children, it is typically spread by skin-to-skin contact or shared towels.

clozeText: Smallpox is classified as a {{c1::Category A}} bioterrorism agent by the CDC.
extraNote: This is due to its high mortality rate and ease of person-to-person spread.

clozeText: The incubation period for Smallpox is approximately {{c1::12::number}} days, followed by a high-fever prodrome.
extraNote: The rash appears several days after the initial fever.

clozeText: Molluscum contagiosum is often persistent and widespread in patients with {{c1::HIV/AIDS}} or other forms of cellular immunodeficiency.
extraNote: Large, numerous, or giant lesions should prompt screening for HIV.

clozeText: Poxviruses acquire their envelope from the {{c1::Golgi apparatus}} or by budding through the cell membrane.
extraNote: The virus is released either by cell lysis or exocytosis.

clozeText: Variola {{c1::major}} was the form of smallpox associated with a 30% mortality rate, while Variola minor had a mortality rate of <1%.
extraNote: The clinical severity depended heavily on which strain infected the patient.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from other staphylococci primarily by its production of {{c1::coagulase}}, an enzyme that activates prothrombin.
extraNote: Coagulase catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot, helping the organism wall itself off from host defenses.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which differentiates them from streptococci, which are catalase-negative.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from oxidative killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting opsonization.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: S. aureus can acquire iron for growth by producing {{c1::hemolysins::toxins}} that lyse red blood cells to retrieve hemoglobin.
extraNote: The iron is utilized by the bacteria to synthesize cytochrome enzymes for energy production.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) occurs when the peptidoglycan precursor {{c1::D-alanine}} is substituted with {{c2::D-lactate}}.
extraNote: This modification is carried on a transposon located on a plasmid, similar to the mechanism found in Enterococci.

clozeText: In the S. aureus cell wall, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These acids also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains are characterized by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, which is less common in hospital-acquired strains.
extraNote: Panton-Valentine leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that targets white blood cells.

clozeText: The typical lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which is characterized by central necrosis and {{c2::pus}} formation.
extraNote: The localized nature of the abscess is largely due to coagulase-induced fibrin clotting.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States and is a frequent cause of {{c2::folliculitis}}.
extraNote: Folliculitis presents as small pustules on hair follicles, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::scalded skin syndrome}}, a condition characterized by widespread desquamation caused by an {{c2::exotoxin}}.
extraNote: This syndrome is typically seen in infants and young children.

clozeText: In the laboratory, S. aureus is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}}.
extraNote: S. aureus turns Mannitol Salt Agar (MSA) yellow due to acid production from fermentation.

clozeText: S. aureus is the leading cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users}}, often resulting in endocarditis.
extraNote: It is also a primary cause of septic arthritis and osteomyelitis in this and other populations.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are highly susceptible to S. aureus because they cannot produce {{c2::hydrogen peroxide}} to kill catalase-positive organisms.
extraNote: CGD is a defect in the NADPH oxidase enzyme of neutrophils.

clozeText: The lesions of {{c1::impetigo}} are crops of vesicles with a characteristic {{c2::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipo-teichoic acids}}, which trigger the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mimics the action of endotoxin (LPS) found in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative species that is distinguished by its {{c1::resistance}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative species that is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin and often infects {{c2::prosthetic}} devices.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora and utilizes biofilms to adhere to foreign bodies.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain plasmids encoding {{c1::β-lactamase}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades the beta-lactam ring of many penicillins.

clozeText: S. aureus is a major cause of hospital-acquired (nosocomial) {{c1::pneumonia}} and {{c2::surgical-wound}} infections.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::peptidoglycan}} has endotoxin-like properties, enabling it to activate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This contributes to the clinical findings of shock even though staphylococci lack true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: In roughly 5% of women, S. aureus is found in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: This condition is often associated with high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating infections caused by methicillin-sensitive S. aureus (MSSA) is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: These are beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::foreign bodies::e.g. sutures}} is a major predisposing factor for S. aureus infection by lowering the required inoculum.
extraNote: Sutures and intravenous catheters provide a nidus for infection.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of bacterial {{c1::conjunctivitis}}, presenting with purulent discharge from the eye.
extraNote: It is also associated with cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis.

clozeText: The S. aureus {{c1::capsule}} is a virulence factor that inhibits phagocytosis, though it is poorly immunogenic.
extraNote: There are 11 serotypes, but types 5 and 8 cause the majority of infections.

clozeText: The most effective way to decrease the transmission of S. aureus in healthcare settings is through consistent {{c1::handwashing}}.
extraNote: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission between hospital personnel and patients.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that differentiates them from streptococci by degrading H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This enzyme allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive cocci, but their arrangement is a key morphological differentiator.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin clots.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is a(n) {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and produces beta-hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a common selective and differential medium for S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus uses {{c1::hemolysins}} to destroy red blood cells and recover {{c2::iron}} for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth during infection.

clozeText: The major virulence protein in the S. aureus cell wall is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by interfering with the binding of IgG to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: MRSA is resistant to nafcillin and methicillin because of the {{c1::mecA::gene}} which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Resistance to vancomycin in VRSA involves a genetic cassette that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursors.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptor for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause septic shock via {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which induce the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}} from macrophages.
extraNote: This mimics the effect of endotoxin (LPS) found in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The most common site of S. aureus colonization in the human body is the {{c1::nose}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic nasal carriers.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is a catalase-positive organism that destroys the host's limited H2O2 in CGD patients.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is specifically associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains produce this toxin.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS) in clinical labs.

clozeText: The lesions of {{c1::impetigo}} are characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored crust}}.
extraNote: This skin infection can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Scalded Skin Syndrome::disease}} is caused by an exotoxin that results in widespread desquamation, particularly in infants.
extraNote: The exotoxin (exfoliatin) acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
