extraNote: This often presents as right-sided endocarditis or skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate the {{c1::complement and coagulation}} cascades, mimicking endotoxin-like properties.
extraNote: This explains the ability of a gram-positive organism to cause septic shock findings.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is typically associated with high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: The {{c1::USA300}} strain is the most common strain of MRSA in the United States.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: S. aureus polysaccharide capsules of serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} cause approximately 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: Most strains of S. aureus (90%+) contain plasmids encoding {{c1::beta-lactamase}}, requiring treatment with drugs like {{c2::nafcillin}}.
extraNote: Beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins are the treatment of choice for MSSA.

clozeText: {{c1::S. saprophyticus}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a frequent cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::joint replacements}}.
extraNote: It is part of the normal skin flora and adheres to foreign bodies via biofilm/slime production.

clozeText: The enzyme coagulase converts {{c1::fibrinogen}} into {{c2::fibrin}}.
extraNote: This reaction produces the visible clot in the coagulase test tube.

clozeText: Transmission of S. aureus is commonly mediated via {{c1::hand contact}}, making {{c2::handwashing}} essential for prevention in hospitals.
extraNote: Fomites like contaminated towels also contribute to transmission.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::phage typing}} is a method used for epidemiologic tracking of strains, utilizing surface receptors containing {{c2::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: Specific bacteriophages infect specific strains, creating a fingerprint for the isolate.

clozeText: HSV-1 remains latent in the {{c1::trigeminal}} ganglia, while HSV-2 remains latent in the {{c1::sacral}} ganglia.
extraNote: Reactivation can be triggered by stress, fever, or UV light, following retrograde transport to the skin.

clozeText: HSV encephalitis characteristically affects the {{c1::temporal}} lobe, often presenting with seizures and olfactory hallucinations.
extraNote: This is the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis in the United States.

clozeText: The classic finding for HSV and VZV on a Tzanck smear is {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}}.
extraNote: The smear is prepared from the base of a ruptured vesicle; it cannot distinguish between HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV.

clozeText: HSV and VZV infections are microscopically characterized by {{c1::Cowdry A}} intranuclear inclusion bodies.
extraNote: These are eosinophilic (pink) inclusions that push chromatin to the periphery of the nucleus.

clozeText: HSV-1 is the most common cause of {{c1::keratoconjunctivitis}}, which typically manifests as {{c1::dendritic}} ulcers on fluorescein staining.
extraNote: Recurrent infections can lead to corneal scarring and blindness.

clozeText: Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) remains latent in the {{c1::dorsal root}} or cranial nerve ganglia.
extraNote: Reactivation results in Herpes Zoster (shingles), which follows a dermatomal distribution.

clozeText: The most common complication of shingles in elderly patients is {{c1::postherpetic neuralgia}}.
extraNote: This is chronic pain persisting for months after the resolution of the rash.

clozeText: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infects B cells by binding to the {{c1::CD21::Cluster of Differentiation}} receptor.
extraNote: The CD21 receptor is also the receptor for the C3d complement component.

clozeText: Atypical lymphocytes seen on a blood smear during EBV infectious mononucleosis are actually reactive {{c1::CD8+ T cells}}.
extraNote: These T cells proliferate in response to infected B cells.

clozeText: The Monospot test for EBV detects {{c1::heterophile}} antibodies that agglutinate horse or sheep red blood cells.
extraNote: Heterophile-negative mononucleosis is most commonly caused by CMV.

clozeText: EBV is strongly associated with {{c1::Burkitt lymphoma}}, which is characterized by a {{c1::t(8;14)}} translocation.
extraNote: This translocation moves the c-myc oncogene next to the heavy-chain Ig promoter.

clozeText: In HIV-positive patients, EBV causes {{c1::oral hairy leukoplakia}}, which appears as white, non-scrapable plaques on the lateral tongue.
extraNote: Unlike Candida (thrush), these plaques cannot be scraped off.

clozeText: Congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is characterized by {{c1::periventricular}} calcifications and sensory hearing loss.
extraNote: Compare this to Toxoplasmosis, which features diffuse intracranial calcifications.

clozeText: The diagnostic hallmark of CMV infection on biopsy is the {{c1::owl's eye}} intranuclear inclusion body.
extraNote: These are large, basophilic, or eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo.

clozeText: In AIDS patients with a CD4 count < {{c1::50}}, CMV can cause {{c1::retinitis::organ}} with a 'pizza pie' funduscopic appearance.
extraNote: CMV can also cause linear esophageal ulcers and colitis in immunocompromised hosts.

clozeText: Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) is the causative agent of {{c1::Roseola infantum}}, which presents as a high fever followed by a {{c1::diffuse maculopapular rash}}.
extraNote: The rash appears once the fever subsides ('fever then rash').

clozeText: Kaposi Sarcoma is caused by {{c1::HHV-8}} and is characterized by the proliferation of {{c1::spindle}} cells.
extraNote: The lesions are vascular and appear as dark violaceous plaques or nodules.

clozeText: Acyclovir is a {{c1::guanosine}} analog that requires monophosphorylation by viral {{c1::thymidine kinase}} to become active.
extraNote: This explains why it selectively targets infected cells.

clozeText: Ganciclovir, used for CMV, requires phosphorylation by the viral kinase {{c1::UL97}}.
extraNote: Resistance to ganciclovir often occurs through mutations in this specific kinase.

clozeText: The drug {{c1::Foscarnet}} is a pyrophosphate analog that does not require phosphorylation by viral kinases.
extraNote: It directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and is used for acyclovir-resistant HSV or ganciclovir-resistant CMV.

clozeText: Cidofovir is a {{c1::nucleotide}} analog that only requires host cellular kinases for activation, bypassing viral kinases.
extraNote: It is used primarily for CMV retinitis; it must be administered with probenecid to reduce nephrotoxicity.

clozeText: The VZV vaccine is a {{c1::live attenuated}} vaccine used to prevent chickenpox and shingles.
extraNote: It is contraindicated in pregnancy and severely immunocompromised patients.

clozeText: EBV is associated with {{c1::nasopharyngeal}} carcinoma, especially in patients of Southern Chinese descent.
extraNote: This association is linked to dietary factors like nitrosamines in salted fish.

clozeText: CMV pneumonia is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in {{c1::transplant}} recipients.
extraNote: It is particularly high-yield in the context of bone marrow or lung transplants.

clozeText: Primary infection with HSV-1 in children typically presents as {{c1::gingivostomatitis}}.
extraNote: This involves painful vesicles and ulcers on the gingiva, tongue, and lips.

clozeText: Herpetic {{c1::whitlow}} is a painful HSV infection of the finger, common in healthcare workers or children who suck their thumbs.
extraNote: It occurs when HSV-1 or HSV-2 enters through a break in the skin.

clozeText: HHV-8 causes {{c1::primary effusion lymphoma}}, which manifests as malignant B-cell effusions in body cavities.
extraNote: It is a rare but high-yield association for Step 1 in HIV/AIDS patients.

clozeText: A significant adverse effect of Ganciclovir is {{c1::bone marrow suppression}} (leukopenia/thrombocytopenia).
extraNote: Foscarnet is more likely to cause nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from Streptococci by the enzyme {{c1::catalase::degrades H2O2}}.
extraNote: Catalase converts hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, allowing the bacteria to survive the oxidative killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive, nonmotile, and non-spore-forming cocci.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike most coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol::sugar}}.
extraNote: This biochemical property is used on Mannitol Salt Agar to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: The mecA gene is typically located on the bacterial chromosome and encodes for an altered penicillin-binding protein.

clozeText: MRSA is resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics due to the production of an altered {{c1::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind to beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: S. aureus cell walls contain {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages because the Fc receptor cannot bind the antibody.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These acids also serve as part of the surface receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids::LTA}} in the staphylococcal cell wall can induce septic shock by stimulating the release of cytokines like {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of endotoxin (LPS) in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) involves a gene cassette that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This mutation prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursor.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers, increasing their risk for infection.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are particularly susceptible to S. aureus because they cannot neutralize catalase.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the neutrophil respiratory burst (NADPH oxidase defect).

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of endocarditis and sepsis in this population.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its sensitivity to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, whereas S. saprophyticus is resistant to novobiocin.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a major cause of infections related to {{c1::prosthetic devices (valves/hips)}}.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora and forms biofilms on plastic surfaces.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young women.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and resistant to novobiocin.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) usually produces {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a toxin that destroys white blood cells and is associated with severe skin and lung infections.

clozeText: S. aureus recovery of {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin is used for the synthesis of {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Hemolysins lyse red blood cells to release hemoglobin for this purpose.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections and necrotizing fasciitis.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, stimulating cytokines and the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite being gram-positive.

clozeText: Staphylococcal capsules of serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the majority (85%) of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess::collection of pus}}.
extraNote: Abscesses undergo central necrosis and often require surgical drainage.

clozeText: Colonization of S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}} of 5% of women predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: The syndrome is typically associated with high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: Infections caused by {{c1::beta-lactamase}}-producing S. aureus are treated with drugs like nafcillin.
extraNote: Over 90% of S. aureus strains carry plasmids encoding this penicillin-degrading enzyme.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of cellulitis and bullous impetigo.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::vasculitis}} is a pediatric disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to specific S. aureus strains.
extraNote: The syndrome involves coronary artery aneurysms and mucocutaneous inflammation.

clozeText: Coagulase-negative staphylococci lack {{c1::Protein A}} on their cell surfaces.
extraNote: This helps distinguish them from S. aureus in laboratory and virulence profiles.

clozeText: Hand contact is the major mode of transmission for S. aureus; therefore, {{c1::handwashing}} is the most effective preventative measure.
extraNote: This is especially critical in hospital settings where healthcare workers can become transient carriers.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci by degrading H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This enzyme serves as an important virulence factor, helping bacteria survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}, which activates prothrombin to form a fibrin clot.
extraNote: Coagulase catalyzes the activation of fibrinogen to fibrin via thrombin formation.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG to prevent phagocytosis.
extraNote: By occupying the Fc region, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a is a transpeptidase that retains its function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This modification is carried on a transposon often acquired from enterococci.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers in the staphylococcal cell wall that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids also play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating macrophage release of IL-1 and TNF.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is specifically associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin rarely found in HCA-MRSA.
extraNote: The most common strain of CA-MRSA in the United States is the USA300 strain.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for Staphylococcus aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, with approximately {{c2::30%}} of the population being chronic carriers.
extraNote: Chronic nasal carriage increases the risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, allowing it to neutralize the limited H2O2 these patients' neutrophils can produce.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and produces {{c2::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar, distinguishing it from S. epidermidis.
extraNote: Hemolysins recover iron from hemoglobin, which the bacteria use to synthesize cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is uniquely {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}, unlike S. saprophyticus.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in clinical samples.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young women and is {{c2::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its resistance to novobiocin and its lack of coagulase.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and drainage of pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus that results in widespread desquamation, particularly in infants.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts}}, can be caused by either {{c2::S. aureus}} or {{c3::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection often seen in children.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90%}} of S. aureus strains produce {{c2::beta-lactamase}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: These strains require treatment with beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can trigger {{c1::septic shock}} by stimulating macrophages to produce cytokines, despite the organism lacking {{c2::endotoxin}}.
extraNote: The peptidoglycan mimics endotoxin-like properties by activating complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora and is a frequent cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} or {{c2::catheters}}.
extraNote: It is known for its ability to produce biofilms on foreign bodies.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users}}, including endocarditis.
extraNote: MRSA is increasingly frequent in this population.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is considered a virulence factor; serotypes {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} cause approximately 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may potentially be triggered by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is a pediatric vasculitis that requires prompt recognition to prevent coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, a factor that predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is typically mediated by the TSST-1 superantigen.

clozeText: {{c1::Phage typing}} of S. aureus strains for epidemiologic studies is possible because of surface receptors composed partly of {{c2::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: This method helps track outbreaks by identifying specific bacteriophage susceptibility patterns.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: Folliculitis can progress to furuncles (boils) or carbuncles.

clozeText: In the hospital setting, the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus is {{c1::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Rigorous handwashing by healthcare personnel is the primary method for decreasing transmission.

clozeText: Bacteria that produce {{c1::catalase}} are able to survive the killing effect of {{c2::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}} inside neutrophils.
extraNote: This is why S. aureus is a classic pathogen in patients with CGD who cannot produce their own H2O2.

clozeText: Staphylococci appear microscopically as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci typically appear in {{c2::chains}}.

clozeText: Predisposing factors for S. aureus infection include reduced humoral immunity, {{c1::diabetes}}, and the presence of {{c2::foreign bodies}} like sutures.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
