clozeText: S. aureus is the leading cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: It is also a common cause of cellulitis, impetigo, and bacterial conjunctivitis.

clozeText: The crops of vesicles with a 'honey-colored' crust seen in {{c1::impetigo}} can be caused by S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.
extraNote: This is a superficial skin infection most common in children.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome::Syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus that results in widespread desquamation.
extraNote: This condition is particularly common in infants and young children.

clozeText: {{c1::S. saprophyticus}} is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its resistance to novobiocin.

clozeText: The vaccine development for S. aureus has been difficult because the {{c1::polysaccharide capsule}} is poorly immunogenic.
extraNote: Serotypes 5 and 8 are responsible for 85% of clinical S. aureus infections.

clozeText: In users of intravenous drugs, {{c1::S. aureus::organism}} is the most common cause of endocarditis and sepsis.
extraNote: MRSA strains are frequently involved in these cases.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing metabolic factor to infections by S. aureus.
extraNote: Reduced humoral immunity and poor neutrophil function in these patients increase risk.

clozeText: S. aureus produces {{c1::β-lactamase}}, an enzyme encoded on plasmids that degrades penicillins.
extraNote: Over 90% of S. aureus strains are now resistant to penicillin G due to this enzyme.

clozeText: Caliciviruses are characterized as {{c1::non-enveloped (naked)}} viruses with an icosahedral capsid.
extraNote: Being non-enveloped makes them highly resistant to environmental degradation and detergents.

clozeText: The genome of Caliciviruses consists of {{c1::positive-sense single-stranded RNA}}.
extraNote: Because it is positive-sense, the genomic RNA can be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Caliciviruses are named for the {{c1::cup-shaped}} depressions seen on the surface of the capsid under electron microscopy.
extraNote: The name is derived from 'calix', the Latin word for cup.

clozeText: {{c1::Norovirus::Genus}} is the most common cause of epidemic viral gastroenteritis worldwide.
extraNote: It is a member of the Caliciviridae family and was formerly known as Norwalk virus.

clozeText: Norovirus outbreaks are classically associated with crowded settings such as {{c1::cruise ships}}, schools, and nursing homes.
extraNote: High infectivity and environmental resilience facilitate rapid spread in these environments.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Caliciviruses is the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route.
extraNote: Transmission can occur through contaminated food, water, or person-to-person contact.

clozeText: Consuming contaminated {{c1::shellfish (e.g., oysters)}} is a high-yield risk factor for Norovirus infection.
extraNote: The virus can be concentrated in the tissues of filter-feeding bivalves.

clozeText: Norovirus has a very low infectious dose, requiring only {{c1::10 to 100}} virions to cause disease.
extraNote: This low threshold contributes to its high transmissibility and epidemic potential.

clozeText: The hallmark clinical symptom of Norovirus gastroenteritis is {{c1::profuse, watery vomiting}}.
extraNote: Vomiting is often more prominent than diarrhea in many patients.

clozeText: Diarrhea associated with Caliciviruses is typically {{c1::watery and non-bloody}}.
extraNote: The lack of blood or mucus indicates a non-invasive, malabsorptive mechanism.

clozeText: Pathogenesis of Norovirus involves the {{c1::blunting or atrophy}} of the villi in the small intestine.
extraNote: This leads to malabsorption and transient lactose intolerance.

clozeText: The gold standard for the diagnosis of Norovirus in clinical samples is {{c1::RT-PCR}}.
extraNote: RT-PCR detects viral RNA in stool specimens with high sensitivity.

clozeText: Norovirus replicates in the cytoplasm and encodes a(n) {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} for genome replication.
extraNote: Like other RNA viruses, it lacks proofreading, leading to significant genetic diversity.

clozeText: {{c1::Sapovirus}} is another genus of Caliciviridae that primarily causes gastroenteritis in children.
extraNote: It is named after Sapporo, Japan, where it was first discovered.

clozeText: Norovirus is highly resistant to {{c1::alcohol-based}} hand sanitizers.
extraNote: Hand washing with soap and water is more effective at removing the virus.

clozeText: For environmental disinfection of Norovirus, {{c1::bleach (sodium hypochlorite)}} is the agent of choice.
extraNote: The virus is stable in the environment and resistant to many standard cleaners.

clozeText: Susceptibility to Norovirus has been linked to the presence of {{c1::histo-blood group antigens (HBGAs)}} on gut epithelial cells.
extraNote: Individuals who do not express certain antigens (non-secretors) may be resistant to some strains.

clozeText: Norovirus gastroenteritis typically has a short incubation period of {{c1::12 to 48}} hours.
extraNote: The illness is usually self-limiting, lasting 1-3 days.

clozeText: Unlike Rotavirus, Norovirus frequently causes disease in {{c1::both children and adults}}.
extraNote: Rotavirus is traditionally more associated with severe disease in infants.

clozeText: Secondary transmission of Norovirus can occur via the {{c1::aerosolization}} of vomitus.
extraNote: This allows the virus to settle on surfaces or be inhaled and swallowed.

clozeText: The Calicivirus genome is translated into a single {{c1::polyprotein}} that is subsequently cleaved by proteases.
extraNote: This is a common feature among many positive-sense RNA viruses.

clozeText: Chronic shedding of Norovirus in the stool can persist for {{c1::weeks}} after symptoms have resolved.
extraNote: This complicates infection control in institutional settings.

clozeText: Caliciviruses are resistant to {{c1::gastric acid}}, allowing them to pass through the stomach to the small intestine.
extraNote: This acid stability is a key trait of many fecal-oral pathogens.

clozeText: The primary treatment for Calicivirus infection is {{c1::supportive care (rehydration)}}.
extraNote: There are no specific antiviral therapies or vaccines currently available.

clozeText: Norovirus outbreaks often peak during the {{c1::winter}} months.
extraNote: It is sometimes referred to as the 'winter vomiting bug'.

clozeText: Immunity to Norovirus is generally {{c1::short-lived (temporary)}}, allowing for repeat infections throughout life.
extraNote: Strain diversity and waning mucosal IgA contribute to re-infection.

clozeText: Caliciviruses lack a lipid envelope; therefore, they do not require {{c1::bile salts}} for infectivity in the gut.
extraNote: In contrast, some enveloped viruses are inactivated by the detergent action of bile.

clozeText: On a molecular level, Norovirus attaches to host cells via {{c1::H-type 1::antigen type}} carbohydrate antigens.
extraNote: This specific binding dictates the host range and tissue tropism.

clozeText: Staphylococci are distinguished from Streptococci biochemically by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide.
extraNote: Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Under the microscope, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: This is a primary morphological distinction in Gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: The classic lesion caused by Staphylococcus aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which characterized by central necrosis and pus drainage.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol::biochemical reaction}} and is β-hemolytic on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides S. aureus with iron, which is required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene, which encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids::genetic element}} that encode β-lactamase, making them resistant to many penicillins.
extraNote: Nafcillin is often used to treat non-MRSA S. aureus because it is resistant to this beta-lactamase.

clozeText: Strains of CA-MRSA (Community-Acquired), such as USA300, almost always produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin::toxin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few strains of HCA-MRSA (Healthcare-Acquired) produce this specific leukocidin.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate::molecule}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This mechanism is acquired from enterococci via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: S. aureus virulence factor {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the Fc portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.
extraNote: Coagulase-negative staphylococci do not produce Protein A.

clozeText: The cell wall component {{c1::teichoic acid}} mediates the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in the S. aureus cell wall induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of endotoxin in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of skin infections.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: MRSA is particularly prevalent in this population.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is a catalase-positive organism, which is a key threat to patients lacking oxidative burst capability.

clozeText: Vaginal colonization by S. aureus in 5% of women predisposes them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: The syndrome is caused by the release of toxic shock syndrome toxin (TSST).

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a pediatric disease caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus, leading to large areas of desquamated skin.
extraNote: It is also known as Ritter's disease.

clozeText: The lesions of {{c1::impetigo}} are crops of vesicles characterized by a "honey-colored" crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, presenting as small pustules on hair follicles.
extraNote: It can progress to furuncles (boils) or carbuncles.

clozeText: S. aureus causes several pyogenic infections, including endocarditis, septic arthritis, and {{c1::osteomyelitis}}.
extraNote: S. aureus is a major cause of surgical-wound infections and infections at cardiac pacemaker sites.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is clinically distinguished by its resistance to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive to novobiocin; this test differentiates the two coagulase-negative species.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora but can cause infections of {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and prosthetic hips.
extraNote: Biofilm formation is a critical virulence factor for S. epidermidis on prosthetic devices.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause findings of septic shock despite lacking {{c1::endotoxin}} because its peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acids stimulate cytokine production.
extraNote: It activates the complement and coagulation cascades similarly to Gram-negative LPS.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::85}}% of S. aureus infections are caused by capsule polysaccharide types 5 and 8.
extraNote: The microcapsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: Predisposing factors to S. aureus infection include foreign bodies such as {{c1::sutures}} and intravenous catheters.
extraNote: These provide a surface for colonization and shield the bacteria from the immune response.

clozeText: A major systemic predisposing factor for S. aureus infections is the metabolic disease {{c1::diabetes}}.
extraNote: Reduced humoral immunity and neutrophil function in these patients increase risk.

clozeText: S. aureus can be identified to the strain level for epidemiology using {{c1::phage typing}}, which utilizes surface receptors including teichoic acids.
extraNote: This method relies on the specific susceptibility of strains to certain bacteriophages.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that differentiates them from streptococci by degrading {{c2::H2O2}} into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This allows catalase-positive bacteria to survive the oxidative killing effect within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}, which activates {{c2::prothrombin}} to form thrombin.
extraNote: Thrombin then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: In addition to being coagulase-positive, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and produces {{c2::β-hemolysis::type of hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: The major protein in the S. aureus cell wall is {{c1::Protein A}}, which functions by binding to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis because the Fc portion is unavailable to bind to receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Strains of S. aureus with full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) employ a mechanism that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This resistance is often carried on a transposon located on a plasmid, originally acquired from enterococci.

clozeText: Nearly all strains of {{c1::Community-Acquired (CA-MRSA)}} produce the virulence factor {{c2::P-V leukocidin}}, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}, with approximately 30% of the population colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: The {{c1::teichoic acids}} of S. aureus are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}} from macrophages.
extraNote: The peptidoglycan also has endotoxin-like properties that can activate complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill {{c2::catalase-positive}} bacteria.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the NADPH oxidase system, preventing the oxidative burst.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which characteristically undergoes central {{c2::necrosis}}.
extraNote: Abscesses often drain pus (furuncles/boils) and can lead to hematogenous dissemination.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users::patient population}}.
extraNote: This includes abscesses, sepsis, and endocarditis.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an S. aureus {{c1::exotoxin}} that leads to widespread desquamation, particularly in infants.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: The honey-colored crusting seen in {{c1::impetigo}} can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of ~5% of women, predisposing them to {{c1::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin (TSST-1) leading to massive cytokine release.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is an important virulence factor, with serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} causing approximately 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90%}} of S. aureus strains possess plasmids encoding {{c2::β-lactamase}}, necessitating the use of penicillinase-resistant drugs like nafcillin.
extraNote: Beta-lactamase breaks the beta-lactam ring, inactivating standard penicillins.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: The major clinical manifestation of Staphylococcus saprophyticus is {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}}.
extraNote: It is a common cause of cystitis in young, sexually active women.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a frequent cause of infections associated with {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a normal member of the skin flora and produces a biofilm (slime layer) to adhere to plastics.

clozeText: Hand contact is a critical mode of transmission for S. aureus, and {{c1::handwashing}} is the most effective way to decrease spread in clinical settings.
extraNote: Healthcare workers are often transient carriers on their skin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial) pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also commonly involved in infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: An important predisposing factor for S. aureus infection is the presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}}, such as sutures or {{c2::intravenous catheters}}.
extraNote: Bacteria utilize these surfaces to establish protected niches (biofilms).

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing systemic factor for infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia and impaired neutrophil function contribute to increased susceptibility.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles characterized by small pustules.
extraNote: If the infection progresses, it can form larger furuncles or carbuncles.

clozeText: S. aureus may be the causative agent of {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}}, a childhood disease of unknown etiology characterized by vasculitis.
extraNote: Staphylococcal superantigens are hypothesized to play a role in the pathogenesis.

clozeText: MRSA currently accounts for more than {{c1::50%}} of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients in the United States.
extraNote: Treatment usually requires vancomycin or newer agents like daptomycin or linezolid.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which differentiates them from streptococci.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades H2O2 into oxygen and water, allowing the bacteria to survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: The classic lesion caused by Staphylococcus aureus is an {{c1::abscess::type of lesion}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: S. aureus causes pyogenic inflammation and can disseminate via the bloodstream.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}, which clots plasma.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: The {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene on the bacterial chromosome encodes altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBP2a) in MRSA.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but does not bind β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Protein A, a major cell wall component of S. aureus, inhibits phagocytosis by binding to the {{c1::Fc portion::part of antibody}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages from binding the antibody, thwarting opsonization.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus recovery of iron for cytochrome synthesis is achieved through the {{c1::hemolysis::process}} of red blood cells.
extraNote: S. aureus usually ferments mannitol and is β-hemolytic, unlike S. epidermidis or S. saprophyticus.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate::molecule}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification is encoded by genes typically located on a transposon on a plasmid, often acquired from enterococci.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus colonization in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are nasal carriers at any given time.

clozeText: In patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}}, S. aureus is a frequent cause of infection because the bacteria produce catalase.
extraNote: CGD patients have a defect in neutrophil killing (NADPH oxidase deficiency) and cannot neutralize catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids::cell wall component}}, which trigger the release of IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: S. aureus peptidoglycan also has endotoxin-like properties that activate the complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains frequently produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin::toxin}}, a virulence factor rarely seen in HCA-MRSA.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust, can be caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: Bullous impetigo is specifically associated with S. aureus strains producing exfoliative toxin.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is also at high risk for right-sided endocarditis caused by S. aureus.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin::type of toxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It causes widespread desquamation of the skin, typically in infants and young children.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis::organism}} is the most common cause of infections related to prosthetic heart valves and artificial joints.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections and is distinguished by its resistance to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: Unlike S. saprophyticus, S. epidermidis is sensitive to novobiocin.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%::percentage}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by TSST-1, a superantigen that causes massive cytokine release.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids::component}} are cell wall polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids::genetic element}} that encode β-lactamase.
extraNote: β-lactamase degrades penicillins like penicillin G, necessitating the use of nafcillin or other penicillinase-resistant drugs.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis::bone condition}}, an infection of the bone.
extraNote: Other pyogenic infections include septic arthritis and endocarditis.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::condition}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It primarily affects children and involves vasculitis of the coronary arteries.

clozeText: The {{c1::USA300::strain name}} strain is currently the most common strain of MRSA in the United States.
extraNote: It is heavily associated with community-acquired infections and skin abscesses.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci are arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: This morphology is due to division in multiple planes, unlike streptococci which divide in one plane to form chains.

clozeText: Staphylococci are gram-{{c1::positive::stain}} cocci that are nonmotile and do not form spores.
extraNote: The Gram stain shows purple spheres in clusters.

clozeText: S. aureus capsule types {{c1::5 and 8::serotypes}} are responsible for about 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes::condition}} is a major predisposing factor to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia and impaired neutrophil function in these patients contribute to increased susceptibility.

clozeText: Folliculitis, characterized by small pustules on the chin or neck, is most commonly caused by {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::organism}}.
extraNote: It involves the infection of hair follicles and can progress to furuncles.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause food poisoning through the ingestion of a preformed {{c1::enterotoxin::type of toxin}}.
extraNote: Symptoms typically include rapid-onset vomiting and diarrhea (within 1-6 hours).

clozeText: The primary biochemical test used to differentiate {{c1::Staphylococcus::genus}} (positive) from {{c1::Streptococcus::genus}} (negative) is the catalase test.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, allowing bacteria to survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, Staphylococci are arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas Streptococci are found in {{c1::chains}}.
extraNote: This morphological distinction is visible on Gram stain; both are Gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::coagulase}} distinguishes S. aureus from other staphylococci by activating prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: Thrombin then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot, potentially walling off the bacteria from immune cells.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: Common presentations include endocarditis (often right-sided) and skin abscesses.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Abscesses are the hallmark of pyogenic (pus-producing) inflammation caused by this organism.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin and methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA::gene}}.
extraNote: This gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) that has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: MRSA strains produce an altered {{c1::PBP2a::protein}} which can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This is the structural basis for resistance to all current beta-lactams except 5th generation cephalosporins.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major virulence factor of S. aureus that binds to the {{c2::Fc::portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids::cell wall component}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: The induction of septic shock by S. aureus involves {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which stimulate macrophages to release {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is analogous to the action of endotoxin (LPS) in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c1::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This modification is acquired via a transposon often originating from Enterococci.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers, increasing their risk for autoinfection.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, meaning it can neutralize the small amount of H2O2 produced by the patient's defective neutrophils.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}}.
extraNote: S. aureus turns Mannitol Salt Agar yellow, while coagulase-negative staph typically do not.

clozeText: Among the coagulase-negative staphylococci, {{c1::S. epidermidis::species}} is sensitive to novobiocin, while {{c2::S. saprophyticus::species}} is resistant.
extraNote: This is a classic 'lab bench' mnemonic (S-S-R: Saprophyticus is Second and Resistant).

clozeText: Almost all strains of Community-Acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin rarely found in HCA-MRSA.
extraNote: Panton-Valentine leukocidin is associated with necrotizing skin lesions and severe pneumonia.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus that results in widespread epidermal desquamation.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein, a protein in desmosomes.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus requires iron for growth, which it obtains by producing {{c1::hemolysins}} to lyse red blood cells and recover iron from hemoglobin.
extraNote: Iron is specifically used for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes in the bacteria.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids}} that encode {{c2::beta-lactamase}}.
extraNote: This enzyme renders standard penicillin G ineffective against most staphylococcal infections.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome can occur in women due to S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}}, which is found in ~5% of women.
extraNote: This is often associated with high-absorbency tampon use, providing a growth environment for the toxin-producing strain.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is a frequent cause of community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: {{c1::S. saprophyticus::species}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is identified as a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant Gram-positive coccus.

clozeText: The S. aureus peptidoglycan has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, stimulating the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus can trigger septic shock even though it lacks true LPS (endotoxin).

clozeText: {{c1::S. epidermidis::species}} is the most common cause of infections associated with prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: Its ability to produce a biofilm (slime layer) allows it to adhere to synthetic surfaces.

clozeText: S. aureus polysaccharide capsule types {{c1::5 and 8::types}} cause approximately 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::disease}} is a pediatric disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is characterized by systemic vasculitis and is a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children.

clozeText: {{c1::Hand contact::transmission}} is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus in healthcare settings.
extraNote: Rigorous handwashing is the primary method used to decrease the spread of the organism.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that differentiates them from streptococci by degrading {{c2::H2O2}} into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the oxidative killing effect within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: In the laboratory, S. aureus can be differentiated from S. epidermidis by its ability to {{c1::ferment mannitol}} and {{c2::hemolyze}} red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::PBP2a::protein}}.
extraNote: This altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP) can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Strains of S. aureus with full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) possess a transposon that encodes enzymes substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This is the same resistance cassette found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE).

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} acts as a virulence factor by binding to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG, preventing phagocytosis.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages from binding the antibody.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose::anatomical site}}, with approximately {{c2::30::%}} of the population colonized.
extraNote: Chronic nasal carriers have an increased risk of developing skin infections.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is characterized by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, which is relatively rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States is USA300.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: S. aureus induces septic shock findings despite lacking endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} and {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} stimulate macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also mediate adherence to mucosal cells.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus, leading to desquamation in infants.
extraNote: The condition presents as widespread areas of 'rolled up' skin.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts::finding}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It often presents as crops of vesicles that rupture.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is uniquely sensitive to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}, distinguishing it from Staphylococcus saprophyticus.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of UTIs and is novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and often gains access via foreign bodies.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: These are common pyogenic complications of hematogenous spread.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is associated with S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}}, which occurs in about 5% of women.
extraNote: The syndrome is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: Over {{c1::90%}} of S. aureus strains produce {{c2::beta-lactamase::enzyme}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: These strains require treatment with beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: The {{c1::capsule}} of S. aureus is an important virulence factor, with serotypes {{c2::5 and 8}} causing the majority of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: Staphylococci are morphologically described as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: This is in contrast to streptococci, which typically form chains.

clozeText: A major predisposing factor for S. aureus infections, besides immune compromise, is {{c1::diabetes}}.
extraNote: Reduced humoral immunity and neutrophils also increase susceptibility.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of {{c1::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: It is a pediatric vasculitis often involving coronary arteries.

clozeText: For epidemiologic purposes, S. aureus strains can be classified using {{c1::phage typing}}.
extraNote: This relies on surface receptors composed in part of teichoic acids.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also frequently found at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertions.

clozeText: {{c1::Handwashing::action}} is the most effective way to decrease the transmission of S. aureus among hospital personnel.
extraNote: Hand contact is the primary mode of transmission.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause food poisoning by producing a preformed {{c1::enterotoxin}}.
extraNote: The text lists food poisoning among the primary diseases caused by the organism.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}} such as sutures or catheters greatly predisposes patients to infection by S. aureus.
extraNote: These surfaces facilitate biofilm formation and protect the bacteria from host defenses.

clozeText: The primary biochemical test used to distinguish {{c1::Staphylococcus}} (positive) from {{c1::Streptococcus}} (negative) is the {{c2::catalase::enzyme}} test.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into O2 and H2O, allowing bacteria to survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: Within the genus Staphylococcus, {{c1::S. aureus}} is distinguished from others by being {{c2::coagulase}}-positive.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: The major virulence factor in the cell wall of S. aureus that binds the {{c1::Fc portion::part of Ig}} of {{c2::IgG}} is {{c3::Protein A}}.
extraNote: By binding the Fc region, Protein A prevents opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: MRSA (Methicillin-resistant S. aureus) is resistant to nafcillin due to the {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: This altered PBP2a maintains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by triggering {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}}.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids act similarly to the endotoxin (LPS) found in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: High-level vancomycin resistance (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This modification is carried on a transposon, often acquired from Enterococcus species.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and {{c2::pus::fluid}} production.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses, furuncles, and boils.

clozeText: Most strains of {{c1::Community-Acquired (CA-MRSA)}} produce the {{c2::P-V leukocidin::toxin}} toxin, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is associated with necrotizing pneumonia and severe skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}} and its {{c2::β (beta)}} hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: The hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}, with approximately {{c2::30}}% of the population colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of autoinoculation leading to skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot produce {{c2::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}}.
extraNote: Since S. aureus is catalase-positive, it destroys the small amount of H2O2 the patient's cells might otherwise use.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is a coagulase-negative staph that is typically {{c2::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from S. epidermidis, which is novobiocin-sensitive.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}, often presenting as right-sided {{c2::endocarditis}}.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis in this population.

clozeText: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} that causes large areas of desquamated skin, particularly in {{c2::infants}}.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the desmosomes of the epidermis.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crusts, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: S. aureus is currently the most common cause of impetigo.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c2::vagina}}, which predisposes them to Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS).
extraNote: TSS is mediated by TSST-1, which acts as a superantigen.

clozeText: S. aureus is a major cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections, including those at {{c2::cardiac pacemaker}} sites.
extraNote: Hand contact is the primary mode of transmission in healthcare settings.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: The S. aureus {{c1::capsule}} is poorly immunogenic and comes in 11 serotypes, with types {{c2::5 and 8}} causing the majority of human infections.
extraNote: The presence of the capsule or microcapsule inhibits phagocytosis.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora and is a frequent cause of infections involving {{c2::prosthetic heart valves::hardware}} and joints.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::peptidoglycan}} possesses endotoxin-like properties, stimulating macrophages to produce {{c2::cytokines}} and activating the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite being Gram-positive and lacking LPS.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicles, often presenting as small pustules, for which {{c2::S. aureus}} is the most common cause.
extraNote: It commonly occurs on the chin and neck.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains possess {{c2::plasmids}} that encode β-lactamase.
extraNote: This enzyme renders standard penicillin G ineffective against most staphylococcal infections.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. epidermidis is the {{c1::skin}}, while the primary reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c2::nose}}.
extraNote: Both are Gram-positive cocci but differ in their coagulase production and typical disease profiles.

clozeText: In terms of morphology, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This distinction is visible on Gram stain of clinical specimens or cultures.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating non-MRSA S. aureus infections that produce β-lactamase is {{c1::nafcillin::drug}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: Nafcillin is a β-lactamase-resistant penicillin.

clozeText: S. aureus can be differentiated from other species by its ability to cause {{c1::β-hemolysis}} on blood agar, which results in a clear zone around the colonies.
extraNote: Hemolysins (alpha-toxin, etc.) lyse red blood cells to release hemoglobin.

clozeText: {{c1::Phage typing}} of S. aureus for epidemiologic studies is possible because the bacteria have surface receptors for specific bacteriophages, which include {{c2::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: This allows clinicians to track outbreaks by identifying specific strain patterns.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase-positive organisms can survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils; patients with Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) are particularly susceptible to these infections.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci typically form {{c2::chains::arrangement}}.
extraNote: Both genera are Gram-positive cocci, but their spatial arrangement is a primary morphological distinction.

clozeText: The primary enzyme used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci is {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}, which activates prothrombin to form a fibrin clot.
extraNote: S. aureus is coagulase-positive, while S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are coagulase-negative (CoNS).

clozeText: The major virulence factor in the cell wall of S. aureus that prevents phagocytosis by binding the {{c1::Fc portion}} of IgG is {{c2::Protein A}}.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on neutrophils and macrophages from binding the antibody, thereby inhibiting opsonization.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and displays {{c2::beta-hemolysis::hemolysis type}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol fermentation on Mannitol Salt Agar (MSA) results in a yellow color change, a key diagnostic feature.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a maintains its transpeptidase function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics, rendering penicillins and cephalosporins (except 5th gen) ineffective.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin that is relatively rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: Panton-Valentine leukocidin is associated with necrotizing pneumonia and severe skin infections.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This mechanism is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE), often transferred via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the leading cause of skin abscesses, furuncles, and carbuncles.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis::bone infection}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::crust color}} crust, is caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most frequent cause of both impetigo and folliculitis.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a condition in infants caused by an exotoxin that results in widespread desquamation.
extraNote: The exotoxin (exfoliatin) cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis, leading to skin sloughing.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have a significantly increased risk of autoinfection and subsequent skin lesions.

clozeText: In users of intravenous drugs, S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::endocarditis::heart infection}}.
extraNote: It often affects the tricuspid valve (right-sided endocarditis) in this population.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is associated with S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}} in approximately 5% of women.
extraNote: TSS involves a superantigen (TSST-1) that causes massive cytokine release (IL-1, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma).

clozeText: The virulence factor {{c1::teichoic acid}} facilitates the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also serve as surface receptors for specific staphylococcal bacteriophages (phage typing).

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acid}} and peptidoglycan can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release cytokines such as {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite lacking traditional Gram-negative endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to destroy red blood cells and recover {{c2::iron}} for use in its cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth during infection.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is distinguished from Staphylococcus saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive; S. saprophyticus is resistant. Remember: 'NO Staph' for saprophyticus (Novobiocin Off/Resistant).

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora but can cause infections of {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It produces a biofilm (extracellular polysaccharide) that allows it to adhere to plastic and metal surfaces.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections}} in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is the second most common cause of cystitis in this demographic after E. coli.

clozeText: The capsule of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic; serotypes {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} account for the majority of human infections.
extraNote: Microcapsules (small amounts of polysaccharide) can also coat certain strains, aiding in the evasion of the immune system.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::diabetes}} and {{c2::Chronic Granulomatous Disease}} are significantly more predisposed to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Neutrophil defects (CGD) or impaired vascular flow/high glucose (diabetes) facilitate staphylococcal survival.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::beta-lactamase::enzyme}}, which is typically encoded on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins like penicillin G; treatment usually requires beta-lactamase-resistant agents like nafcillin.

clozeText: The primary drug of choice for treating non-MRSA S. aureus infections is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: These are beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::bacterial conjunctivitis}}, an infection of the outer layer of the eye.
extraNote: It is also associated with surgical site infections, including pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::disease}}, a condition of unknown etiology involving systemic vasculitis, has been suggested to be caused by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: The disease primarily affects young children and can lead to coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: It is frequently associated with skin and soft tissue infections in the community.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that differentiates them from streptococci by degrading H2O2 into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the oxidative killing effect of hydrogen peroxide within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococci are morphologically described as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: In contrast, streptococci are typically arranged in chains.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}, which activates prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: The resulting thrombin catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot, potentially walling off the bacteria from the immune system.

clozeText: S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c1::β-hemolysis}} on blood agar, whereas S. epidermidis does not.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides a source of iron, which is recovered and used for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: The major protein in the S. aureus cell wall is {{c1::Protein A::virulence factor}}, which prevents phagocytosis by binding to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By occupying the Fc portion, the antibody cannot bind to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: In vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA), resistance is achieved by substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to the terminal part of the peptidoglycan precursor.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill catalase-positive bacteria.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in NADPH oxidase, preventing the production of reactive oxygen species.

clozeText: S. aureus cell wall {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF, leading to septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids trigger the same inflammatory pathways as Gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is unique because almost all strains produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin that kills white blood cells.
extraNote: This toxin contributes to the severity of skin infections and necrotizing pneumonia in healthy individuals.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which features central necrosis and pus drainage.
extraNote: Furuncles and boils are common clinical presentations of these abscesses.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is sensitive to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}, while {{c2::S. saprophyticus}} is resistant.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci in urinary tract infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This often manifests as endocarditis, specifically involving the right-sided valves (tricuspid).

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus that causes widespread desquamation in infants.
extraNote: The skin appears 'rolled up' and denuded, resembling a burn.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately {{c1::5%}} of women, predisposing them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is associated with superantigen production and can be linked to tampon use.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages to produce {{c1::cytokines}} and activate the complement cascade, mimicking the effects of {{c2::endotoxin}}.
extraNote: This explains why Gram-positive bacteria like S. aureus can still cause clinical signs of septic shock.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of hospital-acquired (nosocomial) {{c1::pneumonia}}, septicemia, and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also frequently associated with infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: Regarding S. aureus capsules, there are 11 serotypes, but types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the vast majority (85%) of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of bone and joint infections, specifically {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: Staph aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in the general population.

clozeText: Epidemiologic typing of S. aureus strains can be performed using {{c1::bacteriophages}}, which bind to surface receptors made partly of teichoic acids.
extraNote: This is known as 'phage typing'.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora but can cause serious infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: Its ability to form biofilms is a key factor in these hardware-associated infections.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: It is frequently associated with community-acquired outbreaks.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::food poisoning}} through the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins.
extraNote: Symptoms usually have a rapid onset (within hours) because the toxin is already present in the food.

clozeText: A major predisposing factor to S. aureus infections is {{c1::diabetes}}, which compromises the host's immune response.

clozeText: {{c1::Hand contact}} is an important mode of S. aureus transmission in healthcare settings, emphasizing the need for regular handwashing.

clozeText: MRSA is defined as being resistant to {{c1::nafcillin}} and methicillin, requiring the use of antibiotics like {{c2::vancomycin}}.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) occurs when {{c1::D-lactate}} is substituted for {{c2::D-alanine}} in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This substitution is encoded by a gene cassette often acquired from enterococci via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for S. aureus in approximately 30% of humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nares have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil bacterial killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the respiratory burst to kill catalase-positive organisms.

extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein, disrupting the epidermal layer.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: This often manifests as acute endocarditis, frequently involving the tricuspid valve.

clozeText: Impetigo, which presents as honey-colored crusts, can be caused by either {{c1::S. aureus}} or {{c2::S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}}, a metabolic property that helps distinguish it from coagulase-negative species.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar (MSA) is used in labs; S. aureus turns the agar yellow.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus has endotoxin-like properties, allowing it to induce {{c2::septic shock}} despite being Gram-positive.
extraNote: It can activate the complement and coagulation cascades and stimulate cytokine release.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate the {{c2::adherence}} of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} induce the release of cytokines like {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages, contributing to septic shock.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of LPS/Endotoxin found in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Almost all community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains produce the {{c1::P-V leukocidin::toxin}}, which is rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is associated with necrotizing skin infections and severe pneumonia.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is famously associated with infections of {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a common member of the skin flora and produces biofilms on foreign bodies.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young women.
extraNote: It is typically novobiocin-resistant, unlike S. epidermidis.

clozeText: Coagulase-negative staphylococci are differentiated by their reaction to {{c1::novobiocin}}; S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}} while S. epidermidis is sensitive.
extraNote: This is a standard laboratory mnemonic: NO-Stressed (Saprophyticus-Resistant), On-the-Edge (Epidermidis-Sensitive).

clozeText: {{c1::Nafcillin}} (or oxacillin) is the treatment of choice for {{c2::beta-lactamase}}-producing strains of S. aureus that are not methicillin-resistant.
extraNote: These are known as MSSA (Methicillin-Sensitive S. aureus).

clozeText: The {{c1::capsule}} of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic, making it difficult to develop an effective {{c2::vaccine}}.
extraNote: Serotypes 5 and 8 cause approximately 85% of staphylococcal infections.

clozeText: S. aureus produces {{c1::hemolysins}} to break down red blood cells to obtain {{c2::iron}}, which is required for cytochrome synthesis.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting factor for bacterial growth in the human host.

clozeText: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus, emphasizing the importance of {{c1::handwashing}}.
extraNote: This is especially critical for hospital personnel to prevent healthcare-acquired infections.

clozeText: Presence of S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}} of approximately 5% of women predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is associated with superantigen production (TSST-1) and high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is characterized by multiple small pustules on the chin and neck and is most commonly caused by {{c2::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: It is an infection of the hair follicles that may progress to furuncles.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of sepsis and septicemia in hospitalized patients.

clozeText: Staphylococci typically appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}} on Gram stain, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This morphological difference is a primary microscopic criterion for identification.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections (CA-MRSA).

clozeText: Biochemically, Staphylococci are differentiated from Streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the oxidative burst (killing effect of H2O2) within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, Staphylococci appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas Streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: Both are gram-positive, nonmotile, and non-spore-forming cocci.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other Staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β (beta)}} hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and acts as a virulence factor by binding the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on phagocytes from binding the antibody, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids::cell wall component}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by stimulating cytokine release.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids trigger macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess {{c1::plasmids}} that encode {{c2::β-lactamase::enzyme}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: Nafcillin or oxacillin (beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins) are typically used for these strains.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: High-level vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This cassette of genes is often acquired from vancomycin-resistant enterococci via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: S. aureus causes disease via both pyogenic inflammation and toxin production.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains are distinguished by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of the population is colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of autoinoculation leading to skin infections.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::peptidoglycan}} possesses endotoxin-like properties, stimulating macrophages to produce {{c2::cytokines}} and activating the complement cascade.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock despite being Gram-positive and lacking LPS/endotoxin.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, allowing it to neutralize the limited H2O2 produced in these patients.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users}}.
extraNote: These patients are at high risk for endocarditis and sepsis caused by MRSA.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust, can be caused by either {{c2::S. aureus}} or S. pyogenes.
extraNote: Folliculitis is more commonly caused specifically by S. aureus.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus, leading to widespread desquamation in infants.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause of infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::joint replacements (hips)}}.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and is coagulase-negative.

clozeText: To differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to novobiocin, while S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: S. aureus colonization of the {{c1::vagina}} in ~5% of women predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin (TSST-1).

clozeText: {{c1::Hand contact}} is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus in hospital settings.
extraNote: Handwashing is the most effective way to decrease transmission among hospital personnel.

clozeText: S. aureus produces iron-seeking hemolysins; the recovered iron is used for the synthesis of {{c1::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: This is essential for the bacterial energy production cycle.

clozeText: While S. aureus has a polysaccharide capsule with 11 serotypes, types {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} cause 85% of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: {{c1::Phage typing::method}} of S. aureus strains for epidemiologic purposes is possible because of surface receptors partly composed of teichoic acids.
extraNote: Specific staphylococcal bacteriophages bind to these receptors.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} and the presence of {{c2::foreign bodies}} (e.g., sutures, catheters) are major predisposing factors to S. aureus infection.
extraNote: Foreign bodies provide a surface for biofilm formation and shield bacteria from the immune system.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of hospital-acquired {{c1::pneumonia}}, septicemia, and {{c2::surgical-wound}} infections.
extraNote: It is also a common cause of bacterial conjunctivitis.

clozeText: The enzyme coagulase produced by S. aureus activates {{c1::prothrombin}} to thrombin.
extraNote: This is a key biochemical test used to identify S. aureus in the lab.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: It is a systemic vasculitis primarily affecting children.

clozeText: Staphylococci are characterized microscopically as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci are arranged in chains.
extraNote: This arrangement is due to the plane of cell division in staphylococci.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that degrades {{c2::H2O2::hydrogen peroxide}} into water and oxygen.
extraNote: This test differentiates all staphylococci (positive) from streptococci (negative).

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from other staphylococci because it typically {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β-hemolysis::type of hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: The major virulence factor in the S. aureus cell wall that binds the Fc portion of IgG is {{c1::Protein A}}.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: The component of the S. aureus cell wall that mediates adherence to mucosal cells is {{c1::teichoic acid}}.
extraNote: Teichoic acids are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the receptors for bacteriophages.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating the release of cytokines like {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::two cytokines}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of endotoxin (LPS) in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a functions as a transpeptidase but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves a gene cassette that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan structure.
extraNote: This same resistance mechanism is found in Enterococci and is often carried on transposons.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of the population is colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of developing autologous skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in NADPH oxidase, preventing the production of reactive oxygen species.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and contains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is uniquely associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin::toxin}}, which is rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that targets white blood cells.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This frequently leads to right-sided endocarditis involving the tricuspid valve.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus, leading to large areas of desquamated skin.
extraNote: The toxin is also known as exfoliatin; it cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored crust}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately {{c1::5}}% of women, predisposing them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: Toxic shock is often associated with high-absorptivity tampon use.

clozeText: The S. aureus cell wall component {{c1::peptidoglycan}} possesses endotoxin-like properties, allowing the bacteria to cause {{c2::septic shock}} without having LPS.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines and activate the complement cascade.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: Remember: 'Staph saprophyticus is Second' (resistant), 'Staph epidermidis is E-sensitive'.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints::hips}}.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and forms biofilms on plastic surfaces.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a significant cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is second only to E. coli in this demographic.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is characterized by vasculitis, fever, and 'strawberry tongue'.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::β-lactamase}}, an enzyme typically encoded on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme renders standard penicillin ineffective against most S. aureus infections.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is a frequent cause of community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is one of the most common causes of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of infections at pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: Phage typing of S. aureus strains for epidemiologic purposes is possible because of surface receptors made partly of {{c1::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: Specific bacteriophages infect only certain strains based on these receptors.

clozeText: While S. aureus has 11 serotypes based on capsular polysaccharide, types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the vast majority (85%) of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The first-line treatment for non-MRSA S. aureus infections (MSSA) is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: These are beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins.

clozeText: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a {{c1::defective}} virus because it requires the presence of HBV to provide its envelope.
extraNote: HDV cannot produce its own envelope proteins and relies on HBsAg for virion assembly and infection of hepatocytes.

clozeText: The HDV genome consists of {{c1::negative}}-sense, {{c2::circular}}, single-stranded RNA.
extraNote: The circular nature of the HDV genome is unique among animal viruses and resembles plant viroids.

clozeText: HDV utilizes the {{c1::HBsAg (surface antigen)}} from Hepatitis B virus for its external envelope.
extraNote: This requirement makes HDV an obligate satellite virus of HBV.

clozeText: {{c1::Superinfection}} occurs when a chronic HBV carrier is subsequently infected with HDV, often leading to severe permanent liver damage.
extraNote: Superinfection has a much higher risk of chronicity (nearly 100%) and fulminant hepatitis compared to co-infection.
