clozeText: {{c1::Co-infection}} occurs when a person is infected with both HBV and HDV at the same time.
extraNote: Co-infection usually presents as a severe acute hepatitis but rarely results in chronic HDV infection as HBV is often cleared.

clozeText: HDV replication takes place in the host cell's {{c1::nucleus}}.
extraNote: This is unusual for an RNA virus, as most replicate in the cytoplasm (except Orthomyxoviruses and Retroviruses).

clozeText: HDV is unique among RNA viruses because it uses host cell {{c1::RNA polymerase II}} to replicate its genome.
extraNote: HDV does not encode its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; it subverts the host's DNA-dependent RNA polymerase to work on its RNA template.

clozeText: The HDV genome encodes a single protein known as the {{c1::Delta antigen (HDAg)}}.
extraNote: HDAg exists in two forms (Small and Large), which serve different functions in the viral life cycle.

clozeText: The {{c1::Small}} form of the Delta antigen (S-HDAg) is required for viral {{c2::replication}}.
extraNote: The S-HDAg is produced early in the infection cycle.

clozeText: The {{c1::Large}} form of the Delta antigen (L-HDAg) is required for viral {{c2::assembly}}.
extraNote: L-HDAg also acts as an inhibitor of further HDV genome replication.

clozeText: HDV RNA possesses {{c1::ribozyme}} activity, allowing it to self-cleave and ligate during replication.
extraNote: This catalytic RNA activity is essential for the rolling-circle replication mechanism of the circular genome.

clozeText: The switch from producing Small HDAg to Large HDAg is mediated by the host enzyme {{c1::ADAR1::adenosine deaminase acting on RNA}}.
extraNote: ADAR1 edits the amber stop codon (UAG) to a tryptophan codon (UGG), extending the protein.

clozeText: HDV infection is prevented by administering the {{c1::HBV vaccine}}.
extraNote: Since HDV requires HBsAg, immunity to HBV automatically provides protection against HDV.

clozeText: Chronic HDV superinfection carries a significant risk of progressing to {{c1::cirrhosis}} and {{c2::hepatocellular carcinoma}}.
extraNote: HDV is considered the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis.

clozeText: In the United States, the highest prevalence of HDV is found among {{c1::intravenous drug users}}.
extraNote: Transmission is primarily parenteral, mirroring the risk factors of HBV and HCV.

clozeText: Acute HDV infection is diagnosed by detecting {{c1::IgM anti-HDV}} or HDV RNA in the serum.
extraNote: Persistent HDV RNA indicates chronic infection, which is often seen in superinfected patients.

clozeText: The HDV genome replicates via a {{c1::rolling circle}} mechanism.
extraNote: This involves the synthesis of multi-unit linear concatemers that are cleaved by the viral ribozyme.

clozeText: HDV is the only species in the genus {{c1::Deltavirus}}.
extraNote: It is often categorized as a subviral satellite or a viroid-like agent.

clozeText: The HDV virion is approximately {{c1::35::size in nm}} nm in diameter.
extraNote: It is smaller than the HBV Dane particle (42 nm) but uses the same surface proteins.

clozeText: HDV RNA contains a very high {{c1::G-C}} content, resulting in a rod-like secondary structure.
extraNote: Extensive base pairing (approximately 70%) makes the single-stranded circular RNA appear double-stranded.

clozeText: Unlike HBV, HDV is believed to cause liver damage through {{c1::direct cytopathic effects}} in addition to immune-mediated damage.
extraNote: The Delta antigen itself may be toxic to hepatocytes.

clozeText: The current treatment of choice for chronic HDV, though often with low success rates, is {{c1::Interferon-alpha}}.
extraNote: Nucleoside analogs used for HBV (like entecavir) are generally ineffective against HDV replication.

clozeText: HBsAg-positive patients with sudden worsening of chronic hepatitis should be screened for {{c1::HDV superinfection}}.
extraNote: A "flare" in a previously stable HBV patient is a classic presentation for HDV acquisition.

clozeText: HDV is transmitted via {{c1::blood}} and {{c2::sexual}} contact.
extraNote: Vertical (perinatal) transmission is possible but less common than with HBV alone.

clozeText: Immunity against HDV is mediated by the production of {{c1::anti-HBs}} antibodies.
extraNote: Anti-HBs prevents the entry of both HBV and HDV into the hepatocyte by blocking attachment.

clozeText: The Large Delta Antigen (L-HDAg) undergoes {{c1::prenylation}} at its C-terminus, which is essential for interaction with HBsAg.
extraNote: Prenylation (addition of a farnesyl group) allows the protein to anchor to the viral envelope during assembly.

clozeText: In a patient with HDV/HBV {{c1::co-infection}}, the serologic marker {{c2::anti-HBc IgM}} will be positive.
extraNote: This distinguishes co-infection from superinfection, where anti-HBc IgG would be present instead.

clozeText: HDV is considered a {{c1::subviral satellite::classification}} because it requires a helper virus (HBV) for its infectious cycle.
extraNote: It is the only human pathogen in this category.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide.
extraNote: Catalase converts H2O2 into H2O and O2; it is an important virulence factor that protects the organism from being killed by neutrophils.

clozeText: The primary biochemical test used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci is {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}} production.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta-hemolysis::type}} on blood agar, distinguishing it from S. epidermidis.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron from hemoglobin, which is utilized for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a maintains its transpeptidase function but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics, rendering the bacteria resistant.

clozeText: In vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA), the resistance mechanism involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This change is encoded by a cassette of genes often acquired from enterococci via a transposon on a plasmid.

clozeText: S. aureus virulence factor {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG to prevent phagocytosis.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc portion from binding to receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, inhibiting opsonization.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages (phage typing).

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which stimulate the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: S. aureus lacks endotoxin (LPS), but its cell wall components can trigger the same cytokine cascade.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where it colonizes approximately 30% of the population.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of developing skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill catalase-positive bacteria.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in NADPH oxidase, leading to impaired oxidative burst.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which is characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Foreign bodies like sutures or intravenous catheters are major predisposing factors for these infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: MRSA is particularly prevalent in this population and can lead to sepsis and endocarditis.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a desquamating skin disease in infants caused by an exotoxin produced by certain S. aureus strains.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein, leading to the detachment of the epidermal layer.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: Among coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus epidermidis is sensitive to {{c1::novobiocin}}, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause of infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves::devices}} and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a normal member of the skin flora and utilizes biofilm formation to adhere to synthetic materials.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce the {{c1::P-V leukocidin}} toxin, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also frequently involved in infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}}, a systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology, may be associated with certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: This disease primarily affects young children and can lead to coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, which predisposes them to Toxic Shock Syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by TSST-1, a superantigen that causes massive cytokine release.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus has endotoxin-like properties, allowing it to activate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus causes septic shock despite being Gram-positive and lacking LPS.

clozeText: The S. aureus polysaccharide capsule is an important virulence factor, with serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} causing the majority of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, which complicates the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicles for which S. aureus is the most common causative agent.
extraNote: Presentation usually involves multiple small pustules localized to the chin, neck, or other hair-bearing areas.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains possess plasmids encoding {{c1::beta-lactamase}}, requiring the use of nafcillin or oxacillin.
extraNote: These enzymes specifically target the beta-lactam ring of penicillin G.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear as gram-positive cocci in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This arrangement is due to the plane of cell division; staphylococci divide in multiple planes.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing metabolic factor to infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Elevated glucose and impaired neutrophil function in diabetics contribute to increased susceptibility.

clozeText: The most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States is {{c1::MRSA}}.
extraNote: Community-acquired MRSA has significantly increased the incidence of these pyogenic infections.

clozeText: Organisms with {{c1::intermediate}} resistance to vancomycin are known as VISA, while those with full resistance are VRSA.
extraNote: VISA strains often show a thickened cell wall that 'traps' vancomycin molecules.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses, pneumonia, and sepsis in intravenous drug users.
extraNote: S. aureus is also the leading cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into {{c2::O2 and H2O}}.
extraNote: This enzyme differentiates staphylococci from streptococci, which are catalase-negative.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is distinguished from other medically important staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c2::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin clots.

clozeText: The major cell wall protein and virulence factor of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages because their Fc receptors cannot bind the occupied IgG.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids::cell wall component}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids are ribitol phosphate polymers; lipoteichoic acids can induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF, contributing to septic shock.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin and methicillin (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: The mecA gene is located on the bacterial chromosome and encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein {{c1::PBP2a}} in MRSA retains its {{c2::transpeptidase}} function but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This allows the cell to synthesize peptidoglycan even in the presence of beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) involves a gene cassette that substitutes {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursor.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus typically ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::β-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for energy production via cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce the toxin {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few strains of healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA) produce this specific leukocidin.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where it colonizes approximately 30% of the population.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are highly susceptible to S. aureus because their neutrophils cannot kill {{c2::catalase}}-positive bacteria.
extraNote: In CGD, there is a defect in the NADPH oxidase system, preventing the oxidative burst.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is highly associated with infections of {{c2::prosthetic devices}} such as heart valves and artificial hips.
extraNote: It is a normal member of the skin flora and is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its {{c1::resistance}} to {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of UTIs in young women.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate {{c1::macrophages}} to produce cytokines, explaining its ability to cause {{c2::septic shock}} without possessing endotoxin.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan also activates the complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} that leads to widespread desquamation.
extraNote: This syndrome is most common in infants and young children.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which features central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Foreign bodies like sutures or catheters predispose patients to abscess formation.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can also be caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: {{c1::Folliculitis}} is an infection of the hair follicles for which S. aureus is the most common cause.
extraNote: It appears as multiple small pustules on areas like the chin and neck.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: It is an acute vasculitis primarily affecting children.

clozeText: The enzymes encoded by plasmids in >90% of S. aureus strains that degrade penicillins are called {{c1::β-lactamases}}.
extraNote: Infections caused by these strains are treated with β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: S. aureus capsular types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the vast majority (85%) of human infections.
extraNote: The microcapsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: Surface receptors for {{c1::bacteriophages}} on S. aureus, composed partly of teichoic acids, allow for {{c2::phage typing}} for epidemiologic study.
extraNote: Phage typing is used to track the source of outbreaks.

clozeText: Staphylococci are morphologically described as gram-positive cocci arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: They are nonmotile and do not form spores.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately {{c1::5%}} of women, predisposing them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: Disease risk is increased by the use of high-absorbent tampons.

clozeText: The coagulase test works by activating {{c1::prothrombin}} to form thrombin, which catalyzes the conversion of {{c2::fibrinogen}} to fibrin.
extraNote: Clotted plasma in a test tube indicates a positive result.

clozeText: S. aureus hemolysins recover iron from {{c1::hemoglobin}}, which is then used to synthesize {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: These cytochromes are essential for the bacterium's energy production.

clozeText: Hand contact is a major mode of S. aureus transmission; therefore, {{c1::handwashing}} is the most important preventive measure.
extraNote: Hospital personnel are often carriers on their skin and in their noses.

clozeText: All Paramyxoviruses possess a {{c1::Fusion (F) protein}}, which facilitates the formation of multinucleated giant cells (syncytia).
extraNote: The F protein mediates the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane and host cells with each other.

clozeText: The genome of Paramyxoviruses consists of {{c1::negative-sense, non-segmented SS RNA::segmentation status}}.
extraNote: Because they are non-segmented, they do not undergo reassortment (unlike Orthomyxoviruses/Influenza).

clozeText: In the treatment of Measles (Rubeola), supplementation with {{c1::Vitamin A}} is shown to reduce morbidity and mortality, especially in malnourished children.
extraNote: Vitamin A helps maintain the integrity of the respiratory and GI epithelium.

clozeText: The classic prodrome of Measles includes the '3 Cs': {{c1::Cough, Coryza, and Conjunctivitis}}.
extraNote: This is followed by Koplik spots and then the maculopapular rash.

clozeText: The pathognomonic finding for Measles, consisting of small blue-white spots on a red background on the buccal mucosa, is called {{c1::Koplik spots}}.
extraNote: These usually appear 1-2 days before the rash and are located near the lower molars.

clozeText: A rare, delayed, and fatal complication of Measles that occurs years after the initial infection is {{c1::Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)}}.
extraNote: It is caused by a persistent, defective Measles virus in the CNS; symptoms include personality changes, seizures, and myoclonus.

clozeText: The characteristic histologic finding in Measles pneumonia or lymphoid tissue is the {{c1::Warthin-Finkeldey giant cell}}.
extraNote: These are multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic cytoplasmic and nuclear inclusions.

clozeText: The Measles rash is a maculopapular eruption that typically spreads in a {{c1::cephalocaudal}} direction.
extraNote: It starts at the hairline/behind the ears and moves down to the trunk and extremities (including palms and soles late).

clozeText: Mumps virus infection most commonly presents with painful, often bilateral, swelling of the {{c1::parotid glands (parotitis)}}.
extraNote: Other salivary glands may be involved, but the parotids are the classic target.

clozeText: A significant complication of Mumps in post-pubertal males is {{c1::orchitis}}, which can occasionally lead to infertility.
extraNote: It is usually unilateral and presents with testicular pain and swelling.

clozeText: Mumps is a common cause of {{c1::aseptic meningitis::neurological complication}} and can also cause acute pancreatitis.
extraNote: Mumps-associated pancreatitis may present with epigastric pain and elevated serum amylase.

clozeText: The 'seal-bark' cough and inspiratory stridor seen in Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) are most commonly caused by {{c1::Parainfluenza virus (Type 1)}}.
extraNote: The virus causes inflammation and narrowing of the subglottic larynx and trachea.

clozeText: On an X-ray of a child with Croup, the subglottic narrowing is visualized as the {{c1::Steeple sign}}.
extraNote: This refers to the tapered appearance of the upper airway on an AP neck radiograph.

clozeText: {{c1::Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV)}} is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants less than 1 year of age.
extraNote: It is a major cause of winter-season hospitalizations in pediatric populations.

clozeText: RSV attaches to respiratory epithelium via the {{c1::G protein}}.
extraNote: Unlike Measles and Mumps, RSV lacks hemagglutinin and neuraminidase activities.

clozeText: {{c1::Palivizumab}} is a monoclonal antibody used for RSV prophylaxis in high-risk premature infants.
extraNote: Its mechanism of action is the inhibition of the RSV F (fusion) protein.

clozeText: In severe, hospitalized cases of RSV in children, the guanosine analog {{c1::Ribavirin}} may be used as a treatment option.
extraNote: Ribavirin is administered via aerosol in these cases.

clozeText: Unlike Orthomyxoviruses, Paramyxoviruses replicate entirely within the {{c1::cytoplasm}}.
extraNote: They carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to transcribe negative-strand RNA.

clozeText: The Measles virus enters host cells by binding the {{c1::CD150 (SLAM)}} receptor or the Nectin-4 receptor.
extraNote: CD150 is found on T cells, B cells, and macrophages, explaining the systemic spread.

clozeText: Mumps and Parainfluenza viruses possess both Hemagglutinin and {{c1::Neuraminidase}} activities on a single HN protein.
extraNote: Measles has Hemagglutinin but lacks Neuraminidase activity.

clozeText: Measles can cause a severe, life-threatening {{c1::giant cell pneumonia}} in immunocompromised patients who lack T-cell immunity.
extraNote: This occurs because the cellular immune response is required to clear the virus.

clozeText: The most common cause of death from Measles in children is {{c1::secondary bacterial pneumonia}}.
extraNote: The virus causes transient immunosuppression by depleting T-cells and altering cytokine profiles.

clozeText: Parainfluenza virus infection can lead to severe airway obstruction in children, occasionally requiring the use of {{c1::nebulized epinephrine}} to reduce edema.
extraNote: Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction of the laryngeal mucosa, widening the airway.

clozeText: Paramyxoviruses are {{c1::enveloped::envelope status}} viruses, making them susceptible to detergents and ether.
extraNote: The envelope is derived from the host cell plasma membrane during budding.

clozeText: Mumps virus parotitis results in an elevation of serum {{c1::amylase}}, which is helpful for clinical diagnosis.
extraNote: This occurs due to inflammation of the salivary glands (S-type) or the pancreas (P-type).

clozeText: The Live-attenuated {{c1::MMR}} vaccine provides protection against Measles, Mumps, and Rubella.
extraNote: It is typically given at 12-15 months and 4-6 years of age.

clozeText: In the lung, RSV causes necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium and increased mucus production, leading to {{c1::air trapping}} and hyperinflation.
extraNote: On physical exam, this presents as wheezing, tachypnea, and retractions.

clozeText: The nucleocapsid of Paramyxoviruses has a {{c1::helical}} symmetry.
extraNote: All negative-strand RNA viruses have helical capsids.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses, such as the Rabies virus, are characterized by a unique {{c1::bullet-shaped::shape}} morphology.
extraNote: They are enveloped viruses with a helical nucleocapsid.

clozeText: The genome of Rhabdoviruses consists of {{c1::negative-sense single-stranded RNA::genome type}}.
extraNote: Because they are negative-sense, they must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses possess a {{c1::helical::symmetry}} nucleocapsid surrounded by a lipid envelope.
extraNote: The envelope contains glycoprotein spikes (G protein) which are essential for attachment.

clozeText: The Rabies virus initially binds to the {{c1::nicotinic acetylcholine::receptor}} receptor on the postsynaptic membrane at the neuromuscular junction.
extraNote: This allows the virus to enter the peripheral nervous system after a bite.

clozeText: Following entry into the peripheral nerves, Rhabdoviruses move toward the CNS via {{c1::retrograde::direction}} axonal transport.
extraNote: The virus travels at a rate of approximately 50–100 mm per day.

clozeText: The motor protein used for the retrograde transport of Rabies virus in axons is {{c1::dynein::protein}}.
extraNote: In contrast, kinesin is typically used for anterograde transport.

clozeText: Pathognomonic histological findings in Rhabdovirus-infected neurons are {{c1::Negri bodies::inclusion name}}.
extraNote: These are eosinophilic, sharply outlined inclusion bodies.

clozeText: Negri bodies are most commonly found in the {{c1::Purkinje cells::cell type}} of the cerebellum and pyramidal cells of the hippocampus.
extraNote: They are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions.

clozeText: Negri bodies represent collections of viral {{c1::nucleocapsids::content}} within the cytoplasm of infected neurons.
extraNote: They are found in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus.

clozeText: The most common reservoir for Rabies in the United States is currently {{c1::bats::animal}}.
extraNote: Other reservoirs include raccoons, skunks, and foxes; dog rabies is rare in the US but common globally.

clozeText: The incubation period of Rabies virus is highly variable and depends primarily on the {{c1::distance of the bite from the CNS::factor}}.
extraNote: Bites on the face or neck have a much shorter incubation than bites on the foot.

clozeText: The classic clinical sign of {{c1::hydrophobia::symptom}} in rabies is caused by painful spasms of the pharyngeal muscles when swallowing liquids.
extraNote: This can also be triggered by the sight or sound of water.

clozeText: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for Rabies includes wound cleansing, administration of {{c1::rabies immunoglobulin (RIG)::passive immunity}}, and the rabies vaccine.
extraNote: RIG provides immediate passive immunity while the vaccine stimulates active immunity.

clozeText: The Rabies vaccine used in humans is typically a(n) {{c1::inactivated (killed)::vaccine type}} virus vaccine.
extraNote: The most common form is the Human Diploid Cell Vaccine (HDCV).

clozeText: Once clinical symptoms of Rabies appear, the disease is almost 100% {{c1::fatal::prognosis}}.
extraNote: Prevention is critical because there is no effective treatment after symptom onset.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses replicate in the {{c1::cytoplasm::location}} of the host cell.
extraNote: This is typical for most RNA viruses, with the exception of Orthomyxoviruses and Retroviruses.

clozeText: The genome of Rhabdoviruses is {{c1::non-segmented::segmentation status}}.
extraNote: Unlike Influenza or Rotavirus, the Rhabdovirus genome is a single piece of RNA.

clozeText: Late in the infection, Rabies virus travels {{c1::anterogradely::direction}} from the CNS to the salivary glands.
extraNote: This ensures the virus is present in saliva for transmission to the next host.

clozeText: In the developing world, the most common vector for transmitting Rabies to humans is {{c1::domestic dogs::animal}}.
extraNote: Effective pet vaccination programs have significantly reduced this in the US.

clozeText: The {{c1::G protein::protein}} on the surface of the Rhabdovirus envelope is the target for neutralizing antibodies.
extraNote: It is also the protein that mediates attachment to the host cell receptor.

clozeText: Human rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is injected {{c1::around the wound site::location}} to neutralize the virus locally.
extraNote: The remaining volume is given intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine injection.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are part of the {{c1::Mononegavirales::order}} order, which includes other non-segmented negative-strand RNA viruses like Paramyxoviruses.
extraNote: This classification is based on genome structure and replication strategy.

clozeText: The prodromal phase of Rabies often presents with non-specific symptoms and {{c1::paresthesia::neurologic finding}} at the site of the original wound.
extraNote: Tingling or itching at the bite site is a high-yield early diagnostic clue.

clozeText: Rabies can present in two forms: the common 'furious' (encephalitic) rabies and the less common {{c1::'dumb' (paralytic)::form}} rabies.
extraNote: The paralytic form may mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome.

clozeText: Rhabdoviruses are easily inactivated by {{c1::soap and water::disinfectant}} because they possess a lipid envelope.
extraNote: Immediate and thorough wound cleansing is a vital step in post-exposure prophylaxis.

clozeText: Besides Purkinje cells, Negri bodies are frequently located in the {{c1::hippocampus::brain region}}.
extraNote: Specifically, they are found in the pyramidal cells.

clozeText: Pre-exposure prophylaxis for Rabies is recommended for high-risk individuals and consists of {{c1::3::number}} doses of the killed vaccine.
extraNote: High-risk groups include veterinarians, laboratory workers, and spelunkers.

clozeText: The specific genus for the Rabies virus within the Rhabdoviridae family is {{c1::Lyssavirus::genus}}.
extraNote: From the Greek 'lyssa', meaning madness or rage.

clozeText: Rhabdoviridae (Rabies virus) are characterized by an enveloped, {{c1::bullet}}-shaped morphology.
extraNote: The virion is approximately 75 nm in diameter and 180 nm in length.

clozeText: The genome of Rabies virus consists of {{c1::negative-sense}} {{c2::single}}-stranded RNA.
extraNote: Because it is negative-sense, the virus must carry its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: Rabies virus G-protein binds specifically to the {{c1::nicotinic acetylcholine}} receptor at the neuromuscular junction.
extraNote: It may also utilize NCAM (neural cell adhesion molecule) for entry into the nervous system.

clozeText: After local replication in muscle, Rabies virus travels to the CNS via {{c1::retrograde}} axonal transport.
extraNote: It hitches a ride on the motor protein dynein to move from the periphery to the cell body.

clozeText: The motor protein used for Rabies virus transport along the axon is {{c1::dynein}}.
extraNote: Kinesin is typically used for anterograde (away from cell body) transport.

clozeText: Pathognomonic {{c1::Negri bodies::Inclusion type}} are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in infected neurons.
extraNote: These are most commonly found in the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and pyramidal cells of the hippocampus.

clozeText: Negri bodies are most characteristically found in the {{c1::hippocampus}} and the {{c2::cerebellum (Purkinje cells)}}.
extraNote: These sites represent the areas of highest viral concentration in the CNS.

clozeText: In the United States, the most common animal reservoir for Rabies transmission to humans is {{c1::bats}}.
extraNote: Other common U.S. reservoirs include raccoons, skunks, and foxes; domestic dogs are rare in the U.S. but the global leader.

clozeText: Worldwide, the most common source of human Rabies infection is the bite of an infected {{c1::dog}}.
extraNote: Mass vaccination of domestic animals is the primary prevention strategy in developed nations.

clozeText: The classic rabies presentation involving painful pharyngeal spasms and fear of water is known as {{c1::hydrophobia}}.
extraNote: Hydrophobia occurs because attempts to drink trigger violent, painful spasms of the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles.

clozeText: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for an unvaccinated individual includes both the {{c1::inactivated vaccine}} and {{c2::human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG)}}.
extraNote: HRIG provides immediate passive immunity, while the vaccine induces active immunity.

clozeText: The rabies vaccine is a(n) {{c1::inactivated/killed}} virus vaccine.
extraNote: Because the incubation period is long, the vaccine can be given post-exposure to generate immunity before the virus reaches the CNS.

clozeText: Early clinical Rabies often presents with {{c1::paresthesia}} or tingling at the site of the initial bite wound.
extraNote: This is a key prodromal symptom that precedes neurological decline.

clozeText: The {{c1::encephalitic (furious)}} form of rabies is characterized by agitation, hypersalivation, and hydrophobia.
extraNote: This form accounts for about 80% of clinical cases.

clozeText: The {{c1::paralytic (dumb)}} form of rabies can mimic Guillain-Barré syndrome due to ascending paralysis.
extraNote: Patients are typically less agitated and do not exhibit hydrophobia compared to the furious form.

clozeText: Diagnosis of rabies in a living patient often involves a skin biopsy from the {{c1::nape of the neck}} to look for viral antigen.
extraNote: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing is used to identify viral particles in hair follicles.

clozeText: Rabies virus belongs to the genus {{c1::Lyssavirus}}.
extraNote: The name 'Lyssa' comes from the Greek goddess of rage and frenzy.

clozeText: Once clinical symptoms of Rabies appear, the case-fatality rate is approximately {{c1::100}}%.
extraNote: Survival is extremely rare once the virus has reached the brain and caused encephalopathy.

clozeText: Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) should be administered {{c1::around the bite wound}} to provide immediate protection.
extraNote: Any remaining HRIG should be injected intramuscularly at a site distant from the vaccine injection.

clozeText: The incubation period of rabies is highly variable and depends on the {{c1::distance}} of the wound from the CNS.
extraNote: A bite on the face has a much shorter incubation period than a bite on the foot.

clozeText: Hypersalivation in rabies occurs due to autonomic dysfunction and {{c1::difficulty swallowing}}.
extraNote: This contributes to the 'foaming at the mouth' appearance often associated with the virus.

clozeText: Pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals (e.g., veterinarians) consists of {{c1::3}} doses of the inactivated vaccine.
extraNote: High-risk individuals should also have their antibody titers checked periodically.

clozeText: If a previously vaccinated person is exposed to rabies, they require {{c1::booster doses}} but do NOT require {{c2::HRIG}}.
extraNote: The memory response is sufficient when boosted, making passive immunity unnecessary.

clozeText: Rabies virus is sensitive to {{c1::soap and water}} because it is an enveloped virus.
extraNote: Immediate and thorough wound washing is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of infection.

clozeText: The hallmark of the Encephalitic form of Rabies, besides hydrophobia, is {{c1::aerophobia}}, or fear of drafts.
extraNote: The skin is hypersensitive to air movement, triggering pharyngeal spasms.

clozeText: Rabies virus replicates in the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: Like most RNA viruses (except influenza and retroviruses), replication occurs entirely outside the nucleus.

clozeText: Rabies virus {{c1::glycoprotein (G-protein)}} is the structure that induces neutralizing antibodies.
extraNote: This protein is the primary target for vaccine development.

clozeText: Confirmation of Rabies in animals requires euthanasia and testing of {{c1::brain}} tissue.
extraNote: Testing is performed using direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) on brain smears.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci are arranged in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: Staphylococci are nonmotile and do not form spores.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into {{c2::O2 and H2O}}.
extraNote: This biochemical test differentiates staphylococci (positive) from streptococci (negative).

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and {{c2::hemolyzes::process}} red blood cells.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used to identify S. aureus.

clozeText: The primary mechanism of S. aureus resistance to penicillin is the production of {{c1::β-lactamase::enzyme}}, which is typically encoded on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain these plasmids.

clozeText: MRSA strains are resistant to nafcillin due to alterations in {{c1::penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)}}, specifically {{c2::PBP2a}}.
extraNote: These altered PBPs are encoded by the mecA gene on the bacterial chromosome.

clozeText: The {{c1::mecA::gene}} gene on the bacterial chromosome encodes altered PBPs that allow S. aureus to be resistant to methicillin and nafcillin.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a factor relatively rare in healthcare-acquired MRSA.
extraNote: The most common CA-MRSA strain in the US is USA300.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves enzymes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This resistance cassette is often acquired from enterococci via transposons on plasmids.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} is a major virulence factor that binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages by blocking the Fc receptor binding site.

clozeText: In the cell wall of S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids play a significant role in the induction of septic shock.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus has endotoxin-like properties and can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines, activating {{c2::complement::system}}.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock without possessing true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized at any one time.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because of a defect in {{c2::neutrophil killing}}.
extraNote: CGD involves a deficiency in NADPH oxidase.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains {{c2::pus}}.
extraNote: Foreign bodies like sutures or catheters are major predisposing factors for these infections.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its sensitivity to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive; S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: S. aureus hemolysins recover iron from {{c1::hemoglobin}}, which the bacteria then use to synthesize {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes for energy production.
extraNote: Iron is a strictly required nutrient for the growth of the organism.

clozeText: While 11 serotypes of capsular polysaccharide exist for S. aureus, types {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} cause 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous (IV) drug users}}.
extraNote: This includes skin infections, sepsis, and endocarditis.

clozeText: Staphylococcal surface receptors for {{c1::bacteriophages}} permit "phage typing" of strains; these receptors are partly composed of {{c2::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: This is used primarily for epidemiologic tracking of outbreaks.

clozeText: S. aureus is found in the vagina of approximately {{c1::5%::percentage}} of women, predisposing them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is caused by the release of a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus that results in widespread {{c2::desquamation}}.
extraNote: It is often seen in infants and young children.

clozeText: Impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored crust}} and can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a common superficial skin infection.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Hyperglycemia and vascular compromise contribute to infection risk.

clozeText: MRSA is currently responsible for more than {{c1::50%}} of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients in the United States.
extraNote: USA300 is the dominant community strain.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: It is a vasculitis often affecting children.

clozeText: The coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women is {{c1::S. saprophyticus}}.
extraNote: It is uniquely resistant to novobiocin compared to S. epidermidis.

clozeText: {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora and is known for infecting {{c2::prosthetic heart valves}} and joints.
extraNote: It often produces biofilms on medical devices.

clozeText: Staphylococci are distinguished from streptococci microscopically because they appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: Staphylococci are gram-positive, nonmotile, and do not form spores.

clozeText: Biochemically, all staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into O2 and H2O.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate Staphylococci (+) from Streptococci (-).

clozeText: Bacteria that produce {{c1::catalase}} can survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils, a key virulence factor for S. aureus.
extraNote: This is why patients with Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) are particularly susceptible to S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium for S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus produces hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin, which is utilized for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical growth requirement for the organism to produce energy.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene on the bacterial chromosome.
extraNote: This gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).

clozeText: MRSA is resistant to nafcillin because it possesses {{c1::PBP2a}}, which performs transpeptidase functions but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: Standard beta-lactams cannot inhibit this altered protein.

clozeText: Almost all strains of {{c1::community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA)}} produce P-V leukocidin, unlike most healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: Panton-Valentine (P-V) leukocidin is a toxin that destroys white blood cells.

clozeText: High-level vancomycin resistance (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and is a virulence factor that binds the Fc portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on neutrophils from binding the antibody, inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These also serve as receptors for specific staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in S. aureus play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating the release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: This mimics the action of endotoxin found in Gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages and activate complement, allowing it to cause septic shock without possessing endotoxin.
extraNote: Gram-positive bacteria do not have LPS/endotoxin.

clozeText: The main reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately 30% of the population is colonized.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of skin infections.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Abscesses are the classic pathology of pyogenic (pus-producing) inflammation.

clozeText: {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora and is a leading cause of infections in prosthetic heart valves and joints.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-sensitive.

clozeText: {{c1::S. saprophyticus}} is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is resistant to {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: It is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young women.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a desquamating skin disease in infants caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that cleaves desmoglein in the skin.

clozeText: Lesions of {{c1::impetigo::syndrome}} are characterized by crops of vesicles with a honey-colored crust.
extraNote: It can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection involving small pustules on the hair follicles.
extraNote: It is a common skin and soft tissue infection (SSTI).

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} and intravenous drug use are major predisposing factors for serious infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: MRSA is particularly common in IV drug users.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and {{c1::surgical-wound}} infections.
extraNote: It frequently infects sites of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired infections.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::beta-lactamase}}, which is encoded by plasmids.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins like penicillin G.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States.
extraNote: MRSA is frequently isolated from these lesions in both healthy and immunocompromised patients.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a pediatric disease of unknown etiology that has been linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It presents with fever, strawberry tongue, and coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: The viral family {{c1::Filoviridae}} includes the highly pathogenic Ebola and Marburg viruses.
extraNote: These viruses cause severe viral hemorrhagic fever and have high mortality rates.

clozeText: Filoviruses possess a {{c1::negative-sense}} single-stranded RNA genome.
extraNote: Like other negative-sense RNA viruses, they must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion.

clozeText: On electron microscopy, Filoviruses exhibit a unique {{c1::filamentous}} or pleomorphic morphology, often appearing as a 'shepherd's crook' or '6-shape'.
extraNote: This filamentous shape is the namesake for the 'Filo' prefix (from Latin filum, meaning thread).

clozeText: The Filovirus genome is enclosed by a {{c1::helical}} nucleocapsid and an outer lipid envelope.
extraNote: The envelope is derived from the host cell's plasma membrane during budding.

clozeText: The natural reservoir for Filoviruses such as Ebola and Marburg is believed to be {{c1::fruit bats}} (e.g., Rousettus aegyptiacus).
extraNote: Spillover events to humans often involve contact with bat guano or infected bushmeat.

clozeText: Human-to-human transmission of Filoviruses occurs primarily through {{c1::direct contact}} with infected blood, secretions, or other body fluids.
extraNote: This leads to high risks for healthcare workers and family members during outbreaks.

clozeText: Laboratory handling of Filoviruses requires the highest containment level, known as {{c1::Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4)}}.
extraNote: This level is reserved for dangerous and exotic agents that pose a high risk of aerosol-transmitted laboratory infections.

clozeText: The Ebola virus surface {{c1::glycoprotein (GP)}} is responsible for viral attachment, fusion, and is the primary target for neutralizing antibodies.
extraNote: The GP is also targeted by monoclonal antibody therapies like Inmazeb.

clozeText: Ebola virus infects {{c1::endothelial cells}}, macrophages, and dendritic cells, leading to widespread vascular damage.
extraNote: Endothelial infection contributes to the massive hemorrhage and capillary leak seen in terminal stages.

clozeText: Severe Filovirus infections induce a {{c1::cytokine storm}}, characterized by massive release of pro-inflammatory mediators like TNF-alpha and IL-6.
extraNote: This systemic inflammation leads to increased vascular permeability and hypovolemic shock.

clozeText: The definitive diagnostic test for acute Filovirus infection is {{c1::RT-PCR}} to detect viral RNA in the blood.
extraNote: Viral loads are typically very high during the symptomatic phase, making PCR highly sensitive.

clozeText: {{c1::Marburg}} virus was first identified in 1967 following simultaneous outbreaks in Germany and Serbia linked to imported African green monkeys.
extraNote: While monkeys can transmit the virus, fruit bats are the true natural reservoir.

clozeText: The incubation period for Ebola virus is typically 2 to {{c1::21::range}} days.
extraNote: Contacts are usually monitored for 21 days to ensure they do not develop symptoms.

clozeText: Ebola virus inhibits the host's innate immune response by blocking {{c1::Type I Interferon (IFN)}} signaling.
extraNote: Viral proteins VP24 and VP35 are responsible for inhibiting the IFN pathway.

clozeText: Filoviruses replicate their genome and assemble new virions within the host cell {{c1::cytoplasm}}.
extraNote: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, with the exception of Orthomyxoviruses (e.g., Influenza) and Retroviruses.

clozeText: Ebola virus can persist in immunologically privileged sites, most notably the {{c1::semen}}, long after clinical recovery.
extraNote: Sexual transmission from survivors is a recognized risk for late-onset outbreaks.

clozeText: The host cell receptor {{c1::NPC1 (Niemann-Pick C1)}} is required for the entry of Ebola virus into the cytoplasm.
extraNote: NPC1 is an intracellular cholesterol transporter; cells lacking this protein are resistant to Filovirus infection.

clozeText: In terminal stages, Filovirus infections often progress to {{c1::DIC (Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation)}} and multi-organ failure.
extraNote: This leads to the depletion of clotting factors and severe bleeding from mucosal surfaces and needle stick sites.

clozeText: The {{c1::rVSV-ZEBOV}} vaccine is a live-attenuated recombinant vaccine used to prevent Zaire ebolavirus infection.
extraNote: It uses Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV) as a vector to express the Ebola glycoprotein.

clozeText: Common laboratory findings in Ebola include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and markedly elevated {{c1::transaminases (AST/ALT)}}.
extraNote: Liver involvement is a hallmark of Filovirus pathogenesis, often causing more severe AST elevation than ALT.

clozeText: {{c1::Inmazeb}} is a combination of three monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab, maftivimab, and odesivimab) approved for the treatment of Ebola.
extraNote: It specifically targets the Zaire ebolavirus glycoprotein to prevent cell entry.

clozeText: Exposure to Marburg virus is frequently associated with entering {{c1::caves or mines}} inhabited by Rousettus fruit bats.
extraNote: Tourism or mining in endemic African regions are common exposure histories for Marburg cases.

clozeText: Filoviruses are classified as {{c1::Category A}} bioterrorism agents by the CDC due to their high mortality and potential for public disruption.
extraNote: This category includes agents like Anthrax, Smallpox, and Plague.

clozeText: The 'L' protein of the Filovirus genome functions as the {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: It is the largest protein in the genome and is essential for viral transcription and replication.

clozeText: Healthcare workers prevent nosocomial spread of Filoviruses through strict use of {{c1::PPE (Personal Protective Equipment)}} and barrier nursing.
extraNote: Aerosolization is not a primary mode of transmission, but droplets and contact are highly infectious.

clozeText: Ebola virus was named after the {{c1::Ebola River}} in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, near where the first outbreak occurred in 1976.
extraNote: The two initial outbreaks in 1976 were caused by Zaire and Sudan ebolaviruses.

clozeText: Filovirus infection typically begins with a 'dry' phase of fever and myalgia, followed by a 'wet' phase of {{c1::vomiting and diarrhea}}.
extraNote: Gastrointestinal symptoms contribute significantly to fluid loss and electrolyte imbalances.

clozeText: The mortality rate of {{c1::Zaire ebolavirus}} can reach up to 90% in untreated populations.
extraNote: It is considered the most virulent of the known ebolavirus species.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the oxidative burst within neutrophils.

clozeText: The primary enzyme used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci is {{c1::coagulase}}, which activates prothrombin to form thrombin.
extraNote: Coagulase results in fibrin clot formation, potentially walling off the bacteria from host defenses.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses, pneumonia, and sepsis in {{c1::intravenous drug users::patient population}}.
extraNote: Injection drug use often introduces skin flora directly into the bloodstream.

clozeText: The major cell wall protein of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which functions by binding the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains transpeptidase activity but has a low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: Panton-Valentine leukocidin is associated with severe necrotizing pneumonia and skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from S. epidermidis by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}} and produce {{c2::beta-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium for S. aureus.

clozeText: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} that leads to widespread desquamation of the skin.
extraNote: This is specifically caused by exfoliatin toxin, which cleaves desmoglein in the epidermis.

clozeText: In the cell wall, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also serve as receptors for bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release cytokines like {{c2::IL-1 and TNF::Cytokines}}.
extraNote: This mechanism allows S. aureus to cause shock despite lacking traditional Gram-negative endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is uniquely sensitive to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}, distinguishing it from S. saprophyticus.
extraNote: Mnemonic: 'On the STAPH retreat, there was NO Staph SAP' (Saprophyticus is Resistant).

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This prevents vancomycin from binding to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminal, which is its normal target.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nasopharynx)}}, with chronic carriage occurring in ~30% of the population.
extraNote: Colonization in the nose increases the risk of recurrent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are highly susceptible to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack NADPH oxidase, making them unable to clear catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: The characteristic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which typically features central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: The organism tends to produce localized, walled-off infections rather than spreading through tissues like Streptococci.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: Furuncles (boils) and carbuncles are deeper extensions of this process.

clozeText: S. aureus produces hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from host hemoglobin, which is then used for the synthesis of {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth in the human host.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90%}} of S. aureus strains produce {{c2::beta-lactamase}}, rendering them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: This necessitated the development of penicillinase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::toxic shock syndrome}}, which is often linked to vaginal colonization in women (5%).
extraNote: TSST-1 acts as a superantigen, causing massive cytokine release and multi-organ failure.

clozeText: The most common MRSA strain currently found in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections}} in young sexually active women.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. epidermidis by being novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: Phage typing of staphylococcal strains is possible because {{c1::teichoic acids}} serve as receptors for specific bacteriophages.
extraNote: This was traditionally used for epidemiological tracking of outbreaks.

clozeText: The S. aureus polysaccharide capsule is considered {{c1::poorly immunogenic}}, which has hindered the development of an effective vaccine.
extraNote: Serotypes 5 and 8 account for the majority of human infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}}, a childhood disease of unknown etiology, is hypothesized to be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It presents with fever, conjunctivitis, and strawberry tongue, and can cause coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: S. aureus causes food poisoning via the ingestion of {{c1::preformed enterotoxins}}.
extraNote: Symptoms appear rapidly (within hours) because the toxin is already present in the food.

clozeText: Hospital-acquired MRSA is frequently treated with {{c1::vancomycin}}, though strains with intermediate (VISA) or full (VRSA) resistance exist.
extraNote: Nafcillin and oxacillin are ineffective against MRSA due to the altered PBP2a.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate the production of cytokines and activate the {{c1::complement and coagulation::cascades}} systems.
extraNote: This allows the organism to induce the clinical findings of septic shock without possessing endotoxin.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the {{c1::catalase}} test.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into H2O and O2, protecting the bacteria from neutrophil-mediated killing.

clozeText: The classic lesion of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::organism}} pyogenic infection is an abscess.
extraNote: Abscesses often undergo central necrosis and drain pus.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of infections in intravenous drug users.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron needed for cytochrome enzyme synthesis.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: This gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a).

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA, known as {{c1::PBP2a}}, has low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics but retains its transpeptidase function.
extraNote: This allows cell wall synthesis to continue even in the presence of nafcillin or methicillin.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major S. aureus virulence factor that binds to the Fc portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on phagocytes from binding the antibody, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids::cell wall component}} mediate the adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the bacteriophage receptor.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to how endotoxin (LPS) functions in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin::toxin}}.
extraNote: This is less commonly found in healthcare-acquired strains (HCA-MRSA).

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose::anatomical site}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers in the nares.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to recurrent S. aureus infections.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill catalase-positive bacteria.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles.
extraNote: It also commonly causes impetigo, which presents with honey-colored crusts.

clozeText: Impetigo can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: The lesions are crops of vesicles that develop a honey-colored crust.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is the most common cause of infections associated with prosthetic heart valves and artificial joints.
extraNote: It is a highly common member of the normal skin flora.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its resistance to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections in young women.

clozeText: The {{c1::polysaccharide capsule}} of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine production difficult.
extraNote: Serotypes 5 and 8 are responsible for about 85% of human infections.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause the clinical findings of septic shock even though it lacks {{c1::endotoxin}}.
extraNote: This is due to the ability of its peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acids to stimulate cytokine production.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::beta-lactamase}} is encoded by plasmids in over 90% of S. aureus strains.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins that are not beta-lactamase-resistant.

clozeText: S. aureus colonizes the vagina in approximately {{c1::5::percentage}}% of women, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: Toxic shock syndrome can be associated with tampon use.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} in infants is caused by an exotoxin produced by S. aureus.
extraNote: It presents with widespread desquamation of the skin.

clozeText: Staphylococci typically appear as {{c1::grapelike clusters}} under a microscope.
extraNote: In contrast, streptococci typically appear in chains.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: Reduced humoral immunity and neutrophil defects also increase susceptibility.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently found in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of community-acquired infections.

clozeText: S. aureus-mediated food poisoning is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} rather than direct bacterial infection of the gut.
extraNote: The organism produces heat-stable enterotoxins.

clozeText: Coagulase activates {{c1::prothrombin}} to form thrombin.
extraNote: This is the initial step in the formation of a fibrin clot by S. aureus.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci are found in {{c1::chains}}.
extraNote: Staphylococci divide in multiple planes, while streptococci divide in a single plane.

clozeText: Biochemically, all staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades H2O2 into oxygen and water, allowing organisms to survive neutrophil oxidative bursts.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci primarily by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike the coagulase-negative species, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and produces {{c1::β-hemolysis::type of hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the bacteria with iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: The major virulence protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, the bacterium prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells and serve as part of the {{c2::bacteriophage}} receptors.
extraNote: Teichoic acids are polymers of ribitol phosphate found in the cell wall of Gram-positive bacteria.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} and {{c2::peptidoglycan}}, which stimulate macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Even without endotoxin (LPS), these cell wall components can trigger the same cytokine cascade and complement activation.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin/methicillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c1::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This modification is encoded by a cassette of genes typically acquired from enterococci via transposons on a plasmid.

clozeText: The most common site of S. aureus colonization in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers, which increases their risk for autoinoculation and skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing of catalase-positive organisms.
extraNote: CGD involves a deficiency in NADPH oxidase, preventing the formation of reactive oxygen species.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by S. aureus that causes desquamation of the skin.
extraNote: This condition typically affects infants and presents with widespread 'rolled up' desquamated skin.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored crust}}, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is uniquely associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin that kills white blood cells.
extraNote: This toxin is less common in healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA) and contributes to necrotizing pneumonia and skin abscesses.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is {{c1::sensitive}} to the antibiotic novobiocin, whereas Staphylococcus saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: Mnemonic: 'On the office's STAPH retreat, there's NO-Stressing (Novobiocin Sensitive) about the Epidemic (S. epidermidis).'

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a major member of the normal skin flora and produces biofilms that allow it to adhere to synthetic materials.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a significant cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in young, sexually active women.
extraNote: It is the second most common cause of community-acquired UTIs after E. coli.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} and {{c2::osteomyelitis}}.
extraNote: The classic lesion is an abscess, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::β-lactamase}}, which is encoded by genes found on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillins, necessitating the use of β-lactamase-resistant drugs like nafcillin for MSSA.

clozeText: The primary drug of choice for treating non-MRSA (MSSA) staphylococcal infections is {{c1::nafcillin}} (or oxacillin).
extraNote: These are β-lactamase-resistant penicillins.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This includes serious conditions such as right-sided endocarditis and sepsis.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is associated with high-absorbency tampon use, where the toxin TSST-1 acts as a superantigen.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It frequently infects sites of insertion of cardiac pacemakers and other indwelling devices.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}}, a disease of unknown etiology characterized by vasculitis in children.
extraNote: Certain strains of S. aureus are thought to be potential triggers for the syndrome.

clozeText: The S. aureus capsule is composed of {{c1::polysaccharides}}; types {{c2::5 and 8}} cause the majority of human infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making it a difficult target for vaccine development.

clozeText: Infections caused by S. aureus are more common in patients with {{c1::diabetes}} or reduced {{c2::humoral immunity}} (low antibody/complement).
extraNote: Compromised immune systems cannot effectively opsonize and clear the pyogenic bacteria.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which is characterized by central {{c2::necrosis}} and pus.
extraNote: S. aureus induces pyogenic (pus-producing) inflammation through both toxins and surface proteins.

clozeText: The most common MRSA strain currently in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: This strain is highly associated with community-acquired outbreaks of skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Mumps virus belongs to the {{c1::Paramyxoviridae}} family of viruses.
extraNote: This family also includes Parainfluenza, Measles (Rubeola), and RSV.

clozeText: The genome of Mumps virus consists of {{c1::negative-sense}} single-stranded RNA.
extraNote: Like other paramyxoviruses, the RNA is non-segmented.

clozeText: Mumps virus is an {{c1::enveloped::enveloped or naked?}} virus with a helical nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are generally more susceptible to detergents and heat.

clozeText: Unlike the Orthomyxoviridae (Influenza), the Mumps virus genome is {{c1::non-segmented}}.
extraNote: Non-segmented genomes cannot undergo reassortment.

clozeText: Mumps virus possesses a surface glycoprotein with both {{c1::hemagglutinin and neuraminidase}} activities.
extraNote: This is often denoted as the HN protein.

clozeText: The {{c1::Fusion (F) protein}} of Mumps virus mediates the formation of multinucleated giant cells (syncytia).
extraNote: The F protein allows the viral envelope to fuse with the host cell membrane.

clozeText: Mumps virus is primarily transmitted via {{c1::respiratory droplets}}.
extraNote: It is highly contagious and spreads in close-contact settings.

clozeText: Following initial replication in the upper respiratory tract, Mumps virus spreads to distant organs via {{c1::viremia}}.
extraNote: Viremia allows the virus to reach the parotid glands, testes, and CNS.

clozeText: The classic clinical presentation of Mumps is {{c1::parotitis::inflammation of which gland?}}, which is often bilateral.
extraNote: This results in the characteristic swelling of the cheeks and jaw line.

clozeText: A common complication of Mumps in post-pubertal males is {{c1::orchitis}}, which can lead to testicular atrophy.
extraNote: While it can cause sterility, it is usually unilateral and complete sterility is rare.

clozeText: Mumps virus is a common cause of {{c1::aseptic meningitis::CNS complication}}.
extraNote: Patients present with headache, fever, and nuchal rigidity, but CSF cultures remain sterile for bacteria.

clozeText: The mnemonic 'POM-Poms' for Mumps stands for {{c1::Parotitis, Orchitis, Meningitis, and Pancreatitis}}.
extraNote: These represent the four most high-yield clinical manifestations.

clozeText: In a patient with Mumps, an elevated serum {{c1::amylase}} may indicate either parotitis or pancreatitis.
extraNote: Amylase is produced by both the salivary glands and the pancreas.

clozeText: The Mumps vaccine is a {{c1::live attenuated}} vaccine.
extraNote: It is typically administered as part of the MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) series.

clozeText: Mumps virus replicates within the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, with the exception of Influenza and Retroviruses.

clozeText: The {{c1::F (Fusion) protein}} is a target for neutralizing antibodies that prevent syncytia formation.
extraNote: Palivizumab targets a similar protein in RSV, though there is no equivalent for Mumps.

clozeText: Neutralizing antibodies against the {{c1::hemagglutinin::H, N, or HN?}} protein are protective against reinfection.
extraNote: There is only one serotype of Mumps virus, making the vaccine highly effective.

clozeText: A rare but serious complication of Mumps is sensorineural {{c1::deafness::hearing complication}}.
extraNote: Mumps was a leading cause of childhood deafness before widespread vaccination.

clozeText: The MMR vaccine is contraindicated in {{c1::pregnant women}} and severely immunocompromised individuals.
extraNote: Live vaccines carry a theoretical risk of causing disease in these populations.

clozeText: Mumps virus infection in the pancreas can lead to {{c1::pancreatitis}}, which may present as epigastric pain and vomiting.
extraNote: This is often tested alongside parotitis as a multi-organ involvement scenario.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for Mumps virus is {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: No animal reservoir exists, which theoretically allows for potential eradication.

clozeText: Mumps virus induces the formation of {{c1::syncytia}} (multinucleated cells) in infected tissue culture.
extraNote: This is a characteristic cytopathic effect of the Paramyxoviridae.

clozeText: The {{c1::negative-sense}} RNA genome of Mumps must be transcribed into mRNA by a {{c2::viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}}.
extraNote: The virus must carry this enzyme within its virion.

clozeText: Mumps parotitis is often accompanied by the displacement of the {{c1::earlobe}} upward and outward.
extraNote: This physical exam finding helps distinguish parotid swelling from lymphadenopathy.

clozeText: Epidemiologically, Mumps outbreaks are most common in the {{c1::late winter and spring}}.
extraNote: This seasonal pattern is typical for many respiratory viruses.

clozeText: The incubation period for Mumps is approximately {{c1::2 to 3 weeks}}.
extraNote: Patients are infectious from several days before to several days after the onset of parotitis.

clozeText: Mumps virus is typically identified by {{c1::RT-PCR::Diagnostic method}} or viral culture from saliva or urine.
extraNote: RT-PCR is the preferred diagnostic test for rapid detection.

clozeText: Passive immunity against Mumps is provided to infants by {{c1::maternal IgG}}.
