extraNote: This protection usually lasts for the first 6 months of life.

clozeText: Mumps virus is a member of the {{c1::Paramyxoviridae}} family.
extraNote: This family also includes Measles, RSV, and Parainfluenza viruses.

clozeText: The genome of the Mumps virus is {{c1::negative-sense, single-stranded RNA}}.
extraNote: Because it is negative-sense, the virus must carry its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: Unlike influenza virus, the Mumps virus genome is {{c1::non-segmented}}.
extraNote: Non-segmented genomes cannot undergo reassortment (antigenic shift).

clozeText: The Mumps virus is an {{c1::enveloped}} virus with a helical nucleocapsid.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses are generally more sensitive to detergents and environmental heat.

clozeText: Mumps virus possesses a {{c1::Fusion (F)}} protein that facilitates the formation of multinucleated giant cells (syncytia).
extraNote: This protein allows the viral envelope to fuse with the host cell membrane.

clozeText: The {{c1::Hemagglutinin-Neuraminidase (HN)}} protein on the Mumps envelope mediates both attachment to sialic acid and viral release.
extraNote: Some paramyxoviruses have H or G proteins, but Mumps specifically has the combined HN protein.

clozeText: The most common clinical manifestation of Mumps is {{c1::parotitis::glandular swelling}}.
extraNote: Parotitis is usually bilateral and characterized by the elevation of the earlobe.

clozeText: A high-yield complication of Mumps in post-pubertal males is {{c1::orchitis}}, which can cause testicular atrophy.
extraNote: While it can lead to decreased sperm counts, permanent sterility is rare as it is often unilateral.

clozeText: Mumps is a common cause of {{c1::aseptic meningitis::neurologic complication}} in unvaccinated populations.
extraNote: It is characterized by lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose in the CSF.

clozeText: Inflammation of the pancreas, or {{c1::pancreatitis}}, is a classic complication of Mumps presenting with epigastric pain.
extraNote: It is often identified by elevated serum lipase and amylase.

clozeText: In females, Mumps infection can lead to {{c1::oophoritis::ovarian inflammation}}, though it rarely affects fertility.
extraNote: This is the female equivalent of mumps-induced orchitis.

clozeText: Mumps can lead to permanent {{c1::sensorineural deafness}} due to direct viral damage to the cochlea.
extraNote: This is a classic 'pedia' boards question for sudden hearing loss after a febrile illness.

clozeText: The Mumps vaccine is a {{c1::live attenuated}} vaccine administered as part of the MMR series.
extraNote: It is contraindicated in pregnant women and severely immunocompromised individuals.

clozeText: The first dose of the MMR vaccine is typically given at {{c1::12–15 months}} of age.
extraNote: A second dose is given at 4–6 years of age to ensure long-term immunity.

clozeText: A diagnostic clue for Mumps parotitis is an elevated serum {{c1::amylase}}, which reflects salivary gland inflammation.
extraNote: Amylase will also be elevated if the patient develops pancreatitis.

clozeText: Mumps virus can be detected in clinical samples using {{c1::RT-PCR}} of buccal or oral swabs.
extraNote: RT-PCR is the preferred method for confirmation during outbreaks.

clozeText: The presence of Mumps-specific {{c1::IgM}} antibodies indicates an acute or recent infection.
extraNote: IgG indicates past infection or successful vaccination.

clozeText: The incubation period for Mumps virus is typically {{c1::12 to 25}} days.
extraNote: Symptoms usually appear 16–18 days after exposure.

clozeText: Mumps virus can cause {{c1::hemadsorption}}, where red blood cells adhere to the surface of virus-infected cells.
extraNote: This is due to the presence of the viral hemagglutinin on the host cell membrane.

clozeText: The only natural reservoir for Mumps virus is {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: This makes the virus a potential candidate for eradication through global vaccination.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::bacterium}} can cause a bacterial parotitis that mimics mumps but usually presents with purulent discharge.
extraNote: Mumps parotitis is viral and non-suppurative.

clozeText: Mumps virus is most contagious from {{c1::2 days before}} to 5 days after the onset of parotitis.
extraNote: Isolation of the patient is critical during this window.

clozeText: Mumps-associated meningitis will show {{c1::lymphocytic}} pleocytosis upon lumbar puncture.
extraNote: Viral (aseptic) meningitis typically shows lymphocytes, whereas bacterial shows neutrophils.

clozeText: Primary replication of Mumps virus occurs in the {{c1::upper respiratory tract}} and local lymph nodes.
extraNote: This is followed by a primary viremia that seeds the salivary glands and other organs.

clozeText: Mumps virus contains an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, also known as the {{c1::L protein}}.
extraNote: This protein is essential for transcribing the negative-sense RNA into mRNA.

clozeText: The {{c1::nucleocapsid (N)}} protein protects the viral RNA and is the most abundant protein in the virion.
extraNote: It plays a key role in the transition from transcription to replication.

clozeText: The incidence of Mumps has decreased by over 99% in the US due to the introduction of the {{c1::Jeryl Lynn}} vaccine strain.
extraNote: This is the specific attenuated strain used in most MMR vaccines.

clozeText: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) has a {{c1::double-stranded linear DNA::genome type}} genome.
extraNote: Like all Herpesviruses, it replicates in the nucleus and is enveloped.

clozeText: HSV acquires its envelope from the {{c1::host cell nuclear membrane::specific membrane}} via budding.
extraNote: This is unique compared to many other enveloped viruses that bud from the plasma membrane.

clozeText: The space between the capsid and the envelope in HSV is known as the {{c1::tegument}}.
extraNote: It contains viral proteins and enzymes (like VHS and VP16) that facilitate the initiation of replication.

clozeText: HSV-1 typically establishes latency in the {{c1::trigeminal ganglia}}.
extraNote: Reactivation typically leads to herpes labialis (cold sores).

clozeText: HSV-2 typically establishes latency in the {{c1::sacral ganglia}}.
extraNote: Latency is maintained in a non-replicating state within the sensory neurons.

clozeText: The gold standard for diagnosing HSV encephalitis is {{c1::PCR of the CSF::diagnostic test}}.
extraNote: PCR has replaced brain biopsy for the detection of HSV DNA in the central nervous system.

clozeText: A Tzanck smear showing {{c1::multinucleated giant cells::finding}} is indicative of HSV or VZV infection.
extraNote: This test cannot distinguish between HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV.

clozeText: HSV infections are characterized histologically by {{c1::Cowdry type A::inclusion type}} intranuclear inclusions.
extraNote: These are eosinophilic droplets of nucleic acid and protein surrounded by a clear halo.

clozeText: HSV-1 is the most common cause of {{c1::sporadic encephalitis::clinical syndrome}} in the United States.
extraNote: It typically affects the temporal lobes, causing hemorrhagic necrosis.

clozeText: HSV-1 encephalitis typically presents with localized necrosis and edema in the {{c1::temporal lobes::brain region}}.
extraNote: Clinical signs include personality changes, aphasia, and seizures.

clozeText: HSV-related keratitis classically presents with {{c1::dendritic (branching) ulcers::characteristic finding}} on fluorescein staining.
extraNote: It is a leading cause of corneal blindness in developed countries.

clozeText: The primary infection of HSV-1 in children often presents as {{c1::gingivostomatitis}}.
extraNote: This involves high fever, irritability, and vesicular lesions on the gums and oral mucosa.

clozeText: HSV-2 is more frequently associated with {{c1::aseptic meningitis::neurological complication}} than HSV-1.
extraNote: Often occurs during primary genital infection.

clozeText: Acyclovir must be monophosphorylated by viral {{c1::thymidine kinase::enzyme}} to become active.
extraNote: Host cell kinases then convert it to the triphosphate form which inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: The primary mechanism of acyclovir resistance in HSV is the {{c1::absence or mutation of thymidine kinase::mechanism}}.
extraNote: Without the viral kinase, the drug cannot be phosphorylated to its active form.

clozeText: HSV travel from the site of infection to the sensory ganglia via {{c1::retrograde axonal transport::transport direction}}.
extraNote: This transport is mediated by the motor protein dynein.

clozeText: HSV reactivation and movement from the ganglia back to the skin occurs via {{c1::anterograde axonal transport::transport direction}}.
extraNote: This transport is mediated by the motor protein kinesin.

clozeText: {{c1::Erythema multiforme::skin condition}} is a hypersensitivity reaction frequently triggered by a preceding HSV infection.
extraNote: Classically presents with 'target' or 'bulls-eye' lesions.

clozeText: A painful HSV infection of the finger, common in healthcare workers, is called {{c1::herpetic whitlow}}.
extraNote: It results from direct inoculation of the virus into the skin through a break.

clozeText: In immunocompromised patients, HSV can cause esophagitis characterized by {{c1::punched-out ulcers::lesion description}}.
extraNote: This is in contrast to CMV esophagitis, which typically causes linear ulcers.

clozeText: Neonatal herpes is most commonly transmitted {{c1::perinatally during birth::transmission route}} via the birth canal.
extraNote: Risk is significantly higher during a primary maternal HSV-2 infection than a reactivation.

clozeText: HSV-1 is generally transmitted by {{c1::respiratory secretions/saliva::route}}.
extraNote: HSV-2 is generally transmitted via sexual contact or perinatally.

clozeText: The viral glycoprotein {{c1::gB/gC}} of HSV binds to {{c2::heparan sulfate::host molecule}} on the cell surface for initial attachment.
extraNote: Subsequent binding to Nectin-1 or HVEM leads to membrane fusion.

clozeText: HSV can induce {{c1::syncytia}} formation, which allows the virus to spread directly from cell to cell.
extraNote: This helps the virus evade neutralizing antibodies in the extracellular environment.

clozeText: Herpes gladiatorum is a skin infection caused by HSV-1 that is common among {{c1::wrestlers::population}}.
extraNote: It is spread by skin-to-skin contact during matches.

clozeText: In the CSF of a patient with HSV encephalitis, you may find an increased number of {{c1::red blood cells (RBCs)::cell type}}.
extraNote: This reflects the hemorrhagic nature of the temporal lobe necrosis.

clozeText: Acyclovir acts as a {{c1::guanosine analog::chemical class}} that causes chain termination.
extraNote: It specifically inhibits viral DNA polymerase more than host DNA polymerase.

clozeText: Foscarnet can be used to treat acyclovir-resistant HSV because it does NOT require {{c1::phosphorylation by viral kinase::requirement}}.
extraNote: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: HSV-1 typically remains latent in the {{c1::trigeminal ganglion}}.
extraNote: Reactivation is often triggered by stress, fever, or UV light, leading to herpes labialis (cold sores).

clozeText: HSV-2 typically remains latent in the {{c1::sacral ganglia::be specific}}.
extraNote: This explains the recurrence of genital herpes in the S2-S4 dermatomes.

clozeText: HSV encephalitis characteristically affects the {{c1::temporal lobe::brain region}}.
extraNote: Clinical findings include seizures, olfactory hallucinations, and personality changes; it is the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis.

clozeText: The gold standard for diagnosing HSV encephalitis is {{c1::PCR analysis::test}} of the cerebrospinal fluid.
extraNote: CSF analysis typically shows increased RBCs due to hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes.

clozeText: A Tzanck smear of a vesicle base reveals {{c1::multinucleated giant cells}}.
extraNote: This test identifies HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV, but cannot distinguish between them.

clozeText: The characteristic intranuclear inclusion bodies seen in HSV-infected cells are called {{c1::Cowdry type A}} inclusions.
extraNote: These are eosinophilic inclusions composed of nucleic acid and protein in the nucleus.

clozeText: HSV-1 is the most common trigger for {{c1::erythema multiforme}}, characterized by targetoid lesions.
extraNote: This is an immune-mediated reaction, not a direct infection of the skin lesions by the virus.

clozeText: Primary HSV-1 infection in children typically presents as {{c1::gingivostomatitis::condition}}.
extraNote: It involves high fever, irritability, and painful vesicles on the tongue, gums, and buccal mucosa.

clozeText: HSV infection of the finger, often seen in healthcare workers or dentists, is called {{c1::herpetic whitlow}}.
extraNote: It is caused by direct inoculation of the virus into a break in the skin.

clozeText: On fluorescein staining, HSV keratoconjunctivitis shows characteristic {{c1::dendritic ulcers}}.
extraNote: Recurrent infections can lead to corneal scarring and blindness.

clozeText: Acyclovir must be monophosphorylated by the viral enzyme {{c1::thymidine kinase}} to become active.
extraNote: Host cell kinases then perform the second and third phosphorylations to form acyclovir triphosphate.

clozeText: The mechanism of action for acyclovir involves inhibition of {{c1::viral DNA polymerase}} via chain termination.
extraNote: It acts as a guanosine analog that lacks a 3' hydroxyl group.

clozeText: In cases of acyclovir-resistant HSV (often due to mutated thymidine kinase), {{c1::foscarnet}} is the drug of choice.
extraNote: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog that does not require phosphorylation for activity.

clozeText: {{c1::Cidofovir}} can be used for resistant HSV as it only requires cellular kinases for activation, bypassing viral thymidine kinase.
extraNote: It is a cytidine analog that inhibits viral DNA polymerase.

clozeText: Neonatal herpes is usually acquired via {{c1::the birth canal}} during delivery.
extraNote: It can present as skin-eye-mouth disease, encephalitis, or disseminated infection.

clozeText: HSV esophagitis in immunocompromised patients typically presents with {{c1::punched-out}} ulcers.
extraNote: In contrast, CMV esophagitis presents with linear ulcers.

clozeText: The classic dermatologic description of HSV vesicles is {{c1::dew drops on a rose petal}}.
extraNote: This refers to clear vesicles on an erythematous base.
highYieldKeyword: Dew drops on a rose petal

clozeText: {{c1::Herpes gladiatorum}} is an HSV-1 infection of the skin common among wrestlers.
extraNote: Transmission occurs via direct skin-to-skin contact during matches.

clozeText: HSV virions travel from the periphery to the sensory ganglia cell bodies via {{c1::retrograde}} transport.
extraNote: This process is mediated by the motor protein dynein.

clozeText: Reactivated HSV virions travel from the sensory ganglia to the skin via {{c1::anterograde}} transport.
extraNote: This process is mediated by the motor protein kinesin.

clozeText: {{c1::Valacyclovir}} is a prodrug of acyclovir with better oral bioavailability.
extraNote: It is converted to acyclovir in the liver and intestines.

clozeText: Cerebrospinal fluid in HSV encephalitis often shows a pleocytosis with a predominance of {{c1::lymphocytes}}.
extraNote: Despite the presence of RBCs (hemorrhage), the WBC differential is lymphocytic.

clozeText: HSV is a member of the {{c1::Alphaherpesvirinae}} subfamily.
extraNote: This subfamily is characterized by a short reproductive cycle and latency in sensory ganglia.

clozeText: The structural symmetry of the HSV capsid is {{c1::icosahedral}}.
extraNote: It is an enveloped, double-stranded linear DNA virus.

clozeText: Unlike most DNA viruses, HSV encodes its own {{c1::ribonucleotide reductase}} to facilitate replication in non-dividing cells like neurons.
extraNote: This enzyme converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides.

clozeText: HSV-2 is a major risk factor for the acquisition of {{c1::HIV}}.
extraNote: The mucosal inflammation and ulcers provide a portal of entry for the virus.

clozeText: Eczema herpeticum is a severe HSV infection superimposing on pre-existing {{c1::atopic dermatitis}}.
extraNote: It presents as rapid onset of diffuse vesicles and can be life-threatening.

clozeText: Topical {{c1::trifluridine}} is a primary treatment for HSV-induced keratitis.
extraNote: It is a fluorinated pyrimidine nucleoside analog.

clozeText: The Rabies virus belongs to the {{c1::Rhabdoviridae}} family of viruses.
extraNote: Rhabdoviridae are characterized by their distinct rod or bullet shape.

clozeText: Rabies virus has a characteristic {{c1::bullet-shaped::shape}} morphology under electron microscopy.
extraNote: This shape is due to the envelope and the helical nucleocapsid structure.

clozeText: The genome of the Rabies virus is {{c1::(-) ssRNA::nucleic acid type}}.
extraNote: Negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses must carry their own polymerase in the virion.

clozeText: The Rabies virus genome is {{c1::linear::shape}} and non-segmented.
extraNote: Unlike Orthomyxoviruses or Reoviruses, Rhabdoviridae do not have segmented genomes.

clozeText: Because it is a negative-strand RNA virus, Rabies must carry {{c1::RNA-dependent RNA polymerase}} within its virion.
extraNote: This enzyme is necessary to transcribe the negative-sense RNA into positive-sense mRNA.

clozeText: The Rabies virus is {{c1::enveloped}} and contains glycoprotein spikes.
extraNote: The envelope makes the virus susceptible to detergents and heat.

clozeText: The Rabies virus initially binds to {{c1::Nicotinic Acetylcholine receptors (nAChR)}} at the neuromuscular junction.
extraNote: This allows the virus to enter the peripheral nervous system after a bite.

clozeText: After entry into the peripheral nerves, the Rabies virus travels via {{c1::retrograde::direction}} axonal transport.
extraNote: This transport carries the virus from the site of the bite to the central nervous system.

clozeText: The motor protein responsible for the transport of Rabies virus toward the CNS is {{c1::dynein}}.
extraNote: Dynein moves cargo toward the negative end of microtubules (retrograde).

clozeText: Rabies virus replicates in the {{c1::cytoplasm::cell compartment}} of the host cell.
extraNote: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm, with the notable exception of Influenza and Retroviruses.

clozeText: The pathognomonic histological finding in Rabies is the {{c1::Negri body}}.
extraNote: Negri bodies are eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions.

clozeText: Negri bodies are most commonly found in the {{c1::Purkinje cells}} of the cerebellum.
extraNote: They are also frequently found in the pyramidal cells of the hippocampus.

clozeText: In the hippocampus, Rabies virus Negri bodies are most prominently found in {{c1::pyramidal}} cells.
extraNote: The hippocampus and cerebellum are the two primary sites for post-mortem histological diagnosis.

clozeText: The most common reservoir/source of Rabies in the United States is {{c1::bats}}.
extraNote: While dogs are the main source worldwide, bat-associated strains cause most human cases in the US.

clozeText: Globally, the most common source of human Rabies transmission is {{c1::dogs}}.
extraNote: This is largely controlled in developed countries via mandatory pet vaccination.

clozeText: One of the earliest clinical symptoms of Rabies is {{c1::paresthesia::sensory change}} at the site of the wound.
extraNote: This tingling or burning sensation occurs as the virus replicates in the sensory neurons.

clozeText: {{c1::Hydrophobia}} is a classic clinical sign of Rabies caused by painful pharyngeal spasms when swallowing water.
extraNote: This symptom often leads to fear of water and significant dehydration.

clozeText: Rabies virus glycoproteins bind to the {{c1::p75NTR}} (nerve growth factor receptor) as an alternative receptor.
extraNote: This contributes to its neurotrophic nature.

clozeText: The incubation period of Rabies depends on the {{c1::distance}} of the bite from the central nervous system.
extraNote: Bites on the face have a shorter incubation period than bites on the foot.

clozeText: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for Rabies includes both the {{c1::killed vaccine}} and HRIG.
extraNote: The Rabies vaccine is one of the few that can be given effectively after exposure due to the long incubation period.

clozeText: {{c1::Human Rabies Immune Globulin (HRIG)}} provides passive immunity and should be injected around the wound.
extraNote: HRIG provides immediate protection while the active vaccine stimulates the patient's own immune response.

clozeText: The Rabies vaccine is a {{c1::killed / inactivated::type}} vaccine.
extraNote: It is typically administered in a series of four doses over two weeks.

clozeText: The {{c1::Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA)}} test on brain tissue is the gold standard for diagnosing Rabies in animals.
extraNote: In living humans, skin biopsy from the nape of the neck is often used to look for viral antigen.

clozeText: Besides bats, common terrestrial reservoirs for Rabies in the US include {{c1::raccoons, skunks, and foxes}}.
extraNote: Rodents and rabbits are rarely found to be infected with rabies.

clozeText: The Rabies virus {{c1::G protein}} is the primary target for neutralizing antibodies.
extraNote: The G protein (glycoprotein) mediates attachment to host cell receptors.

clozeText: Progression of Rabies to the {{c1::furious}} form involves agitation, hallucinations, and autonomic instability.
extraNote: The other form is 'paralytic' or 'dumb' rabies, which mimics Guillain-Barré syndrome.

clozeText: Patients found with a {{c1::bat}} in their room while sleeping should receive Rabies PEP, even if a bite is not visible.
extraNote: Bat bites can be small enough to go unnoticed, making this a critical USMLE management point.

clozeText: Rabies virus Negri bodies are described as {{c1::eosinophilic}} cytoplasmic inclusions.
extraNote: This means they stain pink/red with H&E staining.

clozeText: Microscopically, {{c1::Staphylococci}} appear in grapelike clusters, whereas {{c2::Streptococci}} appear in chains.
extraNote: This morphological difference is a primary criterion for initial identification after Gram staining.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that degrades {{c2::H2O2::hydrogen peroxide}} into oxygen and water.
extraNote: The catalase test is used to differentiate Staphylococci (+) from Streptococci (-).

clozeText: The primary enzyme used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from other staphylococci is {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta (β)}} hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar (MSA) is a selective and differential medium often used for S. aureus identification.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and acts as a virulence factor by binding the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: Binding the Fc portion prevents the orientation needed for opsonization and phagocytosis by neutrophils.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids induce the release of cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::PBP2a::protein}}.
extraNote: PBP2a (Penicillin-Binding Protein 2a) can still perform transpeptidation but has low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Strains of {{c1::CA-MRSA (Community-Acquired)}} almost all produce {{c2::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}, whereas HCA-MRSA strains usually do not.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is associated with severe skin infections and necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves enzymes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site, which is normally the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus.

clozeText: The most common human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where approximately {{c2::30}}% of people are colonized.
extraNote: Nasal colonization increases the risk of subsequent skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in the ability of {{c2::neutrophils}} to kill bacteria.
extraNote: S. aureus is a catalase-positive organism, which is particularly dangerous for CGD patients who lack the respiratory burst.

clozeText: The classic pyogenic lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which often undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: Pyogenic inflammation is the result of both toxin production and host immune response.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, can be caused by either {{c2::S. aureus or S. pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a superficial skin infection most common in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, which presents as small pustules on hair follicles.
extraNote: Folliculitis can lead to furuncles (boils) or carbuncles (larger, interconnected abscesses).

clozeText: S. aureus can cause {{c1::scalded skin syndrome}}, a condition characterized by desquamation of the skin in infants caused by an {{c2::exotoxin}}.
extraNote: The specific toxin responsible is exfoliative toxin, which cleaves desmosomes.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV)}} drugs.
extraNote: Common infections in this population include right-sided endocarditis and septic arthritis.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome (TSS)}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin (TSST-1) that causes massive cytokine release.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::peptidoglycan}} has endotoxin-like properties and can activate the {{c2::complement}} and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus can cause septic shock without possessing true LPS (endotoxin).

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is sensitive to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}, whereas Staphylococcus saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is high-yield for differentiating coagulase-negative staphylococci.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common member of the skin flora and is an important cause of infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and joints.
extraNote: It frequently forms biofilms on indwelling medical devices.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is primarily associated with infections of the {{c1::urinary tract}}.
extraNote: It is a common cause of cystitis in young, sexually active women.

clozeText: The primary method of preventing S. aureus transmission, especially in hospitals, is {{c1::handwashing}}.
extraNote: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission between medical personnel and patients.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States.
extraNote: It is also a significant cause of pneumonia and sepsis in immunocompetent patients.

clozeText: More than {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains produce β-lactamase, which degrades many penicillins.
extraNote: These strains remain sensitive to beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin, provided they are not MRSA.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}} such as sutures or catheters is a major predisposing factor to S. aureus infection.
extraNote: Foreign bodies facilitate the establishment of infection with a lower inoculum of bacteria.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to break down red blood cells to recover {{c2::iron}} for energy synthesis.
extraNote: Iron is an essential cofactor for cytochrome enzymes in the bacterial energy chain.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of hospital-acquired {{c1::pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections, including those at {{c2::cardiac pacemaker}} sites.
extraNote: It is a leading cause of nosocomial (healthcare-acquired) infections.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: While the exact cause is unknown, superantigen production by S. aureus has been proposed as a mechanism.

clozeText: Staphylococci are characterized microscopically as {{c1::gram-positive}} cocci arranged in {{c2::grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: In contrast, streptococci are typically arranged in chains.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce the enzyme {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from {{c2::streptococci}}.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from neutrophil-mediated killing.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin, forming a clot.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A::virulence factor}}, which binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by neutrophils and macrophages because the Fc receptor cannot bind the antibody.

clozeText: The {{c1::mecA}} gene in S. aureus encodes for altered {{c2::penicillin-binding proteins (PBP2a)}}, leading to MRSA.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics like methicillin or nafcillin.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate {{c2::adherence}} to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also form part of the surface receptors for specific staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, where it colonizes approximately {{c2::30}}% of people.
extraNote: Chronic carriers have an increased risk of developing skin infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is at high risk for endocarditis and skin abscesses.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD involves a deficiency in NADPH oxidase, making patients vulnerable to catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: Full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) occurs when the bacteria substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This change is encoded by a gene cassette often found on transposons within plasmids.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause septic shock even without endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} and {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids specifically stimulate cytokine release from macrophages.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is distinguished from HCA-MRSA by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin::Toxin}}.
extraNote: Almost all CA-MRSA strains (like USA300) produce this toxin, which is associated with skin abscesses and necrotizing pneumonia.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Abscesses undergo central necrosis and typically drain pus to the outside.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}}.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a common selective and differential medium for S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to destroy red blood cells and recover {{c2::iron}} for cytochrome synthesis.
extraNote: Iron is a critical nutrient for bacterial energy production and growth.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women are colonized by S. aureus in the {{c2::vagina}}, predisposing them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: Menstruation-associated TSS is linked to the use of highly absorbent tampons.

clozeText: Unlike S. aureus, both S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus are {{c1::coagulase-negative}}.
extraNote: They are further differentiated by their sensitivity or resistance to the antibiotic novobiocin.

clozeText: Over {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains produce {{c2::beta-lactamase}}, which is encoded by plasmids.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades penicillin G, necessitating the use of beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::impetigo}}, which presents as vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored crust}}.
extraNote: S. pyogenes (Group A Strep) is another common cause of this condition.

clozeText: S. aureus polysaccharide capsules are poorly immunogenic; types {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} cause 85% of infections.
extraNote: The poor immunogenicity has made the development of an effective vaccine difficult.

clozeText: Hand contact is a major mode of transmission for S. aureus; therefore, {{c1::handwashing}} is a critical preventative measure.
extraNote: Hospital personnel are common vectors for colonization and infection of patients.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing factor to infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Compromised immunity and vascular issues in these patients increase susceptibility.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It results in widespread desquamation, typically in infants.

clozeText: Foreign bodies like {{c1::sutures}} and {{c2::intravenous catheters}} are major predisposing factors for S. aureus infection.
extraNote: These surfaces facilitate biofilm formation and bacterial survival.

clozeText: In the US, {{c1::MRSA}} currently accounts for more than {{c2::50}}% of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients.
extraNote: MRSA is a significant burden in healthcare-acquired (HCA) infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as pustules.
extraNote: It can progress to more severe lesions like furuncles and carbuncles.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also frequently implicated in infections at the site of cardiac pacemaker insertion.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::Disease}} is a condition of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It is an acute febrile vasculitis primarily affecting children.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::Organism}} (MRSA) is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.
extraNote: MRSA is also an important cause of necrotizing fasciitis, pneumonia, and sepsis in immunocompetent individuals.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, whereas streptococci do not, allowing for the degradation of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase allows the bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus, S. aureus typically {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and produces beta-hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron, which is necessary for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in S. aureus is mediated by the {{c1::mecA::gene}}.
extraNote: This gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) that has low affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) almost always produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin relatively rare in healthcare-acquired MRSA.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: High-level vancomycin resistance (VRSA) occurs when the bacteria substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This change prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site in the cell wall.

clozeText: The major cell wall virulence factor of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which binds to the Fc portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, thus inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: In the cell wall of S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: These are polymers of ribitol phosphate and also serve as part of the receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus is often induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which stimulate the release of IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.
extraNote: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus also possesses endotoxin-like properties that contribute to the clinical findings of shock.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic nasal carriers, which increases their risk of skin infections.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome in infants is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: The toxin causes widespread desquamation of the skin, giving it a rolled-up appearance.

clozeText: Lesions of {{c1::impetigo}} present as crops of vesicles with a characteristic honey-colored crust.
extraNote: This infection can be caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, characterized by multiple small pustules at the base of hair follicles.
extraNote: It is also a primary cause of cellulitis and bacterial conjunctivitis.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS).
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen that causes massive cytokine release.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which features central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Abscesses are the classic lesion; S. aureus can also disseminate via the bloodstream to cause osteomyelitis or endocarditis.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::beta-lactamase}}, which is encoded on plasmids and degrades many penicillins.
extraNote: Strains that produce only beta-lactamase can still be treated with nafcillin or oxacillin.

clozeText: The coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is sensitive to novobiocin is {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections on prosthetic heart valves and artificial joints.

clozeText: The coagulase-negative staphylococcus that is resistant to novobiocin is {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: {{c1::Hand contact::Mechanism}} is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus, making handwashing critical for prevention.
extraNote: Hospital personnel are common vectors for transmitting the bacteria to patients.

clozeText: Staphylococcal capsule types {{c1::5 and 8}} cause approximately 85% of human S. aureus infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, which complicates the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users::population}}.
extraNote: This frequently presents as right-sided endocarditis involving the tricuspid valve.

clozeText: Important predisposing factors to S. aureus infection include the presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}}, such as sutures or intravenous catheters.
extraNote: Bacteria can adhere to these surfaces and form biofilms, protecting them from the immune response.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: Kawasaki syndrome typically affects children and involves vasculitis of the coronary arteries.

clozeText: The altered transpeptidase PBP2a in MRSA performs its function in cell wall synthesis but does not {{c1::bind penicillins}}.
extraNote: This allows the bacteria to build their peptidoglycan layer even in the presence of methicillin or nafcillin.

clozeText: The cassette of genes for vancomycin resistance in S. aureus is identical to those found in {{c1::enterococci}}.
extraNote: These genes are typically carried on transposons within plasmids, facilitating horizontal gene transfer.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of surgical-wound infections, including at the insertion site of {{c1::cardiac pacemakers}}.
extraNote: Post-operative monitoring for erythema and purulence at the site is essential.

clozeText: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) belongs to the {{c1::Picornaviridae}} family.
extraNote: It is a small, non-enveloped virus that is a major cause of acute hepatitis worldwide.

clozeText: The genome of Hepatitis A virus consists of {{c1::positive-sense ssRNA::polarity and type}}.
extraNote: Because it is positive-sense, the RNA can be directly translated into a polyprotein by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Hepatitis A virus is a {{c1::naked (non-enveloped)}} virus, making it resistant to detergents and acid.
extraNote: The lack of an envelope allows it to survive the acidic environment of the stomach and remain stable in the environment.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Hepatitis A is the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route.
extraNote: Outbreaks are often linked to contaminated water, food, or poor sanitary conditions.

clozeText: A classic high-yield risk factor for Hepatitis A infection is the consumption of raw {{c1::shellfish (e.g., oysters)}}.
extraNote: Shellfish concentrate the virus from contaminated water; proper cooking inactivates the virus.

clozeText: Hepatitis A outbreaks are common in {{c1::daycare centers}} due to poor hand hygiene during diaper changes.
extraNote: Children are often asymptomatic but shed high concentrations of the virus in their stool.

clozeText: Acute Hepatitis A infection is diagnosed by the presence of {{c1::Anti-HAV IgM}} antibodies.
extraNote: IgM appears early in the infection and usually disappears within 3 to 6 months.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::Anti-HAV IgG}} indicates immunity through prior infection or vaccination.
extraNote: IgG persists for life and provides protection against reinfection.

clozeText: Unlike Hepatitis B and C, Hepatitis A has {{c1::no}} chronic carrier state.
extraNote: Infection is almost always self-limiting and does not lead to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, or hepatocellular carcinoma.

clozeText: A unique clinical symptom of viral hepatitis (especially HAV) is an {{c1::aversion to smoking}}.
extraNote: The mechanism for this sudden change in taste/preference is unknown but frequently tested.

clozeText: Hepatocellular damage in HAV is not caused by the virus itself, but by {{c1::CD8+ T cells}}.
extraNote: Host immune-mediated destruction of infected hepatocytes leads to the clinical symptoms of hepatitis.

clozeText: Histologically, HAV infection can show {{c1::Councilman bodies}}, which represent apoptotic hepatocytes.
extraNote: These appear as intensely eosinophilic (acidophilic) bodies on liver biopsy.

clozeText: Hepatitis A translation is initiated by an {{c1::IRES (Internal Ribosome Entry Site)}}.
extraNote: This allows the virus to bypass the need for a 5' cap on its mRNA during protein synthesis.

clozeText: The Hepatitis A vaccine is a(n) {{c1::inactivated (killed)}} vaccine.
extraNote: It is recommended for travelers to endemic areas, men who have sex with men, and patients with chronic liver disease.

clozeText: For post-exposure prophylaxis in healthy individuals (ages 1-40), the {{c1::HAV vaccine}} is preferred over immune globulin.
extraNote: Immune globulin (IG) is used for those under 1 year old, over 40, or immunocompromised.

clozeText: Hepatitis A virus undergoes replication in the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of hepatocytes.
extraNote: As an RNA virus (excluding influenza and retroviruses), it completes its life cycle without entering the nucleus.

clozeText: The incubation period for Hepatitis A is approximately {{c1::2 to 6 weeks}}.
extraNote: Patients are most infectious during the 2 weeks before the onset of jaundice when stool shedding is highest.

clozeText: The stool of a patient with Hepatitis A contains the highest concentration of virus {{c1::before}} the onset of symptoms.
extraNote: This leads to high transmission rates because the host is unaware they are infected.

clozeText: In acute HAV infection, the serum level of {{c1::ALT}} is usually higher than AST.
extraNote: Very high transaminase levels (>1000 U/L) are characteristic of acute viral hepatitis.

clozeText: Patients with Hepatitis A may develop {{c1::dark urine}} due to conjugated hyperbilirubinuria.
extraNote: This occurs because the liver cannot adequately excrete bilirubin into the bile, leading to its spillover into the blood and urine.

clozeText: Hepatitis A is characterized by {{c1::ballooning degeneration}} and mononuclear cell infiltration on biopsy.
extraNote: Swelling of hepatocytes and inflammation are the hallmarks of the acute phase.

clozeText: Although rare, HAV can cause {{c1::fulminant hepatitis}} leading to acute liver failure.
extraNote: This is more common in patients with pre-existing chronic liver disease (e.g., Hep B or C).

clozeText: There is only {{c1::one}} known serotype of Hepatitis A virus worldwide.
extraNote: This single serotype makes the development of an effective universal vaccine possible.

clozeText: Unlike most other Picornaviruses, HAV is exceptionally {{c1::acid-stable}}.
extraNote: Stability at pH 1 allows the virus to survive stomach acid after ingestion.

clozeText: HAV can be inactivated by {{c1::chlorination (or boiling)}} of water.
extraNote: Standard water treatment processes are usually sufficient to prevent large-scale outbreaks.

clozeText: The jaundice associated with HAV is often accompanied by {{c1::pruritus (itching)}}.
extraNote: This is caused by the deposition of bile salts in the skin during cholestasis.

clozeText: The HAV polyprotein is cleaved into functional proteins by a viral {{c1::protease}}.
extraNote: This is a common feature of the Picornaviridae life cycle.

clozeText: Physical exam of a patient with acute HAV often reveals {{c1::hepatomegaly}}.
extraNote: The liver is often tender to palpation in the Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ).

clozeText: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a member of the {{c1::Picornaviridae}} family.
extraNote: HAV is a non-enveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA virus.

clozeText: The genome of Hepatitis A is described as {{c1::(+)ssRNA::RNA type}} and is non-segmented.
extraNote: Its positive-sense nature allows it to be directly translated by host ribosomes.

clozeText: Unlike many other hepatitis viruses, HAV is {{c1::non-enveloped::enveloped or non-enveloped?}}, which allows it to survive the acidic environment of the stomach.
extraNote: This lack of an envelope facilitates its fecal-oral transmission.

clozeText: Consumption of raw or undercooked {{c1::shellfish::food type}} (e.g., oysters) is a classic high-yield source of HAV infection.
extraNote: Shellfish filter-feed and concentrate the virus from contaminated water.

clozeText: In children, infection with Hepatitis A is typically {{c1::asymptomatic (or subclinical)}}.
extraNote: While children are often asymptomatic, they can still shed the virus and spread it to adults.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::IgM anti-HAV}} is the most important marker for diagnosing an acute infection.
extraNote: IgM appears early in the course of the disease and typically disappears within 3 to 6 months.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::IgG anti-HAV}} indicates prior infection or successful vaccination.
extraNote: IgG anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity and protects against reinfection.

clozeText: Hepatitis A does {{c1::not::does or does not?}} have a chronic carrier state.
extraNote: HAV is almost always self-limiting and does not lead to chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis.

clozeText: Unlike Hepatitis B and C, HAV is not associated with an increased risk of {{c1::hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)}}.
extraNote: The lack of chronicity and integration into the host genome prevents oncogenesis.

clozeText: A high-yield clinical finding is that smokers with HAV may report a sudden {{c1::aversion to smoking}}.
extraNote: This is a classic but unexplained symptom found in the prodromal phase of viral hepatitis.

clozeText: The Hepatitis A vaccine is a(n) {{c1::inactivated::vaccine type}} vaccine.
extraNote: It is recommended for travelers to endemic areas, men who have sex with men, and patients with chronic liver disease.

clozeText: Histopathology of the liver during HAV infection shows {{c1::Councilman bodies::finding}}, which are apoptotic hepatocytes.
extraNote: These are also known as acidophilic bodies and appear as intensely eosinophilic circles on H&E stain.

clozeText: The incubation period for HAV is relatively short, usually lasting {{c1::2 to 6::range}} weeks.
extraNote: This is shorter than the incubation periods for Hepatitis B or C.

clozeText: Common symptoms of acute HAV include fever, jaundice, and {{c1::right upper quadrant (RUQ)}} pain.
extraNote: Hepatomegaly and dark urine (due to conjugated bilirubin) are also common.

clozeText: Outbreaks of HAV are frequently seen in {{c1::daycare centers::location}} due to fecal-oral spread among children.
extraNote: Infected children who are asymptomatic are major drivers of transmission in these settings.

clozeText: In the liver, HAV causes hepatocyte swelling and {{c1::monocytic::cell type}} infiltration.
extraNote: The damage to hepatocytes is largely due to the host's immune response (CD8+ T cells) rather than direct viral cytopathic effect.

clozeText: Post-exposure prophylaxis for healthy individuals aged 1–40 consists of the {{c1::HAV vaccine}}.
extraNote: Individuals outside this age range or those who are immunocompromised may require HAV immunoglobulin.

clozeText: Hepatitis A is a {{c1::self-limiting}} disease that typically requires only supportive care.
extraNote: No specific antiviral therapy is indicated for acute HAV.

clozeText: Viral shedding in the stool occurs primarily {{c1::before::before or after?}} the onset of clinical jaundice.
extraNote: This timing makes it difficult to prevent spread because the patient is most infectious while still asymptomatic.

clozeText: Serum levels of {{c1::ALT::enzyme}} are typically much higher than AST in the acute phase of HAV.
extraNote: Levels often exceed 1000 U/L during the symptomatic phase.

clozeText: HAV enters host hepatocytes by binding to the {{c1::HAVCR-1}} (or TIM-1) receptor.
extraNote: This receptor is expressed on the surface of liver cells.

clozeText: Dark urine in HAV is a result of {{c1::conjugated hyperbilirubinemia}}.
extraNote: The liver can conjugate bilirubin, but the inflamed hepatocytes/bile canaliculi prevent its excretion into bile, leading to spillover into the blood and urine.

clozeText: A rare but life-threatening complication of HAV is {{c1::fulminant hepatitis}}.
extraNote: This presents as acute liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.

clozeText: International travelers should receive the first dose of the HAV vaccine at least {{c1::2}} weeks before departure.
extraNote: This allows for the development of protective antibody titers.

clozeText: The stools of patients with HAV often become {{c1::pale (clay-colored)}} due to decreased bile pigment excretion.
extraNote: This occurs during the icteric phase when cholestasis is present.

clozeText: Pruritus in HAV results from the accumulation of {{c1::bile salts}} in the skin.
extraNote: This is common in the icteric phase of any obstructive or hepatocellular jaundice.

clozeText: HAV does not have {{c1::DNA polymerase}} because it is an RNA virus.
extraNote: It utilizes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for replication.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococci}} appear in grapelike clusters, whereas {{c2::streptococci}} are arranged in chains.
extraNote: This microscopic distinction is a primary criterion for differentiating gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into {{c2::O2 and H2O}}.
extraNote: No streptococci produce catalase, making this the primary biochemical test to differentiate the two genera.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus by its production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen into a fibrin clot.

clozeText: S. aureus typically {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta}}-hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Coagulase-negative staphylococci generally do not ferment mannitol or cause hemolysis.

extraNote: PBP2a can perform its transpeptidase function but does not bind penicillins effectively.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA in the United States is {{c1::USA300}}.
extraNote: It is a frequent cause of community-acquired staphylococcal infections.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, while few healthcare-acquired strains do.
extraNote: This toxin contributes to the severity of skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) involves genes that substitute {{c1::d-lactate}} for {{c2::d-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding its target.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is the major cell wall protein of S. aureus and binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, it prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils, inhibiting phagocytosis.

extraNote: These cytokines are the primary mediators of the systemic inflammatory response in sepsis.

clozeText: The S. aureus polysaccharide capsule is an important virulence factor, with serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus possesses endotoxin-like properties, even though the organism lacks true endotoxin (LPS).
extraNote: It can activate the complement and coagulation cascades and stimulate macrophages.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill catalase-positive bacteria.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This population is at high risk for endocarditis and skin abscesses.
