extraNote: It presents as multiple small pustules, often on the chin or neck.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome::disease}} in infants is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It features widespread areas of desquamated skin.

clozeText: Impetigo is a skin infection characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored crust}}.
extraNote: It is caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: S. aureus is considered a possible causative agent in some theories.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is sensitive to {{c1::novobiocin}}, whereas S. saprophyticus is {{c2::resistant}}.
extraNote: This test is used to differentiate coagulase-negative staphylococci, particularly in urinary tract infections.

clozeText: S. aureus is one of the most common causes of {{c1::hospital-acquired pneumonia}} and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of infections at pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: {{c1::Foreign bodies::factor}} such as sutures and intravenous catheters are major predisposing factors for S. aureus infection.
extraNote: They provide a surface for biofilm formation and protect the bacteria from host defenses.

clozeText: Staphylococci are characterized as {{c1::Gram-positive cocci}} arranged in {{c1::irregular grapelike clusters}}.
extraNote: In contrast, Streptococci are typically arranged in chains.

clozeText: The biochemical test used to distinguish Staphylococci from Streptococci is {{c1::catalase}}.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.

clozeText: Catalase is a virulence factor because it allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of {{c1::H2O2 (hydrogen peroxide)}} within neutrophils.
extraNote: Bacteria that lack this enzyme are more easily killed by oxidative bursts.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by its ability to produce {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and produces {{c1::β-hemolysis}} on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a common selective and differential medium for S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to recover {{c1::iron::nutrient}} from red blood cells for energy production.
extraNote: The iron is specifically used in the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains contain plasmids encoding {{c1::β-lactamase}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: This led to the clinical use of beta-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene located on the bacterial chromosome.
extraNote: This gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein.

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA is called {{c1::PBP2a}}, which functions as a transpeptidase but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This renders all standard beta-lactams ineffective.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains frequently produce {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, a toxin relatively rare in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves enzymes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c1::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding to its target site.

clozeText: S. aureus {{c1::Protein A}} acts as a virulence factor by binding to the {{c1::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on phagocytes from binding the antibody, inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: Adherence of staphylococci to mucosal cells is mediated by {{c1::teichoic acids}}.
extraNote: These are polymers of ribitol phosphate found in the cell wall.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}}, which trigger the release of {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}} from macrophages.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids mimic the action of Gram-negative endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The S. aureus {{c1::peptidoglycan}} possesses endotoxin-like properties, allowing it to activate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains why S. aureus can cause septic shock without having true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers in this site.

clozeText: In the hospital setting, the most important mode of S. aureus transmission is {{c1::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Frequent handwashing is critical for infection control.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the neutrophil's ability to produce reactive oxygen species to kill catalase-positive bacteria.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: These lesions typically undergo central necrosis and drain pus.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by a specific {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} produced by S. aureus.
extraNote: It results in widespread desquamation, particularly in infants.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, can be caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a common superficial skin infection in children.

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis}} and {{c2::septic arthritis}}.
extraNote: It is also a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is associated with high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is distinguished from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is resistant to novobiocin.

clozeText: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} in sexually active young women.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant.

clozeText: S. epidermidis is a common cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::prosthetic joints}}.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and frequently forms biofilms on devices.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing metabolic factor to infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: Other factors include compromised humoral immunity and presence of foreign bodies like sutures.

clozeText: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) belongs to the {{c1::Flaviviridae}} family.
extraNote: This family also includes Yellow Fever, Dengue, and West Nile viruses.

clozeText: The HCV genome consists of {{c1::(+)ssRNA::polarity and type}}.
extraNote: It is linear and approximately 9.6 kb in length.

clozeText: HCV is an {{c1::enveloped}} virus, making it sensitive to detergents and heat.
extraNote: Enveloped viruses generally do not survive well in the GI tract.

clozeText: HCV lacks {{c1::3' to 5' exonuclease::proofreading}} activity in its RNA polymerase, leading to high genetic variability.
extraNote: This frequent mutation prevents the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: The {{c1::NS5B}} protein in HCV functions as the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
extraNote: It is a major target for direct-acting antiviral (DAA) drugs like Sofosbuvir.

clozeText: Antigenic variation in HCV occurs most frequently in the {{c1::hypervariable region 1 (HVR1)}} of the E2 envelope protein.
extraNote: Host antibodies cannot keep up with the rapid mutations in this region.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::80}}% of patients infected with acute HCV will progress to chronic infection.
extraNote: This is much higher than the chronicity rate of HBV in adults (~5%).

clozeText: The most common mode of HCV transmission in the United States is {{c1::IV drug use}}.
extraNote: Post-transfusion HCV has drastically decreased since the introduction of blood screening in 1992.

clozeText: HCV protease inhibitors, such as Simeprevir, target the {{c1::NS3/4A}} protease.
extraNote: These drugs prevent the cleavage of the viral polyprotein into functional units.

clozeText: {{c1::NS5A}} inhibitors (e.g., Ledipasvir, Velpatasvir) play a crucial role in inhibiting viral replication and assembly.
extraNote: NS5A is a phosphoprotein essential for RNA replication.

clozeText: Chronic HCV is strongly associated with {{c1::mixed cryoglobulinemia}}, a form of small-vessel vasculitis.
extraNote: Presents with the triad of palpable purpura, arthralgias, and fatigue.

clozeText: The renal disease most classically associated with Hepatitis C is {{c1::Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)}}.
extraNote: Often shows a 'tram-track' appearance on basement membrane staining.

clozeText: {{c1::Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)}} is a dermatologic manifestation of HCV characterized by blisters and hyperpigmentation on sun-exposed skin.
extraNote: Caused by a deficiency in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

clozeText: Initial screening for HCV infection is performed using the {{c1::anti-HCV antibody}} test.
extraNote: A positive antibody test must be confirmed with an HCV RNA PCR test.

clozeText: Confirmation of active HCV infection requires a positive {{c1::HCV RNA PCR}} test.
extraNote: This distinguishes between a resolved past infection and an active chronic infection.

clozeText: HCV replicates entirely within the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the host cell.
extraNote: Like other (+)ssRNA viruses, it does not require entry into the nucleus.

clozeText: Liver damage in HCV is primarily mediated by {{c1::cytotoxic T cells (CD8+)}} rather than direct viral cytopathicity.
extraNote: The immune response causes chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis.

clozeText: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in HCV patients typically occurs only after the development of {{c1::cirrhosis}}.
extraNote: HCV does not integrate into the host genome, unlike HBV.

clozeText: {{c1::Lichen planus}} is an extrahepatic manifestation of HCV that presents as pruritic, purple, polygonal papules.
extraNote: Often found on the wrists or as Wickham striae in the mouth.

clozeText: In chronic HCV, serum {{c1::ALT}} levels often show episodic elevations or 'waxing and waning' patterns.
extraNote: ALT levels may even be normal in some patients with significant liver damage.

clozeText: HCV infection increases the risk of developing {{c1::Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus}} and insulin resistance.
extraNote: The virus interferes with insulin signaling pathways in hepatocytes.

clozeText: Unlike Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C infection does NOT involve a {{c1::DNA intermediate}}.
extraNote: HBV uses reverse transcriptase; HCV uses an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

clozeText: The primary mechanism of action for Sofosbuvir is the inhibition of {{c1::NS5B}} as a chain terminator.
extraNote: It is a uridine nucleotide analog.

clozeText: {{c1::Ribavirin}}'s mechanism in HCV treatment includes the inhibition of IMP dehydrogenase and inducing lethal viral mutations.
extraNote: It is now less commonly used due to the efficacy of DAAs.

clozeText: Patients with HCV-related cirrhosis should be screened for HCC every 6 months using {{c1::liver ultrasound}}.
extraNote: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) may also be checked but is less specific.

clozeText: HCV is translated into a single large {{c1::polyprotein}} which is then cleaved by both host and viral proteases.
extraNote: This is a characteristic feature of the Flaviviridae family.

clozeText: {{c1::Genotype 1}} is the most common HCV genotype found in North America and Europe.
extraNote: Genotype 1 was historically the most difficult to treat before DAAs.

clozeText: Interferon-alpha (IFN-α) treats HCV by inducing {{c1::ribonuclease L}} and protein kinase R to inhibit viral protein synthesis.
extraNote: This therapy has largely been replaced by direct-acting antivirals.

clozeText: Methicillin-resistant {{c1::S. aureus}} (MRSA) is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.
extraNote: It also causes necrotizing fasciitis and sepsis in immunocompetent patients.

clozeText: {{c1::S. aureus::Organism}} is the most common cause of infections in intravenous drug users (IVDU).
extraNote: It is also associated with Kawasaki syndrome, though the etiology of the syndrome remains unknown.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into water and oxygen.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::catalase}} allows bacteria to survive the killing effect of H2O2 within {{c2::neutrophils}}.
extraNote: This is a key virulence factor helping the bacteria evade the respiratory burst.

clozeText: S. aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Biochemically, S. aureus typically {{c1::ferments mannitol}} and is {{c2::β-hemolytic::hemolysis type}}.
extraNote: In contrast, S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus do not ferment mannitol or cause hemolysis.

clozeText: More than 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::β-lactamase::enzyme}}, which is typically encoded on {{c2::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades many penicillins, making them ineffective against the organism.

clozeText: Resistance to nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP)}}.
extraNote: The specific protein is PBP2a, which retains transpeptidase activity but does not bind penicillins.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is distinguished from healthcare-acquired MRSA by the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is an exotoxin that can cause tissue necrosis and leukocyte destruction.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus involves enzymes that substitute {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This modification prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall precursor.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major cell wall protein of S. aureus that binds the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG, preventing phagocytosis.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, the antibody is oriented incorrectly to be recognized by neutrophil receptors.

clozeText: The {{c1::teichoic acids}} in the cell wall of staphylococci mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They are polymers of ribitol phosphate.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release cytokines like {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is analogous to the action of Gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus has {{c1::endotoxin-like}} properties, allowing it to activate complement and the coagulation cascade.
extraNote: This explains why Gram-positive organisms can still cause the clinical findings of septic shock.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized at any one time.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because of a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is catalase-positive, allowing it to neutralize the small amount of H2O2 these patients' cells might produce.

clozeText: The classic lesion of a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Common examples include furuncles and boils.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, which presents as small pustules on hair follicles.
extraNote: Other common skin infections include cellulitis and impetigo.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by {{c1::honey-colored crusts}}, is caused by either S. aureus or {{c2::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It results in large areas of desquamated skin, especially in infants.

clozeText: S. aureus can be spread via {{c1::fomites}} such as contaminated towels or clothing, and by {{c2::hand contact}}.
extraNote: Handwashing is critical for decreasing transmission, especially in hospital settings.

clozeText: The microcapsule of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic, making the development of a {{c1::vaccine}} difficult.
extraNote: Types 5 and 8 are responsible for 85% of S. aureus infections.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a common member of the skin flora that frequently infects prosthetic heart valves and hips.
extraNote: It is distinguished from S. saprophyticus by being sensitive to novobiocin.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections}} and is {{c2::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: It is coagulase-negative and does not produce hemolysis.

clozeText: The bacteria utilize hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin for the synthesis of {{c2::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is an essential nutrient required for bacterial growth and energy production.

clozeText: Staphylococci appear microscopically as {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: Both are Gram-positive, nonmotile, and non-spore-forming cocci.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5%}} of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, which predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: This condition is often associated with high-absorbency tampon use.

clozeText: Vancoymcin-resistant strains (VRSA) carry resistance genes on a {{c1::transposon}} located on a {{c2::plasmid}}.
extraNote: These genes were likely acquired from enterococci.

clozeText: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a {{c1::defective}} virus that requires the presence of Hepatitis B virus to cause infection.
extraNote: HDV is unable to produce its own envelope proteins and must 'steal' them from HBV.

clozeText: HDV requires the {{c1::HBsAg::surface antigen}} from HBV for its envelope to package its genome and infect hepatocytes.
extraNote: Without HBsAg, the HDV genome can replicate within a cell but cannot form new virions to spread.

clozeText: The genome of Hepatitis D virus is a {{c1::circular::shape}}, {{c2::negative::polarity}}-sense single-stranded RNA.
extraNote: It is unique among animal viruses for its circular RNA structure, resembling viroids in plants.

clozeText: A {{c1::co-infection::type}} occurs when a patient is infected with both HBV and HDV simultaneously.
extraNote: This typically results in an acute hepatitis that is usually self-limiting and rarely becomes chronic.

clozeText: A {{c1::superinfection::type}} occurs when a chronic HBV carrier is subsequently infected with HDV.
extraNote: This is much more dangerous than co-infection, leading to a high risk of chronic HDV and fulminant hepatitis.

clozeText: Superinfection of HDV on top of chronic HBV leads to {{c1::fulminant::severity}} hepatitis in roughly 20% of cases.
extraNote: This carries a significantly higher mortality rate compared to HBV infection alone.

clozeText: HDV is classified within the genus {{c1::Deltavirus}}.
extraNote: It is the only member of this genus known to infect humans.

clozeText: The only protein encoded by the HDV genome is the {{c1::HDAg::Delta antigen}}.
extraNote: HDAg exists in two forms: Small (S-HDAg) for replication and Large (L-HDAg) for virion assembly.

clozeText: HDV utilizes the host's {{c1::RNA polymerase II}} to replicate its RNA genome in the nucleus.
extraNote: This is unusual as RNA polymerase II typically transcribes DNA into mRNA.

clozeText: HDV RNA possesses {{c1::ribozyme::enzymatic activity}} activity, allowing it to self-cleave and ligate during replication.
extraNote: Replication occurs via a rolling-circle mechanism.

clozeText: Prevention of HDV is primarily achieved through {{c1::HBV vaccination}}.
extraNote: Because HDV cannot survive without HBV, immunity to HBV confers immunity to HDV.

clozeText: In a superinfection, the risk of developing chronic HD infection is approximately {{c1::90::%}}.
extraNote: In contrast, co-infection results in chronic disease in less than 5% of cases.

clozeText: Unlike HBV, which is mostly immunopathic, HDV is believed to have a {{c1::direct cytopathic}} effect on hepatocytes.
extraNote: This contributes to the rapid progression of liver damage seen in superinfections.

clozeText: The diagnosis of active HDV infection is typically confirmed by the presence of {{c1::HDV RNA}} in the serum.
extraNote: Anti-HDV antibodies (IgM and IgG) are also used for screening and diagnosis.

clozeText: HDV virions are approximately {{c1::35::size}} nm in diameter.
extraNote: They are composed of the HDV RNA-HDAg complex surrounded by an HBsAg-containing lipid envelope.

clozeText: HDV replication occurs within the {{c1::nucleus::organelle}} of the host hepatocyte.
extraNote: Most other RNA viruses (except influenza and retroviruses) replicate in the cytoplasm.

clozeText: The {{c1::Large::form}} Delta antigen (L-HDAg) inhibits replication and promotes the assembly of new virions.
extraNote: It undergoes post-translational prenylation which is essential for its interaction with HBsAg.

clozeText: The {{c1::Small::form}} Delta antigen (S-HDAg) is essential for the initiation of viral RNA replication.
extraNote: It acts as a trans-activator of HDV RNA synthesis.

clozeText: HDV transmission occurs via {{c1::parenteral::route}} routes, including blood transfusions and IV drug use.
extraNote: Transmission routes are identical to HBV (blood, sexual, perinatal).

clozeText: In the US, HDV is most commonly found in the {{c1::IV drug use::population}} population.
extraNote: Routine screening is recommended for HBV-positive patients in high-risk groups.

clozeText: The progression to {{c1::cirrhosis}} is significantly faster in patients with chronic HBV/HDV dual infection than with HBV alone.
extraNote: It is considered the most severe form of chronic viral hepatitis.

clozeText: Treatment for chronic HDV is difficult, but {{c1::Interferon-alpha::drug}} is sometimes used to reduce viral load.
extraNote: Nucleoside analogs that target HBV polymerase are generally ineffective against HDV.

clozeText: HDV RNA is synthesized using a {{c1::rolling-circle}} model of replication.
extraNote: This results in long multimeric strands that are then cleaved by the ribozyme.

clozeText: During HDV infection, the presence of {{c1::IgM anti-HDV}} indicates an acute or recent infection.
extraNote: Persistence of IgM anti-HDV may also indicate ongoing chronic infection.

clozeText: HDV is highly prevalent in the {{c1::Mediterranean::region}} basin and parts of South America (Amazon).
extraNote: These are known 'hotspots' for HDV endemicity.

clozeText: HDV requires the host enzyme {{c1::ADAR1::enzyme}} (Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA) to produce the Large HDAg.
extraNote: ADAR1 edits the viral RNA to change a stop codon, allowing the translation of the longer protein.

clozeText: Chronic HDV infection increases the risk of {{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma::cancer}} compared to HBV infection alone.
extraNote: The increased inflammatory and cytopathic environment accelerates oncogenesis.

clozeText: HDV cannot infect a person who is {{c1::immune}} to Hepatitis B.
extraNote: This is why the HBV vaccine is effective 'indirect' protection against HDV.

clozeText: Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a {{c1::defective}} virus that requires the presence of Hepatitis B virus to replicate.
extraNote: HDV lacks the genes to produce its own envelope proteins.

clozeText: HDV utilizes the {{c1::HBsAg::surface antigen}} from HBV to package its RNA genome into infectious virions.
extraNote: The HBV surface antigen provides the necessary envelope for HDV entry into hepatocytes.

clozeText: The HDV genome consists of a {{c1::circular}}, single-stranded {{c2::negative}}-sense RNA.
extraNote: This structure is unique among animal viruses and resembles plant viroids.

clozeText: {{c1::Coinfection::Term}} occurs when a patient is infected with both HBV and HDV simultaneously.
extraNote: Coinfection usually results in an acute hepatitis that resolves, similar to HBV alone.

clozeText: {{c1::Superinfection::Term}} occurs when a chronic HBV carrier is subsequently infected with HDV.
extraNote: Superinfection is associated with a much higher risk of chronic liver disease and fulminant hepatitis.

clozeText: HDV superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier leads to a {{c1::chronic}} HDV infection in approximately {{c2::80::%}} of cases.
extraNote: In contrast, coinfection only leads to chronicity in <5% of cases.

clozeText: HDV replication is unique because the genome is replicated by the host cell's {{c1::RNA polymerase II}}.
extraNote: The host RNA polymerase is 'redirected' to use the HDV RNA as a template.

clozeText: Preventing infection with {{c1::HBV::virus name}} effectively prevents infection with HDV.
extraNote: The HBV vaccine is the primary means of preventing HDV since HDV cannot exist without HBsAg.

clozeText: A significant clinical complication of HDV superinfection is an increased risk of {{c1::fulminant::type}} hepatitis.
extraNote: This is characterized by rapid liver failure and massive hepatic necrosis.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::IgM anti-HDV::serology marker}} indicates an acute HDV infection or a recent flare.
extraNote: Detection of HDV RNA by PCR is the most sensitive method for diagnosing active replication.

clozeText: Long-term infection with HBV and HDV significantly increases the risk of {{c1::Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)}} and cirrhosis.
extraNote: HDV accelerates the progression of liver damage compared to HBV monoinfection.

clozeText: The treatment of choice for chronic HDV infection is {{c1::Pegylated Interferon-alpha}}.
extraNote: Standard HBV nucleoside analogs (like tenofovir) are ineffective against HDV directly.

clozeText: HDV is primarily transmitted through {{c1::parenteral::route}} routes, such as IV drug use or blood transfusions.
extraNote: It can also be transmitted sexually, though less efficiently than HBV.

clozeText: In the context of serology, HDV superinfection often causes a {{c1::decrease}} in HBV DNA levels.
extraNote: HDV often suppresses the replication of its helper virus (HBV).

clozeText: The HDV genome is characterized as a {{c1::ribozyme}}, meaning it possesses catalytic RNA activity.
extraNote: This activity is used to cleave the multimeric RNA transcripts produced during replication.

clozeText: HDV replicates via a {{c1::rolling circle::mechanism}} model.
extraNote: This mechanism produces long concatemers that are cleaved by the ribozyme.

clozeText: Liver biopsy in HDV infection may show intense inflammation and {{c1::acidophilic bodies::histology}} (Councilman bodies).
extraNote: These represent apoptotic hepatocytes, common in viral hepatitis.

clozeText: Chronic HDV is defined by the persistence of HDV RNA for more than {{c1::6 months}}.
extraNote: Most superinfections lead to this chronic state.

clozeText: The incubation period for HDV superinfection is typically {{c1::2 to 8 weeks}}.
extraNote: The clinical course is often much more severe than that of the original HBV infection.

clozeText: In a patient with chronic HBV, a sudden clinical worsening or "flare" should prompt testing for {{c1::HDV superinfection}}.
extraNote: This is a high-yield clinical pearl for USMLE examinations.

clozeText: Unlike HBV, HDV is believed to have a {{c1::direct cytopathic}} effect on hepatocytes.
extraNote: HBV liver damage is primarily mediated by CD8+ T-cell response, but HDV proteins may be directly toxic.

clozeText: The "Large" Delta Antigen (L-HDAg) is produced via {{c1::RNA editing}} by the host enzyme ADAR1.
extraNote: ADAR1 converts an amber stop codon (UAG) to a tryptophan codon (UGG).

clozeText: The {{c1::Small}} Delta Antigen (S-HDAg) is required for the initiation of HDV RNA {{c2::replication}}.
extraNote: S-HDAg promotes replication, while L-HDAg inhibits replication and promotes assembly.

clozeText: Geographically, HDV is highly prevalent in the {{c1::Mediterranean}} basin, parts of Africa, and the Amazon.
extraNote: Global prevalence has decreased in areas with high HBV vaccination rates.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::Total anti-HDV::marker}} (IgG and IgM) without HDV RNA indicates a {{c2::past}} infection.
extraNote: If HDV RNA is present, the infection is active.

clozeText: Bulevirtide is a newer agent that treats HDV by blocking the {{c1::NTCP::receptor}} receptor.
extraNote: NTCP is the entry receptor for both HBV and HDV on hepatocytes.

clozeText: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) belongs to the {{c1::Hepeviridae}} family.
extraNote: It was previously classified as a Calcivirus but is now in its own family.

clozeText: The Hepatitis E virus genome consists of {{c1::ssRNA::nucleic acid}} that is {{c2::positive-sense}} and linear.
extraNote: Like HAV, it is an RNA virus, which helps differentiate it from HBV (DNA).

clozeText: Hepatitis E virus is a {{c1::naked::enveloped/naked}} virus with an {{c2::icosahedral}} capsid.
extraNote: The lack of an envelope allows it to survive the acidic environment of the GI tract.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for Hepatitis E is the {{c1::fecal-oral}} route, usually via contaminated {{c2::water::vehicle}}.
extraNote: Outbreaks are common in developing countries following heavy rains or floods.

clozeText: Hepatitis E infection is particularly dangerous in {{c1::pregnant women::specific population}}, where it carries a mortality rate of approximately {{c2::20}}%.
extraNote: This is a classic USMLE board fact used to distinguish HEV from HAV.

clozeText: In pregnant patients, HEV infection often progresses to {{c1::fulminant hepatitis::syndrome}}.
extraNote: Characterized by rapid liver failure, hepatic encephalopathy, and DIC.

clozeText: Unlike Hepatitis B and C, Hepatitis E usually does {{c1::not}} cause chronic infection in immunocompetent hosts.
extraNote: It typically causes an acute, self-limiting illness similar to Hepatitis A.

clozeText: Chronic Hepatitis E infection can occur in {{c1::immunocompromised}} patients, particularly {{c2::solid organ transplant}} recipients.
extraNote: HEV Genotype 3 is most commonly associated with these chronic cases.

clozeText: The incubation period for Hepatitis E ranges from {{c1::2 to 6 weeks::time range}}.
extraNote: This is similar to the incubation period of Hepatitis A.

clozeText: Diagnosis of acute Hepatitis E is typically confirmed by detecting {{c1::IgM anti-HEV}} in the serum.
extraNote: IgG anti-HEV appears later and provides long-term immunity.

clozeText: In chronic HEV cases or early acute infection, {{c1::HEV RNA::test type}} can be detected in the stool or serum using PCR.
extraNote: PCR is the gold standard for diagnosing HEV in immunocompromised patients who may not mount an antibody response.

clozeText: In developed countries, HEV (Genotype 3) is often a {{c1::zoonotic}} infection transmitted via undercooked {{c2::pork::meat}} or deer meat.
extraNote: This differs from Genotypes 1 and 2, which are strictly human and waterborne.

clozeText: Pathologically, HEV causes liver damage primarily through {{c1::host immune response (T-cells)}} rather than direct cytopathic effects.
extraNote: Like most hepatitis viruses, the inflammation is caused by the body's reaction to infected hepatocytes.

clozeText: Hepatitis E {{c1::does not}} have an FDA-approved vaccine available in the United States.
extraNote: A vaccine (Hecolin) is currently used in China but is not globally available.

clozeText: The best way to prevent Hepatitis E in endemic areas is through {{c1::clean water supplies}} and proper sanitation.
extraNote: Boiling water and adequate sewage disposal are key.

clozeText: Treatment for chronic Hepatitis E in transplant patients often involves the administration of {{c1::Ribavirin}}.
extraNote: Reduction of immunosuppressive therapy is also an initial strategy.

clozeText: HEV Genotypes {{c1::1 and 2}} are associated with large-scale waterborne epidemics in Asia and Africa.
extraNote: Genotypes 3 and 4 are more often sporadic or zoonotic.

clozeText: Liver biopsies in HEV may show {{c1::canalicular cholestasis}} and acidophilic bodies (Councilman bodies).
extraNote: Councilman bodies represent apoptotic hepatocytes, common to all viral hepatitides.

clozeText: Hepatitis E virus replicates in the {{c1::cytoplasm}} of the hepatocyte.
extraNote: Most RNA viruses (except influenza and retroviruses) replicate in the cytoplasm.

clozeText: A key mnemonic for HEV and HAV is 'The vowels (A and E) hit the {{c1::bowels}}'.
extraNote: This highlights the fecal-oral transmission route for both Hepatitis A and Hepatitis E.

clozeText: HEV particles found in feces are {{c1::non-enveloped}}, while those found in the blood are {{c2::quasi-enveloped}}.
extraNote: The lipid membrane protects the virus from neutralizing antibodies while in the bloodstream.

clozeText: HEV Genotypes 1 and 2 are restricted to {{c1::humans}}.
extraNote: This makes them targets for potential eradication through sanitation.

clozeText: HEV infection during pregnancy is associated with a high risk of {{c1::disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)}}.
extraNote: This contributes to the high maternal mortality rate.

clozeText: Elevated {{c1::ALT::enzyme}} and {{c2::AST::enzyme}} are typical laboratory findings in acute HEV infection.
extraNote: ALT is usually higher than AST, indicating viral liver injury.

clozeText: In the United States, the majority of HEV cases are caused by Genotype {{c1::3}}.
extraNote: It is often asymptomatic or mild unless the patient is immunocompromised.

clozeText: HEV does not possess a {{c1::reverse transcriptase}} enzyme.
extraNote: This distinguishes it from Hepatitis B and HIV.

clozeText: The HEV genome contains {{c1::three}} open reading frames (ORFs).
extraNote: ORF2 encodes the viral capsid; ORF1 encodes non-structural proteins.

clozeText: Hepatitis E should be suspected in a traveler returning from {{c1::Mexico, Africa, or Asia}} with jaundice.
extraNote: Travel history is critical for differentiating between hepatitis etiologies.

clozeText: Staphylococci are differentiated from streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: This is a primary biochemical test: Staphylococci are catalase-positive, while Streptococci are catalase-negative.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from other staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which سپس catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: The major protein in the cell wall of S. aureus is {{c1::Protein A}}, which inhibits phagocytosis by binding the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a retains its transpeptidase function but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics, rendering them ineffective.

clozeText: In the United States, the most common strain of MRSA is the {{c1::USA300::strain name}} strain.
extraNote: USA300 is highly associated with community-acquired infections and skin abscesses.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from S. epidermidis by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}} and its typical {{c2::β (beta)}} hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Coagulase-negative staphylococci like S. epidermidis generally do not ferment mannitol or cause hemolysis.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance (VRSA) in S. aureus occurs when {{c1::D-lactate::molecule}} is substituted for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This mechanism is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) and is often carried on a transposon.

clozeText: The primary site of S. aureus colonization in the human body is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers; nasal carriage increases the risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are particularly susceptible to S. aureus because of a defect in neutrophil oxidative killing.
extraNote: Because S. aureus is catalase-positive, it degrades the small amount of H2O2 these patients' neutrophils produce, preventing bacterial death.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion produced by a pyogenic S. aureus infection is an {{c1::abscess}}.
extraNote: Abscesses typically undergo central necrosis and drain pus; they are localized infections that can potentially disseminate.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs), including {{c1::folliculitis}}, cellulitis, and {{c2::impetigo}}.
extraNote: Impetigo is characterized by vesicles that rupture to form honey-colored crusts.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is unique because almost all strains produce {{c1::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}.
extraNote: This toxin is less common in hospital-acquired (HCA-MRSA) and contributes to necrotizing skin lesions and pneumonia.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} in the S. aureus cell wall are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the receptor for staphylococcal bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: S. aureus can induce septic shock despite being Gram-positive because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} and {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} stimulate cytokine release.
extraNote: These components act like endotoxin, inducing IL-1 and TNF from macrophages to trigger the systemic inflammatory response.

clozeText: S. aureus recovery of iron for energy production via cytochrome enzymes is facilitated by the {{c1::hemolysis::process}} of red blood cells.
extraNote: Iron in hemoglobin is a critical growth factor for the bacteria and is harvested using hemolysins.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users (IVDU)}}.
extraNote: Common presentations in this population include endocarditis and skin/soft tissue infections.

clozeText: In approximately 5% of women, S. aureus colonizes the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: TSS is associated with the use of high-absorbency tampons and the production of TSST-1.

clozeText: Staphylococcus {{c1::saprophyticus}} is a common cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and is distinguished by its resistance to {{c2::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis, by contrast, is sensitive to novobiocin.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by a specific {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} produced by S. aureus that leads to large areas of desquamated skin.
extraNote: This is most commonly seen in infants and young children (Ritter's disease).

clozeText: S. aureus is a leading cause of {{c1::hospital-acquired (nosocomial)}} pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is also a significant cause of infections at cardiac pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a major cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves::device}} and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a member of the normal skin flora and frequently contaminates blood cultures.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains produce {{c1::β-lactamase::enzyme}}, making them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: These strains are treated with β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin or oxacillin.

clozeText: Staphylococci appear microscopically as Gram-positive cocci in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This morphological difference is a key initial step in laboratory identification.

clozeText: The {{c1::capsule}} of S. aureus is poorly immunogenic, containing 11 serotypes with types {{c2::5 and 8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The poor immunogenicity has significantly hindered the development of an effective vaccine.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause disease via two main mechanisms: {{c1::toxin production}} and {{c2::pyogenic inflammation}}.
extraNote: Pyogenic inflammation results in abscess formation, while toxins cause syndromes like food poisoning and TSS.

clozeText: {{c1::Handwashing}} is the most effective way to decrease the transmission of S. aureus, especially among hospital personnel.
extraNote: Hand contact is the primary mode of transmission for both MRSA and MSSA.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is part of the staphylococci group that is {{c1::coagulase-negative}}.
extraNote: Along with S. epidermidis, it lacks the ability to clot plasma.

clozeText: The substitution of D-lactate for D-alanine in VRSA occurs within the {{c1::peptidoglycan}} layer of the cell wall.
extraNote: This alteration prevents vancomycin from binding to its target, which is normally the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus.

clozeText: Staphylococci are distinguished from Streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: This enzyme allows Staphylococci to survive the oxidative killing mechanism (H2O2) within neutrophils.

clozeText: Microscopically, Staphylococci appear as {{c1::gram-positive cocci in clusters::arrangement}}, whereas Streptococci appear in chains.
extraNote: The clusters are often described as "grapelike."

clozeText: The primary biochemical test used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus from coagulase-negative staphylococci is {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is characterized by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}} and produce {{c1::β-hemolysis::hemolysis type}} on blood agar.
extraNote: S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus typically do not ferment mannitol or cause hemolysis.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes hemolysins to recover {{c1::iron}} from hemoglobin for use in the synthesis of {{c1::cytochrome}} enzymes.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth during infection.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c1::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but has a low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the {{c1::Fc portion::part of antibody}} of IgG, preventing phagocytosis by neutrophils.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc receptor on phagocytes from binding the antibody-antigen complex.

clozeText: The major cell wall component responsible for adherence to mucosal cells in Staphylococci is {{c1::teichoic acid}}.
extraNote: Teichoic acids are polymers of ribitol phosphate.

clozeText: Lipoteichoic acids in S. aureus can induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release {{c1::IL-1 and TNF::cytokines}}.
extraNote: This mechanism is similar to the action of endotoxin in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c1::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan precursor.
extraNote: This cassette of genes is typically acquired via transposons on a plasmid from enterococci.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for Staphylococcus aureus in the human body is the {{c1::nose (anterior nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers in the nose.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to recurrent S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: CGD patients lack the respiratory burst necessary to kill catalase-positive organisms.

clozeText: Almost all strains of community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) produce the toxin {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: This toxin is less commonly produced by healthcare-acquired MRSA (HCA-MRSA).

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This often leads to complications like right-sided endocarditis.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate macrophages to produce cytokines, explaining why it can cause {{c1::septic shock}} despite lacking endotoxin.
extraNote: Peptidoglycan also activates the complement and coagulation cascades.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is a leading cause of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs).

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, which presents as small pustules on the hair follicles.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of cellulitis and impetigo.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust, is caused by either S. aureus or {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: This is a common superficial skin infection in children.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin::toxin type}} produced by S. aureus that results in large areas of desquamated skin.
extraNote: It is most common in infants and young children.

clozeText: A predisposing factor for toxic shock syndrome is the presence of S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which occurs in approximately 5% of women.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin (TSST-1).

clozeText: Strains of S. aureus are typed for epidemiologic purposes using {{c1::bacteriophages::method}} that recognize specific surface receptors.
extraNote: Teichoic acids make up part of the phage receptors.

clozeText: S. aureus serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} are responsible for approximately 85% of infections caused by encapsulated strains.
extraNote: The polysaccharide capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: The enzyme {{c1::β-lactamase}} is encoded by plasmids in over 90% of S. aureus strains, rendering them resistant to penicillin G.
extraNote: Nafcillin or oxacillin are used to treat β-lactamase-producing (but methicillin-susceptible) strains.

clozeText: The USA300 strain is currently the most common strain of {{c1::MRSA}} in the United States.
extraNote: It is frequently associated with community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Foreign bodies, such as {{c1::sutures or catheters}}, are major predisposing factors that facilitate S. aureus infection.
extraNote: These surfaces provide a niche for bacterial adherence and biofilm formation.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}}.
extraNote: It involves systemic vasculitis, primarily in children.

clozeText: Staphylococci are nonmotile and {{c1::do not::do/do not}} form spores.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from gram-positive rods like Bacillus and Clostridium.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is distinguished from Staphylococcus saprophyticus by its sensitivity to the antibiotic {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, which distinguishes them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from neutrophil killing.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the iron required for the synthesis of cytochrome enzymes.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: This gene is located on the bacterial chromosome and encodes altered penicillin-binding proteins.

clozeText: The altered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA, known as {{c1::PBP2a::specific protein name}}, provides transpeptidase activity without binding to beta-lactam antibiotics.
extraNote: This allows cell wall synthesis to continue despite the presence of methicillin or nafcillin.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is specifically associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: Relatively few healthcare-acquired (HCA-MRSA) strains produce this specific toxin.

clozeText: Vancomycin resistance in S. aureus (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate::molecule}} for D-alanine in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This mechanism is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: The major virulence factor {{c1::Protein A}} binds to the {{c2::Fc portion}} of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis by occupying the site that would normally bind to receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate the adherence of S. aureus to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the receptors for specific staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: The induction of septic shock by S. aureus is partly due to {{c1::lipoteichoic acids}} inducing the release of IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.
extraNote: This is a similar cytokine cascade as seen in Gram-negative endotoxin shock.

clozeText: Approximately 85% of S. aureus infections are caused by polysaccharide capsule serotypes {{c1::5 and 8::numbers}}.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus possesses endotoxin-like properties, allowing it to stimulate complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus causes septic shock despite lacking true LPS endotoxin.

clozeText: The primary reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose::anatomical site}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are colonized at any given time.

clozeText: Approximately 5% of women carry S. aureus in the {{c1::vagina}}, which predisposes them to Toxic Shock Syndrome.
extraNote: Colonization is a key risk factor for toxin-mediated disease in this population.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are particularly prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is a catalase-positive organism, which CGD patients cannot neutralize effectively.

clozeText: {{c1::Diabetes}} is a major predisposing metabolic factor to infections caused by S. aureus.
extraNote: High blood glucose levels and impaired immune response facilitate infection.

clozeText: The typical lesion of a S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, characterized by central necrosis and pus.
extraNote: Furuncles and boils are common examples of these lesions.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs}}.
extraNote: This often presents as endocarditis or skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: MRSA is currently the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses}} in the United States.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common strain identified in these community-acquired cases.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome::disease name}} is a condition of unknown etiology that may be linked to certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: The disease involves inflammation of blood vessels and is often seen in children.

clozeText: Microscopically, staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, while streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This morphology is a hallmark of Gram-positive cocci differentiation.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is differentiated from S. epidermidis by its resistance to {{c1::novobiocin}}.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive to novobiocin.

clozeText: Infections of prosthetic heart valves and artificial joints are most commonly associated with {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}}.
extraNote: It is a common member of the skin flora and produces biofilms on prosthetic materials.

clozeText: {{c1::Beta-lactamase::enzyme}} is encoded by plasmids in more than 90% of S. aureus strains.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades standard penicillins like penicillin G.

clozeText: S. aureus skin infections include impetigo, which is characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::description}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is caused by an exotoxin produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: It presents as widespread desquamated skin, typically in infants.

clozeText: The substitution of D-lactate for D-alanine in VRSA occurs on the {{c1::peptidoglycan}} precursor.
extraNote: This change reduces the binding affinity of vancomycin to the cell wall components.

clozeText: Hand contact is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus, and {{c1::handwashing}} is the most effective prevention.
extraNote: This is critical for preventing healthcare-acquired infections.

clozeText: The main site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose}}.

clozeText: The classic pathological lesion caused by S. aureus is an {{c1::abscess}}, which is characterized by central necrosis and pus.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for *S. aureus* in the human reservoir is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of people are colonized in the nose at any given time.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is distinguished from hospital-acquired MRSA by the frequent production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States.

clozeText: Full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) occurs when the bacteria substitute {{c1::d-lactate}} for {{c2::d-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This cassette of genes is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci.

clozeText: In *S. aureus*, {{c1::teichoic acids}} mediate adherence to mucosal cells, while {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can induce septic shock.
extraNote: Lipoteichoic acids induce cytokines like IL-1 and TNF from macrophages.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to recurrent *S. aureus* infections.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill catalase-positive bacteria.

clozeText: {{c1::Scalded skin syndrome}} is a condition in infants caused by an exotoxin produced by *S. aureus* that leads to widespread desquamation.
extraNote: It presents with large areas of 'rolled up' skin.

clozeText: Impetigo, presenting with "honey-colored" crusts, can be caused by either *S. aureus* or {{c1::Streptococcus pyogenes}}.
extraNote: Both organisms are common causes of skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs).

clozeText: *S. aureus* is the most common cause of {{c1::methicillin-resistant (MRSA)}} skin abscesses and is the leading cause of infections in {{c2::intravenous drug}} users.
extraNote: MRSA is also a common cause of necrotizing fasciitis and sepsis.

clozeText: Staphylococci are characterized by being {{c1::nonmotile}} and do {{c2::not}} form spores.
extraNote: This differentiates them from other gram-positive rods like Bacillus or Clostridium.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry *S. aureus* in the vagina, which predisposes them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.
extraNote: TSS is mediated by a superantigen toxin.

clozeText: For *S. aureus* strains that are not methicillin-resistant, the drug of choice is a β-lactamase–resistant penicillin such as {{c1::nafcillin}}.
extraNote: Over 90% of S. aureus produce β-lactamase, making them resistant to penicillin G.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of *S. aureus* has endotoxin-like properties and can stimulate macrophages to produce {{c2::cytokines}}.
extraNote: This allows S. aureus to cause septic shock despite lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: *S. aureus* is a common cause of hospital-acquired infections, including {{c1::pneumonia}}, septicemia, and infections of {{c2::surgical wounds}}.
extraNote: It is also frequently associated with infections at cardiac pacemaker insertion sites.

clozeText: Epidemiologic typing of *S. aureus* strains can be performed using {{c1::phage typing}}, which relies on surface receptors composed of teichoic acids.
extraNote: Receptors for specific bacteriophages allow for strain differentiation.

clozeText: The *S. aureus* polysaccharide capsule is poorly immunogenic, with types {{c1::5 and 8}} causing the majority of human infections.
extraNote: Some strains possess a very thin capsule known as a microcapsule.

clozeText: A major predisposing factor for *S. aureus* infections is {{c1::diabetes}}, which compromises the immune system.
extraNote: Other factors include reduced humoral immunity or low levels of complement.

clozeText: In a Gram stain of *S. aureus*, the bacteria appear as {{c1::Gram-positive}} cocci, often seen alongside {{c2::neutrophils}} with pink segmented nuclei.
extraNote: Gram-positive cocci appear purple under microscopy.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a childhood disease of unknown origin that has been hypothesized to be caused by specific strains of *S. aureus*.
extraNote: The clinical presentation includes fever, rash, and vasculitis.

clozeText: The risk of skin infection by *S. aureus* is significantly increased in individuals who are {{c1::chronic carriers}} of the organism in their nose.
extraNote: The primary mode of transmission is often hand contact.

clozeText: The presence of {{c1::foreign bodies}} such as sutures or intravenous catheters significantly predisposes a patient to infection by *S. aureus*.
extraNote: Bacteria can adhere to these surfaces and form biofilms.

clozeText: Staphylococcal {{c1::food poisoning}} is a common toxinoses caused by *S. aureus*.
extraNote: This occurs via the ingestion of preformed enterotoxins in contaminated food.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase}}, an enzyme that degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: This distinguishes them from streptococci, which are catalase-negative. Catalase allows bacteria to survive H2O2 killing within neutrophils.

clozeText: Staphylococcus aureus is primarily distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: Coagulase activates prothrombin to form thrombin, which then converts fibrinogen to a fibrin clot.

clozeText: S. aureus is unique among staphylococci because it usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and hemolyzes red blood cells.
extraNote: Hemolysis provides the organism with iron, which is utilized to synthesize cytochrome enzymes for energy production.

clozeText: Over 90% of S. aureus strains produce β-lactamase, which is typically encoded on {{c1::plasmids}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades many penicillins, requiring the use of β-lactamase-resistant penicillins like nafcillin.

clozeText: Methicillin resistance in S. aureus (MRSA) is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene on the bacterial chromosome.
extraNote: This gene encodes for altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs).

clozeText: The altered PBP produced by MRSA is named {{c1::PBP2a}}, which functions as a transpeptidase but does not bind penicillins.
extraNote: This makes the organism resistant to nearly all β-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: Almost all strains of {{c1::community-acquired (CA-MRSA)}} produce P-V leukocidin, unlike many healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: USA300 is the most common strain of CA-MRSA in the United States.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) utilizes a transposon that encodes enzymes substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in peptidoglycan.
extraNote: This is the same resistance mechanism used by vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE).

clozeText: The major cell wall protein of S. aureus, {{c1::Protein A}}, binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents phagocytosis because the Fc portion cannot bind to receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as receptors for bacteriophages used in phage typing.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in S. aureus play a role in inducing septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: This mechanism is analogous to the action of endotoxin in gram-negative bacteria.

clozeText: S. aureus polysaccharide capsule types {{c1::5 and 8}} are responsible for approximately 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, making vaccine development difficult.

clozeText: The {{c1::peptidoglycan}} of S. aureus possesses endotoxin-like properties, enabling it to stimulate the complement and coagulation cascades.
extraNote: This explains how S. aureus can cause septic shock despite lacking true endotoxin (LPS).

clozeText: The primary human reservoir for S. aureus is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population is colonized at any given time.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in {{c1::intravenous drug users::specific patient population}}.
extraNote: MRSA is a particularly high risk in this group.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are specifically predisposed to S. aureus infections because the organism is catalase-positive.
extraNote: CGD involves a defect in the ability of neutrophils to kill bacteria using oxidative bursts.

clozeText: The classic lesion associated with S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which typically contains pus and central necrosis.
extraNote: These lesions (furuncles/boils) often drain to the outside but can lead to bacteremia.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::skin abscesses::pathology}} in the United States, largely due to MRSA.
extraNote: It is also a major cause of necrotizing fasciitis and sepsis in immunocompetent patients.

clozeText: In hospital settings, {{c1::hand contact}} is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus.
extraNote: Handwashing is the primary intervention to decrease transmission between healthcare workers and patients.

clozeText: Vaginal colonization by S. aureus in approximately {{c1::5}}% of women predisposes them to toxic shock syndrome.
extraNote: This syndrome is mediated by superantigen toxins.

clozeText: {{c1::Foreign bodies::Predisposing factor}} such as sutures and intravenous catheters significantly increase the risk of S. aureus infection.
extraNote: These provide a surface for colonization and protect the bacteria from immune defenses.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is differentiated from S. saprophyticus by its {{c1::sensitivity}} to the antibiotic novobiocin.
extraNote: S. epidermidis is sensitive, while S. saprophyticus is resistant.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of {{c1::urinary tract infections (UTIs)}} and is resistant to novobiocin.
extraNote: It is typically seen in young, sexually active women.

clozeText: S. aureus causes {{c1::scalded skin syndrome}} through the production of an exotoxin that causes desquamation in infants.
extraNote: This is also known as Ritter's disease.

clozeText: Staphylococcal impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Both S. aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes can cause this clinical presentation.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of {{c1::folliculitis}}, an infection of the hair follicles presenting as small pustules.
extraNote: It may progress to more severe lesions like furuncles or carbuncles.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a leading cause of infections in {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora that readily adheres to plastic surfaces.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a disease of unknown etiology that some evidence suggests may be linked to certain S. aureus strains.
extraNote: It is a pediatric vasculitis that can lead to coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: Staphylococci appear in {{c1::grapelike clusters}}, whereas streptococci appear in {{c2::chains}}.
extraNote: This microscopic difference is a primary diagnostic criterion for gram-positive cocci.

clozeText: All staphylococci produce {{c1::catalase::enzyme}}, which differentiates them from streptococci.
extraNote: Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into water and oxygen, protecting the bacteria from neutrophil-mediated killing.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the only medically important staphylococcus that is coagulase-positive.
extraNote: Coagulase is an enzyme that activates prothrombin to form thrombin, leading to fibrin clot formation.

clozeText: {{c1::Protein A}} is a major S. aureus virulence factor that binds to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: This prevents the Fc portion from binding to receptors on phagocytes, thereby inhibiting phagocytosis.

clozeText: MRSA resistance to nafcillin and methicillin is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene.
extraNote: The mecA gene encodes PBP2a, an altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for beta-lactams.

clozeText: In vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA), resistance is caused by the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in peptidoglycan precursors.
extraNote: This prevents vancomycin from binding to the cell wall subunits.

clozeText: The {{c1::nose::anatomical site}} is the primary human reservoir for Staphylococcus aureus.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic carriers in the anterior nares.

clozeText: {{c1::Lipoteichoic acids}} in the S. aureus cell wall induce septic shock by stimulating macrophages to release {{c2::IL-1 and TNF}}.
extraNote: While S. aureus lacks endotoxin (LPS), its cell wall components can trigger similar inflammatory cascades.

clozeText: S. aureus serotypes {{c1::5 and 8}} cause the vast majority of human infections involving the polysaccharide capsule.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus epidermidis}} is a major cause of infections in prosthetic heart valves and prosthetic joints.
extraNote: It is a common member of the normal skin flora and forms biofilms on foreign bodies.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus saprophyticus}} is distinguished from S. epidermidis by its {{c2::resistance}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: Mnemonic: Saprophyticus is Resistant (S-R), Epidermidis is Sensitive (E-S).

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} that leads to widespread desquamation in infants.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a protease that disrupts cell-to-cell adhesion in the epidermis.

clozeText: {{c1::Impetigo}} caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes is characterized by vesicles with a {{c2::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: It is a highly contagious superficial skin infection common in children.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::chronic granulomatous disease (CGD)}} are particularly susceptible to S. aureus because the bacteria produce catalase.
extraNote: CGD neutrophils cannot produce H2O2; catalase-positive organisms further deplete available peroxide, preventing oxidative killing.

clozeText: The drug of choice for treating non-MRSA (MSSA) infections is {{c1::nafcillin::or oxacillin}}.
extraNote: Nafcillin is a beta-lactamase-resistant penicillin.

clozeText: Most community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) strains produce the {{c1::P-V leukocidin}} toxin.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is associated with necrotizing skin lesions and severe pneumonia.

clozeText: S. aureus produces {{c1::coagulase}}, which converts {{c2::fibrinogen}} to fibrin.
extraNote: This helps the bacteria sequester themselves within a clot to evade the immune system.

clozeText: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus}} is the most common cause of skin abscesses, including folliculitis and furuncles.
extraNote: Abscesses are the hallmark pyogenic lesion of S. aureus.

clozeText: S. aureus can be differentiated from S. epidermidis by its ability to ferment {{c1::mannitol}}.
extraNote: S. aureus turns Mannitol Salt Agar yellow.

clozeText: {{c1::Teichoic acids}} are ribitol phosphate polymers that mediate the {{c2::adherence}} of staphylococci to mucosal cells.
extraNote: They also serve as part of the receptor for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: These patients are at high risk for endocarditis and sepsis.

clozeText: {{c1::Kawasaki syndrome}} is a systemic vasculitis of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain S. aureus strains.
extraNote: It typically affects young children and can lead to coronary artery aneurysms.

clozeText: {{c1::S. aureus}} is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and surgical-wound infections.
extraNote: It is a leading cause of nosocomial morbidity.

clozeText: Unlike S. epidermidis, S. aureus is typically {{c1::beta-hemolytic}} on blood agar.
extraNote: The hemolysins also allow the bacteria to acquire iron from hemoglobin.

clozeText: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by a toxin that can be found in the {{c1::vagina}} of approximately 5% of women.
extraNote: The toxin acts as a superantigen, causing massive cytokine release.

clozeText: The peptidoglycan of S. aureus can stimulate {{c1::macrophages}} to produce cytokines, mimicking the effects of endotoxin.
extraNote: This explains why gram-positive organisms can still cause septic shock.

clozeText: {{c1::Hand contact}} is the most important mode of transmission for S. aureus in clinical settings.
extraNote: Handwashing is the primary preventive measure to decrease transmission.

clozeText: MRSA accounts for more than {{c1::50%}} of S. aureus strains isolated from hospital patients in the United States.
extraNote: The USA300 strain is the most common MRSA strain currently.

clozeText: Staphylococci are distinguished from Streptococci by the production of {{c1::catalase}}, which degrades hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
extraNote: Catalase allows bacteria to survive the oxidative burst (H2O2) within neutrophils.

clozeText: The classic lesion of S. aureus pyogenic infection is an {{c1::abscess}}, which undergoes central necrosis and drains pus.
extraNote: S. aureus is the most common cause of skin abscesses in the United States.

clozeText: S. aureus is distinguished from coagulase-negative staphylococci by the production of {{c1::coagulase::enzyme}}, which activates prothrombin to form a fibrin clot.
extraNote: Coagulase-negative species include S. epidermidis and S. saprophyticus.

clozeText: The major cell wall protein of S. aureus, {{c1::Protein A}}, prevents phagocytosis by binding to the {{c2::Fc}} portion of IgG.
extraNote: By binding the Fc portion, Protein A prevents the antibody from binding to Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages.

clozeText: Resistance to methicillin and nafcillin in MRSA is mediated by the {{c1::mecA}} gene, which encodes an altered {{c2::penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a)}}.
extraNote: PBP2a can perform transpeptidase functions but does not bind beta-lactam antibiotics.

clozeText: In S. aureus, {{c1::teichoic acids}} are polymers of ribitol phosphate that mediate adherence to mucosal cells.
extraNote: Teichoic acids also serve as part of the surface receptors for staphylococcal bacteriophages.

clozeText: Septic shock caused by S. aureus can be induced by {{c1::lipoteichoic acids::cell wall component}}, which stimulate macrophages to release IL-1 and TNF.
extraNote: S. aureus can cause septic shock despite lacking endotoxin (LPS), as its cell wall components (peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid) mimic endotoxin properties.

clozeText: Full resistance to vancomycin (VRSA) involves the substitution of {{c1::D-lactate}} for {{c2::D-alanine}} in the peptidoglycan chain.
extraNote: This cassette of genes is the same as that found in vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) and is carried on a transposon.

clozeText: The main reservoir for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}, with approximately 30% colonization rate.
extraNote: Chronic carriers in the nose have an increased risk of subsequent skin infections.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) is uniquely associated with the production of {{c1::P-V leukocidin}}, which is rarely found in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: P-V leukocidin is a pore-forming toxin that kills white blood cells and is linked to severe skin infections.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections because their neutrophils cannot kill catalase-positive organisms.
extraNote: CGD is characterized by a defect in NADPH oxidase, preventing the respiratory burst.

clozeText: S. aureus can be distinguished from other staphylococci because it usually ferments {{c1::mannitol}} and causes {{c2::beta}}-hemolysis on blood agar.
extraNote: Mannitol salt agar is a selective and differential medium used for S. aureus.

clozeText: The primary mode of transmission for S. aureus in clinical settings is {{c1::hand contact::mechanism}}.
extraNote: Handwashing is the most important intervention to decrease transmission.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous drugs::population}}.
extraNote: This includes endocarditis, sepsis, and skin abscesses.

clozeText: Scalded skin syndrome is caused by an {{c1::exotoxin}} produced by certain strains of S. aureus.
extraNote: The toxin causes widespread desquamation (rolled up skin) in infants.

clozeText: Staphylococcal impetigo is characterized by crops of vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored}} crust.
extraNote: Impetigo can be caused by either S. aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::90}}% of S. aureus strains contain plasmids encoding {{c2::beta-lactamase::enzyme}}.
extraNote: This enzyme degrades many penicillins, requiring the use of beta-lactamase-resistant drugs like nafcillin.

clozeText: S. aureus utilizes {{c1::hemolysins}} to destroy red blood cells and recover {{c2::iron}} for cytochrome synthesis.
extraNote: Iron is a critical limiting nutrient for bacterial growth in the host.

clozeText: The most common strain of MRSA currently identified in the United States is the {{c1::USA300}} strain.
extraNote: USA300 is a major cause of community-acquired skin and soft tissue infections.

clozeText: Predisposing factors to S. aureus infection include {{c1::diabetes}}, reduced humoral immunity, and the presence of {{c2::foreign bodies}}.
extraNote: Foreign bodies include sutures, cardiac pacemakers, and intravenous catheters.

clozeText: Unlike S. aureus, {{c1::S. epidermidis}} is sensitive to the antibiotic novobiocin.
extraNote: Novobiocin sensitivity is used to distinguish S. epidermidis from S. saprophyticus (which is resistant).

clozeText: S. aureus microcapsules are considered important virulence factors, with types {{c1::5}} and {{c2::8}} causing 85% of infections.
extraNote: The capsule is poorly immunogenic, complicating vaccine development.

clozeText: In the coagulase test, S. aureus produces a clot by activating {{c1::prothrombin}} to form thrombin.
extraNote: Thrombin then catalyzes the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.

clozeText: S. aureus is a common cause of {{c1::osteomyelitis::bone infection}} and {{c2::septic arthritis::joint infection}}.
extraNote: Pyogenic inflammation is a hallmark of staphylococcal pathogenesis.

clozeText: Strains of S. aureus that have intermediate resistance to vancomycin are termed {{c1::VISA}}.
extraNote: Full resistance is termed VRSA.

clozeText: Kawasaki syndrome is a disease of unknown etiology that may be associated with certain strains of {{c1::S. aureus}}.
extraNote: While the exact cause is unknown, staphylococcal toxins are sometimes implicated.

clozeText: Approximately {{c1::5}}% of women carry S. aureus in the vagina, predisposing them to {{c2::toxic shock syndrome}}.

clozeText: Protein A, the major cell wall protein of S. aureus, prevents phagocytosis by binding to the {{c1::Fc}} portion of IgG.

clozeText: Vancomycin-resistant S. aureus (VRSA) arises by substituting {{c1::D-lactate}} for D-alanine in the peptidoglycan.
extraNote: The genes for this resistance are typically carried on a transposon located on a plasmid.

clozeText: The most common site of colonization for S. aureus in humans is the {{c1::nose (nares)}}.
extraNote: Approximately 30% of the population are chronic nasal carriers.

clozeText: Patients with {{c1::Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD)}} are especially prone to S. aureus infections due to a defect in neutrophil killing.
extraNote: S. aureus is a catalase-positive organism that degrades the small amount of H2O2 these patients can produce.

clozeText: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is clinically distinguished from S. epidermidis by being {{c1::resistant}} to novobiocin.
extraNote: S. saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections in sexually active young women.

clozeText: Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) usually produces {{c1::P-V (Panton-Valentine) leukocidin}}, which is less common in healthcare-acquired strains.
extraNote: The most common CA-MRSA strain in the United States is USA300.

clozeText: S. aureus can cause septic shock without endotoxin because its {{c1::peptidoglycan}} and {{c2::lipoteichoic acids}} can stimulate macrophage cytokines (IL-1, TNF).
extraNote: These components activate the complement and coagulation cascades similarly to Gram-negative endotoxin.

clozeText: Impetigo, characterized by vesicles with a {{c1::honey-colored::color}} crust, can be caused by either S. aureus or S. pyogenes.

clozeText: S. aureus is the most common cause of infections in users of {{c1::intravenous (IV) drugs}}.
extraNote: It is also a leading cause of endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and septic arthritis.

clozeText: Vaginal colonization by S. aureus in 5% of women predisposes them to {{c1::Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS)}}.

clozeText: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a major cause of infections involving {{c1::prosthetic heart valves}} and {{c2::hip joints}}.
